docs.title: 1. Sources
docs.text: Public, on this machine: [RM13] doc/hardware/s32k1xx/S32K-RM.pdf (S32K1xx Reference Manual Rev. 13: ch. 5, 36.1.2.4, 36.5.11.11, 36.5.11.14, 36.5.13), [DS13] the data sheet (Table 38 NVM reliability), [AN11983] Using the S32K1xx EEPROM Functionality Rev. 2 (§2.2.2.1, §3.1, §7, §8.2), [MAP] S32K1xx_Memory_Map.xlsx (attachment of [RM13]: FlexRAM and CSE_PRAM per derivative), [AN5401] Getting Started with CSEc Security module (§4, Tables 9 and 10, Appendix A). A vendor safety document under doc/confidential/ was searched for CSEc content and contains nothing; no statement here rests on it. The HIS SHE specification 1.0.1 is not available here; [RM13] 36.5.13 does not repeat it.

docs.title: 2. What CSEc is on this part, in facts
docs.text:
• CSEc is a feature set of the flash module (FTFC), not a separate peripheral: AES-128 (ECB, CBC), CMAC, TRNG and PRNG, secure boot, and a key store in flash ([RM13] 5.2.2, 36.5.13). It follows the SHE specification.
  • It only exists when the FlexNVM is configured for emulated EEPROM. "To access the command feature set, the part must be configured for EEE operation, using the PGMPART command" ([RM13] 36.5.13). On a non-CSEc part, and on a CSEc part with key size 0, access to the CSEc parameter RAM is not even guaranteed ([RM13] 5.2). CSEc and the emulated EEPROM are one decision, not two.
  • The keys live in the EEPROM RAM. The key space is subtracted from the end of the EEERAM address range and becomes unaddressable ([RM13] 5.2, 36.5.13). It is backed up in the EEPROM backup inside the FlexNVM.
  • No concurrency. EEPROM operations, ordinary flash commands and CSEc commands cannot run at the same time; one operation of any kind at a time ([RM13] 36.5.13, [AN11983] §8.1).
  • Not in HSRUN. Flash writes/erases, EEPROM writes and CSEc commands are not supported above RUN mode; in HSRUN (112 MHz) they raise error flags ([DS13] Table 38 notes 2 and 5; [RM13] introduction, footnote 1 to the S32K14x feature list: switch back to RUN at 80 MHz to execute CSEc or EEPROM writes). The demo project runs at 80 MHz (projects/evalboard_s32k144_demo/project.yaml, clock.system_hz), so this is a check to add, not a problem today.
  • The parameter RAM lies behind the FlexRAM, not in it — and moves with the FlexRAM size. CSE_PRAM (128 bytes) is at 0x1400_1000 on the S32K14x/S32K14xW (4 KB FlexRAM) and at 0x1400_0800 on the S32K11x (2 KB) ([MAP] S32K1xx_Memory_Map.xlsx, file attachment of [RM13], sheet "Overview Memory Map"). No device header of the family has it. On an S32K14x, 0x1400_0800 is FlexRAM offset 0x800, i.e. the emulated EEPROM: a write there is an EEPROM record, and a second write before CCIF returns ends in a transfer error ([RM13] 36.5.2.3). That is what did on the board on 2026-09-30 with the address of the S32K116 SVD; bspCsec now picks the address from SIM_SDID SUBSERIES at run time (csec/CsecPramAddress.h) and refuses an unknown sub-series.
  • Key slots are fixed by SHE, not by us. Slot 1 MASTER_ECU_KEY, slot 2 BOOT_MAC_KEY, slot 3 BOOT_MAC, then KEY_1…KEY_17 ([RM13] Table 36-75). If any key at all is allocated, those first three slots are assumed to be taken, so of 20 slots 17 are free for our own use ([RM13] 36.5.11.14).

docs.title: 3. What CSEc should be used for
docs.text:
Test applied to each candidate: does CSEc do something here that software on this MCU cannot do as well, and is the gain worth a permanent decision?

Candidate CSEc the right means? Slots needed now Reason SecOC CMAC on CAN (3.1) yes, later 1 AES-128 CMAC is the SecOC primitive and the key stays unreadable; but no freshness manager, PDU configuration or key distribution exists (libs/bsw/e2e protects against faults, not attackers); a SecOC concept is its own task Secure boot of the bootloader (3.2) yes, only CSEc can do it BOOT_MAC_KEY + BOOT_MAC (slots 2, 3) the flash module checks a CMAC over the program flash from address 0 at every reset; no software can check its own first instruction Application Security Access 0x27 (3.3) no, software path stays; CSEc as a later option of security[].method 1 HMAC-SHA256 with a per-device key is proven, family-neutral and works without CSEc; the gain would be defence in depth only Bootloader Security Access (3.4) no, but hal_random() via CMD_RND is a free win 0 the bootloader must keep the software path anyway, so CSEc would add code; the weak seed (UID and timers) gets a real hardware random source Device key / identity (3.5) yes in principle, no partner today 1 component protection needs a partner that challenges Signed application image no, Ed25519 stays 0 a symmetric CMAC would put a forging key on every device and the build machine

Secure-boot flavours ([RM13] 36.5.13.2, 5.2.3):

Flavour Behaviour on a MAC mismatch Suitable here Sequential core starts only after the check; keys with the boot-protection attribute stay locked possible Parallel core starts immediately, the check runs beside it; keys stay locked on failure recommended Strict the part stays in reset never – "Strict" is one-time and cannot be undone ([RM13] 36.5.13.25); a single mismatch, e.g. an interrupted bootloader update, bricks the device permanently

Relation to a separate task. Two links of one chain, not alternatives:

CSEc secure boot Ed25519 Protects the bootloader (0x0…0x7FFF today) the application image Checked by the flash module, at every reset the bootloader, before it starts the application Key on the device symmetric BOOT_MAC_KEY – whoever can verify can also forge only the public key – a stolen device yields no signing key Answers "is the root of trust still the one we installed?" "did this image come from us?"

Constraints for a separate task and a later bootloader task: BOOT_SIZE covers the bootloader area only (memory.bootloader.size), never the application; the flash configuration field at 0x400 lies inside that area; with secure boot active canflash blupdate writes the new BOOT_MAC in the same operation, before the reset (second reason against Strict); the boot MAC is checked by hardware, so the bootloader core needs no code for it.

docs.title: 4. How many key slots, and what each one is for
docs.text:
The part's ceiling is 20 slots, of which 3 are taken by SHE itself, leaving 17 of our own ([RM13] Table 36-62 and the text after it). Slots cannot be bought singly: FCCOB1[1:0] selects one of four steps, and each step costs a fixed number of bytes out of the EEERAM.

FCCOB1[1:0] Slots Of those, free for us Cost from the EEERAM 00 none (CSEc off) – 0 bytes 01 1 to 5 2 128 bytes 10 1 to 10 7 256 bytes 11 1 to 20 17 512 bytes

Source: [RM13] Table 36-62 "CSEc/SHE key size" (p. 865). The byte figures are larger than 16 bytes per key because the store holds each key's attributes as well; the RM gives only the totals and so does this table.

Proposed allocation (17 free slots, FCCOB1 = 11):

Slot SHE name Purpose Needed when 1 MASTER_ECU_KEY authorises loading every other key, and the debug authentication that is the only way back at once, in production, as the first key 2 BOOT_MAC_KEY key of the secure-boot CMAC over the bootloader (3.2) with secure boot 3 BOOT_MAC the expected CMAC of the boot area (a slot, though it is a MAC) with secure boot KEY_1 CAN message authentication (SecOC) – one bus (3.1) later KEY_2 bootloader Security Access, if it ever moves to CSEc (3.4) probably never KEY_3 application Security Access 0x27, as an option (3.3) later KEY_4 ECU identity / component protection (3.5) later KEY_5…KEY_17 reserve: second bus, key rotation, application keys unknown

Why the largest step and not 10. The difference between 10 and 11 is 256 bytes of emulated EEPROM out of 4096 — 6 %. The difference in what it buys is 7 usable slots against 17. The project has no NvM blocks defined at all yet (nvm.blocks is absent from project.yaml), so nothing is known to be short of those 256 bytes, while the cost of finding out later that 7 slots were not enough is a device that has to go through the debug authentication and be re-partitioned (the way back in stages is in 6.3; the partition step alone is reversible). Buy the headroom.

docs.title: 5. Interaction with the partition: the table for a separate task
docs.text:
Three values go into one PGMPART command and can never be separated afterwards ([RM13] Table 36-61): FCCOB1 key size, FCCOB2 SFE, FCCOB3 load-on-reset, FCCOB4 EEESIZE, FCCOB5 DEPART.

Fixed by the part, not a choice. On a CSEc part with 4 KB FlexRAM the EEPROM size must be 0010b = 4096 bytes ([RM13] 36.1.2.4.1, Table 36-15 note 2, pp. 793-794). 1111b (0 bytes) is only allowed when DEPART says "no EEPROM", and that in turn switches CSEc off. On the S32K11x family with 2 KB FlexRAM the corresponding value is 0011b = 2048 bytes ([RM13] Table 36-3 note 2) — which is why this belongs in mcudb, per derivative, and not in the code.

Usable EEPROM per key-size code (S32K144, EEESIZE 0x2 = 4096 bytes; the key space is subtracted from the end of the EEERAM, [RM13] 5.2 and 36.5.13):

FCCOB1 Key space Usable emulated EEPROM Against 4096 bytes 00 (CSEc off) 0 4096 bytes – 01 (5 slots) 128 3968 bytes −3 % 10 (10 slots) 256 3840 bytes −6 % 11 (20 slots) 512 3584 bytes −12,5 %

[AN11983] §8.2 states the same result for the family in one line: with CSEc enabled up to 512 B go to key storage, leaving 3.5 kB on S32K14x and 1.5 kB on S32K11x. So nobody may plan with 4 KB: with the recommended code the application gets 3584 bytes, and tools/nxconfig and the display before writing must say so.

Concretely for a separate task: tools/nxconfig/nvm.py, check() sets usable = partition.eeprom_bytes today. That is the one line where the key bytes have to be subtracted, so that every NvM block placement downstream counts with the real size instead of the programmed one. NvmPartitionPlan.describe() is where the two extra lines of the display belong (key slots and usable bytes). The second effect, and the one that surprises: the partition split. The key space is backed up inside the EEPROM backup, and the endurance of the emulated EEPROM depends on the ratio of backup to FlexRAM:

  • [DS13] Table 38 "NVM reliability specifications": write endurance 100 K writes at an EEPROM-backup-to-FlexRAM ratio of 16, and 1.6 M writes at a ratio of 256. Below a ratio of 16 the data sheet specifies no figure.
  • [AN11983] §7: to reach the data sheet endurance the backup must be at least 16 times the EEERAM size; the whole FlexNVM as E-flash (64 KB on S32K14x) with the maximum EEERAM (4 KB) is exactly that ratio.
  • [AN11983] §2.2.2.1: if EEE is used at all, at least 32 KB of the FlexNVM must be E-flash on S32K14x.
  • [AN11983] §8.2, for the CSEc case explicitly: "Program partition command must use the maximum available E-Flash size (64 kB for S32K14x devices)".

Applied to the codes the S32K144 offers ([RM13] Table 36-17, already in mcudb/s32k1xx/S32K144.yaml):

DEPART Data flash EEPROM backup Backup : 4 KB FlexRAM Data sheet endurance figure 0x0 / 0xC 64 KB 0 KB – not possible with CSEc (no EEPROM → no CSEc) 0xA 16 KB 48 KB 12 below 16 – no specified figure 0x3 / 0xB 32 KB 32 KB 8 below 16 – no specified figure 0x4 / 0x8 0 KB 64 KB 16 100 K writes

Finding. The value in the project today is partition_code: 0xB — 32 KB data flash, 32 KB backup, ratio 8. That is the bare minimum [AN11983] allows for EEE at all, and it is half the ratio at which the data sheet gives an endurance figure. It was chosen before CSEc was on the table and while it was assumed that data flash would be wanted; no project value uses data flash today (nvm.blocks does not exist, data_flash_bytes is used by nothing but the partition check). With CSEc, both NXP notes point the same way: give the FlexNVM entirely to the backup.

Recommendation for a separate task: EEESIZE = 0x2, DEPART = 0x4 (0 KB data flash, 64 KB backup), FCCOB1 = 0b11, FCCOB2 = 0x00, FCCOB3 = 0 (load on reset — with CSEc the FlexRAM is loaded at reset anyway, [RM13] Table 36-15). Result: 3584 bytes of usable emulated EEPROM at the data sheet's 100 K write endurance, and 17 free key slots. If data flash is wanted after all, 0xA (16 KB data flash, 48 KB backup, ratio 12) is the compromise — but then the 100 K figure is gone and the concept must say so out loud.

FCCOB2 (SFE) stays 0x00: it only enables the non-SHE "verify only" key attribute ([RM13] Table 36-63), we have no use for it, and FCCOB1 > 0 together with SFE = 1 is an error condition in the command ([RM13] Table 36-69).

docs.title: 5.1 What the commands cost ([AN5401] Tables 9 and 10)
docs.text:
NXP's nominal figures (Cortex-M4 at 80 MHz, 112 bytes of data per command), not our measurements. GENERATE_MAC 0.0229 ms, VERIFY_MAC 0.0363 ms; an 8-byte CAN frame is far below the 112 bytes, so about 23 µs per generated and 36 µs per verified MAC are upper bounds (0.23 % of a 10 ms task per protected frame). The command interface is serial and a CCOB command cancels a running one, so the queue needs designing, not the arithmetic. Secure boot, which matters for start-up time:

Flavour Size Clock Time Sequential (and strict sequential) 128 KB 25 MHz and 12.5 MHz IPG 5.09 ms — identical Parallel 32 KB LPBOOT = 1 (48 MHz) 2.06 ms Parallel 128 KB LPBOOT = 1 (48 MHz) 8.33 ms Parallel 32 KB LPBOOT = 0 (24 MHz) 4.17 ms Parallel 128 KB LPBOOT = 0 (24 MHz) 16.60 ms

The sequential figure does not depend on the IPG clock (the FTFC uses its own 50 MHz source); the parallel flavour takes the MCU clock. Sequential is the predictable one; for a bootloader-sized region it is both simpler to argue and, at LPBOOT = 0, the faster one.

docs.title: 6.1 Who generates them, and when are they written
docs.text:
The scheme that exists stays: a project master key outside the repository (%LOCALAPPDATA%/neXtBSW/keys/<name>.key), per-device keys derived from it and the chip UID; CSEc only changes where the derived key ends up (a key slot, loaded with the SHE LOAD_KEY protocol). Production order ([AN11983] §3.1, [RM13] 36.5.11.14):

  1. PGMPART with the values of section 5, once per device, at the very beginning.
  2. Reset (the codes take effect at the next reset).
  3. LOAD_KEY(MASTER_ECU_KEY) with the per-device value, before anything else.
  4. Bootloader and application over the debugger, key record of the software path as today.
  5. The remaining keys as needed: BOOT_MAC_KEY, then CMD_BOOT_DEFINE with flavour and BOOT_SIZE, then the boot MAC.

Never provision at first power-up in the field. No key may get the WRITE_PROTECTION attribute: it makes the debug authentication impossible, with it the mass erase and NXP's failure analysis; there is no way back. A replacement device has a different UID and therefore different derived keys; whatever holds the counterpart (partner ECU, backend) has to learn the new device, which is an integrator duty.

docs.title: 6.3 How a development board gets back to a blank state
docs.text:
The block on the ordinary mass erase hangs on the presence of keys ([RM13] 36.5.11.11 and 36.5.11.13, [AN5401] §4.2.2.3). Sector erase and programming of the program flash are not affected, so flashing an application or a bootloader keeps working in every case. State of 2026-09-23:

State Way back Costs PGMPART run, key space reserved, no key loaded the ordinary mass erase (Erase All Blocks, the J-Link unlock, the external erase-all request of 36.5.11.11.1) — it is not blocked, because no key is present nothing but the flash content at least one key loaded, none write protected CMD_DBG_CHAL → CMD_DBG_AUTH → reset. [AN5401] §4.5 states the result: all keys erased, FlexRAM back to ordinary RAM (RAMRDY = 1) and FlexNVM back to all data flash (EEERDY = 0). The partition itself is undone, not only the keys the MASTER_ECU_KEY must be known; INIT_RNG first any key with WRITE_PROTECTION none, ever — for us and for NXP's own failure analysis the part stays as it is

Superseded in part on 2026-09-29: already a PGMPART with key space blocks the mass erase, with or without a loaded key; the table above is kept as the record of 2026-09-23. The way back is therefore needed in every stage except "write protected", and it is implemented (host-verified only): device side platforms/s32k1xx/bsp/bspCsec (LOAD_KEY of the MASTER_ECU_KEY into its empty slot, INIT_RNG, GET_ID, DBG_CHAL, DBG_AUTH, from RAM, typed confirmations, no key flag can pass), host side tools/csec (SHE KDF, M1..M5, debug authorisation). The proof on the board is part of a separate task.

The documented way back ([RM13] 36.5.13.26/27): CMD_DBG_CHAL returns a 128-bit challenge; the workstation computes the authorisation from MASTER_ECU_KEY, challenge and UID; CMD_DBG_AUTH erases all keys and the maintainer IFR (factory status); after a reset EEERDY is 0, RAMRDY is 1 and PGMPART may be issued again. The master key must be kept: losing it leaves every provisioned device re-flashable but never re-partitionable. Operational risks: interrupting a PGMPART can leave the partition codes indeterminate and the command runs from RAM, not from flash ([RM13] 36.5.11.14); the data flash IFR must be erased before PGMPART ([AN5401] §4.1); re-partitioning loses the stored data and the endurance guarantee ([AN11983] §3.1). Prove the way back once, on a sample.

docs.title: 6.4 What it means for the bootloader and for canflash
docs.text: With key space allocated canflash erase/program of the application unchanged — program flash sectors are not blocked canflash blupdate unchanged today; with secure boot active it has to rewrite BOOT_MAC in the same operation, before the reset J-Link flashing of the bootloader unchanged J-Link "unlock" / mass erase as a rescue path unchanged while no key is loaded; gone once a key exists, and then replaced by DBG_CHAL/DBG_AUTH with the master key (6.3). The rule in the project rules file is reworded accordingly, not deleted Bootloader security access unchanged (software path stays, 3.4) Bootloader seed quality better – hal_random() can be implemented with CMD_RND (3.4) Emulated EEPROM of the application 3584 bytes instead of 4096 (section 5)

docs.title: 6.5 The MASTER_ECU_KEY of development boards, and the lock on WRITE_PROTECTION
docs.text:
On a development board the MASTER_ECU_KEY is a project secret shared by every board of the project, known by construction, so the debug authentication of 6.3 can bring any of them back. It never stands in the repository; it lives in the key store of the workstation (a folder in the per-user application data: outside every worktree, protected by the maintainer account, one folder to back up; an environment variable would leak into child processes and logs):

Folder %LOCALAPPDATA%/neXtBSW/keys/csec/ (elsewhere ~/.local/share/neXtBSW/keys/csec/); NX_CSEC_KEY_DIR moves it (tests, CI) File <name>.key, UTF-8; lines starting with # are comments, the rest is 32 hex digits = the 16 key bytes, most significant byte first Name project.yaml security.master_ecu_key; left out: the board name (one key for every project of a board, as for the bootloader master key of a separate task) Refused all-zero, all-one (the empty slot) and the public SHE/AES test values; a project value that looks like key material Created python tools/nxconfig csec-key new <project> — random, never overwrites an existing file; csec-key where <project> shows the path and a fingerprint, never the key

Host interface (tools/nxconfig/keystore.py, standard library only): security.master_ecu_key_name(cfg), keystore.load_master_ecu_key(name), keystore.checked_flags([...]) (raises WriteProtectionRefused). tools/csec uses it: python -m tools.csec load-master --project <project> (or --key-name, --key-file; a file inside the repository is refused). *.key is in .gitignore; python tools/nxconfig csec-key scan searches every file git would commit for every key of the store (hex in any spelling, spread over lines, or raw bytes) and names file and key name, never the key; the host test nxconfig-security runs the same scan.

The lock. The project describes keys and flags in security.keys (SHE names, checked against nvm.partition.key_slots). The schema offers boot_protection, debugger_protection, key_usage, wildcard and verify_only; WRITE_PROTECTION is deliberately not offered and is refused three times, each with the YAML path: by the schema validators, by tools/nxconfig/security.py on the loaded project, and by keystore.checked_flags in the tool that builds the LOAD_KEY message. Stage production is refused as a whole until per-device keys are designed.

docs.title: 7. What it means for the architecture
7.1 Where a CSEc driver sits
docs.text: CSEc is a feature of the FTFC, i.e. MCU hardware of one family. The platform rule (README section 6, P1 to P3) puts it per family in the OpenBSW layout: platforms/s32k1xx/bsp/bspCsec, beside bspFlexNvm, not in platforms/common. Above it a neutral contract libs/bsp/bspCrypto (CMAC over a buffer and a flash range with a key handle, random bytes, key load, secure-boot state, "key not available" as an ordinary result) with a contract test, in the shape of IFlashDriver/IEepromDriver. Services in libs/bsw/<module> ask for a role (crypto_cmac); a board without CSEc fills it with a software module built from the bootloader's SHA-256/HMAC code. The bootloader keeps its own way: C without OpenBSW, the CSEc access in bootloader/platforms/s32k1xx, hal_random() as the existing hook.

docs.title: 7.2 Which configuration level holds which value
docs.text:
Value Level Why Does the family/derivative offer CSEc at all; the FCCOB1 codes with their slot counts and byte cost; the EEESIZE the derivative forces on a CSEc part (4096 on 4 KB FlexRAM, 2048 on 2 KB) Derivative (mcudb/<family>/<derivative>.yaml, beside eeprom_emulation) manufacturer fact, the same for every board Address of the parameter RAM CSE_PRAM Family code, chosen at run time from SIM_SDID SUBSERIES (bspCsec csec/CsecPramAddress.h); test_csec.py checks it against the FlexRAM region of every derivative in mcudb manufacturer fact of the sub-series; the silicon says which one it is, the S32K144 builds with the S32K148 header. A cse_pram region in mcudb with a generated constant is the alternative Whether the fitted chip is a security part — the ordering part number (FS32K144U**A**VLL) Board (boards/<board>/board.yaml, a new mcu_part beside mcu/package) a property of this PCB; the derivative name S32K144 covers both variants Number of key slots (FCCOB1), SFE, which slot serves which purpose, secure-boot flavour and BOOT_SIZE, whether the Security Access uses the hardware key Project (project.yaml, nvm.partition and a new security: section) a decision of this ECU software The usable EEPROM that results, the endurance ratio, the register encoding of the command derived by tools/nxconfig and shown by bswgen / flexnvm show before writing README section 4: the generator derives what is derived

Run time keeps its own check: SIM_SDID FEATURES bit 7 says whether the chip has CSEc (platforms/s32k1xx/bsp/bspFlexNvm/include/flexnvm/FlexNvmChip.h). Key slots on a board whose part number says "no security" are an nxconfig error with a YAML path, a mismatch at start-up a reported fault.

docs.title: 7.3 What is board- and family-neutral
docs.text: Neutral: the contract bspCrypto, the role crypto_cmac, the software fallback, the project values "how many slots, what for", addressing a key by a handle. Family-specific, never reaching the neutral contract: that the key space comes out of the EEERAM, the four steps, the common write with the FlexNVM partition, that CSEc needs EEE operation (on the S32K3 the counterpart is the HSE firmware with its own key store; STM32 and rm4x have none in the current scope). Board-specific: only "is a security part fitted".

docs.title: 8. What this does not decide
docs.text: No SecOC profile, no freshness-value handling, no key distribution; no general provisioning tool (the LOAD_KEY protocol is implemented for the first MASTER_ECU_KEY); PGMPART stays blocked until a follow-up task and the decision on Q1 to Q7 are in.

docs.title: 9. Open gaps
docs.text:
# Gap Effect G4 Whether the external, debugger-triggered erase-all is also refused when keys are allocated but none is write-protected ([RM13] 36.5.11.11.1 says that path ignores ACCERR) the remaining rescue path of a development board is uncertain; Q6 treats it as blocked G5 Which S32K1 part numbers carry the security option is not in [RM13]; for this board settled (FS32K144UAVLL) mcudb/board.yaml need the part number as a source G6 Nothing here has been run on hardware verification stays mock until a follow-up task and a board run

Closed: G1 (command times, [AN5401] Tables 9 and 10), G2 (the mass erase is blocked by the presence of keys, not by the key space), G3 (LOAD_KEY M1..M5 implemented in tools/csec).

docs.title: 10. Decision proposal
docs.text:
# Question Recommendation Reason Q1 (irreversible) Allocate key space, how much? yes, FCCOB1 = 0b11: 20 slots, 17 free, 512 bytes of EEERAM cannot be raised later without debug authentication and re-partition; the largest step costs 256 bytes (6 %) more than the next Q2 (irreversible) Which FlexNVM split? DEPART = 0x4 (0 KB data flash, 64 KB backup) instead of today's 0xB; EEESIZE 0x2, FCCOB2 = 0, FCCOB3 = 0; if data flash is wanted, 0xA (ratio 12, no 100 K figure) only at ratio 16 does [DS13] Table 38 give an endurance figure; no project value uses data flash Q3 Secure boot? yes as a target, BOOT_SIZE = bootloader only, flavour parallel, never Strict; reserve the slots now, secure boot later (csec-q3-secureboot) only CSEc can check the first code; Strict cannot be undone Q4 Security Access 0x27 to CSEc? no; keep HMAC-SHA256 with the per-device key, reserve one slot, CSEc later as an option proven, works without CSEc Q5 Does (Ed25519) stay? yes, unchanged different protection goals (3.2) Q6 (risky) Way back before the first PGMPART with key space master key recorded outside the repository and the chip's MASTER_ECU_KEY computed beforehand; the first session stops after PGMPART; DBG_CHAL/DBG_AUTH proven before the first key is loaded for good; never WRITE_PROTECTION (answered csec-q6-rueckweg: no second eval board, S32K146 boards exist, they confirm the procedure, not the numbers) the only truly irreversible act is a write-protected key Q7 Checks nxconfig refuses key slots on a non-security part; key slots with an EEESIZE other than the derivative's CSEc value; key slots with a DEPART without EEPROM backup (errors); backup ratio below 16 and clock.system_hz above the RUN limit with EEPROM or CSEc use (warnings); the display before writing names usable EEPROM, slot count, ratio and that the mass erase will be refused each with a YAML path

Written for a separate task on 2026-09-23. No code changed, nothing written to any chip, no board touched.

Status: 2026-09-22, umgesetzt (N1 bis N20 unten); am 2026-10-04 auf die Entwurfsentscheidungen gekürzt. Schrittfolge, Befehle und Beispielausgaben stehen im Guide "Your own ECU repository"; die Abwägungen, offenen Fragen Q1 bis Q12 und der Studio-Wizard-Entwurf stehen in der Versionshistorie dieser Datei (Commit vor). Das Dokument ist dem verbindlichen Zielbild README.md nachgeordnet.

Entscheidungen des Maintainers vom 2026-09-22:

Key Decision studio-neues-projekt-ablage In production, every ECU project has its own repository. (same) neXtBSW is referenced there at a fixed version. After the project has started, the newest neXtBSW state is never pulled in automatically; an update is a deliberate step. studio-neues-projekt-* The Studio wizard "New project" is built on this design: location free to choose, start empty for a board or as a copy of a project. iso-q3 A neXtBSW release is an annotated tag vX.Y.Z on master, preceded by a green CI run with an archived report.

docs.title: 1. Guiding sentence
docs.text:
A customer repository contains only what the ECU decides: its projects, its own boards, components, modules and tests, and one pin that names exactly one released neXtBSW. Everything neXtBSW provides is read from that pinned tree and never copied or modified. Generated output is reproducible from the two and is therefore not checked in.

Consequences:

  • The three configuration levels (derivative, board, project; README.md section 4) stay as they are. The pin is not a fourth configuration level: it carries no value of the ECU, only where neXtBSW and the customer's extensions are found (same stance as the multi-MCU concept, see planned.md).
  • Everything is board-neutral: the customer's boards are ordinary board.yaml files, found by path like the boards of neXtBSW. The examples below use invented names (acme_bcm, acme_bcm_b2); no neXtBSW board is special.
  • The same rule serves the development case: the projects under projects/ of the neXtBSW repository are a workspace whose pin is "this working tree" (section 6.4).

docs.title: 2. Terms
docs.text: Term Meaning neXtBSW tree one checked-out or unpacked neXtBSW release (or, for development, the working tree of the neXtBSW repository) Workspace the customer repository root: the folder that holds the pin file nextbsw.yaml; one workspace has exactly one neXtBSW tree Pin the reference to exactly one neXtBSW version (section 4), recorded in nextbsw.yaml and, for the recommended variant, in the git submodule entry Release an annotated tag vX.Y.Z on master of neXtBSW with its CI report; for a licensed line, the same version of the licensed export or overlay Update moving the pin from one release to another, as a reviewed change of its own (section 5.5)

docs.title: 3. Example tree of a customer repository
docs.text:
acme-bcm/                              customer repository: one ECU (possibly several MCUs = several projects)
  nextbsw.yaml                         [in]  the pin: version, source, path of the tree, search paths (section 3.1)
  nextbsw/                             [ref] git submodule -> neXtBSW, checked out at tag v1.4.2
                                             (the gitlink is checked in, the content is not)
  CMakeLists.txt                       [in]  thin root, written once by the wizard: includes the build of the
                                             neXtBSW tree (gap N4); no logic of its own
  CMakePresets.json                    [in]  one visible preset per project, inherits the base presets of the tree
  CMakeUserPresets.json                [--]  workstation (compiler path, CAN adapter), in .gitignore as today
  .gitignore  .gitattributes           [in]  build/, .venv/, doc/confidential/; eol rules for YAML/DBC
  .github/workflows/ci.yml             [in]  provider file only: checkout with submodules, then python -m tools.ci
                                             of the neXtBSW tree with --workspace . (gap N12)
  ci/
    pipeline.toml                      [in]  which projects the CI builds, allowed skips (format of tools/ci)
    tests.yaml                         [in]  host tests of the workspace (format of tools/test/tests.yaml)
  projects/
    bcm_main/
      project.yaml                     [in]  board: ../../boards/acme_bcm_b2 ; rte: rte.yaml ; diag: diag.yaml
      rte.yaml                         [in]  components, connections, tasks, CAN (paths relative to this file, gap N3)
      diag.yaml                        [in]  DIDs, routines, sessions, DTCs (ARCH-51)
      can/BCM_Body.dbc                 [in]  the project's CAN database (or a submodule of a vehicle network repo)
      swc/
        DoorLogic/                     Simulink component (swc/README.md)
          DoorLogic.slx                [in]  the source
          DoorLogic_data.m             [in]  calibration values
          generated/{src,arxml}/       [in]  Embedded Coder output, as in neXtBSW: builds and CI need no MATLAB
          generated/model.sha256       [in]  hash of the .slx, configure warns when the code is stale
          test/                        [in]  SIL/MIL stimuli
        LevelMon/                      hand-written C component (RTE-20)
          swc.yaml                     [in]  implementation: c - the master of the component
          LevelMon_data.m              [in]  calibration values (read without MATLAB)
          src/LevelMon.c               [in]  hand-written code
          test/                        [in]  host test of the component
    bcm_io_slave/                      second MCU of the same ECU ([`planned.md`](planned.md)): its own project.yaml ...
  swc/                                 [in]  components shared by several projects of this repository
  boards/
    acme_bcm_b2/
      board.yaml                       [in]  the customer's PCB, same schema as neXtBSW boards
      README.md                        [in]  board notes, safety rules of the board
  mcudb/<family>/<derivative>.yaml     [in]  only if a derivative is missing in the pinned release; should flow
                                             upstream, found through search paths (gap N2)
  libs/<module>/module.yaml ...        [in]  the customer's own device drivers or services with manifest
  doc/
    nextbsw-updates/v1.4.2-v1.5.0.md   [in]  update report of every pin move (section 5.5)
    safety/ ...                        [in]  the integrator's work products; they cite the neXtBSW baseline tag
  build/                               [--]  build directories, one per project and preset (or a short build root)
  .venv/                               [--]  Python environment of this workspace, made from the pinned tree

[in] checked in, [--] never checked in, [ref] referenced (only the pointer is checked in).

docs.title: 3.1 The pin file nextbsw.yaml
docs.text:
Implemented in N2: schema WorkspacePin in tools/nxconfig/model.py, discovery and checks in tools/nxconfig/workspace.py. Step by step: guide, step 1.

# acme-bcm/nextbsw.yaml - which neXtBSW this workspace is built with. Not an ECU configuration level.
schema_version: 1
nextbsw:
  version: 1.4.2                 # the release; must equal the tree's VERSION file (error otherwise)
  source: submodule              # submodule | archive (section 4); decides how tools check the pin
  path: nextbsw                  # the neXtBSW tree, relative to this file
  profile: open                  # open | licensed | nda: the distribution line (lizenz-und-release.md 5.2), default open
  # archive only (required there, refused for a submodule): url: ..., sha256: <64 hex digits>
search:                          # the workspace's own extensions, searched BEFORE the tree's own folders
  mcudb: [mcudb]                 # <dir>/<family>/<derivative>.yaml
  modules: [libs]                # <dir>/**/<module>/module.yaml
  boards: [boards]               # <dir>/<board>/board.yaml - offered by tools; a project still names its board by path
  # overlays (licensed modules, model B, N16): further trees with their own version, checked against nextbsw.version
  # overlays: [{ path: nextbsw-licensed, version: 1.4.2 }]

Rules as implemented (every message with file, line and YAML path of nextbsw.yaml):

  • Discovery walks up from the folder of project.yaml to the first folder that holds nextbsw.yaml, is the root of a neXtBSW tree (VERSION plus tools/nxconfig) or of a git repository. No pin: the tree the tool runs from.
  • Tree: nextbsw.path must be the neXtBSW tree the tool runs from; nextbsw.version must equal its VERSION.
  • Search paths lie outside the tree. A derivative or module found twice, or a board name that exists in two board folders, is an error naming both paths. Unknown keys are errors, so ECU values cannot creep into the pin.
  • One file at the root, no per-project version in project.yaml: every value exactly once (README.md section 4); fitting formats are decided by schema_version of each YAML level, with a migration when a release raises it (N11).

docs.title: 3.2 What is checked in, and why
docs.text:
Artefact Checked in? Reason project.yaml, rte.yaml, diag.yaml, DBC, board.yaml, own mcudb/modules yes the sources of the ECU; reviewed as text .slx, _data.m, swc.yaml, hand-written src/ yes the sources of the components swc/<Swc>/generated/{src,arxml}, model.sha256 yes same rule as in neXtBSW: the firmware and the CI build without MATLAB; the hash makes stale code visible at configure build/<preset>/generated/ (bswgen, rtegen, dbcgen, diaggen, memory layout, A2L) no fully determined by the workspace sources plus the pinned tree; checking it in would create a second truth that can drift. For traceability each customer release archives it as a CI artefact next to ELF/HEX/MAP, and the image carries the generator identity update report doc/nextbsw-updates/*.md yes the evidence of the impact analysis of a pin move (section 5.5), small text; the full generated diff is a CI artefact gitlink of the submodule yes it is the pin for variant 1 (a commit SHA) content of nextbsw/, .venv/, build/, CMakeUserPresets.json no referenced, workstation or derived

Whether a customer wants generated code in git anyway (some reviews ask for it) is question Q6; the design allows it as an export step without making it a second source.

docs.title: 4. Variants for referencing neXtBSW at a fixed version
docs.text:
Rated ++ very good, + good, o neutral, - weak, -- unsuitable.

Criterion 1 submodule on tag 2 FetchContent 3 release archive + SHA-256 4a pip package 4b vendored copy Reproducibility ++ gitlink is the commit SHA + SHA or URL_HASH ++ archive hash + --require-hashes + release identity only by convention Offline build + mirror via insteadOf - cache per build directory ++ one shared cache + wheelhouse ++ Licensed lines + repository permission o credentials in CMake + one archive per profile + private index o licensed files enter the history Python tools before CMake o .venv from the tree -- tree appears only at configure + wheelhouse ++ o Studio matches the pin + VERSION, tag at a fixed place -- + from nextbsw.yaml + o Deliberate, traceable update ++ one reviewed diff, git log vA..vB + hash diff only + hash diff, release notes o -- huge diffs Safety baseline ++ tag reachable from master, dirty submodule visible + + hash, origin needs a signature o --

Decisive facts: the tree is needed before CMake (nxconfig check, Studio live check, RTE and component tools, MATLAB read it directly; the root CMakeLists.txt selects the toolchain before project()); the Studio bundles the generator modules of its build, so its version must match the pin; OpenBSW is a nested submodule (git variants need --recursive); licensed content never shares an object store with the public line.

docs.title: 4.4 Recommendation
docs.text:
Variant 1: git submodule nextbsw/ on a release tag, declared in nextbsw.yaml. The pin is a commit SHA in the customer's own history, so nothing moves it except a commit; the update is a normal reviewed change. The safety baseline is checkable by a tool (N10: annotated tag v<version> reachable from master, clean submodule). It fits both licence models (lizenz-und-release.md (not published, available on request) 4.4) and needs the least new infrastructure.

Variant 3 is the documented fallback for air-gapped build machines: the same nextbsw.yaml with source: archive, url and sha256; the tools read only path and version, so switching changes one file. Variants 2 and 4b are not recommended; 4a is a candidate for the web app, not for the firmware tree.

Rules: only release tags in a workspace that builds a customer release (CI flag --release; an untagged pin is a warning during development); the submodule is never edited; git clone --recurse-submodules is the documented clone.

docs.title: 5. How the parts work together
docs.text: Commands and examples: guide. The rules:

docs.title: 5.1 Finding things
docs.text: The tree comes from nextbsw.yaml (walk up from project.yaml), without the file the tree the tool runs from; for a project the Studio takes the tree of its pin, not its own. A board is named by path in project.board (explicit and diff-visible, no name lookup); derivatives and modules are searched in the workspace search paths first, then in the tree; rte.yaml paths are relative to the file; the Python .venv and the build directory belong to the workspace.

docs.title: 5.2 Building
docs.text: The workspace root gets a thin CMakeLists.txt that hands over to the tree. The root build separates the tree root (NX_ROOT: generators, platforms, libs, OpenBSW) from the workspace root (NX_WORKSPACE: projects, boards, .venv, build); no board port is needed, because the feature switches come from the project (N5). cmake --preset <project> works in the workspace like in the neXtBSW repository. See guide, step 5.

docs.title: 5.3 Python environment
docs.text: tools/requirements.txt and tools/ci/constraints.txt of the pinned tree define the environment; the workspace gets its own .venv, made by one command of the tree (N8, tools/setup) that writes a marker with the hash of the constraints; tools warn when it does not match the pinned tree. See guide, step 2.

docs.title: 5.4 Studio and version
docs.text: The Studio bundles the generator modules of its build, so its version must match the pin (N7). On opening a project it reads the pin: same version opens normally, a different version is said so, the installed Studio build of the pinned version is offered, otherwise the project opens read-only with a warning. External steps (CMake, generators) always run from the pinned tree with the workspace .venv. Exact match instead of a compatibility range is the only rule a tool qualification can state. See guide, step 8.

docs.title: 5.5 Update workflow (deliberate and traceable)
docs.text: One command in the core (tools/nxupdate, N9), run on a branch: generate every project with the current pin; move the pin (fetch, check out the new tag, check it, update nextbsw.yaml, recreate .venv); run the format migrations of every raised schema_version (N11); generate again, compile, run the workspace tests; write doc/nextbsw-updates/v<old>-v<new>.md (skipped releases, changelog excerpt, migrated files, new and gone nxconfig messages, generated-file diff, ELF size change, and a prominent list of field-relevant changes: memory layout, bootloader identity, CAN IDs, diagnostic addresses, record formats); commit the gitlink, nextbsw.yaml, migrated files and the report as one change. Nothing runs automatically; the Studio may inform that a newer release exists but never moves the pin.

docs.title: 5.6 CI in the customer repository
docs.text: The provider file only checks out (with submodules and credentials for private lines) and calls python nextbsw/tools/ci with --workspace . (N12); compiler versions come from the tree, the workspace adds ci/pipeline.toml and ci/tests.yaml, and --release runs the pin check (N10). See guide, step 6.

docs.title: 5.7 Safety
docs.text:
• The customer (integrator) cites two baselines: the neXtBSW release tag (with commit) and the customer's own tag. The image identifies both (N13, next section).
  • Assumption of use for the safety concept: the integrator uses a released neXtBSW baseline unmodified and performs an impact analysis on every update; the update report is that analysis's input, and the pin check (N10) turns the assumption into a CI error.

docs.title: 5.7.1 What the image says about the customer baselines (N13)
docs.text:
Implemented in separate tasks. Four values, each with one source and one place in the image:

Value Source (one) Console (info) DID Build header neXtBSW version VERSION of the tree the build runs from (PROJECT_VERSION) neXtBSW, also in version 0xF195, first word - neXtBSW commit git describe --tags --always --dirty of the tree, plus a hash of uncommitted changes (tools/diaggen/buildid.py, same rule as the EPK) commit 0xF195, second word NX_DIAG_NEXTBSW_COMMIT / NX_DIAG_NEXTBSW_VERSION Configuration and generators SHA-256 over the configuration files (pin file nextbsw.yaml included) and the generator sources (tools/nxconfig/identity.py) configuration (also in version), identity, ... 0xF1F1 identity/nxIdentityFields.h Workspace (customer) commit git describe of the workspace root, same rule workspace 0xF1F2 (workspace.version, 48 bytes) NX_DIAG_WORKSPACE_VERSION
  • One header for the git state: diag/DiagBuildId.h is written by buildid.py at every build; DiagSystem and the console read the same macros, so console and DID cannot disagree.
  • The tree is the pin; the workspace is NX_WORKSPACE. In a submodule git describe names the release tag, not the customer's commit. An archive has no .git and shows nogit. The workspace value is - in the development case (NX_WORKSPACE equals NX_ROOT) and carries a hash of uncommitted changes, so a build from uncommitted files never looks like a release.
  • No git state in the configuration identity: 0xF1F1 stays reproducible in every checkout; the pin file is one of its inputs, neither commit is.
  • Identifier 0xF1F2 is the next free one in the supplier-specific identification group of tools/diaggen/standard_diag.yaml. The release CI (--release) refuses a dirty or untagged pin.

docs.title: 5.8 Licensed modules
docs.text:
Model (lizenz-und-release.md (not published, available on request) 4.4) What the workspace references C (now): monorepo + export per profile one submodule: the export repository of the customer's profile (open, licensed-<line>); profile in nextbsw.yaml names it B (goal): open repository + overlays submodule nextbsw/ (open) plus overlay submodules (nextbsw-licensed, per class); overlays listed in nextbsw.yaml with their version, found through the module search path, checked to equal nextbsw.version

In both, a project that uses a module above its profile is reported by nxconfig (the planned distribution_profile check of a separate task section 5.2 moves into the workspace pin).

docs.title: 6. Studio wizard "New project" and the development case
docs.text: The wizard (core function without Qt plus GUI) asks where (new repository, existing workspace, development in the neXtBSW repository), which neXtBSW release, what to start from (empty for a board, copy of a project), the name, and shows a summary before anything is written; failed checks leave the files in place and open the project with the messages. See guide, step 1, "In the Studio".

docs.title: 6.4 The demo and development case
docs.text:
projects/ in the neXtBSW repository stays: examples, build tests, the projects the neXtBSW CI builds, and the place where neXtBSW itself is developed and tested. Such a project has no nextbsw.yaml; the tools fall back to "the tree I run from", its version is the working tree (git describe), presets stay in the root CMakePresets.json or none (explicit NX_PROJECT). These projects are not for production.

A consequence worth naming: the maintainer's own non-public projects (for example those on private boards, F10) fit the workspace model directly - in model B the "private integration repository" of a separate task is exactly a workspace with a pin.

docs.title: 7. Gaps in today's neXtBSW and task proposals
docs.text:
Status is kept in the task list; the IDs N1 to N20 stay as references. Done and described in the guide or in code: N2 (pin and discovery), N5 (no board port needed), N9 (tools/nxupdate), N10 (pin check, tools/nxconfig/pincheck.py), N11 (format migrations, nxconfig migrate), N13 (image identity, section 5.7.1), N15 (release publication, tools/ci/release.py), N17 (the guide), N19 (coverage and static analysis of the customer's own code), N20 (empty project on a board of an existing workspace).

# Title N1 neXtBSW version identity: one VERSION file at the tree root, checked against the tag vX.Y.Z N2 Workspace pin nextbsw.yaml and discovery (section 3.1) N3 Paths in rte.yaml relative to the file, schema_version: 2 with migration N4 Build a workspace outside the tree: NX_ROOT and NX_WORKSPACE separated N5 Feature switches from the project instead of ecu/platforms/<board>/Options.cmake N6 Studio: tree, interpreter and build root per project N7 Studio and pin version rule (exact match, warning, read-only) N8 Workspace Python environment from the tree's requirements and constraints, with a marker N9 Update workflow: before/after generation, pin move, migrations, report N10 Pin check: annotated tag on master, clean, overlays equal in version N11 Format migrations when a schema_version rises N12 tools/test and tools/ci for workspaces (--workspace) N13 neXtBSW version and workspace commit in the image identity N14 Studio git page in a workspace (submodule as its own category, commit blocked on a dirty submodule) N15 Release publication: tag, archived CI report, export per profile, optional archive with SHA-256 N16 Licensed overlays in a workspace N17 Guide "Customer project" N18 Safety: assumption of use for the pin N19 Coverage and static analysis of the customer's own code N20 Empty project on a board of an existing workspace

Out of scope: the format of a vehicle-network description shared by several ECU repositories, OTA packages and multi-ECU composition (planned.md), signing of releases and archives.

Review questions (README.md section 11): the design touches no ECU value (questions 1 to 5), keeps the pin in one file (6), is tested with synthetic workspaces outside the repository (7) and keeps the core free of Qt (8).

docs.title: Calibration in neXtBSW: parameters, maps, a versioned calibration database, measurement signals
docs.text:
Status: 2026-09-28, concept; decisions E1 to E6 taken by the maintainer (all recommendations a, section 11); stages K1, K2, K3 and K6 are implemented (section 10). Am 2026-10-04 gekürzt: Optionenvergleiche, Ist-Zustand vor der Umsetzung, Umsetzungsnotizen (7.6, 7.7) und die Langfassung der Entscheidungen stehen in der Versionshistorie dieser Datei (Commit vor), die Umsetzung in den Readmes der Werkzeuge.
