Status: variant A decided and implemented (a project decision; concept); am 2026-10-04 gekürzt: Bestandsaufnahme, Varianten B und C im Detail und die Fragen F1 bis F4 stehen in der Versionshistorie dieser Datei (Commit vor). Finding of the Studio user test 2026-09-25: interrupts on pins (edge, priority) could not be configured. Reference: architecture target picture (sections 3–5, review questions in section 11), safety concept section 1.4, coexistence, dependent failures DF-37.

docs.title: 1.1 Pins in the configuration
docs.text: The board lists inputs in dio.inputs[] (name, pin, pad, active level, pull); the project says which are used (use.dio) and may give a rank (interrupts.ranks[], source: dio); the RTE offers dio.in.<NAME> sampled per task cycle. The derivative knew nothing about which pins can raise an interrupt.

docs.title: 1.2 Existing users of pin interrupts
docs.text:
User How Remark Hall sensors (platforms/s32k1xx/bsp/bspHall) PORT_PCR.IRQC = either edge, NVIC level from the dio rank of the three signals update 2026-09-29: the vectors belong to the family dispatcher platforms/s32k1xx/bsp/bspPinIrq, the Hall pins are one consumer of it; since an earlier change tools/bswgen generates the whole table (bsp/pinIrq/pinIrqConfiguration.h: Hall pins and pin events, vectors from the derivative fact pin_interrupts, one rank per vector), so a Hall sensor also builds on the S32K11x (vector PORT) Pin events (libs/bsp/bspPinEvent) project pin_events; edge of the detector: both while debouncing, else the physical edge of the logical one second consumer of the dispatcher through the s32k1xx adapter bios::PinEventAdapter; the port starts every consumer once (bsp::startPinInterrupts()), the RTE cycles the events in one task and offers pinevent.<NAME>.count/.time_us/.qlf; console pinevent SBC INTN (sbcUja113x) polled every 10 ms over SPI, deliberately no ISR the INTN pins are ordinary dio inputs Wake-up through the supply (SBC local wake inputs LOCAL0..7, CAN wake), exposed as ecu.wakeup[.<source>] the MCU itself has no low-power mode in use; with the SBC in sleep the MCU is unpowered Input capture timer channel, polled by a task not a pin interrupt

All four device drivers of the safety concept poll their FAULT/INT lines (concept section 13, "Polling, not interrupts").

docs.title: 1.3 Interrupt priorities
docs.text: Priorities are ranks in the project (interrupts.ranks): NVIC level = max_syscall_level + rank, VIM: the ranks order the free channels. Levels above max_syscall_level stay reserved for interrupts that never call the RTOS (halt deadman SM-06). tools/elfcheck compares the programmed levels with the ranks.

docs.title: 1.4 Vector topology differs per family
docs.text:
This is what makes "one flag per pin" insufficient:

Family / derivative Edge detection Vectors Consequence s32k1xx S32K14x PORT_PCR.IRQC per pin (rising, falling, either, level; DMA variants) one vector per port (A–E) all event pins of one port share one priority level s32k1xx S32K11x as above one vector for all ports all pin events of the MCU share one level s32k3xx SIUL2 external interrupt lines EIRQn, reachable only from certain pins (already in the pinmux table as signal EIRQn) lines grouped onto a few vectors not every pin can raise an interrupt; the pin mux decides stm32 EXTI line n serves pin n of one port (selected in SYSCFG) lines 0–4 own vectors, 5–9 and 10–15 shared PA3 and PB3 cannot both be event inputs rm4x (RM46) GIO: only ports GIOA/GIOB, every pin of them two VIM requests (high/low line), chosen per pin only 16 pins (fewer bonded on LQFP144) can raise an interrupt

S32K1 additionally has a digital glitch filter per port (one filter width for all enabled pins of that port); other families have different or no filters.

docs.title: 2. Which level owns which value
docs.text:
The user test asked for "edge and priority on a pin". Split according to section 4 of the target picture, fact and decision separated:

Value Level Reason Which pin can raise an interrupt, which line/vector it belongs to, which pins share a vector or a line, filter capability Derivative (new, mcudb) manufacturer fact, the same on every board. Not the board: the board wizard would otherwise ask the maintainer for a datasheet fact The input itself: pin, active level, pull Board (unchanged, dio.inputs) property of the PCB Optional: nature of the signal (mechanical contact that bounces, open-drain line) Board (optional fact, proposal) property of the circuit; allows a warning "contact input without debounce" That the input raises events at all, edge, debounce time, maximum event rate, rank, wake-up source yes/no Project usage decision of the ECU software

So the answer to "board or project" is: the project configures pin interrupts; the board stays as it is; the capability comes from the derivative. The board wizard needs no new step (section 5).

Edges are proposed relative to the active level of the board (activate, deactivate, both), not as physical rising/falling: the board already says whether the input is active low, and the project then does not have to know it. This is open question F2.

Sketch (project, not a schema yet):

pin_events:
  - input: DOOR_SW          # board dio.inputs[].name, must be in use.dio
    edge: activate          # activate | deactivate | both
    debounce_us: 2000       # 0 = none
    max_rate_hz: 200        # storm limit, required
    wakeup: false           # prepared for an MCU low-power mode, see 3.5
interrupts:
  ranks:
    - { source: dio, name: DOOR_SW, rank: 6 }

docs.title: 3. Driver interface and path into the application
3.1 Layering
docs.text:
L5  SWC  reads pinevent.<NAME>.count / .time_us / .qlf        (variant A)
          or is activated by the event                         (variant B)
 L4  RTE  (generated) copies the snapshot per task cycle
 L3/L2    pinEvent (family neutral, host-tested): debounce, rate limit, counter, time stamp, qualifier
 L1       pin interrupt contract libs/bsp/<pinIrq>: arm(edge), disarm, callback per pin
          family implementation platforms/<family>/bsp: one dispatcher per vector,
          clears only the flags of its own pins, calls the registered consumer
          consumers: pinEvent, Hall (moved onto the dispatcher, IO-23), later BSW users
  • One dispatcher per vector in the family (this is the item "pin-interrupt dispatcher per port"). It owns PORTx_IRQHandler (or the EXTI/SIUL2/GIO vector), reads the flag register once, clears only the flags of pins that have a consumer, and calls the consumer with the pin and a time stamp. Hall and pin events are two consumers of the same dispatcher; the generator assigns each pin to exactly one consumer.
  • The consumer is chosen by the generator, not registered at run time. A generated table (pin → consumer, edge code) keeps the wiring checkable (elfcheck, host tests) and avoids function pointers written at run time.
  • Edge codes stay in the family generator (IRQC 9/10/11 on S32K1, EXTI_RTSR/FTSR, GIOPOL + both-edge emulation on rm4x). The contract only knows activate/deactivate/both after the inversion of the board.
  • No level-sensitive interrupts for events: a stuck level would be an endless interrupt. Only edges.

docs.title: 3.2 Three ways into the application
docs.text:
Way What the SWC sees Latency Fits the RTE today? Signal: counter, time stamp, level, qualifier pinevent.<NAME>.count (uint32, wraps), .time_us (time of the last accepted edge), .qlf (QLF_* values of a separate task) as RTE inputs like capture.* and hall.* one task cycle for the reaction; no edge is lost and the time stamp is exact yes: a new input kind, like separate tasks Activation: the event starts a runnable a runnable with an event instead of a period interrupt + task switch no: needs a new RTE event kind, a sporadic task with a minimum inter-arrival time, schedule analysis and deadline monitoring for it Callback nothing; only BSW modules get a function call in interrupt context shortest not meant for SWCs (interrupt context, no RTE consistency, no Simulink mapping)

A callback into application code is not proposed at all: an SWC running in interrupt context would bypass the task model, the RTE data consistency and every timing argument.

docs.title: 3.3 Run-time limits (interrupt storms)
docs.text:
A pin interrupt preempts every task, including the safety task. Without a limit, a bouncing contact, a broken wire picking up noise, or a fault on the line can starve the system (DF-37, "interrupt storm").

Proposal for the pinEvent module (driver-level robustness, see 4.2):

  • Rate limit per pin: at most max_rate_hz accepted edges over a sliding window (token bucket). On overflow the module disarms the pin (edge code 0), sets .qlf = QLF_ERROR and counts the overflow. Re-arming is open question F4 (automatic after a hold-off, or on request).
  • Debounce in software as a lock-out: after an accepted edge further edges are counted as glitches for debounce_us, then the level is sampled once more to confirm it. Hardware filters (S32K1 port filter) are an optional family optimisation, not the contract, because their width is per port and other families lack them (open question F3).
  • ISR budget: the dispatcher and the consumer have a bounded, short path (no loops over unused pins, no RTOS call except where the variant needs a task notification). The worst-case load is max_rate_hz × ISR time per pin and is reported by nxconfig as a load figure.

docs.title: 3.4 Priority
docs.text: Pin interrupts use the existing rank mechanism (source: dio). The rank is per input, but the hardware level is per vector: nxconfig checks that all event inputs (and Hall signals) sharing a vector have the same rank and says which ones they are (as bswgen already does for Hall). Ranks are ≥ 0 and therefore always at or below max_syscall_level: a pin event can never preempt the deadman or other levels reserved above the RTOS boundary.

docs.title: 3.5 Low power and wake-up
docs.text: Today the ECU sleeps through the SBC, which switches the MCU supply off; a pin interrupt cannot wake an unpowered MCU, so wake-up inputs are the SBC local inputs (wakeup_local, ecu.wakeup.LOCALn). An MCU low-power mode (IEcuPowerStateController, S32K1 VLPS/STOP, noted as future in ecuState.md) would use pin interrupts as wake sources. The concept therefore only reserves wakeup: true in the project entry: in stage 2 nxconfig rejects it with a message until an MCU low-power implementation exists; later it adds a source ecu.wakeup.<NAME> in the same way as wakeup_local, and the same rule applies as a separate task: a wake-up input must be chosen explicitly (default off), because an unterminated line wakes the ECU at random. Whether edge detection works in the chosen stop mode of each family is a derivative fact to be confirmed from the reference manual at that time.

docs.title: 4.1 Temporal interference
docs.text:
• A pin interrupt is a new interrupt source above every task. Its effect on the safety task is bounded by the rate limit (3.3) and the ISR budget; the credited detection of a delay stays what it is today: SM-04 period check of the safety task, SM-06 halt deadman, SM-01 watchdog (DF-37). No new claim is made for application tasks — that remains F10 (activation of application tasks is not supervised).
  • Variant B adds a sporadic activation of application tasks. This is exactly the unsupervised case of F10: the schedule analysis (tools/schedana) would need the minimum inter-arrival time, and SM-05 would need deadlines for event runnables. This is the main reason to postpone variant B (section 6).
  • The dispatcher runs inside the SafePreIsrHook/SafePostIsrHook frame like the CAN, UART and Hall vectors; it is not a safety context: it may not write safety RAM (MPU, SM-10), and the static rule safety-context must not list its files.

docs.title: 4.2 Classification: driver mechanism, not a base-software safety mechanism
docs.text:
Part Classification Reason Rate limit, debounce, disarm on storm, qualifier driver robustness / quality measure (QM), not credited as a safety mechanism it protects availability of the CPU; the credited detection of a stall remains SM-04/SM-06/SM-01. Crediting it would mix a driver-level measure into the stage-1 argument, which the strict separation forbids Dispatcher, vector entries part of the interrupt infrastructure (S-INT, coexistence class B-SEP) it is a vector entry and shares the hook frame; so it is developed and reviewed like the other ISR entries pinEvent module QM module with a new coexistence row (timing: interrupt storm; argued with rate limit + SM-04, like CA-06/CA-14/CA-23) new row in coexistence.md in stage 2 Pin event used as input of a safety function by the integrator integrator's responsibility (assumption of use) the qualifier gives the SWC the information; the base software does not claim a detection for it

No stage-1 mechanism depends on pin interrupts, and none is changed by this concept. If a later safety mechanism needs a pin interrupt (e.g. a FAULT line of a gate driver as an interrupt instead of polling), it is a stage-2 device-driver mechanism and gets its own analysis.

docs.title: 4.3 Checks in nxconfig (stage 2)
docs.text:
Errors with YAML path unless marked as warning:

  1. The input exists on the board, is in use.dio, and has a rank (interrupts.ranks, source: dio).
  2. The pin can raise an interrupt on this derivative (new derivative fact); on s32k3xx the EIRQ function is reachable at this pin.
  3. Inputs that share a vector (S32K14x: port; S32K11x: all; STM32: EXTI 5–9/10–15) have the same rank; inputs that share a line (STM32 EXTI n) are mutually exclusive.
  4. A pin has exactly one consumer: not both Hall signal and pin event; not a pin of safety, not a safe_off output (already covered by the pin claim check).
  5. max_rate_hz is set and > 0; debounce_us < 1/max_rate_hz; warning when the sum of max_rate_hz × ISR budget over all pins exceeds a configurable share of CPU time (initial proposal 5 %).
  6. Warning for a board input marked as mechanical contact without debounce_us.
  7. wakeup: true is an error until an MCU low-power implementation exists (3.5).

Family-specific details (edge codes, filter register values) stay in the family generator as today.

docs.title: 5. Studio
docs.text: Where What Board wizard (tools/studio/gui/newboard.py, step "Digitaler Eingang") no new input. Only a read-only hint per pin from the derivative fact: "interruptfähig (Vektor PORTC)" or "nicht interruptfähig", and a note when two inputs share an STM32 EXTI line Project configuration (step config) new card "Pin-Ereignisse": table of used digital inputs with switch "Ereignis", edge (aktivieren / deaktivieren / beide), debounce, maximum rate, rank; messages of nxconfig in the row as elsewhere (live check) Tasks & schedule (step tasks) an overview of all interrupt ranks (CAN, UART, pin vectors) with the resulting NVIC level, grouped per vector, so the maintainer sees that pins of one port share a level. Today no Studio page shows the ranks at all Connections (step connections) the new targets pinevent.<NAME>.count/.time_us/.qlf in the BSW input group

docs.title: 6. Variants and decision
docs.text:
Variant What Pro Contra Result A pin events as RTE signals the project enables events per input; a family dispatcher per vector feeds a family-neutral pinEvent module (debounce, rate limit); the RTE offers pinevent.<NAME>.count, .time_us, .qlf no edge lost, exact time stamp, no new RTE event kind, task model and timing argument unchanged except for the bounded ISR; the dispatcher also serves Hall the reaction waits for the next cycle of the reading task decided and implemented B: A plus runnable activation by the event a runnable started by the event in a sporadic task with a minimum inter-arrival time fast reaction without a fast periodic task new RTE event kind and task type, schedule analysis and SM-05 deadlines for sporadic activation, enlarges the unsupervised activation gap F10 until a follow-up task later, only after a later change C: BSW service only dispatcher and a BSW-internal consumer interface; the application keeps reading dio.in.<NAME> smallest change does not answer the user-test finding contained in A

Decisions: edges are written logically relative to the board's active level (activate/deactivate/both), debounce is a software lock-out with level confirmation (a hardware filter stays a later family optimisation), and a tripped rate limit disarms the pin, sets QLF_ERROR and re-arms after a hold-off. The derivative fact (which pin can raise an interrupt, vector and line sharing) is kept for all four families at once, so the configuration model is not shaped by the S32K14x "one vector per port" case (review question 3).

docs.title: Schnelle Regelschleife
docs.text:
Zielbild für Stromregelung im PWM-Takt (FOC, DC/DC, Lader); es gibt weder Schema noch Generatorcode für die Schleife selbst (Entscheidungen F1–F8 vom 2026-09-29, Entwicklungszweig der Entwicklungszweig).

%%{init: {'theme':'base','flowchart':{'curve':'basis'},'themeVariables':{'fontFamily':'Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif','fontSize':'14px','background':'#ffffff','primaryColor':'#ffffff','primaryBorderColor':'#64748b','primaryTextColor':'#0f172a','lineColor':'#475569','edgeLabelBackground':'#ffffff','tertiaryColor':'#f8fafc','clusterBkg':'#f8fafc','clusterBorder':'#cbd5e1'}}}%%
flowchart LR
    PWM("PWM group<br/>timer") -- hardware trigger --> ADC("ADC sample group<br/>i_u i_v i_w u_dc")
    ADC -- "group complete (IRQ)" --> DISP(["generated dispatcher<br/>(no RTOS call, no RTE lock)"])
    DISP --> FAST("fast runnable<br/>(Simulink, T_pwm)")
    FAST -- "3 duties, one sync step" --> PWM
    DISP -. "budget, overrun" .-> SUP("safe supervisor<br/>(mailbox)")
    FAST <-. "double buffer / seqlock" .-> SLOW("slow runnables<br/>(RTE tasks, ms)")

    classDef own fill:#ccfbf1,stroke:#0f766e,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#0f172a
    classDef gen fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#0f172a
    classDef app fill:#ede9fe,stroke:#6d28d9,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#0f172a
    class PWM,ADC,SUP own
    class DISP gen
    class FAST,SLOW app
  • Der RTE kennt nur Timing-Events in ganzen Millisekunden. Die schnelle Schleife ist ein zweiter, generierter Ausführungspfad: ein Runnable, das direkt aus dem Interrupt "Messgruppe vollständig" einer Hardware-Triggerkette PWM → ADC läuft.
  • Das Ereignis liefert ein L1-Vertrag (bspSampleGroup, je Familie umgesetzt; beschrieben im Modul bspSampleGroup); rtegen kennt nur Vertrag und Schleifenname, nie ein Register.
  • Das Simulink-Modell bleibt eine mit autosar.tlc gebaute AUTOSAR-Komponente; Sub-Millisekunden-Perioden gibt es nur für Runnables einer schnellen Schleife. Zwischen schnell und langsam sorgt eine generierte, sperrfreie Übergabe für Konsistenz.
  • Laufzeit und Überlauf werden je Zyklus am PWM-Timer gemessen und als Ereignis an den Safe-Supervisor gemeldet; die Schleife läuft über CAN, UART und allen Tasks, unter dem Halt-Deadman.

Verweise: Zielbild, Pin-Interrupts, Safety-Konzept.

docs.title: Mehrere MCUs in einem Steuergerät und Flash-Master
docs.text:
Ein Steuergerät mit mehr als einer MCU: Eine MCU wird über CAN programmiert, die übrigen programmiert sie über SPI (Umsetzung).

%%{init: {'theme':'base','flowchart':{'curve':'basis'},'themeVariables':{'fontFamily':'Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif','fontSize':'14px','background':'#ffffff','primaryColor':'#ffffff','primaryBorderColor':'#64748b','primaryTextColor':'#0f172a','lineColor':'#475569','edgeLabelBackground':'#ffffff','tertiaryColor':'#f8fafc','clusterBkg':'#f8fafc','clusterBorder':'#cbd5e1'}}}%%
flowchart LR
    T("Tester<br/>canflash / OTA") -- "CAN, UDS<br/>addr M, S1, S2" --> M
    subgraph ECU
        M("Master MCU<br/>bootloader = flash master<br/>(gateway, no image store)")
        S1("Slave 1<br/>bootloader")
        S2("Slave 2<br/>bootloader")
        M -- "SPI + CS0<br/>(+ reset, boot, ready)" --> S1
        M -- "SPI + CS1" --> S2
    end

    classDef own fill:#ccfbf1,stroke:#0f766e,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#0f172a
    classDef grp fill:#f8fafc,stroke:#cbd5e1,rx:8,ry:8
    class T,M,S1,S2 own
    class ECU grp

Ein Steuergerät mit mehreren MCUs sieht für den Tester aus wie mehrere Steuergeräte an einem Bus. Der Master ergänzt eine Route, kein Protokoll.

Schlüssel Entscheidung fm-slave-bootloader Der Slave läuft mit dem neXtBSW-Bootloader, Transport ist SPI; kein ROM-Bootloader des Herstellers. fm-adressierung Der Tester erreicht jeden Slave durch Weiterleitung, jede MCU hat eine eigene Diagnoseadresse; der Master ist Gateway und speichert kein Image. fm-master-ort Die Weiterleitung liegt im Bootloader des Masters; Slaves bleiben aktualisierbar, wenn die Master-Applikation defekt ist. fm-slave-einstieg Einstieg des Slaves in den Bootloader: Reset und Boot-Leitung, nur Reset mit Bootfenster oder Kommando über SPI; alle drei müssen beschreibbar sein. fm-testaufbau Boardnachweis später mit Eval-Board S32K144 als Master und Nucleo F446RE als Slave.

Ein Projekt ohne Slaves erzeugt unverändert das, was es heute erzeugt. Heute vorhanden: der Link-Kern mcuLink.

docs.title: 2. S32K116 (Cortex-M0+)
docs.text:
Unterschiede zur S32K144; alle Werte stehen mit Beleg in mcudb/s32k1xx/S32K116.yaml. Die früheren Stellen mit M4F-Annahme (Toolchain, FreeRTOS-Port, Interruptsperre, NVIC-Prioritätsbits, CMSIS-Header, Cache, Hard-Fault-Handler, Startup, MPU, Takt, Watchdog-Test, Bootloader-HAL) sind über Familienvorlagen nach NX_CORE_ARCHITECTURE gelöst .

Eigenschaft S32K116 S32K144 Kern Cortex-M0+ (ARMv6-M), keine FPU Cortex-M4F NVIC-Prioritätsbits 2 (der NXP-Header sagt fälschlich 4; die Anpassungsschicht korrigiert) 4 Interrupts 32 externe; CAN0_ORed_0_31_MB_IRQn, WDOG_IRQn CAN0_ORed_0_15_MB_IRQn/_16_31_, WDOG_EWM_IRQn P-Flash 128 KB, Sektor 2 KB 512 KB, 4 KB D-Flash / FlexRAM 32 KB / 2 KB 64 KB / 4 KB SRAM 1 KB SRAM_L + 14 KB SRAM_U 32 KB + 28 KB Takt kein SPLL, FIRC 48 MHz SPLL vorhanden Instanzen ADC0, FTM0/1, LPSPI0, LPUART0/1, FlexCAN0 (CAN FD), LPI2C0, FlexIO, MPU mit 8 Regionen ADC0/1, FTM0–3, LPSPI0–2, FlexCAN0–2, LMEM-Cache

Speicherbudget (größtes Risiko): Das Abbild des Eval-Boards (Text ca. 121 KB, bss ca. 37 KB) passt weder in 128 KB Flash noch in rund 15 KB nutzbares RAM; allein der OpenBSW-Logpuffer belegt 8 KB. Ein S32K116-Projekt braucht ein mageres Funktionsprofil (ohne Konsole/Logger oder mit kleinem Puffer, ein bis zwei Tasks, kleine Stacks, kleine UDS-Puffer). Das ist Projektkonfiguration (README Abschnitt 4).

docs.title: 3. Toolchain per core and interrupt controller
docs.text:
Core (derivative.core) -mcpu -mfloat-abi -mfpu Architecture (.arch in the start-up) FreeRTOS port cortex-m0plus (S32K116/118) cortex-m0plus soft – armv6-m GCC/ARM_CM0 + setupApplicationsIsr cortex-m4f (S32K14x, STM32F4, today) cortex-m4 hard fpv4-sp-d16 armv7e-m (today armv7-m) OpenBSW freertos_cm4_sysTick cortex-m7f (S32K3, proposal) cortex-m7 hard fpv5-sp-d16 or fpv5-d16 (depending on the derivative's FPU, assumption) armv7e-m GCC/ARM_CM7 or ARM_CM4F cortex-m33 (test profile only, repo:tools/nxconfig/test_build_integration.py:67) cortex-m33 hard fpv5-sp-d16 armv8-m.main GCC/ARM_CM33_NTZ cortex-r4f (family rm4x, proof target RM46L852; today only test profile TESTR4F) cortex-r4f hard vfpv3-d16 armv7-r (start-up in ARM state, .arm) none yet – candidate GCC/ARM_CRx_No_GIC, source open until a follow-up task (D14)

Core table in nxconfig (status). The table above is CORES in repo:tools/nxconfig/config.py; per core -mcpu, FPU variants (derivative.fpu → -mfpu), architecture (NX_CORE_ARCHITECTURE: armv6m, armv7m, armv8m, armv7r) and interrupt controller:

Controller Cores Derivative (mcudb) Project interrupts Mapping, RTOS boundary nvic Cortex-M0+/M4F/M7F/M33 derivative.nvic_priority_bits (limits per core: ARMv6-M 2, otherwise 3..8) ranks, optional max_syscall_level level = max_syscall_level + rank (checks.InterruptPriorities); ARMv6-M without BASEPRI → level 0 vim Cortex-R4F vim.channels, vim.fixed[] (channel, request, irq/fiq), source only ranks; max_syscall_level is an error the ranks order the non-fixed channels from the lowest number (same rank: YAML order, checks.VimChannelOrder); every rank source is an IRQ and may call the RTOS, FIQ never
  • The NVIC fields (nvic_priority_bits, max_syscall_default) only exist for nvic cores; Core checks this when it is created. nvic_priority_bits on a VIM derivative and vim on an NVIC derivative are errors with the YAML path.
  • Evidence: architecture ARMv7-R, FPU VFPv3-D16 (double precision) and "Cortex-R4 without its own interrupt controller, locking via CPSR I/F" are general ARM facts [ARM, audit section 0]; the VIM principle (priority = channel number, channels IRQ or FIQ) is TI Hercules knowledge [TRM, audit 4.1]. The channel count and fixed channels of a real derivative are not yet anywhere in the repository – the values in TESTR4F (48 channels, 0/1 fixed) are synthetic. RM46L852 follows with evidence in the sources/licence.
  • The controller is attached to the core entry because all Cortex-R4F derivatives of the target picture (rm4x, D13) have the VIM. A Cortex-R derivative with a different controller (e.g. GIC) gets a core entry of its own, or the choice moves into the derivative – decision only with the second such derivative.
  • How many channels an instance needs (e.g. two requests per DCAN) and how the requests are remapped onto their channels via CHANCTRL is only known to the family generator. nxconfig only checks the lower limit "one channel per rank entry".
  • Platform code without an armv7r variant aborts loudly (FreeRTOS port, hard fault handler, updater cycle counter), checked with the test profile in repo:tools/nxconfig/test_build_integration.py (ArmV7rStopsLoudlyTest).

docs.title: Legende
docs.text:
Quelle Lizenz ins Repository? Empfehlung HALCoGen (Werkzeug) TI-Lizenz im Installer, Text nicht geprüft nein nur Werkzeug am Arbeitsplatz zum Nachschlagen HALCoGen-Ausgabe (reg_*.h, sys_core.S, ...) docs.title: Signal qualifiers for received messages
docs.text: Status: 2026-09-15, decisions of the maintainer (Q1–Q7) incorporated. Binding for separate tasks. Reference: architecture target picture (L3 ECU services, L4 RTE; configuration level project).

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: For every received message a software component gets, in addition to the signal values, a qualifier that says whether the values are valid. Timeout, counter and checksum checks run in the generated RTE, not in the model. The old MBDT project (SYSCONST.QLF_*, BACE_lib TimeoutDetection, CheckAliveSignal, BACE_CrcCheck, GenerateQualifier) had this logic in every model; the values of the constants stay the same, so that model logic such as Qlf == QLF_OK still fits.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text: # Question Decision Q1 Where is it checked? In the RTE (BSW), tested once; the model contains no checking logic Q2 Representation Own port: RTE target can.qlf.<message>, data type uint8 Q3 Granularity One qualifier per message Q4 Several faults One value with precedence: bus > timeout > CRC > counter Q5 Signal value in the fault case Configurable per message, default hold (last valid value), alternatively init (start value from the DBC) Q6 Checksum and counter AUTOSAR E2E profiles (see below) Q7 Recovery QLF_OK again after one valid message

docs.title: Qualifier values
docs.text:
Value Name Meaning 0 QLF_DEBOUNCE not yet valid: after start-up until the first valid message, and while a fault is being debounced 1 QLF_OK all checks passed 2 QLF_ERROR_ALIVE E2E counter repeated or wrong sequence, for longer than debounce_ms 4 QLF_ERROR_CRC E2E checksum wrong, for longer than debounce_ms 8 QLF_ERROR_TIMEOUT no message for timeout_ms 16 QLF_ERROR bus fault (bus-off, transceiver not ready): immediately, for all receive messages of the bus 32 QLF_ERROR_RANGE measured value outside its valid range, for longer than debounce_ms (library block NxSwcLib/SensorQualifier in the model)

Precedence for simultaneous faults: QLF_ERROR > QLF_ERROR_TIMEOUT > QLF_ERROR_CRC > QLF_ERROR_ALIVE > QLF_ERROR_RANGE. The sensor qualifier passes a source qualifier other than QLF_OK through unchanged and checks the range only when the source is valid; a range violation is reported as QLF_DEBOUNCE during debounce_ms, recovery is immediate. The numeric value is not the order of precedence. The RTE generates the constants as Rte_Qlf.h (C) and as a MATLAB file for the models (QLF_*, same values).

docs.title: E2E profiles
docs.text:
The profiles for classic CAN are supported; CAN FD follows with a separate task:

Profile Checksum Counter Data ID Use P01 CRC8 SAE J1850 (polynomial 0x1D) 4 bit 16 bit, mode BOTH / ALT / LOW / NIBBLE classic CAN, widespread P02 CRC8H2F (polynomial 0x2F) 4 bit list with 16 entries (one per counter value) classic CAN P11 CRC8 SAE J1850 4 bit 16 bit, mode BOTH / NIBBLE successor of P01 for CAN
  • Library libs/bsw/e2e: C99, without an OpenBSW dependency, so that the RTE, tester tools (host build via Zig/Python) and later other stacks can use it. Functions per profile: Protect (transmit: increment the counter, insert the CRC) and Check (receive: status OK, REPEATED, WRONGSEQUENCE, ERROR, NOTAVAILABLE, NONEWDATA). Host tests against the check values of the specification (e.g. CRC8 SAE J1850 over "123456789" = 0x4B, CRC8H2F = 0xDF) and against a Python reference model that tools/canflash/tests can use too.
  • Mapping onto the qualifier: ERROR → QLF_ERROR_CRC; REPEATED, WRONGSEQUENCE → QLF_ERROR_ALIVE; NONEWDATA/NOTAVAILABLE → timeout monitoring. Instead of the E2E state machine (window/counter), the time-based debouncing from the old project (debounce_ms) and recovery after one valid message (Q7) apply.
  • Position of the fields: named via DBC signals, not via bit offsets by hand. rtegen derives the offsets and checks length (CRC 8 bit, counter 4 bit), byte alignment and overlap with payload signals.

docs.title: Configuration (project level, ECU description)
docs.text:
can:
  qualifiers:
    PC_Command:
      timeout_ms: 1000                  # if not given: GenMsgTimeoutTime of the DBC, otherwise 3 x cycle
      debounce_ms: 200                  # debouncing for E2E faults (CRC and counter)
      on_error: hold                    # hold | init
      e2e:
        profile: P11
        data_id: 0x0100
        data_id_mode: NIBBLE            # P01/P11
        crc: PC_Crc                     # DBC signal
        counter: PC_Counter             # DBC signal
    EVB_Status:                         # transmit message: the RTE protects it automatically
      e2e: { profile: P11, data_id: 0x0200, data_id_mode: BOTH, crc: EVB_Crc, counter: EVB_Counter }

connections:
  MotorCtrl.SpeedCmd.SpeedCmd:  can.rx.PC_Command.Speed
  MotorCtrl.PcCommandQlf.Qlf:   can.qlf.PC_Command
  • Receive messages without a qualifiers entry only get timeout monitoring; can.qlf.<message> can still be connected.
  • Transmit messages with e2e get counter and CRC from the RTE; CRC and counter signals must not be connected to ports (rtegen rejects that).
  • Board-neutral: none of this depends on board or derivative; bus faults come through the CAN transceiver role (can_phy) and the CAN controller of the respective bus.

docs.title: Added during implementation
docs.text:
Decisions Q1–Q7 remain unchanged; this section only lists additions and deviations that were needed during the implementation in tools/rtegen.

  • data_id_nibble: in data ID mode NIBBLE the high nibble of the data ID goes into the message. Its position is a DBC signal, like CRC and counter: e2e.data_id_nibble: <signal> (mandatory in this mode, forbidden in the other modes).
  • Fixed E2E parameters: e2e.max_delta_counter is configurable (default 1). The RTE sets MaxNoNewOrRepeatedData to the saturation value (P01 14, P02 15), MapStatusToSM runs with profileBehavior = true (R4.2); the time-based debouncing replaces the state machine of the specification (as foreseen in the section E2E profiles). SyncCounterInit is 1: a counter with a wrong sequence becomes the new reference, a stuck counter stays REPEATED, the next message in sequence is SYNC (→ E2E_P_OK) and recovers. With 0, a stuck counter came back once as OKSOMELOST after delta − 1 messages and recovered the qualifier for one cycle (board capture 2026-09-16).
  • Check only on reception: the RTE calls E2E_PxxCheck only when a message has arrived, not with NULL in every task cycle. Reason: P01 and P02 increase the counter tolerance with every call; with a 10 ms task and 100 ms messages it would accept any counter value. NONEWDATA is not needed; the qualifier does the time monitoring.
  • Precedence within one fault phase: CRC and counter faults cannot occur at the same time (one check returns one status). What is remembered is which kinds of fault occurred since the last valid message; after debounce_ms the RTE reports QLF_ERROR_CRC if a CRC fault was among them, otherwise QLF_ERROR_ALIVE. The debounce time keeps running in real time from the first fault, not only on reception.
  • on_error applies to every receive message, even without an e2e section. This changes the behaviour from a separate task: previously the signals always fell back to GenSigStartValue after a timeout; now hold is the default (on_error: init restores the old behaviour). Signal values are only taken over from valid messages.
  • timeout_ms: 0 switches off the time monitoring (like a DBC without GenMsgTimeoutTime and without a cycle).
  • Bus faults are read by the RTE at the transceiver of the bus: getState() != OPEN (muted, closed – the CAN layer mutes when the can_phy role is not ready) or getCANTransceiverState() != ACTIVE (bus-off). As long as the RTE is not yet attached to the transceiver (CAN comes up in an earlier lifecycle level), this does not count as a fault; the messages stay QLF_DEBOUNCE. Corrected with a separate task (2026-09-16): the earlier assumption that CanFlex2Transceiver::cyclicTask() is never called has been disproved - open() schedules it itself in the task can every 10 ms. What was wrong was the value: OpenBSW's FlexCANDevice::getBusOffState() reads FLTCONF with the NXP setter macro and therefore permanently reported bus-off (on the board the qualifier of every message was stuck at QLF_ERROR). systems::CanSystem overrides getCANTransceiverState() and reads the field correctly; OpenBSW stays unchanged. Explicitly not a bus fault is error passive: without a counterpart node, TEC on the eval board runs up to 128, and the qualifier should then keep showing timeout and CRC. A bus fault is only BUS_OFF.
  • Qualifier buffer for every receive message: can.qlf.<message> is always an RTE buffer, even without a port. It therefore appears in rte signals and is visible for board tests. Permitted port types are uint8 (default of the decision), uint16 and uint32; several ports may read the same qualifier.
  • Constants: Rte_Qlf.h (C/C++, QLF_* as Rte_QlfType = uint8_t) and Rte_Qlf.m (MATLAB script, QLF_* = uint8(...)) are always generated, even without CAN, so that models can include them.
  • Counters in rte::CAN_RX_STATUS: qlf, debounceMs, errorMs, crcErrors, aliveErrors and startOnError supplement the timeout fields; transmit messages get protectErrors.

docs.title: Extensibility
docs.text:
The pattern <source>.qlf.<name> is intended for other BSW sources (e.g. adc.qlf.<channel> for conversion faults, values from device drivers). Each is implemented as a task of its own.

Implemented for ADC sensors: adc.qlf.<channel> belongs to adc.phys.<channel> and uses the same values: QLF_OK valid; QLF_ERROR_RANGE (32) at the ADC limits (raw value 0 or full scale), outside the output range of an amplifier, with an open pull-up or outside the breakpoints of a load – the value is taken over nevertheless (end value), immediately and without debouncing, because it is a property of the individual conversion; QLF_ERROR (16) on a failed conversion, the value is held; QLF_DEBOUNCE only as the start value before the first transfer. QLF_ERROR_RANGE was chosen instead of QLF_ERROR because according to a separate task the numeric value means exactly "measured value outside its valid range"; a downstream SensorQualifier passes it through unchanged as a source qualifier other than QLF_OK. Formulas and configuration: README.md section 4 "Sensor characteristics on ADC channels".

docs.title: neXtBSW – binding device drivers to the system: analysis of the hand-written integration
docs.text:
Status: 2026-09-21 step 1 (analysis); am 2026-10-04 auf Messergebnis, Variantenvergleich und Entscheidung gekürzt. Die Zeilenmessung je Treiber, die Manifest-Sprache als Entwurf, der Abschnitt zur Sperre im sicheren Zustand und die Folgeschritte stehen in der Versionshistorie dieser Datei (Commit vor). Umgesetzt (2026-09-30): Schritte 3 bis 5 in a separate task (Manifestfelder, Generator, synthetischer vierter Treiber) hat highSideSwitch auf die generierte Anbindung gebracht. gdTmc6200 ist noch von Hand geschrieben, siehe README.md Abschnitt 5, "Generated binding of a device driver".

Decision of the maintainer of 2026-09-21: measure first, then decide between (a) the binding described declaratively in the manifest, the generator writes the whole block, and (b) a small trait class per driver, the generator writes the rest, or a justified mixture. Basis: README.md sections 3, 5 and 6, treiber-granularitaet.md.

docs.title: 1. Measurement (basis: commit bd13071)
docs.text:
Configuration, checks, parameters, CMake linking and console of a device driver came completely from its module.yaml; its binding to the system did not: platforms/s32k1xx/port/main/src/integration/Integration.cpp held a hand-written block per driver type (X macros, configuration check, adapters for SPI and pins, system object, lifecycle registration, safe_off adapters, RTE reader). Every code line was classified: class 1 the same for all drivers, class 2 a parameter that is in the manifest or derivable from it, class 3 driver-specific logic (3h: specific only by convention).

Owner Code lines Class 1 Class 2 Class 3 (3h) highSideSwitch 61 45 16 0 gdTmc6200 121 62 34 25 (24) sbcUja113x (roles) 46 27 18 1 canPhyPassive, shared safe_off and CAN role blocks 52 47 5 0 module wiring total 280 181 (65 %) 73 (26 %) 26 (9 %)
  • 91 % of the module wiring is class 1 or 2; 128 of the class-1 lines are preprocessor scaffolding that a generator does not need. Only 2 code lines are truly driver specific (the GCONF interface mode derived from the board PWM wiring; a board fact the schema could not express yet). The 24 class-3h lines are all in gdTmc6200 because it was integrated differently from the high-side switch (own SPI access interface, label check, RTE snapshot); the high-side switch is 100 % class 1 and 2.
  • About 1 420 lines of per-driver code sat in the family port outside Integration.cpp, none of them family specific. The family-specific part of the whole chain is about 17 lines and belongs to two contracts, not to drivers: the SPI master of a board bus (spi_device) and the ADC channel with its characteristic (analog_input). Digital pins are OpenBSW contracts.

docs.title: 2. The variants
docs.text:
Criterion (a) manifest only (b) trait in the family port Mixture: manifest + trait in the module + binders per contract Contribution without knowledge of the family port + no port line, but C++ fragments in YAML -- one trait per driver in every family port ++ manifest and one header in the contributor's module; no port line Path to other families + templates per family -- drivers x families ++ families x contracts (2 to 4 binders per family), independent of the number of drivers Platform rule (P2/P3) o family knowledge moves into generator templates + per family, but duplicated ++ per-driver code in libs/, per-contract code per family, nothing in platforms/common Checkable in nxconfig o structure yes, C++ names and expressions no + manifest as today + manifest plus the new fields Host tests o only by compiling the generated file + per family ++ trait and system in the module; generated block compiled on the host Diagnostics - in a generated file + in the trait + in the trait, messages by the module author Tool change for a new driver shape -- the language grows + none + none

Variant (a) turns the class-3 lines into C++ expressions in YAML that nxconfig cannot check (an error shows only in a generated file) and duplicates the constructor argument order. Variant (b) in the family port would need every trait again for S32K3, STM32 and rm4x, although nothing in it is family specific.

docs.title: 3. Decision: the mixture
docs.text:
1. The manifest declares what is wired and stays checkable: existing fields are finally bound (lifecycle level and task, console group); added connect.<x>.optional, a maximum number of instances, a short binding: entry (header and name of the trait, no expressions), the readable RTE values, later the roles.
  2. A small trait per driver in the module (libs/bsw/<module>, not the family port) holds the few C++-specific lines: construction and validity of the configuration, SPI device facts, access to the safe-off interface, RTE snapshot:
struct Tmc6200Binding                              // libs/bsw/gdTmc6200, no family code
{
    using System = Tmc6200System;
    static constexpr ::bsp::spi::SpiDeviceFacts SPI{40U, true, true, 1000000U, 5000U};
    template<class P, class B> static constexpr Tmc6200Config config();   // from generated parameters and board facts
    static constexpr bool valid(Tmc6200Config const& c);
    static ::safeoff::ISafeOffOutput& drv_en(System& s);                  // the driver implements the neutral interface
    static RteSnapshot rte(System const& s);
};
  1. The family provides binders per contract, once (SPI device on a board bus, ADC channel with characteristic).
  2. bswgen writes the per-instance block (family neutral): instances, storage, lifecycle registration, safe_off list, RTE readers, and a static_assert on the validity with the YAML path. The framework part of Integration.cpp (BSP, CAN system, shutdown sequence) stays hand-written.

A power function without a safe_off pin (cell balancing over SPI, bccMc33771) is not covered by connect.<x>.safe_off; a module-level declaration is needed (question for separate tasks). The generic safe-state lock needs one neutral interface for the safe-off output that the driver implements, which makes the two adapter headers of the family port unnecessary.

Review questions (README.md section 11): the proposal removes the only obstacle this analysis found for other families (3), puts RTE values, lifecycle binding and optional connections into the manifest exactly once (6), is proven by a synthetic fourth driver in a test profile (7), extends only nxconfig and bswgen (8), and keeps the per-contract binders per family with nothing in platforms/common (10).

docs.title: neXtBSW – granularity of device drivers
docs.text: Status: 2026-09-16. Decision of the maintainer on the fundamental question "a generic driver that abstracts several specific parts, or hardware-near drivers?" – both, but the boundary runs along the protocol, not along the part. Binding for all modules in libs/bsw and for contributor tasks on device drivers. Basis: target picture README.md, sections 3 (layers), 4 (configuration levels), 5 (manifests).

docs.title: 1. The decision rule
docs.text:
For a new part, the following applies in this order:

  1. Does the part differ from one already supported only in numbers – thresholds, sense ratio, times, resolution – with the same control and the same diagnostics? → No new driver. The part goes into the parts: list of the existing module, its values into the configuration.
  2. Does the part bring its own protocol – register model, fault latches with their own semantics, its own start or unlock sequence, CRC over register accesses? → Hardware-near driver, named after the part family (sbcUja113x, not sbc), with its own register file and its own host tests.
  3. Does the part have the same behaviour but a different access path – for example multiplexed current sensing via DSEL instead of one line per channel, or SPI instead of pins? → The behaviour module stays, with a thin adapter underneath as the implementation of the access interface (IHighSideSwitchIo). No further parameter at the top.

What never happens: a generic driver whose parameter set is the union of all part capabilities. Then only subsets of the parameters apply per instance, and tools/nxconfig can no longer check which combination makes sense. That is the MCAL failure.

What also never happens: rewriting part-independent behaviour for each part. Debouncing, turn-on blanking, overcurrent shutdown, open-load detection and plausibility in the off state are not part knowledge – they belong in one place with host tests, otherwise they are wrong in a different way for each part.

docs.title: 2. Where the abstraction sits
docs.text:
The abstraction never goes into the hardware-near driver, but one layer above it:

L3 service         IGateDriver, IBatteryMonitor, ...    (only from the second part on, section 3)
L2 device driver   tmc6200        mc33771b              sbcUja113x
                   register model, protocol, fault latches of the part
L1 contract        bspSpi, bspAdcAccess, digital inputs/outputs

A hardware-near driver may use the terms of its datasheet – that is its purpose and makes it reviewable against the datasheet. A generic behaviour module may not: its terms are those of the function (overcurrent, open_load), and its access interface names signals, not registers.

docs.title: 3. Rule of two: interfaces only from the second instance on
docs.text:
An abstraction over parts of the same kind (gate driver, battery monitor, SBC) is created only when a second part of that kind is actually needed. An interface derived from a single instance is always just that instance under a different name – it creates work without carrying variance, and it breaks exactly when the second part arrives.

Conversely: as soon as the second part is there, the interface is derived from both datasheets, not taken over from the first.

docs.title: 4. parts: only grows with a datasheet check
docs.text:
The parts: list in the manifest is a commitment, not a guess. A part only goes in when its datasheet is at hand and it has been checked that control and diagnostic behaviour fit the module's state machine (for the high-side switch: IS behaviour, fault current, DEN). The check note belongs as a comment on the list, and the source as source: in board.yaml. tools/nxconfig rejects a board part whose part matches no pattern – that is intended and must not be circumvented with a * pattern.

This includes the datasheet rule: before a work package on a hardware part starts, the maintainer is asked for available documents. The exception is the Hall sensor, which is deliberately developed without known hardware – there the configuration carries the variance (arrangement, pole pairs, inversion, debouncing).

docs.title: 5. Units at the module boundary: physical, not part-related
docs.text:
A behaviour module is only truly generic when its project parameters survive a change of part. Therefore: at the boundary to the project stand physical quantities of the function (load current in mA, speed, temperature), not measured quantities of the part's signal path (voltage at IS in mV).

The conversion is board and part knowledge (sense ratio k_ILIS, sense resistor R_IS, ADC scaling) and belongs in the board profile and the adapter. Two reasons:

  • Correctness: otherwise every project value silently depends on part and shunt. If the project swaps the switch, all thresholds are wrong without any generator being able to notice.
  • Reviewability: "shutdown at 12 A" can be checked against the load, "shutdown at 380 mV" cannot.

Permitted exception: a value that really is defined at the pin because it says nothing about the function (for example a plausibility limit for the open input). It is justified in the manifest.

docs.title: 6. Review questions
docs.text: The review question for device drivers is question 9 of README.md section 11; the reasoning for the case of section 1 goes into the changelog fragment.

docs.title: 7. Current state in the repository
docs.text: Module Kind Reason libs/bsw/highSideSwitch generic behaviour + IHighSideSwitchIo PROFET class: the variance is in numbers; parts: today BTS5030-1EJA libs/bsw/sbcUja113x hardware-near (family 113x) own register model, MTPNV, reset counter, watchdog sequence libs/bsw/canPhyPassive generic no protocol and no part facts, only the role; parts: are the transceivers whose mode pin the board may hard-wire platforms/s32k1xx/bsp/* family-near L1 implementations, not device drivers planned: TMC6200, MC33771B hardware-near own registers and protocols; abstraction only from the second instance on planned: Hall generic, without a part no protocol, only edges – the extreme case at the other end

docs.title: neXtBSW – Versionierung und Support
docs.text: Stand: 2026-10-04. Diese Seite sagt, wie neXtBSW-Versionen nummeriert werden, was sich zwischen zwei Versionen nicht ändern darf und welchen Support es gibt. Grundlage ist die Entscheidung des Maintainers vom 2026-10-04 (doc-r1-support-policy). Sprache: vorerst Deutsch, die englische Fassung kommt mit einer eigenen Aufgabe.

Teil Stabil? Was das heißt Konfigurationsformate board.yaml, project.yaml, rte.yaml ja Eine gültige Datei bleibt innerhalb einer MAJOR-Version gültig und hat dieselbe Bedeutung. Neue optionale Felder sind möglich. RTE-Schnittstelle der SWCs ja Die Aufrufe, über die eine Software-Komponente mit der RTE spricht, ändern sich innerhalb einer MAJOR-Version nicht. interne C++-APIs (libs/, platforms/, ecu/, bootloader/) nein Dürfen sich in jeder Version ändern, auch in PATCH. Wer sie direkt aufruft, trägt den Aufwand beim Update. Werkzeuge (tools/), Ausgabeformate der Generatoren im Einzelnen nein Die Eingabe (Formate oben) ist stabil, der erzeugte Code im Einzelnen nicht.

docs.title: Nummerierung
docs.text:
neXtBSW folgt Semantic Versioning 2.0.0: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, die aktuelle Version steht in VERSION im Wurzelverzeichnis.

Stelle Wird erhöht bei MAJOR einer Änderung, die eine gültige Konfigurationsdatei oder eine bestehende RTE-Schnittstelle unbrauchbar macht MINOR neuen Funktionen und neuen optionalen Feldern, ohne dass Bestehendes bricht PATCH Fehlerkorrekturen ohne Änderung der stabilen Teile

Änderungen an den internen C++-APIs lösen für sich keinen MAJOR-Sprung aus. Vorabversionen (zum Beispiel ein Release Candidate) tragen die SemVer-Vorabkennung und sind keine Zusage, dass die stabilen Teile bis zur Freigabe unverändert bleiben.

Die Formate tragen ihre eigene Versionsnummer in schema_version (heute 1). Sie wird nur bei einem Bruch erhöht; mit ihr erhöht sich auch die MAJOR-Version von neXtBSW. Die Felder der Formate beschreibt die generierte Referenz, die RTE-Konfiguration insbesondere rte.md.

docs.title: Support
docs.text:
Version Support erster Release Candidate (rc1) keiner: wird ohne Support-Zusage veröffentlicht Freigaben nach rc1 „best effort“: Es gibt keine Zusage zu Antwortzeit, Fehlerbehebung oder Rückportierung auf ältere Versionen. Der jeweils neueste Stand wird zuerst angesehen. Entwicklungszweig kein Support

„Best effort“ ist kein Service-Level. Das Projekt wird von einer Person neben anderer Arbeit gepflegt. Die Freigabe macht keine Sicherheitszusage; was für den Einsatz anzunehmen ist, steht im Safety-Handbuch.

docs.title: Sicherheitslücken
docs.text: Schwachstellen werden nicht per E-Mail und nicht in einem öffentlichen Issue gemeldet, sondern über GitHub Private Vulnerability Reporting. Grund: Das Projekt enthält einen UDS-Bootloader mit Seed/Key-Zugriff und CSEc-Schlüsselverwaltung; eine öffentlich bekannte Lücke dort betrifft Geräte im Feld. Meldeweg, Umfang und unterstützte Versionen: SECURITY.md im Wurzelverzeichnis (englisch, damit GitHub sie als Sicherheitsrichtlinie anzeigt).

docs.title: Lizenz und Fremdteile
docs.text: neXtBSW steht unter Apache-2.0. Fremdteile (Eclipse OpenBSW, FreeRTOS, Zephyr hal_nxp, CMSIS, STMicroelectronics) mit Lizenz, Copyright und Fundort listet NOTICE (englisch, wie bei Lizenzhinweisen üblich). Beiträge laufen unter dem DCO, siehe CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: neXtBSW in Bildern
docs.text:
Je Seite ein Bild, Text nur als Legende. Die Bilder sind Mermaid direkt im Markdown und werden von GitHub gezeichnet. Beschriftungen sind sprachneutral (Fachbegriffe, IDs, Modulnamen); die Legenden sind vorerst deutsch, die englische Fassung folgt mit einer eigenen Aufgabe. Jede Seite nennt ihre Quellen im Repository; bei einem Widerspruch gilt die Quelle.

    F1("1 layers") --> F2("2 configuration flow") --> F3("3 start-up")
    F3 --> F4("4 UDS flash")
    F3 --> F5("5 ECU states") --> F6("6 safety chain")
    F7("7 module map")
    F8("8 reading paths")
Nr. Bild Zeigt 1 Schichten L0 bis L5, was von OpenBSW kommt, wo der Bootloader steht 2 Konfigurationsfluss Derivat → board.yaml → project.yaml → rte.yaml → Generatoren → Build → Flash 3 Startablauf Reset → Bootloader → Abbildprüfung → Anwendung → Lifecycle → Run 4 Flash-Ablauf über UDS Sequenz von canflash flash bis zum Reset in die neue Anwendung 5 ECU-Zustandsautomat Startup, Run, Nachlauf, Sleep und die Reaktionen bis zum sicheren Zustand 6 Safety-Kette Erkennung → handle() → S1/S2/S1 held/S3/SD → sicherer Zustand, mit SM-Nummern 7 Modulkarte alle Module, Farbe = Prüfstand (Board oder Mock), dazu die Statusmatrix; von tools/docgen erzeugt 8 Lesepfade Verweis auf die Lesepfade in README.md und doc/README.md

Bilder zu den langen Safety-Dokumenten, als ergänzende Darstellung ohne inhaltliche Änderung der freigegebenen Ausgaben:

  • Bilder zum Sicherheitskonzept (Konzept Ausgabe 3): Ziele → Mechanismen, Reaktionen, drei Ebenen, Zeitbudget.
  • Bilder zur Fehleranalyse (FMEA Ausgabe 2): Blöcke → Fehlerarten → Mechanismen, Abdeckung, Urteile zu den Zielen, Zeitbegriffe.

docs.title: Farben und Formen (Stil B1)
docs.text:
Alle Diagramme der Dokumentation haben dieselbe Kopfzeile und dieselben sechs Farben; die Farbe sagt, woher etwas kommt, nicht wie wichtig es ist.

Farbe Bedeutung Türkis neXtBSW (eigener Code) Grau Fremdcode und Fremdgeräte: OpenBSW, FreeRTOS, Hardware, externe Werkzeuge Gelb generiert, Generator Hellgrau Datei, Konfiguration, Daten Violett Anwendung, SWC Rot Safety-Reaktion, sicherer Zustand ohne Farbe neutral (Lesewege, Schrittfolgen)

Status nur in Statusbildern, jeweils mit eigener Legende: Grün = erfüllt, Gelb = teilweise, Rot = nicht erfüllt. Formen: abgerundetes Rechteck = Baustein, Pille = Werkzeuglauf, Zylinder = Datei oder Daten, Kreis = Entscheidung oder Verteiler. Durchgezogene Linie = Fluss oder Aufruf, gestrichelt = optional oder indirekt. Gruppen (Subgraphs) sind hellgrau und gerundet.

Prüfung. tools/test -k docgen-mermaid prüft jeden Mermaid-Block in doc/ und README.md (Diagrammtyp, Klammern, Anführungszeichen, keine leeren Knoten, Stil B1: Kopfzeile, erlaubte Farben, keine eckigen Knoten, Rauten oder style-Zeilen) und die Links dieser Seiten. Die Modulkarte wird wie die Modulreferenz aus den Manifesten erzeugt (tools/docgen); tools/docgen --check und tools/test -k docgen melden, sobald sie abweicht.

    RST --> INIT --> BREQ
    BREQ -- yes --> STAY
    BREQ -- no --> VALID
    VALID -- no --> STAY
    VALID -- yes --> SKIP
    SKIP -- "yes: 0 ms" --> CONF
    SKIP -- no --> WIN
    WIN -- "10 02 received" --> STAY
    WIN -- "window over" --> CONF

Legende

  • Der Bootloader läuft nach jedem Reset zuerst. Er bleibt bei Boot-Anforderung (Anwendung hat 10 02 beantwortet) oder bei ungültigem Abbild; sonst wartet er das Startfenster ab (Eval Board: 200 ms) und springt.
  • Die beiden Resets des Watchdog-Schnelltests (SM-07) erkennt die Familie (hal_reset_skips_startup_window()): dann ohne Startfenster. Die CRC-32 über das Abbild läuft einmal je Start; vor dem Sprung prüft app_image_confirm() Record, Kompatibilität und Einsprung erneut und vergleicht die CRC aus bl_init().
  • Der Bootloader läuft ohne MCU-Watchdog (Sicherheitshandbuch Abschnitt 4).
  • Lifecycle: neun Ebenen (MaxNumLevels = 9); die RTE startet bewusst zuletzt. ecuState wechselt nach Run, wenn Ebene 9 erreicht ist (Bild 5).
  • Türkis: neXtBSW-Code. Kreis: Entscheidung.
  • Gestrichelt: der Schnelltest löst absichtlich zwei Resets aus; danach läuft derselbe Weg erneut.

Quellen: Architekturüberblick, Abschnitt 7, bootloader/src/core/bl_main.c, Bootloader-Doku, Abschnitt 4, Sicherheitshandbuch, Abschnitt 4.

docs.title: Bild 4: Flash-Ablauf über UDS
docs.text:
%%{init: {'theme':'base','flowchart':{'curve':'basis'},'themeVariables':{'fontFamily':'Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif','fontSize':'14px','background':'#ffffff','primaryColor':'#ffffff','primaryBorderColor':'#64748b','primaryTextColor':'#0f172a','lineColor':'#475569','edgeLabelBackground':'#ffffff','tertiaryColor':'#f8fafc','clusterBkg':'#f8fafc','clusterBorder':'#cbd5e1'}}}%%
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant T as Tester canflash
    participant A as Application ecu/uds
    participant B as Bootloader

    Note over T,A: pre-programming, best effort
    T->>A: 10 03, 85 02, 28 03
    T->>A: 10 02
    A-->>T: 50 02
    A->>A: boot request, software reset
    loop until the bootloader answers
        T->>B: 10 02
    end
    B-->>T: 50 02
    T->>B: 10 02 programmingSession
    T->>B: 27 01 requestSeed
    B-->>T: seed
    T->>B: 27 02 sendKey, HMAC-SHA256
    T->>B: 22 F180 boot software id
    T->>B: 22 F1A0, 31 01 F1A0 compatibility
    T->>B: 2E F184 fingerprint
    T->>B: 31 01 FF00 eraseMemory
    B-->>T: 7F 31 78 responsePending
    B-->>T: 71 01 FF00
    T->>B: 34 RequestDownload
    loop each block
        T->>B: 36 TransferData
        B-->>T: 76
    end
    T->>B: 37 RequestTransferExit
    T->>B: 31 01 FF01 checkMemory, CRC-32
    B-->>T: 71 01 FF01 status 00
    T->>B: 11 01 hardReset
    Note over B,A: start check, jump into the new application

Legende

  • Ablauf von canflash flash bzw. dem CMake-Ziel flash-can. Ohne --wait schaltet der Tester eine laufende Anwendung selbst in den Bootloader (Schritte 2 bis 6).
  • Die Vorbereitung (Schritt 1) ist best effort: ein älterer Stand lehnt sie ab, der Flash-Lauf geht weiter.
  • Ohne Fingerprint (2E F184) lehnt der Bootloader Löschen und Download mit NRC 0x22 ab.
  • Passt das Abbild nicht zum Ziel (lokale Prüfung oder Routine F1A0), wird vor dem Löschen abgebrochen und mit 11 01 zurückgesetzt; die installierte Anwendung startet wieder, wenn sie gültig ist.
  • 7F 31 78 steht hier stellvertretend für jeden langen Auftragsschritt (Löschen, CRC, Programmieren); der Bootloader sendet ihn nur, wenn der nächste Schritt P2* überschreiten könnte.
  • Bootloader vor 0.3.4 prüfen die Kompatibilität unter Routine FF02; canflash wählt nach DID F180.

Quellen: tools/canflash/README.md, tools/canflash/canflash.py (flash_over_bus, flash_application, pre_programming_step), Bootloader-Doku, Abschnitte 2 und 4, ecu/uds/src/systems/DiagSystem.cpp (enterBootloader).

docs.title: Bild 5: ECU-Zustandsautomat
docs.text:
%%{init: {'theme':'base','flowchart':{'curve':'basis'},'themeVariables':{'fontFamily':'Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif','fontSize':'14px','background':'#ffffff','primaryColor':'#ffffff','primaryBorderColor':'#64748b','primaryTextColor':'#0f172a','lineColor':'#475569','edgeLabelBackground':'#ffffff','tertiaryColor':'#f8fafc','clusterBkg':'#f8fafc','clusterBorder':'#cbd5e1'}}}%%
stateDiagram-v2
    state "ecuState" as ECU {
        [*] --> Startup
        Startup --> Run: lifecycle level 9
        Run --> Standby: sleep request, min_run_ms
        Standby --> Run: request withdrawn
        Standby --> Rundown: post_run_ms
        Rundown --> Shutdown: NVM, CAN_STOP, SAFE_OUTPUTS done
        Rundown --> Restart: step failed or timeout
        Shutdown --> Sleep: lifecycle level 1
        Shutdown --> Restart: shutdown_timeout_ms or wake-up
        Sleep --> Restart: refused or sleep_timeout_ms
        Sleep --> [*]: MCU unpowered
        Restart --> Startup: lifecycle level 0, reset
    }

    S1: S1 outputs off
    HELD: S1 held, no reset
    S1S2: S1 + S2 reset
    SD: SD groups degraded

    [*] --> ECU: reset or wake-up
    ECU --> S1: SM-22
    ECU --> HELD: SM-07, SM-14, SM-50, SM-34
    ECU --> S1S2: most SM events
    ECU --> SD: mapped DEVICE_FAULT, HW_SHUTOFF
    S1S2 --> ECU: restart
    S1S2 --> HELD: reset-loop limit
    SD --> S1: last group
    HELD --> [*]: power cycle

Legende

  • Kasten ecuState: Normalbetrieb nach ecuState.md. Nachlauf = Standby (Anwendung, CAN und RTE laufen weiter) und Rundown (Schritte NVM, CAN_STOP, SAFE_OUTPUTS in fester Reihenfolge, je Schritt eine Zeitgrenze). Ab Rundown gibt es keinen Rückweg nach Run.
  • Restart heißt Lifecycle-Ebene 0 und damit Software-Reset; der neue Start läuft über den Bootloader (Bild 3).
  • Außen: Reaktionen des Safe Supervisors, unabhängig vom ECU-Zustand (Bild 6). SD gibt es nur, wenn das Projekt Ereignisse auf Ausgangsgruppen abbildet; die letzte Gruppe führt zu S1 ohne Reset.
  • Was nach einem Watchdog-Reset passiert, ist einstellbar (modules.ecuState.after_watchdog_reset: sleep, SM-50).

Quellen: ecuState.md, Zustände und Übergänge, Sicherheitskonzept Ausgabe 3, Abschnitt 3, Sicherheitshandbuch, Abschnitt 4.

    classDef own fill:#ccfbf1,stroke:#0f766e,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#0f172a

    class S3,SD,S1,HELD,S1S2,TAB,RST,HOLD safety

Legende

  • Rot: Reaktion und sicherer Zustand. Türkis: Erkennung und die Entscheidung in handle() (Kreis).
  • Drei Ebenen: Erkennung meldet nur ein Ereignis, entschieden wird an genau einer Stelle (SafeSupervisor::handle()), danach folgt die Wiederherstellung (Start nach dem Reset).
  • S1: Ausgänge stromlos über die eine Tabelle des Projekts. S2: Software-Reset, immer erst nach S1 (SM-25). S1 held: S1 ohne Reset, alle Interrupts gesperrt, die Tabelle wird zyklisch erneut geschrieben, Ende nur durch Aus- und Einschalten. S3: nur Log. SD: nur die abgebildeten Ausgangsgruppen, ohne Reset.
  • SM-34 erscheint dreimal: Meldung → S3, Fehler der Klasse IDENTITY → S1 held, andere Klassen → S1 + S2 oder, wenn das Projekt sie abbildet, SD.
  • Ohne handle(): Fault-Handler (SM-17), Halt-Deadman (SM-06) und der Watchdog-Warn-Interrupt (SM-01) schreiben die Tabelle direkt, weil der Code, der sonst entscheidet, in diesem Moment nicht vertrauenswürdig ist.
  • Nicht über handle(): SM-30/SM-31 (die Anwendung entscheidet), SM-32 (Senden gesperrt), SM-51 (Bootloader startet ein ungültiges Abbild nicht).

Quellen: Sicherheitskonzept Ausgabe 3, Abschnitte 3 und 5, Sicherheitshandbuch, Abschnitt 4, Mechanismen-Katalog mechanisms.sdoc (Feld REACTION).

docs.title: Board README template
docs.text: Every board folder has two files: board.yaml, which describes the hardware as data, and README.md, which tells the person at the bench what the data cannot. This page gives you a template for the README, the rules behind it, and a filled-in example.

docs.title: What the README is for
docs.text:
board.yaml answers what is fitted and how it is wired — nxconfig and the generators read it (Your first board). Some knowledge about a board is not a configuration value but still decides whether a session at the bench ends well:

  • which actions can cut the supply, damage hardware or cannot be undone, and therefore need a person at the board;
  • how the debug probe is connected, and how to get the board back when an image does not start;
  • where the assembled board differs from its schematic;
  • how far each of these facts has been confirmed, and when.

That goes into boards/<board>/README.md. The README does not repeat the pin tables of board.yaml; it names entries of board.yaml where it needs them, so there is only one place for each value.

docs.title: Rules for the README
docs.text:
• English, like all published documentation (../../CONTRIBUTING.md).
  • The safety section is never deleted. If you know of no rule, write "None known" and say what you checked. A board that exists only to be built says so in one line, and that is its safety rule.
  • Every rule says why. A rule without its reason gets broken the first time it is inconvenient. Name the effect ("switches off the MCU supply"), and where it was found (a document, a measurement, a task).
  • Say what is confirmed. Mark facts taken from a schematic you could only read as a picture, or from a document you could not get, the same way board.yaml does with verify: true, and date the state of the safety rules.
  • No workstation settings. Serial port numbers, probe serial numbers and install paths belong to a computer, not to the board (../architecture/README.md, section 4: "Arbeitsplatz"). Write "the serial port of the USB-to-serial converter", not a port name.
  • Public sources only. Cite data sheets, reference manuals and schematics by name and page. Content from a document its maker has not published does not go into the README, and such documents are not checked in (the rule for mcudb/ is the same, see Adding a derivative).
  • Board-neutral wording. The template has to fit a board with a system basis chip, one with a plain linear regulator, and a build-only profile. Remove rows that do not apply; do not invent them.

docs.title: The template
docs.text:
Copy everything between the two ~~~ lines into boards/<board>/README.md and fill in the angle brackets. Comments in <!-- … --> are instructions; delete them when you are done.

# <Board name> (<MCU> <package>)

<!-- One paragraph: what the board is, who made it, which revision this README describes, and its purpose in
     neXtBSW (running target, bring-up pending, build-only profile). -->
<Board name>, revision <rev>, with <MCU> in <package>. Hardware description: [`board.yaml`](board.yaml).
Schematic: <document, revision, where it can be obtained>. Projects on this board: <projects/...>.

## Status

<!-- What runs, what only builds, what was measured on the board and when. Link the task or changelog entry. -->
| Item | State | Confirmed by | Date |
|---|---|---|---|
| Configuration (`nxconfig check`) | <ok / not yet> | host run | <date> |
| Target build | <builds / does not link / not supported by the family yet> | host run | <date> |
| Bring-up on hardware | <running / pending / no hardware> | <measurement, task> | <date> |

## Fitted parts

<!-- Only parts the software talks to or that constrain it (supply, reset, transceivers, drivers, sensors).
     Name the entry of board.yaml (devices[].name) so the reader can find the wiring. -->
| Reference | Part | Function | `board.yaml` entry | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| <U1> | <part number> | <function> | `devices: <NAME>` | <data sheet, revision> |

## Supply

<!-- Input voltage range, what feeds the MCU, and above all: what can switch the MCU supply off (a system basis
     chip, a power switch, a supervisor). If nothing can, say so. -->
- Input: <range, connector>
- MCU supply: <regulator / SBC output>, <voltage>
- Can software switch off the MCU supply? <no / yes: which part, which command or register>

## Debug set-up

<!-- Probe, interface, clock of the debug interface, connector, jumpers that must be in a given position. The probe
     and interface are also in board.yaml (board.debug); do not repeat install paths. -->
- Probe and interface: <probe> over <SWD/JTAG> at <kHz>, connector <Jx>
- Jumpers for debugging: <jumper: position, why>
- **Rescue path** when an image does not start: <how the probe regains the core (connect under reset, boot pin,
  mass erase), and how the bootloader is restored>

## Console and CAN

<!-- Name the board.yaml entries; say what has to be attached outside the board. -->
- Console: `uart: <NAME>` (<instance>), reached through <USB-to-serial converter / probe virtual COM port / header>.
  Baud rate: set by the project.
- CAN: one line per `can:` entry — transceiver (`phy`), connector, termination on the board yes/no, what an adapter
  needs (external transceiver, common ground).

## Safety rules

State of these rules: <date>. <!-- Update the date whenever a rule changes. -->

### Never without a person at the board

<!-- Actions that can cut the supply, drive a load or a power stage, or leave the board unreachable. For each:
     the action, the effect, the condition under which it becomes allowed. -->
- <action> — <what happens> — allowed only <condition>.

### Irreversible or hard to undo

<!-- Examples of what belongs here: flash partitioning that only a mass erase undoes; one-time or few-times
     programmable memories (fuses, OTP areas, non-volatile configuration of an SBC or PMIC); flash security or
     protection bytes that can lock out the debugger; replacing the bootloader in the field. -->
- <action> — <why it cannot be taken back> — <rule>.

### Debugging pitfalls

<!-- Behaviour that surprises: a jumper that lets an external part count resets, a watchdog outside the MCU that
     keeps running while the core is halted, a probe that resets and halts the core on connect, licence dialogs of
     debug software that block scripted runs. -->
- <pitfall> — <what you see> — <what to do>.

## Schematic versus assembled board

<!-- Every place where the assembled board differs from the schematic, and every schematic value that could not be
     read. Say where board.yaml records it (entry, comment, verify: true). -->
| Item | Schematic says | Assembled / measured | Recorded in `board.yaml` | Confirmed by, date |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| <item> | <value> | <value> | <entry> | <measurement> |

## Check and build

```sh
.venv/Scripts/python tools/nxconfig check projects/<project>/project.yaml
cmake --preset <preset>
cmake --build --preset <preset>
```

## Sources

- <schematic, revision>
- <data sheets of the fitted parts, revision>
- <board user manual, if the board is a vendor board>

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A filled-in README in this tree: boards/buildtest_s32k148/README.md, a profile with no hardware behind it, which states that in one line: no flashing, no debugging, no console, no CAN access. For a real board the template asks for the same habits in more places: facts that are only assumed stay visible as such (unconfirmed, verify: true, a dash in the "confirmed" column), a rule such as "never program the non-volatile configuration of the chip" carries its reason, and a board where nothing in software can cut the supply says so in one short safety section.

docs.text:

docs.title: Build and flash
docs.text:
Steps 6 to 8 of the route: turn the configuration into an image, put it on the board, and talk to it.

The configure and build commands and outputs below come from real runs. The flash commands and the console need a connected board and were not run for this page; they are the targets and settings that exist in the build.

docs.title: Step 6: configure and build
docs.text:
The project is the only thing you select; board, derivative, family, core and compiler options follow from the configuration. Each project has a CMake preset; the open tree has buildtest-s32k148-min (projects/buildtest_s32k148_min). For your project add a preset to CMakePresets.json that inherits from nx-arm-gcc and sets NX_PROJECT to your project.yaml (Your own ECU repository, step 5); without a preset, pass NX_PROJECT directly (../../projects/README.md, section "Bauen", German).

cmake --preset buildtest-s32k148-min
cmake --build --preset buildtest-s32k148-min

On Windows the build path is limited: in a deep checkout or worktree pass a short folder with -B <short folder>.

docs.title: What the configure run does
docs.text:
Tool Does nxconfig loads and checks project, board and derivative (the same check as nxconfig check) and writes the build settings bswgen generates the board configuration of the basic software: clock, pins, CAN, UART, ADC, PWM, interrupt priorities, memory layout, bootloader values, module integration rtegen generates the RTE from rte.yaml

Each reports under its name; the log ends Configuring done, Generating done. The run validates the project again before any generator writes a file, so an error carries file, line and YAML path and stops the run:

project.yaml:106 (interrupts.ranks): error: CAN bus CAN1 is used, but has no interrupt rank: the board port cannot set the level of its message buffer interrupts (interrupts.ranks: {source: can, name: CAN1, rank: <n>})

Fix the entry and configure again. The generated files are in <build>/generated/ (board/ from bswgen, rte/ from rtegen, nxconfig/project.cmake) and are never edited by hand.

docs.title: The build
docs.text:
The build compiles the application, the bootloader and a bootloader updater and links them, with warnings as errors (-Werror). The images are ecu/application/RelWithDebInfo/app.ecu.elf (and .hex) and bootloader/RelWithDebInfo/bootloader.elf in the build folder; the last steps print the size table and the A2L generation ([337/338] A2L of app.ecu (tools/a2lgen)).

The example project buildtest_s32k148_min doubles as a check of board neutrality: another derivative than the maintainers' board, an 8 MHz crystal, passive transceivers, two CAN buses with different bit rates, no hardware behind it. If a change breaks it, the change assumed something about one particular board. The maintainers' S32K116 (Cortex-M0+) profile, which does the same for small memory, is not in this tree yet (see Getting started). The complete run with all host tests is .venv/Scripts/python tools/test --group all --jobs 4, see ../../CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: Step 7: flash
docs.text:
Every project gets three flash targets:

Target Puts on the board Through flash-bootloader the bootloader, once per board and again for a bootloader update the debug probe flash application and its validity record the debug probe flash-can the application CAN, through the bootloader (UDS) 
cmake --build --preset <preset> --target flash-bootloader
cmake --build --preset <preset> --target flash
cmake --build --preset <preset> --target flash-can

Flash the bootloader first; after that flash-can needs no probe. Which probe and tool is decided by the board (board.debug.probe, board.debug.interface), where it is installed by your workstation (PATH, an environment variable or a CMake cache variable). The configure run names the tool it found (-- flash targets: jlink (…) for probe J-Link); a missing tool leaves the target in place and it stops with the reason. Supported: J-Link, ST-LINK, CMSIS-DAP/DAPLink, XDS110; the table of tools and variables is in ../../projects/README.md (section "Flash-Ziele je Debug-Probe", German). A target writes a command file next to the image (ecu/application/<configuration>/flash.jlink for a J-Link) that you can read before running it.

On hardware, the J-Link path has been used on one maintainer board and the ST-LINK path on a platform build-test image; the command lines of the other probes are tested against the generated commands only and are to be confirmed at the first use. Flashing over CAN needs a CAN adapter supported by python-can (../../tools/canflash/README.md). Read the README of your board before flashing it (its safety rules, board README template) and write one for your own board.

docs.title: Step 8: the console
docs.text:
The application has a text console on the UART the board describes (board.yaml, uart), with the baud rate from project.yaml (uart.<name>.baudrate), 8 data bits, no parity, one stop bit. Open the serial port with any terminal program.

Command Answers with help the command groups built into this application lc lifecycle: which components are running stats runtime statistics of the tasks rte the RTE: signals of the components, CAN messages with qualifier and counters can status state of each CAN bus the project uses

More groups appear with what the project uses (one per driver module with a console: name in project.yaml). Commands that act on hardware able to cut its own supply are listed with their safety rules in the board's README. Every command with syntax and the build or module it needs: console reference.
