Safety documents built on this concept: the safety plan safety-plan.md (lifecycle, roles and the confirmation measures, among them CM-07 for this concept), the argument over the admissible configuration range config-range.md (the range of configurations for which this concept holds), the safety manual safety-manual.md (section 2: the external interfaces of the element as the integrator uses them), the gap analysis against ISO 26262 iso26262-gap.md (not published, available on request), the coexistence argument coexistence.md, the component qualification component-qualification.md and the dependent failure analysis dfa.md.

docs.title: 0. How to read this document, and what it deliberately does not do
docs.text:
The standard and this document. ISO 26262:2018 is licensed to the maintainer since 2026-09-22; it is not part of the repository. The comparison of neXtBSW with it is the gap analysis iso26262-gap.md (not published, available on request). This document is written in the vocabulary the field has made common (SEooC, ASIL, assumption of use, safe state, fault tolerant time interval, fault handling time interval, diagnostic coverage, freedom from interference, tool confidence level) and explains each term in its own words where it is first used. Where it refers to the standard it cites part and clause only (for example "6-7.4.9" = ISO 26262-6:2018, clause 7.4.9) and never reproduces its text, tables or figures; the requirements behind such a reference are in the gap analysis in its own words. The questions issues 1 and 2 had to leave open for lack of the standard are answered there (section 9.4); the gap analysis's proposals for this document and their disposition are listed in section 9.6. Issue 3 (C1, decision ZH of CM-07): until issue 2 this paragraph said that the standard was not available and that the document contains no clause references.

No invented numbers. This concept states no failure rates, no FIT values and no diagnostic coverage percentages. Every time given here is a constant of the code (and the file it comes from is named), a configured value of the project, a value derived from those (the derivation is named), or a measurement with its date and record. Where a number would be needed but does not exist, the entry says so. The diagnostic coverage of each stage-1 mechanism is rated as an ordinal class in the failure analysis fmea.md; for the device drivers it is the later stage which additionally needs manufacturer documents that we do not have (section 13).

What this document is. The concept level: what the element is, what it assumes, which mechanisms exist, what they react to and how fast, and where the boundary to non-qualified third-party software runs. It is the input for the failure analysis, the freedom-from-interference work, the requirements with traceability and the safety manual for integrators.

What this document is not. It is not a safety case, not a proof of compliance, and not a promise that an ECU built on neXtBSW is ASIL B capable. neXtBSW is a hobby project; nothing here has been assessed by anyone outside it.

docs.title: 1.1 What "out of context" means here
docs.text:
neXtBSW is developed without knowing the vehicle, the ECU or the hazard it will be part of. An element built that way makes its assumptions explicit instead: it states which safety goals it assumes the item has, which ASIL it aims at, and which duties it hands to the integrator. The integrator then checks the assumptions against his own item and either accepts them or replaces them — and where he replaces one, the mechanisms in section 6 have to be re-evaluated for his case.

This is exactly the shape of the rest of the project: the architecture already refuses to let the eval board decide anything (guiding principle), configuration is separated from code in three levels, and every module declares what it needs and what it provides. The safety concept is the same idea applied to the hazard side: the element declares what it needs from its context.

docs.title: 1.2 Scope: what is part of the element
docs.text:
The safety manager decided on 2026-09-21: everything, including the device drivers — not only the core. The element is therefore the whole of neXtBSW as it is built into an ECU image, plus the tools that produce parts of that image.

With the acceptance of issue 1 (same day) the safety manager staged that scope: the safety argument for ASIL B is built from mechanisms of the base software alone (stage 1, now); the device drivers' own safety mechanisms follow later and encapsulated (stage 2). The device drivers stay in the table below, because their code runs in the image and the rules of stage 1 apply to it (static analysis, freedom from interference, the safe_off declaration of their outputs), but their diagnostics are not credited in stage 1. Section 1.4 draws the line.

In scope — software that runs on the target

Group Modules Role in the concept Safety supervision ecu/safety/safeSupervisor, ecu/safety/safeWatchdog central event handling and reaction, MCU watchdog Family safety port (s32k1xx) platforms/s32k1xx/port/safety/{safeLifecycle,safeMemory,safeIo,safeSystem,adcSafetyConsole} MPU, ROM check, ECC, register locking and checking, ADC reference and internal supplies, safe state Fault handlers platforms/s32k1xx/hardFaultHandler (HardFaultDump.h, hardFaultDumpLayout.h, safeOutputs.h) first action on a fault: switch the power outputs off; then the dump Debug-halt guard platforms/s32k1xx/port/main/src/integration (DebugHaltGuardSystem.h, LpitHaltDeadman), ISR LPIT0_Ch1_IRQHandler (Integration.cpp) a core halt or a software stall longer than 10 ms de-energises the power stage RTE and its run-time supervision tools/rtegen output, ecu/application/src/systems/RteSystem.cpp task and runnable deadlines as events ECU state and start reasons libs/bsw/ecuState, platforms/s32k1xx/port/mcuResetReason defined start-up, run-down and shutdown; start reason from two sources Data protection libs/bsw/e2e (P01, P02, P11), signal qualifier of the RTE protection of safety-related signals on CAN Communication libs/bsw/canSystem (transmit gate, bus state, bus-off), libs/bsw/canPhyPassive controlled behaviour of a bus that is not healthy Analogue input path libs/bsp/bspAdcAccess and the generated sensor conversion value plus quality qualifier per channel Device drivers libs/bsw/gdTmc6200 (TMC6200), libs/bsw/bccMc33771 (MC33771C), libs/bsw/sbcUja113x (UJA113x), libs/bsw/highSideSwitch (BTS5030), libs/bsw/hallDecoder stage 1: code in the image, safe_off declaration of their power outputs (feeds SM-23/SM-24); stage 2: the diagnostic functions of the parts and the driver rules around them (section 13) MCU drivers of the family platforms/s32k1xx/bsp/*, platforms/s32k1xx/port/bspConfiguration/* everything a mechanism above reads or writes Bootloader bootloader/ (core, family HAL, updater, validity record) image integrity before the application starts

In scope — off-target parts that decide what the image contains

  • The configuration data: mcudb/<family>/<derivative>.yaml, boards/<board>/board.yaml, projects/<project>/{project.yaml,rte.yaml,*.dbc}. These are safety-related data, not comments: the safe outputs table, the watchdog settings, the deadlines of a separate task and the ADC reference band all come from them.
  • The generators that turn them into code: tools/nxconfig, tools/bswgen, tools/rtegen, tools/dbcgen, blgen (tools/bswgen/blgen.py) and tools/a2lgen (issue 3: issue 2 said "later a2lgen"; the tool exists). Their classification and the safeguards against a wrong generated file are a separate task (tool-classification.md). Corrected by an earlier change: issue 2 also listed tools/intgen, which does not exist (TF3 of the tool classification), and gave blgen a folder of its own.

Out of scope

  • The application itself. SWCs from Simulink are the integrator's; neXtBSW carries them, protects their communication and supervises their timing, but says nothing about what they compute.
  • The hardware. No claim is made about the failure rates, the single-point fault metric or the latent-fault metric of the MCU, the board or any fitted part. Those are the integrator's (AoU-09).
  • The item-level safety concept: the hazard analysis, the safety goals of the actual vehicle function, the ASIL determination and the fault tolerant time interval (AoU-01).

The external interfaces of the element as the integrator uses them (safe supervisor, RTE, configuration files, hardware-software interface) are listed in section 2 of the safety manual safety-manual.md (proposal C3 of the gap analysis).

Everything in the image is ASIL B unless argued otherwise (proposal C4, 6-7.4.8 and 9-6 in the reading of the gap analysis). Without a coexistence argument, all software in the image — the application and also neXtBSW's own QM parts (console, UDS, logger, CAN stack, NvM) and the OpenBSW code — would have to be developed at ASIL B. Which module is argued free from interference and which still counts as ASIL B is decided per module in coexistence.md; AoU-17 carries the consequence to the integrator.

docs.title: 1.3 Platform status
docs.text: The concept is written for the s32k1xx family, because that is the only family with a safety port today. The mechanisms of section 6 are split deliberately into a family-neutral part (the supervisor, its events and reactions, the safe outputs table semantics, the RTE deadlines, E2E, ecuState) and a family part (MPU, ERM/ECC, CRC, LPIT deadman, SIM supply monitor, watchdog registers). For stm32, s32k3xx and rm4x the family part does not exist yet; an integrator on those families gets the neutral part and nothing else. That is a gap, not a silence — see section 9.2.

docs.title: 1.4 Two stages: base-software mechanisms now, device-driver mechanisms later
docs.text:
The line between the two stages follows who detects and who executes, not which file a line of code lives in:

Stage 1 — base software (credited now) Stage 2 — device drivers (later, encapsulated, not credited now) mechanisms whose detection runs on the MCU and uses only the MCU, its peripherals and the configuration: supervisor, watchdog, MPU, ECC, ROM check, supply and reference supervision, register lock/check, halt deadman, fault handlers, RTE deadlines, E2E, signal qualifier, CAN gate, ecuState, bootloader image check diagnostics that a part outside the MCU performs or reports over a bus, and the driver rules that react to them: SM-40 (TMC6200), SM-41 (MC33771C), SM-42 (UJA113x), SM-43 (BTS5030), and the device-dependent parts of SM-33 (transceiver status through the SBC) and SM-52 (SBC reset counter) the safe outputs table and its walk (SM-23 … SM-25) — including the entries a device driver declares with safe_off, because the table walk writes MCU port registers and needs no driver code anything that needs the driver to run, a bus to work or the part to answer in order to take effect

The consequence is deliberate and stated per goal in section 2.2: a safety goal whose detection lives in a part outside the MCU (cell voltages, balancing) has no stage-1 coverage, and the gap is named (section 9.5), not filled with driver diagnostics. The interface through which stage 2 will report into the base software — a fault or qualifier word to the safe supervisor — is itself a base-software mechanism and is proposed for stage 1 (gap G5, section 10.9).

docs.title: 2. Assumed safety goals and target ASIL
2.1 Target ASIL
docs.text:
ASIL B, confirmed for the first implementation with the acceptance of issue 1. First intended applications named by the safety manager: motor control and battery management.

Consequences taken in this concept:

  • Freedom from interference between safety-related and QM software is treated as required — but without the independence and decomposition arguments that a higher ASIL would need. The work is a separate task; today all tasks share one address space and the MPU protects only the safety manager's data (section 6.3).
  • Structural coverage at unit level (proposal C5): at ASIL B the standard expects statement and branch coverage strongly and recommends modified condition/decision coverage (MC/DC), which it expects strongly only at ASIL D; it sets no number, but a missing or unjustified target counts as insufficient (6-9.4.4, in the reading of iso26262-gap.md (not published, available on request) section 4 point 7). The measurement infrastructure exists and reports statement and branch coverage against thresholds per module (tools/test/coverage.yaml); the path to MC/DC is named there for the case of a higher ASIL. Enforcing the thresholds with a rationale per shortfall is proposal C17 (after release R1). Issue 3: issue 2 called MC/DC "desirable but not required" and left out a clause reference "because the standard was not available".
  • A single ECU without a redundant channel is assumed. No lockstep core, no second MCU voting — the S32K1 has neither, and the multi-MCU work is about flashing, not about redundancy.

ASIL C and D are to be considered later. The element makes no claim for them today, but the safety manager's decision asks the base software to implement its mechanisms "um ASIL B (oder höher) erreichen zu können" — so no mechanism should be built in a way that closes the path upwards. What a later stage for C/D would have to add is kept visible rather than struck out:

  • independence of the supervising channel from the supervised one — today supervision runs in the same core and the same clock domain (AoU-13), which is the main single-channel limit;
  • decomposition arguments between partitions, on top of the partitioning of a separate task;
  • the MC/DC path of a separate task, named there and not built;
  • the replacement of the non-qualified RTOS, compiler and libraries (section 8) rather than their argument from use.

Which mechanisms would have to be replaced rather than extended for C/D is a question for the later stage; the single-channel supervision inside one core and the non-qualified RTOS and compiler are the known candidates. AoU-03 carries the integrator's side.

docs.title: 2.2 Assumed safety goals
docs.text:
These are assumptions about the item, not statements about a real vehicle. Each is written so that it can be checked off or replaced by the integrator. The element does not fulfil any of them by itself; it contributes the mechanisms listed in the column "stage 1".

Strict separation. Only base-software mechanisms (section 1.4) are credited. The column "later device contribution" names what the device drivers will add in stage 2 (section 13); it is not part of the argument today and must not be counted by earlier changes. Where the base software alone does not cover a goal, the column "coverage at stage 1" says so and points to a gap in section 9.5.

The goals (ASG-01, ASG-02, ASG-03, ASG-04, ASG-05, ASG-06 and ASG-07, all ASIL B assumed) are the nodes of goals.sdoc (moved from this table by an earlier change). Each node holds the goal, the ASIL assumed, the base-software mechanisms credited at stage 1 (field STAGE1_CONTRIBUTION), the coverage at stage 1 (COVERAGE with the lead word covered / limited / partial / none and COVERAGE_NOTE with the full statement and the gaps of section 9.5) and the later device contribution, which is not credited (LATER_CONTRIBUTION).

What changed against issue 1: ASG-01, ASG-03 and ASG-04 were argued with SM-40 and SM-41 there; under the strict separation they lose that support, and the honest result is one partial and two uncovered goals. ASG-07 was argued with a run-time ROM check that — as a separate task found — never runs. The mechanism numbers in this table were also corrected: issue 1 cited SM-20/21/22 for the safe outputs, the fault handlers and the halt deadman (catalogue: SM-23, SM-17, SM-06), SM-13 for the register lock and check (catalogue: SM-21/SM-22) and SM-11 for the ROM check (catalogue: SM-14).

If an integrator's safety goal requires the function to keep working (a fail-operational goal) rather than to stop, neXtBSW supports it only within the limits of AoU-04 and AoU-32: for the events the supervisor declares degradable — faults of one attached device and, since an earlier change, the trip of a hardware shut-off path (SM-58, report HW_SHUTOFF), never a fault of the MCU itself and never a finding of the shut-off path — a project may switch only the affected safe-output groups and keep the rest running (SD, section 3). A function that must continue after a fault of the MCU is not supported; every other reaction stays fail-safe — de-energise, or reset, or both. Issue 3 (CM-07 decision ZA, F-01): the text released in review (R8) named the device fault only; the trip of a hardware shut-off path is the second case, decided by the safety manager in the safety review of separate tasks (C1).

docs.title: 3. Safe states
docs.text:
neXtBSW knows two reactions of its own, plus "report and continue" — and, since an earlier change, a held variant of the first (S1 held, below), decided by the safety manager on 2026-09-21 (option a; corrected by an earlier change, issue 2 called the decision still open). Since an earlier change a project may choose a fifth, SD — degraded, for the few events the supervisor declares degradable (below).

S1 — de-energised outputs ("safe state"). The generated safe outputs table of the project is walked: every PWM group of the project is forced to its inactive level through the FTM software output control, and every output that a module manifest declares connect.<name>.safe_off (for example the enable of a gate driver) is driven inactive. The walk needs no stack, no RAM and no driver object, it skips a peripheral whose clock is gated, and it ends with a data synchronisation barrier — so it is callable from a task, from the supervisor and from an interrupt (platforms/s32k1xx/hardFaultHandler/include/hardFaultHandler/safeOutputs.h).

S1 is a one-way street upwards. leaveSafeState() releases only the indicator output (an LED on the eval board). No power output is switched back on there, because the safe-state code does not know the state a driver would have to return to. A power stage comes back only through an explicit enable() of its own driver. The indicator comes back with the level the application last wrote to it, which is why it must be no power output and should not be written by the application at all (AoU-30).

On a board without power outputs the table is empty and entering S1 writes no peripheral register at all. That is the board-neutral case and it is covered by the second build profile (buildtest_s32k148_min, NX_SAFE_OUTPUT_COUNT 0).

Selected safe state of a PWM group (decisions C1 … C6 of 2026-09-29). "Inactive level" above is freewheel, and it stays the only safe state of every group whose project lists no active short. A project may allow per group active_short_low and/or active_short_high (pwm.<group>.safe_states, freewheel always listed); the application selects the state in force at run time through a service that accepts only an allowed, not withdrawn state. Every walk of the table - S1, S1 held, SD, the fault handlers, the halt deadman - then writes, per entry of the group, the value of the selected state: for the timer the short pattern (all channels forced, the low-side resp. high-side ones to their active level, before dead-time insertion), for the gate-driver enable bound to the group a store that leaves it as it is. The selection word is read once per entry from ordinary RAM and must hold exactly the pattern of an allowed short; any other value (0 after a reset, a corrupted word, the pattern of a short the group does not allow) and a gated clock of the group's timer give freewheel. A bridge fault of a device bound to the group withdraws the short for the power cycle before any walk of the reaction (decision C4, in the safe supervisor since an earlier change, NX_SAFE_BRIDGE_FAULT_CLASSES, SSR-091), the family port keeps the short in S1, in a degraded group and after a debug halt (C2, NX_SAFE_STATE_SHORT_HOLD, SSR-092), and the hardware fault input of the timer forces freewheel by itself (SM-58). Every reaction that resets ends the short: during reset and restart the bridge is in the board's reset state (C3, AoU-33 (c)). With both code facts in the tree nxconfig accepts an active short (7f82689e, b9eac59c, 2026-09-30; before it refused every short). The application requests the state through the RTE port safety.safe_state.<GROUP>, a refused request leaves the selection as it is and is reported (C6). The integrator's side is AoU-33 (section 4.3).

Start-up test of the active short (SM-27). RteSystem::init() builds every short whose project enables the test once, before the init runnables, only after a power-on: the pattern is forced and read back from the timer, the state found before is restored and read back, and the gate-driver enable bound to the group must read off before and after (read through the driver). After any other reset the outcome of the power-on test is taken from a record in no-init RAM; without an intact record of a passed test the group has freewheel only until the next power-on. The hold is a busy wait whose sum over all groups tools/rtegen bounds to a third of the MCU watchdog time-out. A failed test removes the shorts of the group until the next power-on; the phase voltages are not measured. The integrator's side is AoU-38.

Not credited for release R1. SM-26 and SM-27 are described and host verified (safe-state-select, short-hold, safe-supervisor-bridge-fault, nxconfig-safestate, the start-test tests of tools/rtegen); their board proof is open (fmea.md SM-26, SM-27, B12 … B14). Decision ZD of CM-07: for R1 they are not credited (CREDITED: no in mechanisms.sdoc, as the safety manual already reads them); the requirements SSR-089 … SSR-092 stay and specify SM-23 or SM-34 (section 6.5). Issue 3 (F-02, F-04): issue 2 called AoU-33 "announced" and the RTE port a follow-up here, and credited SM-26/SM-27 in the catalogue.

S2 — software system reset. softwareSystemReset() after enterLimpHome() and after S1. A reset is a reaction, not a repair: what happens afterwards depends on the board. With a system basis chip in the loop, the SBC counts resets (RCC) and goes to forced sleep on the fourth, which removes the MCU supply until a wake-up; on the eval board that path is armed only with JP1 closed. The ECU state management reads the start reason from two sources since an earlier change and can be configured to go to sleep after a watchdog reset (modules.ecuState.after_watchdog_reset: sleep).

S1 held — safe state held without reset. For a fault that a reset cannot remove, S1 + S2 would only restart into the same fault, in a loop. SafeSupervisor::holdSafeState() (ecu/safety/safeSupervisor/src/safeSupervisor/SafeSupervisor.cpp) therefore enters limp home and S1 and then stays: it runs with all interrupts suspended (the lock taken in handle()), so no task, no interrupt and in particular no application runs any more; it walks the safe outputs table again in every round, so S1 stays asserted even if a register is changed in between; and it services the MCU watchdog in every round, because otherwise the watchdog would end the hold after at most 250 ms with a reset into the same loop. An external watchdog (SBC) is deliberately not serviced — with one, its reset and reset counter decide (SM-52). Once, after the first table walk and before the loop, it writes one synchronous console line (SAFE STATE HELD (<event>): outputs off, no reset - power cycle required) so that a board in the hold is not silent. It ends only with a power cycle or a reset from outside. Used at first by exactly two events: WATCHDOG_STARTUP_CHECK_FAILURE (SM-07) and ROM_CHECK_FAILURE (SM-14). State issue 3: also the reset-loop limit (SM-50), a DEVICE_FAULT of the class IDENTITY (SM-34) and a finding of a hardware shut-off path (HW_SHUTOFF with findings; safety manual section 4).

Decision: (a) - S1 held without reset stays as implemented. Rejected were S1 + S2 for the ROM check (the bootloader CRC at start covers only corruption after flashing and only projects with the bootloader) and a "blocked start" in no-init RAM (needs; may come later as an improvement). The hold services the MCU watchdog. Accepted consequence: a debugger that halts the core during the 6 ms start-up self-test makes the self-test fail and leads into the hold; a power cycle ends it.

S3 — report and continue. The event is logged. The error memory exists since an earlier change; an S3 event is stored there only where a DTC is defined for it (today the take-back of a foreign safe_off level), while RTE_TIMING_VIOLATION stays a log entry (left it out of the DTC table on purpose). This is the reaction for events where a reset would do more harm than good — today a single RTE timing violation. In issue 1 it was also, unintentionally, the reaction for two events that should have one (finding F1); since an earlier change those two go to S1 held.

When S3 is admissible (proposal C18, the answer of iso26262-gap.md (not published, available on request) section 4 point 6): the standard prescribes no reaction; a fault counts as handled only if the safe state is reached within the fault tolerant time interval (FTTI) of the item. "Report and continue" is therefore admissible only where the analysis shows that the detected condition cannot violate a safety requirement within the FTTI, or where the reaction is allocated to another element with its own fault handling time. For the RTE timing violation (SM-05) the reaction is allocated to the application: AoU-18 (extended in issue 3). A latent fault of a safety mechanism is never only reported - that is why F1 ended in S1 held.

SD — degraded (decisions B1 … B6 of 2026-09-29). For an event on the supervisor's closed list of degradable events (NX_SAFE_DEGRADABLE_EVENTS, safeSupervisor/Degraded.h; today DEVICE_FAULT of a well-formed report whose class is not IDENTITY; the trip of a hardware shut-off path is the second case, below) that the project maps to safe-output groups (project.yaml safety.output_groups, safety.degraded), handle() drives only the entries of the safe outputs table that belong to those groups to their safe state (the same table and the same walk as S1, restricted by an entry mask), then latches the groups, records them in no-init RAM and reports them (log; RTE signal safety.degraded to the application, which a DTC samples for the error memory). No reset, no limp home, every other group, task and mechanism keeps running. Groups only accumulate and are walked again in every safety cycle; leaving S1 releases none; only a power cycle ends SD — a safety reset re-applies the record before the BSP starts, and an implausible record or latch counts as every group degraded. When the last group that still works is degraded, SD becomes S1 without a reset. Faults of the MCU itself (program flow, time base, watchdog, memory, image, kernel, clock, supply, MPU) are never on the list: they put the supervision of the remaining function in doubt; nxconfig refuses such a mapping with its YAML path, and the supervisor refuses it once more at compile time. A device fault on a bus the supervisor regards as lost (F5) is degraded only if every device on that bus is mapped. A project without a mapping gets not one line of SD compiled in. Limits and residuals: fmea.md SM-23; the interplay with the partner supervision and the active short: partner-and-degraded.md section 4.5.

The second degradable case: the trip of a hardware shut-off path. Decided by the safety manager as safety responsible in the safety review of the point C1: the latched trip of a hardware shut-off path (SM-58, report HW_SHUTOFF of a separate task) need not hold S1 for the whole ECU. A project may map it with safety.degraded: [{event: HW_SHUTOFF, groups: [<group>]}] to exactly the safe-output group of the PWM group the path switches off; a trip then degrades only that group, without a reset (the path stays latched until reset, H1), the rest of the ECU keeps running, and the last group escalates to S1 without a reset. The report is on a second closed list of the supervisor (NX_SAFE_DEGRADABLE_REPORTS in safeSupervisor/Degraded.h), because it is no event of SafeSupervisor::Event. Only "tripped and nothing else" is degraded: a finding of the path (switched off, reconfigured, stuck, not latched), a report without context, an unmapped timer and an implausible record keep S1 held - they may stem from a fault of the MCU, which is never degraded. Without the mapping nothing changes. SM-58 itself stays not credited (section 6.5), and its start test needs AoU-37. Issue 3 (CM-07 decision ZA, F-01): the texts released in review (R8) - this paragraph on SD, the last paragraph of section 2.2, AoU-04 and AoU-32 - now name this case; issue 2 described it only in the update block of a separate task.

Which event leads to which reaction is decided in exactly one place: ecu/safety/safeSupervisor/src/safeSupervisor/SafeSupervisor.cpp, function handle(). Every mechanism below only raises an event; it never decides the reaction itself. That separation is the load-bearing design decision of the whole concept, and both re-confirmed it.

docs.title: 4. Assumptions of use (AoU)
docs.text:
These are the duties neXtBSW hands to the integrator. An integrator who cannot meet one of them either does not get the corresponding claim, or must add his own measure. A related task turns this list into the integrator-facing safety manual with "how to fulfil it" for each entry.

The assumptions themselves are the nodes of assumptions.sdoc (moved from the tables of 4.1 … 4.5 by an earlier change, each with its statement verbatim, a short title and the status concept); the subsections below name the IDs of each group. Issue 3 (CM-07 decisions ZF and ZG): every assumption of the document has the status concept and is binding. AoU-33 (the active short of a PWM group, proposed in partner-and-degraded.md 7.1 and in force through the safety manual since CM-10) is a node of 4.3 with the points (a) … (d); AoU-24 and AoU-25, proposed by the failure analysis and binding through the safety manual since its acceptance (review, D3), are nodes of 4.3 and 4.2; AoU-40 is binding in 4.4. Issue 2 called AoU-24/AoU-25 and AoU-40 "proposed" and AoU-33 "announced" here. AoU-01 and AoU-05 speak of the fault tolerant time interval (FTTI) of the item and the maximum fault handling time interval (FHTI) of the element (C7), AoU-18 allocates the reaction to a timing violation to the application (C18), AoU-04 and AoU-32 name the trip of a hardware shut-off path (ZA).

docs.title: 4.1 Item, goals and ASIL

Proposed by an earlier change in tool-classification.md section 6, carried into the safety manual by an earlier change and into this section by an earlier change (review, D2 and D3). The full wording with the tool rows it rests on is in the tool classification; the entries below state the duty.

docs.title: 5. How the mechanisms are organised
docs.text:
Three levels, and it matters which one a reader is looking at:

  1. Detection. A piece of code notices something. It raises an event on a monitor of the safe supervisor (trigger(), check(), hit()), optionally with a context word.
  2. Reaction. SafeSupervisor::handle() decides: log and return (S3), only the mapped safe-output groups to their safe state without reset (SD, for the degradable events a project maps), safe state without reset (S1), limp home + safe state held without reset (S1 held, holdSafeState()), or limp home + safe state + reset (S1 + S2).
  3. Recovery. Whatever happens after the reset — start reason, ECU state, the reset counter of the SBC, the configured after_watchdog_reset behaviour.

Two mechanisms bypass level 1 and 2 on purpose, because the code that would run them cannot be trusted at that moment: the assembler fault handlers and the halt deadman interrupt walk the safe outputs table directly, before anything else, and only afterwards report. That is the reason the table exists as a plain array of address / value / clock-gate words rather than as driver calls.

docs.title: 6. Catalogue of safety mechanisms
docs.text:
The catalogue itself is mechanisms.sdoc (moved from the tables of 6.1 … 6.7 by an earlier change, fields FAULT_MODEL, DETECTION, REACTION, WORST_CASE; STAGE 2 for the device-dependent rows, CREDITED: no for a stage-1 row marked not credited). The subsections below name the IDs and keep the notes.

How to read the fields. Fault model is what the mechanism is meant to catch, written as the failure, not as the cause. Detection names the code and the period at which it runs. Reaction uses the safe states S1, S2, S3 of section 3. Worst case to reaction is the time from the fault being present to the reaction having taken effect, derived from the periods; where a part of it is not measured, that is said. Evidence names the test entry in tools/test/tests.yaml (run with .venv/Scripts/python tools/test -k <name>), or "board" where CHANGELOG.md records a board run.

Everything in this catalogue is a mechanism that exists in the code today. Mechanisms that are planned are in section 9.

docs.title: 6.1 Program flow and time
docs.text:
SM-01, SM-02, SM-03, SM-04, SM-05, SM-06 and SM-07 - section 6.1 of mechanisms.sdoc.

Notes.

  • SM-01 and SM-06 overlap on purpose and cover different windows. The watchdog catches a stall of more than 250 ms and answers with a reset; the deadman catches a stall of more than 10 ms and answers by de-energising without a reset. A halt longer than 250 ms hits the watchdog warning interrupt first (IRQ 22, WDOG_EWM), whose handler runs the same safe outputs walk as its first action, before the dump and before any output — measured on the board on 2026-09-18 (EXC_RETURN 0xffffffed, DRV_EN off afterwards).
  • SM-06's residual window. A halt shorter than 10 ms is seen only through the DFSR, and only if the debug probe leaves it standing — the J-Link Commander clears it when it resumes the core (reproduced twice on the board on 2026-09-18). Halt below 10 ms and a probe that clears the DFSR is a gap the safety manager accepted knowingly (question 2). Software can never react during a halt; only the hardware change documented in gdTmc6200.md (DRV_EN behind an alive latch) closes that.
  • SM-06 on ARMv6-M. Cortex-M0+ has no priority level above the RTOS syscall boundary; the handler takes the highest level there but can be delayed by a critical section for the length of that section. That is a property of the core, not of the mechanism.

docs.title: 6.2 Memory
docs.text:
SM-10, SM-11, SM-12, SM-13, SM-14, SM-15, SM-16, SM-55, SM-17 and SM-60 (not credited, proposed by an earlier change) - section 6.2 of mechanisms.sdoc.

Notes.

  • The ECC detection is a status poll, not an exception route. A double-bit error is found at the next safety cycle, not at the access that caused it. The ERM double-fault interrupt vector exists and is wrapped (ERM_double_fault_IRQHandler in IsrWrapper.h), but the reaction path we rely on is the poll. Whether that is sufficient for the fault tolerant time interval of the integrator's goal is an AoU-05 question.
  • SM-14 was not active until a follow-up task (found by an earlier change; confirmed on the board in session d3, 2026-09-21: the list address read 0xFF, a changed byte stopped nothing). Three things were missing against OpenBSW: the reference application calls RomCheck.idle() from its idle handler (app.cpp), neXtBSW's did not; OpenBSW runs tools/safety/crcCheck.py after the link (only with PLATFORM_SUPPORT_ROM_CHECK, a script with a fixed build path and pyelftools, which this repository does not install), neXtBSW had no such step; and neXtBSW removed .checksum from the HEX because at the end of the flash it stretched the CAN download. Had the check run, RomCheck would have taken the erased word 0xFFFFFFFF as the number of areas and walked the addresses 0xFFFFFFFF.
  • No false alarm by construction — a false ROM_CHECK_FAILURE holds the ECU until a power cycle (S1 held): the check is only compiled into an image whose reference the build wrote (NX_ROM_CHECK_IMAGE, set by nx_rom_check_image()), the post-link step verifies the finished HEX (list present, result present and equal to the CRC over the areas as the flash will hold them, gaps as 0xFF like canflash downloads them), and every flash byte of the image is inside an area or is the list itself. The CRC of the tool is checked against a register model of the CRC unit, and the real RomCheck.cpp runs against the same model in the host test rom-check.
  • Interplay with the bootloader (SM-51): the post-link step runs before canflash record, so the validity record covers the image including list and reference (demo: 0x8000…0x320FC, the record's length 0x2A0FC). canflash flash computes its CRC over whatever file it is given, so an image changed after the build passes the bootloader and is caught by SM-14 at run time — that is the board test of a separate task. The bootloader protects the list and the reference themselves at every start; SM-14 does not cover them (they are not in any area).
  • SM-14's run time is not bounded per call: the CRC runs over all areas in one go (demo: 172 196 bytes at a separate task, 197 044 bytes at a separate task) in the idle context. That was finding F3 decided that no slicing is needed at idle priority without a lock (fmea.md 5.1). Since an earlier change the pass is repeated with the period of the project.
  • No false alarm from flash writes: a write that begins during a pass discards the pass instead of reporting it, and no pass starts while one is open. The write indicator lies in ordinary RAM (library romCheckFlashWrites), so every writer can update it without access to the protected RAM; a wild write into it can only postpone the check, and postponement beyond one period is itself reported.

docs.title: 6.3 Freedom from interference — what exists and what does not
docs.text:
Today: one address space for all tasks; the MPU separates the safety manager's data and stack from everything else (FUSA_REGION, SAFETY_STACK_REGION), and the fusa gate plus the ISR hooks make sure that window is as narrow as possible. That is protection of the supervisor from the rest — it is not partitioning of the application.

Missing for ASIL B, and therefore the content of a separate task:

  • partitions (safety-related / QM) with memory regions and tasks derived from the configuration;
  • an access violation from a QM partition as an event to the safe supervisor rather than a plain fault;
  • temporal freedom from interference: an execution budget per partition, building on SM-05;
  • the communication between partitions: E2E or protected RTE buffers rather than shared variables.

Until then AoU-17 applies: the integrator treats all application code at the target ASIL, or partitions it himself.

The coexistence argument per module — which modules are ASIL B (mechanisms, the separating element FreeRTOS with task layout and interrupt lock, and the drivers the mechanisms call), which QM modules are argued free from interference and which rows are still open — is in coexistence.md; its section 7 is the list of evidence has to produce, and its findings CX-1 … CX-3 are interference paths into the reaction itself (logger before the safe state, lifecycle shutdown disabling the watchdog, ETL assert reset without the safe outputs table).

docs.title: 6.4 MCU periphery, supply and registers
docs.text:
SM-18, SM-19, SM-20, SM-21, SM-22 and SM-59 (not credited) - section 6.4 of mechanisms.sdoc.

Note on SM-21/SM-22 (brought to the state of separate tasks in issue 3, proposal C11, CM-07 decision ZJ; issue 2 said they were still the OpenBSW demonstration with one locked and one checked pin): the pattern of the OpenBSW demonstration stays - lock what must not move, check the rest cyclically - but the lists are generated from the configuration since an earlier change (tools/bswgen, test bswgen-safe-io): the lock list holds the pins of the used PWM groups, every safe_off output and the role pin (class PIN_FUNCTION), the check list the classes PIN_FUNCTION, GPIO_DIRECTION, CLOCK_GATE and PWM_TIMER (27 entries on the demo, board check 2026-09-22) and, since an earlier change, SUPERVISION (PMC_LVDSC1, the LVD reset of SM-59). A deviation raises the event with class and index as context. Still missing is the class SYSTEM_CLOCK (the SCG configuration, HSI H5): finding F4 stays open until a follow-up task (anomaly AN-004). The re-rating of the coverage class of SM-21/SM-22 in fmea.md (proposal M7 of the gap analysis) belongs to the review of the failure analysis CM-02.

Note on SM-22's reaction: CHECK_REGISTER_ERROR is the only event that enters the safe state without a reset and continues running, and the only one that can leave it again. (Since an earlier change two further events enter S1 without a reset, but they hold it and stop all other code — S1 held, section 3.) On the eval board it is reachable from the console (safety dst / safety est), which is how the board proof of a separate task is meant to be run.

Note on SM-20 and SM-59: SM-20 measures the MCU's internal supplies (1.2 V core, 3.3 V flash and oscillator), not VDD; on a 5 V board it sees a falling VDD only once the internal regulators drop out. SM-59 watches VDD itself, in hardware, and resets below VLVD. Together they cover a falling supply from the regulator's drop-out down to VLVD, SM-59 alone below that; the LVR stays as the last stage. SM-59 does not detect a supply that is too high, and it does not replace an external supply supervisor where the integrator's concept needs one (AoU-09).

docs.title: 6.5 Outputs and the safe state
docs.text:
SM-23, SM-24, SM-25, SM-26 (not credited for release R1), SM-27 (not credited for release R1) and SM-58 (not credited) - section 6.5 of mechanisms.sdoc.

Note on the credit (issue 3, CM-07 decision ZD, F-04): the catalogue states the credit of every stage-1 mechanism explicitly. Not credited are SM-26 and SM-27 (selectable safe state and its start test: host verified, board proof open; section 3), SM-58 (hardware threshold, optional; review H3), SM-59 (LVD reset, section 6.4) and SM-60 (lock of the FlexNVM block, section 6.2); a requirement may specify none of them (the trace check refuses it). SSR-089 and SSR-092 therefore specify SM-23, whose walk and locks they extend, SSR-091 the device report path SM-34, and SSR-090 (the configuration check) no mechanism. Issue 2 credited SM-26/SM-27 in the catalogue while the safety manual did not.

Note: one list, not two. The question "which registers switch the energy off?" has exactly one right answer per project, and it is already derived from the module instances. A second, hand-maintained list inside the safety code would drift apart at the next new power output — unnoticed, because the safe state is rarely entered. The price is that the table semantics exist twice in code (once in assembler for handlers that must not touch the stack, once in C for handlers that return); the host test of the debug-halt guard and the disassembly test safe-outputs-order check the two against each other.

docs.text:

That is correct for a BSW — the meaning of a stale wheel-speed signal is an application question — but it means the safety argument for these two is only complete together with the application, and the integrator carries that part (AoU-11, AoU-12).

docs.title: 6.8 Device drivers — moved to the later stage (section 13)
docs.text:
Issue 1 listed the diagnostics of the four device drivers here, as SM-40 (TMC6200), SM-41 (MC33771C), SM-42 (UJA113x) and SM-43 (BTS5030). Under the strict separation of a separate task they are not mechanisms of the base software and are not credited in stage 1. Their description, unchanged in substance and with the same numbers, is now in section 13, together with the interface through which stage 2 reports into the base software.

What stays in stage 1 from the device side is only what needs no driver code to take effect: the safe_off declaration of a driver's power output in its module manifest (TMC6200 drv_en, BTS5030 in), which puts the output into the safe outputs table (SM-23) and forces an adapter at build time (SM-24).

docs.title: 7. Timing: what the element guarantees, and what the integrator must check
7.1 Where the times come from
docs.text:
Only four numbers set the times, and everything else follows from them. Corrected in issue 2: issue 1 called the safety task period a project value found that all of them are code constants, none is a board or project value. Corrected by an earlier change (that was the state of issue 2): since an earlier change (2026-09-22) the safety task period and the watchdog time-out are module parameters of the project and the service interval is derived from them by nxconfig, as the table shows; only the halt deadman values are still constants of the family port (AoU-08):

Value Where it is set Today (demo project) Safety task period project.yaml modules.safeLifecycle.task_period_ms (generated into integration/safeLifecycleConfiguration.h, read by SafetySystem.cpp and SafetyManager.h) 10 ms Watchdog service interval derived by nxconfig at the fastest LPO of the data sheet: SafetyManager::WATCHDOG_CYCLIC_COUNTER = floor(watchdog_timeout_ms × 1000 / (3 × period × lpo_max_per_mille)) = 7 safety cycles 70 ms MCU watchdog time-out project.yaml modules.safeLifecycle.watchdog_timeout_ms (read by SafeWatchdog::WATCHDOG_TIMEOUT_MS) 250 ms Halt deadman time-out / poll constants of the family port (decision 9: deliberately not a configuration value yet) 10 ms / 1 ms

The relation that must hold is 3 × service interval ≤ time-out: three service opportunities before the watchdog fires (3 × 7 × 10 = 210 ≤ 230.2 ms, the 250 ms time-out at the fastest LPO, 139 kHz). Since an earlier change the relation is computed at the fastest LPO of the derivative (mcudb clock.lpo); before, 3 × 8 × 10 = 240 ms held only at the nominal LPO. Since an earlier change the interval is derived and the relation is checked again (tools/nxconfig/checks.py, safety_timing, with the check watchdog_timing_messages as a cross-check); every message names the YAML path modules.safeLifecycle.<value> and stops the configure run (test nxconfig-watchdog). The hardware limit of the S32K1 watchdog (16-bit time-out value at 128 kHz) is checked too: at most 511 ms.

docs.title: 7.2 Worst-case time to the reaction, per class
docs.text:
The last column is the maximum fault handling time interval (FHTI) of the element: detection plus reaction until the outputs are de-energised (proposal C7; issue 2 called it "total, worst case"). The integrator compares it with the fault tolerant time interval (FTTI) of his goal (AoU-05). Every time says whether it is a constant, derived or measured; the derived ones follow from the four values of section 7.1 and hold for the defaults of the demo project.

Class Mechanisms Detection latency Reaction FHTI (worst case to de-energised) Cyclic checks in the safety task SM-02…SM-04, SM-11…SM-13, SM-15, SM-16, SM-18, SM-20, SM-22 ≤ 1 safety cycle = 10 ms nominal (plus whatever preemption the integrator's task set allows); since an earlier change guaranteed 17 ms while the task runs — a later cycle raises SM-04 before its checks (fmea.md section 2; derived from the period and the configured lateness) safe outputs walk (< 1 µs computed; board bound ≤ 21 µs, fmea.md 8.1 B3) and, for most, a software reset 17 ms guaranteed (10 ms nominal) plus the walk, to de-energised; the restart time after the reset is measured on the eval board: up to 1 077 ms through the watchdog path and up to 858 ms through an MPU fault, the stated values; with bootloader 0.3.9 MPU 699.7 ms and watchdog 883 … 933 ms (fmea.md 8.1 B2, safety-manual.md section 4). Issue 3 (F-07): issue 2 said "≈ 10 ms" here Repeated-failure limits SM-19 10 consecutive cycles = 100 ms nominal, 170 ms guaranteed (derived; safety manual section 5) as above 170 ms guaranteed plus the walk Supply multiplexer round SM-20 full round = 6 cycles = 60 ms per supply nominal, 102 ms guaranteed (derived; safety manual section 5) as above 102 ms guaranteed plus the walk Loss of program execution SM-01 up to 250 ms from the last successful service at the nominal LPO; 230 … 283 ms over the LPO range of the derivative (derived, hsi-s32k1xx.md WDOG_TOVAL) warning interrupt walks the table, then hardware reset ≤ 283 ms (derived) Stopped time base of the supervision: OpenBSW system time stands still SM-06, SM-01 (the period check SM-04 does not run: the safety task is scheduled on this time base) the halt deadman's counter does not depend on the system time: 10 ms (constant of the family port) SM-06 walks the table; the reset follows through SM-01 outputs off after about 10 ms (SM-06); reset after about 160 … 283 ms — derived: the watchdog time-out over the LPO range (230 … 283 ms) minus at most one service interval (70 ms); board 2026-10-03/04 (dfa.md DFA-6, safety manual section 5) Stopped time base of the supervision: LPIT clock gated SM-17 the next access to the LPIT is a bus fault: within one poll of the halt guard, about 1 ms (derived from the poll period) fault handler walks the table, dump, reset about 1 ms plus the walk (derived; board 2026-10-03) Stopped time base of the supervision: LPIT clock too slow SM-06 progress check (DFA-2) within a few safety cycles (two LPIT ticks of budget per cycle, derived from the clock plan) S1 + S2 a few safety cycles plus the walk (board 2026-10-04) Stopped time base of the supervision: SIRC lost while the core runs — residual risk none in time; SM-01 by its hardware reset SM-06 runs on the same clock and stops; no log line, no walk was observed hardware reset of the MCU watchdog (outputs go to their reset state, AoU-07) not shown to be de-energised before the watchdog reset, at most about 283 ms (derived from the watchdog time-out; board 2026-10-03/04). Residual risk DF-05 of dfa.md, investigation and architecture with a separate task after release R1; the integrator takes this time for his FTTI or provides an independent shut-off path (AoU-13). Issue 3 (F-06): issue 2 had no row for the faults of the time bases Core halted or stalled SM-06 10 ms exception entry + table walk on the first instruction after the core runs again 10 ms + < 1 µs (computed at 80 MHz); on the board the walk from the timer to the gate-driver enable is bounded at ≤ 21 µs (oscilloscope 2026-09-22, fmea.md 8.1 B3, AN-008); the < 1 µs is not resolved by that measurement Fault exception SM-17 immediate safe outputs walk as the first action, before the dump exception entry + walk Faults a reset cannot remove SM-07, SM-14 at start-up (SM-07); SM-14 one CRC run in the idle context after lifecycle level 2, then once per modules.safeMemory.rom_check_period_ms (a corruption during operation within one period plus one pass) S1 held: table walk, then the hold without reset (section 3) table walk as above; the ECU stays de-energised until a power cycle Device diagnostics — stage 2, not credited (section 13) SM-40, SM-41, SM-43 the part reacts in µs by itself; the software learns of it after one driver cycle (10 ms, 20 ms for the cell monitor) latched fault, output off, no automatic retry part: µs; software: one driver cycle Timing violation of a runnable SM-05 end of the offending cycle log only no de-energising reaction Degraded reaction the event's own detection: DEVICE_FAULT (SM-34) and, since an earlier change, the trip of a hardware shut-off path (HW_SHUTOFF, SM-58, not credited) as the mechanism that raises the event walk of the mapped groups' entries of the table (as SM-23, fewer entries), no reset; walked again every safety cycle as S1 for the mapped groups; the rest keeps running. After a safety reset the groups are forced before the BSP starts; the PWM driver's initialisation releases them until the first safety cycle (≤ 1 safety cycle, fmea.md SM-23) Selected safe state the path's own trigger (every row above that walks the table) as that path the same walk with one read of the selection word per entry of a group; short pattern or freewheel as that path; every reset ends the short (board reset state, AoU-33). Accepted by nxconfig since earlier changes (host verified); board proof open; SM-26/SM-27 not credited for release R1 (section 3)

docs.title: 7.3 What this means for the integrator
docs.text:
The element does not define a fault tolerant time interval (FTTI) — it cannot, because the FTTI belongs to the item it does not know (AoU-01). What it offers instead is the maximum fault handling time interval (FHTI) per class in the table above (proposal C7). The integrator's check is:

For every safety goal, and for every mechanism this concept lists as contributing to it: is the FTTI of that goal longer than the FHTI in section 7.2 (AoU-05)? The rows of the time bases count as well — in particular the residual risk of a lost SIRC (DF-05).

Two answers are easy to get wrong and are called out:

  • A reset is not instantaneous. The de-energising happens in microseconds, but the ECU is then out of service for the restart time — bootloader check, clock set-up, start-up of the lifecycle levels. That time is measured on the eval board (section 7.2, F6; safety-manual.md section 4 states the values to use). If the item's safe state requires the ECU to be back, this time counts (finding F6, AoU-05).
  • 10 ms is the floor for anything in the safety task, not a guarantee. Preemption by higher-priority tasks and interrupts adds to it, and the schedule analysis (tools/schedana) is where that must be shown. Whether the safety task is actually the right priority in a given project is an integrator decision (AoU-08).

docs.title: 8. Demarcation: software we use and did not develop for safety
docs.text: Nothing in this section is a criticism of the projects named. They are used because they are good; they were just not built to be evidence in a safety argument.

docs.title: 8.1 Eclipse OpenBSW
docs.text:
• What it is here. An unchanged submodule (v0.1.0-698-g3b6e7021, 2026-09-14; issue 2 named v0.1.0-677-g00e3cab1, updated by an earlier change from git describe of the pinned submodule) providing async, lifecycle, cpp2can, docan, transport, uds, logger, console, time, util, storage, and the safety libraries libs/safety/safeMonitor and libs/safety/safeUtils.
  • The honest statement. A large part of our safety code is a copy of OpenBSW's reference-application safety demonstration, tracked as such in tools/openbswsync/copies.yaml: safeSupervisor, safeWatchdog, safeLifecycle, safeMemory, safeIo, safeSystem are all listed there as identical or modified. A demonstration is what it says: it shows the pattern - upstream with one locked pin and one checked pin. We have extended it where the work required it — the safe state is now the project's power outputs, the reference band comes from the configuration, the MPU check knows the derivative's region count the RTE reports timing, and since earlier changes the register lock and check lists of SM-21/SM-22 are generated from the configuration (section 6.4; issue 3, issue 2 still said "one locked pin and one checked pin" here) — but the skeleton is a demo's skeleton.
  • No qualification claim. OpenBSW is developed under Apache-2.0 as open source; it carries no safety qualification, and the safety demo is documented as a demo.
  • Qualification path. Three options, in increasing cost: (a) treat the OpenBSW parts we use as third-party software and qualify them ourselves — argue from the field use, from our own tests and from the analysis of a separate task, which requires our test coverage on those files to be real (today the OpenBSW submodule is excluded from our coverage measurement, by design); (b) reduce the dependency by re-implementing the few pieces the safety path actually needs (safeMonitor is small); (c) replace it. Option (a) is the realistic one and its scope is a task should size. The copies.yaml mechanism already tells us exactly which files are ours and which are upstream's — that list is the input.
  • The path split by kind of part (proposal C12, issue 3). The decision is taken in component-qualification.md: unchanged OpenBSW parts that serve a safety requirement are pre-existing software components and are qualified (8-12; the plan is its section 4, the first report QR-01 for safeMonitor its section 5); modified copies cannot be qualified as components — they are developed as our own code (6, in the reading of 10-9.1), and the static analysis gates them like our own code (its section 3, anomaly AN-031).

docs.title: 8.2 FreeRTOS
docs.text:
• What it is here. FreeRTOS V10.6.2 from external/openbsw/libs/3rdparty/freeRtos, through OpenBSW's asyncFreeRtos layer, with the port selected per architecture (platforms/common/3rdparty/freertosPort, ports per family).
  • No qualification claim. The kernel in this form carries none. The safety-relevant properties we rely on — that a task runs at its period, that priorities are honoured, that a critical section really masks — are assumed, tested by our own tests, and observed on the board. They are not proven.
  • Qualification path.
  • SAFERTOS (WITTENSTEIN high integrity systems) is the obvious candidate: the same programming model, and it is offered with a certification package for automotive and industrial use. The exact scope of that package and which of our ports and derivatives it covers must be checked with the supplier — it is not verified here. The migration cost is not the API (it is close) but OpenBSW's asyncFreeRtos layer and the two RTOS ports we maintain. It is a commercial licence, which conflicts with the open-source branch — a product using it would be a licensed branch.
  • Qualifying FreeRTOS ourselves is possible in principle for ASIL B: a validation argument backed by the kernel's field use plus our own tests against the properties we depend on. It is a large piece of work and it has to be redone at each kernel update.
  • ThreadX is already a second RTOS in the build matrix (target-buildtest-s32k148-threadx) and, as Eclipse ThreadX, has a certification history of its own. Same caveat: the scope must be checked, not assumed.
  • No RTOS at all. A single-loop variant for small safety functions is a real option that the architecture does not forbid, and it would remove the largest single qualification item. It is not on the roadmap today.
  • Route decided (proposal C13, issue 3). The safety manager decided on 2026-09-22 (rtos-u1-anfrage) to stay on FreeRTOS and qualify it as a pre-existing software component (8-12: requirements-based verification including the failure behaviour; structural coverage of the component is expected only at ASIL D); "proven in use" (8-14) is not a realistic route, because it needs field data we do not have. The kernel is also the element that implements the partitioning of a separate task and is then ASIL B itself (6-7.4.9). The plan of the package, including the kernel internals of OpenBSW's async layer, is component-qualification.md section 4.3 (anomaly AN-057).

docs.title: 8.3 Compiler, run-time and libraries
docs.text:
• What it is here. arm-none-eabi-gcc 11.3.1, the xPack build pinned in tools/ci/versions.toml and set up by python -m tools.ci setup (or taken from NX_ARM_GCC_BIN), C++17, -Os/-Werror, with newlib (stubs in platforms/common/newlib), ETL, and the CMSIS core headers. Issue 3 (F-07): issues 1 and 2 named GCC 11.4 from the NXP S32DS installation, which is no longer installed (dev-environment.md DE1).
  • Components and tools (proposal C14, issue 3). The libraries linked into the image (newlib, ETL, the CMSIS headers) are pre-existing software components (8-12), routed in component-qualification.md section 2; the compiler and the generators are tools (8-11), classified in tool-classification.md.
  • No qualification claim. GCC is not a qualified compiler, the C library is not a qualified library, and the standard C++ library features we use are whatever GCC 11 ships.
  • Qualification path. Two directions.
  • A qualified toolchain. Commercial compilers are offered with functional-safety packages (for example IAR's functional-safety edition, Green Hills, TASKING). Whether any of them covers our core profiles and what the package contains has not been checked; naming them is a starting point, not a recommendation. Cost is a licence plus a port of the build (ours is CMake with GCC-specific flags; the linker scripts and the startup assembler are the awkward part).
  • Qualifying the toolchain we have. The usual shape is a validation suite that exercises the language constructs we actually use, plus the argument that our own tests would catch a mis-compilation. Commercial test suites for this exist (Solid Sands' SuperTest is the one usually named). Not evaluated here. The cheaper partial measure that costs us nothing and is already half in place: the back-to-back checks against the target code that this project already does in places — the disassembly test safe-outputs-order proves that the compiled watchdog vector really walks the table before it calls anything; the ELF checks of a separate task prove the static constructor is in .init_array. Extending that pattern to the other mechanisms is a mitigation the integrator can see and check, and it belongs in a separate task.
  • Host test toolchain. The host tests are built with zig cc (clang 21.1.0) and the coverage is measured through gcov with a small runtime of our own. The test toolchain is a different compiler from the target toolchain. That is a strength (two front-ends see the same code) and a weakness (a host test proves the logic, not the emitted target code). The disassembly tests above are the bridge.

docs.title: 8.4 Tools and generated code
docs.text:
nxconfig, bswgen (with blgen), rtegen, dbcgen, schedana and the Studio produce or check parts of the image, including safety-relevant parts: the safe outputs table, the MPU region count and the RAM layout (the MPU region descriptors themselves are computed at run time from them), the ADC reference band, the interrupt priorities, the task list and the deadlines of SM-05. Corrected by an earlier change after TF2 and TF3 of tool-classification.md: issue 2 named generated MPU descriptors and a tool intgen, which does not exist. A wrong generator output is a fault mode of the element.

The classification of each tool by how much it can damage the product and how likely we are to notice — and the safeguards that follow from it — is a separate task. What already exists and should be counted there:

  • generated output compared against checked-in reference output, with the generators' own test profiles rather than the eval board (tools/test -k bswgen, -k rtegen, -k nxconfig, and others); the reference outputs exist since an earlier change (bswgen-reference, rtegen-reference; issue 2 claimed them before they existed, TF1);
  • validation with severities and a YAML path for every message (nxconfig), so that a wrong configuration is rejected rather than silently generated;
  • checks that run against the target artefact, not the generator: safe-outputs-order (disassembly), application-linker, the ELF checks of a separate task;
  • deliberate fault injection: several tests are checked for meaningfulness by breaking the production code and confirming the test goes red (three mutants; four; seven; one; ten for the supervisor, five for the watchdog relation check);
  • static analysis (static-analysis.md): cppcheck with the MISRA C:2012 add-on and clang-tidy over the compile database of the target build, gating in the CI (a new finding fails the run), OpenBSW copies reported separately via copies.yaml. It is a development-process measure, not a mechanism — it has no SM number. Its limits are part of the argument: only the demo profile is analysed, MISRA C++:2023 is not checked by any free tool, the deviations are approved by the safety manager (DEV-001 … DEV-014 on 2026-09-21, entered by an earlier change; DEV-015 … DEV-024 on 2026-09-30 and 2026-10-01, each with its approved_by in tools/misra/deviations.yaml), and the three real faults it found are tasks of their own (the latter two touch SM-53 and SM-06). The integrator's side is AoU-22. The classification of cppcheck and clang-tidy themselves belongs to a separate task.

docs.title: 9.2 Coverage gaps by platform and by module
docs.text:
• Families other than s32k1xx have no safety port. stm32, s32k3xx and rm4x get the neutral part only (supervisor, events, E2E, ecuState, RTE deadlines). Everything in sections 6.2 and 6.4 is s32k1xx today. The mechanism patterns were kept family-neutral where it was cheap (the halt deadman is documented with its equivalents on S32K3, STM32 and RM4x), but no second family implements them.
  • Test coverage of the safety modules is below the thresholds the project set itself. measured 92.4 % statements / 56.5 % branches overall on 2026-09-21 and proposed 95 % / 70 % for the safety-relevant modules. Of those, the branch threshold is met by none: e2e 58.3 %, canSystem 60.0 %, safeSystem 62.5 %. ecuState reads 70.8 % / 50.0 % only because most of its host tests are built by a Python script and fall outside the measurement. Of the family safety port, safeMemory escapes the measurement the same way (its MPU host test is compiled and run by the Python test bswgen-mpu), and safeLifecycle and safeWatchdog have no test entry of their own at all. safeSupervisor gained one with a separate task (safe-supervisor, safe-supervisor-bare: the real SafeSupervisor.cpp against recording stubs, reactions of all 16 events), after the measurement. safeIo gained an entry with a separate task (safe-state), after the measurement was taken, so it is missing from that table but will appear in the next run. Closing the rest is part of what makes provable. State issue 3 (CM-07 decision ZK, F-07): the figures above are those of the measurement of 2026-09-21 and are not re-measured in this issue; the thresholds per module are in tools/test/coverage.yaml. Since an earlier change safeWatchdog has its test entry safe-watchdog and safeLifecycle (the SafetyManager of the safety cycle) the entries safety-cycle and cycle-timer-off, each with built-in faults (F15 closed); so the sentence "no test entry of their own at all" is history.
  • Board proofs for the mechanisms merged on 2026-09-21: a load test really raises the timing event, the safe state really de-energises the bridge — safety dst / safety est with an oscilloscope, halt 30 s and 60 s, no square wave after g; plus 10 minutes of operation without a false trip, wake-up sources 0x00000006 after safety wdg, and (the SBC watchdog in operation). State 2026-10-04: passed on the board on 2026-09-21 (owner lines in the task list; records in tools/boardtest/captures/evalboard_s32k144_demo/2026-09-21_board/: 02_sys18_poweron_baseline.console.txt … 06_sys18_power_cycle.console.txt for a separate task, 07_io32_halt_log.console.txt, 15_sys06_dst.console.txt, 16_sys06_est.console.txt, 25_sys05_loadtest_log.console.txt, 26_sys05_rte_runnables.console.txt, 48_sys05_loadtest.console.txt, 49_sys05_runnables.console.txt) is still open.

docs.title: 9.4 Questions to the standard — answered by the gap analysis
docs.text:
Issues 1 and 2 listed seven questions here that could not be decided without the standard. Since the standard is available to the maintainer, the gap analysis iso26262-gap.md (not published, available on request) section 4 answers each of them in its own words, citing part and clause only; the full answers are there (proposal C15, CM-07 decision ZH, finding F-05). In short, and what this concept does with them:

# Question of issues 1 and 2 Answer in short (gap analysis section 4) Where this concept or its documents carry it 1 Are the assumed goals at the right level; what must an assumption of use contain? for a software SEooC the checkable level is a set of assumed technical safety requirements allocated to the element, each with ASIL, safe state and maximum fault handling time; assumed item goals are useful context (10-9.2.4; 2-6.4.5.7) ASG-01 … ASG-07 stay as context (section 2.2); the assumed technical safety requirements ATSR-1 … ATSR-6 are in safety-manual.md section 3.2 (C2) 2 What evidence is expected at ASIL B? the work products of part 6, part 8 and part 9 and, from part 2, safety plan, safety case and confirmation reviews the list with its status is the gap analysis section 2; the plan is safety-plan.md (C16) 3 Can a pure software element claim ASIL B without hardware metrics? yes, as an ASIL capability (10-9.1); the metrics may stay with the integrator, but the element must deliver per mechanism what his metrics need, and the dependent failures between mechanisms and hardware AoU-09, AoU-36; per mechanism in the safety manual section 5; dfa.md 4 Which non-qualified parts must be qualified, which argued from use? unchanged pre-existing software that serves a safety requirement is qualified (8-12); modified copies are own development; proven in use (8-14) needs field data; compiler and generators are tools (8-11) section 8 (C12 … C14), component-qualification.md, tool-classification.md 5 What must freedom from interference show; is an MPU partition on one core enough? timing and execution, memory, exchange of information; hardware-supported partitioning is required only at ASIL D, but the partitioning software is developed at the highest ASIL of the partitions and its effect shown in integration (6-7.4.9) section 6.3, coexistence.md; the structure by the three kinds is C6/C10 (after release R1) 6 Is "log and continue" (S3) admissible? only where the condition cannot violate a safety requirement within the FTTI, or the reaction is allocated to another element; a latent fault of a safety mechanism is not only reported section 3 (S3), AoU-18 (C18); F1 ended in S1 held 7 Which coverage measure; are the thresholds right? statement and branch coverage strongly expected at ASIL B, MC/DC recommended; no number, but a target without rationale counts as insufficient (6-9.4.4) section 2.1 (C5); enforcing the thresholds with a rationale per shortfall is C17 (after release R1)

docs.title: 9.5 Coverage gaps of the base software made visible by the strict separation (new in issue 2)
docs.text:
When the device diagnostics are no longer counted (section 1.4), some assumed goals lose their support. The entries below say which base-software mechanism is missing. Each was checked against the code at fa04ed1: none of them exists today, not even in part, unless the entry says so. They are proposals, not decisions; section 10.9 turns them into proposed tasks. They follow the maintainer's direction that the base software itself implements "alle notwendigen Sicherheitsmechanismen" for ASIL B.

ID Missing base-software mechanism Goals affected What exists today (checked in the code) G1 Verification of the safe state by read-back. After the safe outputs walk, read back what took effect: the port data/pin level of every safe_off output and the FTM software output control of every PWM group, and raise an event if S1 did not take effect (then the reaction can only be S1 held or a reset — the point is that the element knows) ASG-01, ASG-02 nxSafeOutputsSwitchOff() (platforms/s32k1xx/hardFaultHandler/include/hardFaultHandler/safeOutputs.h) writes and ends with dsb; it reads only the clock gate, never the result. The only read-back of an enable today is the TMC6200 driver's ENABLE_MISMATCH through IOIN — stage 2. Closed for S1 on the host by an earlier change: a read-back entry per table entry (software output control, pin level), read by SafeIo every safety cycle while S1 is latched, LOCK_REGISTER_ERROR (S1 + S2) if S1 did not take effect. Open after a later change: S1 held, SD, the fault handlers' path, board proof. Since an earlier change (host verified, 53dea2fc): read back in every round of S1 held, for the groups of SD in every safety cycle, and after the walk of every S1 + S2 sequence of the safe supervisor (safe-io, safe-io-mutations, safe-supervisor-degraded). Open: the hard fault and watchdog handlers and the halt deadman of the family port, board proof (fmea.md B15, B16) G2 Plausibility between two independent measurement paths, as a configurable base-software service: pairs of signals declared in the project (for example commanded PWM duty or phase state against a measured phase current on an MCU ADC channel; pack voltage on an MCU ADC channel against the sum of cell voltages from a device), a tolerance and a debounce time in physical units, an event to the safe supervisor on violation ASG-01, ASG-03 nothing generic. The signal qualifier (SM-30) judges one channel against its own limits; there is no comparison of two sources. Individual drivers check their own inputs (the Hall decoder's sector table, the high-side switch's current levels) — stage 2 or application G3 Age supervision of safety-relevant signals (freshness): a value that is not refreshed within its configured period becomes invalid, its qualifier is set, and an event can be raised — for signals from on-board devices, not only for CAN messages ASG-03, ASG-05 E2E counters (SM-31) cover CAN messages with a configured profile. SM-05 supervises that a runnable runs on time, not that the data it should deliver is new. A device value that stops updating is not detected by the base software. Since an earlier change (host verified): the RTE sets an age qualifier age.qlf per port element whose value is not refreshed within its configured period (rtegen-age). Open: the event to the safe supervisor, the board proof with a device package G4 Safe state for actuators switched by a bus command (not by a pin): a base-software permission per such actuator, declared in the module manifest like safe_off, revoked by every S1 entry (including S1 held and the fault handlers' path, which needs it as a plain flag without driver code), and checked by the driver before it commands the actuator; plus a cyclic read-back through the driver interface that reports a commanded-off actuator that is on ASG-04, ASG-01 (enable over SPI where a part has one) nothing. The safe outputs table holds port registers only. In S1 held no task runs, so the part is not commanded any more — whether it then switches off depends on the part (for the MC33771C its communication time-out), which is stage 2 and not credited G5 Base-software side of the device interface (section 13.1): an event class for device reports with a defined context word, the reaction of each class decided in SafeSupervisor::handle(), and the qualifier path for device values into the RTE. Without it, stage 2 has nowhere to report to, and G2–G4 have no uniform way to raise their events ASG-01, ASG-03, ASG-04 the supervisor has 16 events, none for devices; no driver includes SafeSupervisor. The gate driver's fault word reaches the RTE (gd.<device>.faults), the cell controller's does not. Closed on the base-software side by an earlier change (SM-34, host verified): DEVICE_REPORT/DEVICE_FAULT with the context word, reaction per class in handle(), correlation per bus (F5), bus verdict in gd.<device>.qlf. Open: no driver reports yet, the permission of G4. Since an earlier change the family port delivers one box: the take-backs of foreign safe_off levels by its 1-ms hold (DEVICE_REPORT, S3) G6 Run-time ROM check actually active (SM-14): checksum generated in the build for the application image, the check called from a defined context with a bounded run time per call (areas in slices), and a re-check period, with the reaction of section 3 ASG-07, ASG-06 partly closed by an earlier change: checksum generated and verified in the build for every application image of the family (build error instead of a missing list), the check called once per start from the idle context (component romcheck), an implausible list refused with ROM_CHECK_FAILURE (S1 held). Open: bounded run time per call (areas in slices) and the re-check period (F3). Closed on the host by an earlier change: slices not needed (fmea.md 5.1, idle priority without a lock); re-check period as module parameter, known-answer test, suspension during flash writes. Open: board proof (fmea.md B1, B9)

Two things this list deliberately does not do. It does not relabel a driver diagnostic as a base-software mechanism (the TMC6200 IOIN read-back stays SM-40, stage 2, even though G1 does something similar from the MCU side). And it does not claim that closing G1–G6 makes the goals fully covered: G2 and G3 detect, but the comparison of a cell voltage against the safe operating area remains an application function, and without the device stage the cell values themselves have no diagnostic behind them. For ASG-03 and ASG-04 the base software can at best provide the frame (freshness, plausibility, permission, report path); AoU-23 carries the rest until stage 2 exists.

docs.title: 9.6 Proposals C1 … C18 of the gap analysis — disposition in issue 3 (new in issue 3)
docs.text:
The gap analysis iso26262-gap.md (not published, available on request) section 5.1 proposes eighteen changes to this document.
