docs.title: 10. Task breakdown — confirmed or changed
docs.text:
The task cut of the task list was reviewed against this concept. All seven tasks stay; five get additions, none is removed, and two new tasks are proposed. The changes are recorded here for the maintainer to carry into the task list (contributors must not edit it).

Issue 2. Sections 10.1 to 10.8 are the review of issue 1 and stay as the record of what was proposed and were created from 10.8 came later. Where the acceptance changed a point, it is marked Issue 2 in place. Section 10.9 proposes the tasks for the gaps G1–G6.

State at issue 3 (CM-07 decision ZK, F-07). Sections 10.1 … 10.9 stay the record of the task review of issues 1 and 2; their figures are of that time. Today: the catalogue runs from SM-01 to SM-60 (10.1 names "SM-01 … SM-53"; added since: SM-26, SM-27, SM-34, SM-55, SM-58, SM-59, SM-60), section 4 has 41 assumptions in assumptions.sdoc (AoU-01 … AoU-30 and AoU-32 … AoU-42, all binding; AoU-31 is announced for a separate task and not a node; 10.7 names 21 and 23) and the safety manual carries 62 rows with those of the other analyses are done is open; the state of the gap tasks of 10.9 is in section 9.5 and in the anomaly register (AN-017 … AN-022).

docs.title: 10.1 Failure analysis, diagnostic coverage, fault tolerance times — confirmed, extended
docs.text:
Stays as scoped: per mechanism, the faults considered, detection, reaction, detection and reaction time against the fault tolerance time, diagnostic coverage with a justification, and the evidence.

Additions from this concept:

  • Use the mechanism IDs SM-01 … SM-53 of section 6 as the spine of the analysis, so the concept, the analysis, the requirements and the safety manual all speak about the same objects.
  • Decide findings F1 (no reaction on watchdog self-test and ROM check failure), F3 (unbounded ROM check), F4 (register checks still at demo scope) and F5 (SPI as a common cause). Each is either a change with its own task or an accepted residual risk with a reason. Issue 2: F1 is implemented by an earlier change (decision taken: S1 held); F3 now includes that SM-14 does not run at all (G6).
  • Device drivers are blocked on the manufacturer documents. The analysis of SM-40 … SM-43 must not start before the decision-board item is answered, and it must not invent coverage figures if the answer is "we have nothing". If the answer stays empty, the honest result is: "the part diagnostics are described, no coverage is claimed, and the integrator must obtain the documents himself" — which is AoU-21, and a legitimate outcome for an out-of-context element. Issue 2 — superseded: analyses the stage-1 mechanisms only and is no longer blocked by safety-bausteinunterlagen; SM-40 … SM-43 and their documents belong to the section 13. The rule "no invented coverage" carries over to a separate task unchanged.
  • Issue 2: Analyse the goals, not only the mechanisms. Section 2.2 now says per assumed goal whether stage 1 covers it. A related task should confirm or correct those verdicts — in particular "partial" for ASG-01 and ASG-07 and "not covered" for ASG-03 and ASG-04 — and weigh the gaps G1–G6 against them.
  • Coverage of the safety modules is an input, not an afterthought. safeLifecycle, safeSupervisor and safeWatchdog have no test of their own, safeMemory is measured only inside a Python test, and e2e, canSystem and safeSystem miss the branch threshold. An analysis that claims a mechanism works needs a test that shows it (section 9.2). Issue 2: safeSupervisor has its own test since an earlier change.

docs.title: 10.2 Freedom from interference — confirmed, scope sharpened
docs.text:
Stays. Sharpened by section 6.3: what exists today is protection of the safety manager's data and stack, not partitioning of the application. Add to the done-when list:

  • the timing side explicitly builds on SM-05 (the deadlines already exist; what is missing is a budget per partition and a reaction);
  • the SPI common cause (F5) touches this task too, because several partitions would share that resource;
  • the S32K1 has no memory-protection support for more than a handful of regions — the number per derivative is already in mcudb (NX_MPU_REGIONS, used by SM-12), so the partition count is bounded by the derivative and that bound belongs in the configuration check.
  • Issue 2: the independence and decomposition arguments and the MC/DC path that ASIL C and D would need are to be carried as a later stage of this task — named in its record, not struck out (section 2.1). The partitioning of stage 1 should not be built in a way that blocks them.

docs.title: 10.3 Safety requirements with traceability — confirmed, extended
docs.text:
Stays as decided (safety-anforderungen: YAML in the repository, IDs, link to code through a comment tag and to tests through covers in tools/test/tests.yaml, matrix generated and checked in the CI).

Additions:

  • The ID spaces of this concept are the starting content: ASG-* (assumed safety goals), AoU-* (assumptions of use) and SM-* (mechanisms). A requirement should be traceable up to an ASG-* or an AoU-* and down to a test.
  • Finding F2 becomes a requirement with a check: the watchdog relation 3 × service interval ≤ time-out has to be a validated property of the configuration, not an accident of three constants.
  • The tool must also report the reverse direction the concept needs: a mechanism without a test and an AoU without a place in the safety manual.

docs.title: 10.4 MISRA and static analysis — confirmed, no change to the scope
docs.text:
Stays as decided (safety-analyse: cppcheck with the MISRA add-on and clang-tidy, free tools; inventory first, then a justified deviation list, then new findings break the run; OpenBSW copies reported separately).

One addition that costs nothing and helps section 8.1: the separation the task already requires — our code versus the OpenBSW copies — should use tools/openbswsync/copies.yaml as its source, because that file already knows which files are upstream, which are modified copies and why. It is the same list the OpenBSW qualification argument needs.

Delivered: rule set, tool, inventory and deviation handling in static-analysis.md.

docs.title: 10.5 Tool classification — confirmed, priority questioned
docs.text:
Stays. Two remarks:

  • Priority. It is P3 today while everything else in this group is P2. Given that the safe outputs table, the MPU descriptors, the interrupt priorities and the SM-05 deadlines are all generated, a wrong generator output is a direct fault mode of the element. Suggestion to the maintainer: raise to P2, after a later change.
  • Credit what exists. Section 8.4 lists the safeguards already in place (reference outputs with own test profiles, validation messages with a YAML path, checks against the target artefact, deliberate fault injection). should start from that inventory rather than from zero, and its result should say per tool which of the four safeguard kinds applies.

docs.title: 10.6 Coverage — confirmed, already delivered in part
docs.text:
Status review; the measurement, the CI stage and the proposed thresholds exist since 2026-09-21. From this concept:

  • The threshold list should gain platforms/s32k1xx/port/safety/safeIo, which the safe-state entry of a separate task now measures but which has no threshold, and it should name the safety modules that are not measured at all so that their absence is visible rather than silent: safeLifecycle, safeSupervisor and safeWatchdog (no test entry of their own) and safeMemory (its MPU test runs inside the Python test bswgen-mpu, like the ecuState tests inside their script). A threshold on a module nobody measures is worth nothing; so is a measurement nobody has a threshold for.
  • The MC/DC path stays as it is: named, not built, and triggered only by an ASIL above B.

docs.title: 10.7 Safety manual — confirmed, input list fixed
docs.text:
Stays, and this concept fixes what it takes as input: section 2.2 (assumed goals), section 4 (all 21 AoUs, each to be turned into "what the integrator does about it"), section 3 (the safe states), section 6 (the mechanisms the integrator may rely on and what each requires from him), section 7 (the times he must compare with his fault tolerance time), section 8 (the honest list of non-qualified parts) and section 9 (the gaps he inherits). Issue 2: section 4 now has 23 AoUs (AoU-22, AoU-23 added); section 2.2 states per goal what stage 1 covers, and the manual must pass that on unchanged — in particular that ASG-03 and ASG-04 are not covered by the base software (AoU-23). The device packages of section 13 get their own chapter only once a related task exists.

The dependency list is right and should gain, because the manual has to tell the integrator what the tool situation is.

docs.title: 10.8 Two new tasks proposed
docs.text:
Title Why Reaction for the events that have none, and the watchdog timing relation as a checked property Findings F1 and F2 are small, concrete code and configuration changes with their own tests. Bundling them keeps an analysis task rather than an implementation task. Touches ecu/safety/safeSupervisor, tools/nxconfig Register lock and register check from the configuration instead of one demo pin Finding F4. The list of registers that must be locked and checked is board and project knowledge and belongs in the configuration, exactly like the safe outputs table. Depends on a separate task for the scope

Not proposed as new tasks, deliberately: the ROM check (F3) and the SPI common cause (F5) — both need the analysis of a separate task before anyone can say what the right change is.

docs.title: 10.9 Issue 2: tasks proposed for the coverage gaps G1–G6
docs.text:
For the maintainer to carry into the task list; IDs to be assigned there. All are base-software work (stage 1) and none depends on the manufacturer documents. Suggested priority follows the project's order (safety before OTA and multi-MCU ECU).

Gap Proposed title Suggested priority, dependencies Touches (expected) Why G5 Device reports to the safe supervisor: event class, context word, reaction in handle(), qualifier path of device values into the RTE P2; docs.title: 11. Review questions of the architecture (section 11)
docs.text:
This task changed no reusable code, no generator and no bootloader — it added one document. The questions are answered for the concept rather than for code, i.e. does the concept force anything board-specific into the architecture. Issue 2 again changes no code; where its additions (stage split, gaps G1–G6) touch a question, the answer says so. Issue 3 changes no code, no generator and no configuration value either: it corrects texts after the confirmation review CM-07. Its new statements are board-neutral — the second degradable case (HW_SHUTOFF) exists only where a project configures a hardware threshold, the time-base rows of section 7.2 are derived from the four values of section 7.1 and marked as eval-board measurements where they are, and the credit of SM-26/SM-27 is a statement of the catalogue, not of a board.

  1. Board without an SBC? Yes. The concept treats the SBC as one possible provider of the roles power_supply and watchdog_trigger and says so (AoU-13, SM-42, SM-52). A board without one keeps the MCU watchdog (SM-01), loses the independent time base and the reset counter, and the concept names that as a difference rather than assuming the SBC. Issue 2: the SBC-dependent mechanisms (SM-33, SM-42, SM-52) are now explicitly not credited in stage 1, so the stage-1 argument is the same with and without an SBC.
  2. Different crystal and system clock? Yes. No time in this document is written as a frequency. The four values that set the times (safety task period, service interval, watchdog time-out, deadman time-out) are times — since an earlier change configured as times in the project, the deadman time-out a constant of the family port (section 7.1); the one place a frequency appears is the computed walk duration in section 7.2, and it is labelled "at 80 MHz".
  3. Different derivative, and S32K3 / STM32 / Cortex-R not blocked? Yes, and the concept makes the split explicit (section 1.3): neutral mechanisms versus family mechanisms, with the family equivalents of the halt deadman named for S32K3, STM32 and RM4x. The derivative-dependent parts already read the derivative database (MPU region count, ERM channel count).
  4. Two or more CAN buses and different IDs? Yes. SM-31 and SM-32 are per bus and per message by construction; nothing in the concept assumes one bus.
  5. Several tasks and freely chosen priorities? Yes — and the concept turns it into an explicit duty (AoU-08) and an explicit residual risk (the "10 ms is a floor, not a guarantee" note in section 7.3), instead of assuming the demo's task set.
  6. Every new value in exactly one configuration level? No new configuration value is introduced by this document. Where it says a value should become one, it names the level: the register list of F4 is board and project data, the watchdog relation of F2 is a check over existing values, not a new value. Issue 2: the gap proposals name their level too — plausibility pairs, tolerances and debounce times (G2) and signal periods for the age supervision (G3) are project data; whether an actuator needs a bus-level permission (G4) is declared by the module manifest, like safe_off; the read-back addresses of G1 are derived by the generator from the same table, not configured.
  7. Host test with its own test profile? Not applicable — no code. The concept does, however, make the coverage of the safety modules a stated gap (section 9.2) and hands it to separate tasks.
  8. Tool core free of Qt, validation messages with a YAML path? Not applicable — no tool changed. Section 8.4 records that messages with a YAML path are an existing safeguard that should count.
  9. Device driver granularity and physical units? Not applicable — no driver changed. Section 13 (6.8 in issue 1) describes the drivers as they are cut today and states their project parameters in the physical units of the function (mA, ms, mV, °C), consistent with treiber-granularitaet.md.
  10. Placement under platforms/? Not applicable — the only new file is doc/safety/concept.md. The concept respects the platform rule in how it talks about the family safety port (platforms/s32k1xx/port/safety/* today, at the OpenBSW location).

Board peculiarity forced into the architecture? None. One is reported instead of built in: the eval board runs the SBC watchdog off (development mode), and rather than treating that as normal, the concept makes it AoU-13 with the sentence that an integrator must not copy it into a product.

docs.title: 12. Sources
docs.text:
Everything in this document comes from inside the repository. No external document was consulted for issues 1 and 2, and in particular ISO 26262 was not. Added by an earlier change: since then the gap analysis iso26262-gap.md (not published, available on request) has compared neXtBSW with the standard, which is licensed to the maintainer and not part of the repository; later updates of this document refer to that analysis and to other documents of doc/safety and cite the standard by part and clause at most, never by its text.

Issue 3: the record of the confirmation review reviews/records/CR-07-1.md (not published, available on request) (answers, findings and decisions ZA … ZM of the safety manager); the gap analysis sections 4 and 5.1 (questions to the standard, proposals C1 … C18), read by part and clause only; dfa.md DF-05 and DFA-6 and the safety manual section 5 (faults of the time bases, board 2026-10-03/04); component-qualification.md sections 2, 3 and 4.3; coexistence.md; dev-environment.md DE1 and tools/ci/versions.toml (the pinned compiler); the code of the active short at dev aaa22c86 (ecu/application/src/systems/safeState/SafeStateRte.h, safeSupervisor/Degraded.h).

  • Module documentation: libs/bsw/*/doc/*.md, platforms/s32k1xx/port/safety/safeSystem/doc/safeSystem.md, and the generated catalogue ../reference/modules.md.
  • Architecture: ../architecture/README.md (binding target picture, decisions D1–D15), ../architecture/treiber-granularitaet.md, ../architecture/openbsw-naehe.md, ../architecture/signal-qualifier.md, a design note (not published, available on request).

  • Configuration and tests: tools/test/tests.yaml, tools/test/coverage.yaml, tools/openbswsync/copies.yaml, projects/evalboard_s32k144_demo/project.yaml, boards/evalboard_s32k144/board.yaml, mcudb/s32k1xx/*.yaml.
  • Decisions of the safety manager: decision items, safety-umfang, safety-analyse, safety-anforderungen (2026-09-21), 2026-09-19, the acceptance (2026-09-21, issue 2), the decision (2026-09-21), and the entries in the task list.
  • Issue 2 additionally: the CHANGELOG.md entries checked against the code at fa04ed1 — ecu/safety/safeSupervisor/src/safeSupervisor/SafeSupervisor.cpp (holdSafeState()), platforms/s32k1xx/port/safety/safeMemory/src/safeMemory/RomCheck.cpp and its (missing) callers, ecu/application/CMakeLists.txt (.checksum removed from the HEX), the three watchdog constants, platforms/s32k1xx/hardFaultHandler/include/hardFaultHandler/safeOutputs.h, libs/bsw/{gdTmc6200,highSideSwitch}/module.yaml, bootloader/src/core/app_image.c, and static-analysis.md.

docs.title: 13. Later stage: encapsulated safety packages of the device drivers
docs.text: Standing. Stage 2 of the element (section 1.4), decided by the safety manager with a separate task: "Sicherheitsmechanismen der Gerätetreiber (z. B. Gate-Treiber TMC6200, MC33771C) kommen später, gekapselt." Nothing in this section is part of the ASIL B argument of stage 1, and the argument of stage 1 does not depend on it. The work is a separate task (per part: mechanisms, fault model, diagnostic coverage from the manufacturer documents, report to the safe supervisor over a defined interface). The mechanism numbers SM-40 … SM-43 are kept and so that can refer to them unchanged.

docs.title: 13.1 "Encapsulated" — the interface to the base software
docs.text:
Encapsulated means: a device package decides nothing about the ECU's reaction, exactly like every mechanism of stage 1 (section 3: the reaction is decided in one place). A package detects, and it reports. What it may rely on from the base software, and what the base software expects from it:

Direction Content Status today package → base software a fault or qualifier report to the safe supervisor: an event per device class with a context word (device instance, fault class), raised through the same monitor pattern as every stage-1 mechanism; the reaction (S3, S1, S1 + S2) is chosen in SafeSupervisor::handle(), not in the driver base-software side exists since an earlier change (SM-34): events DEVICE_REPORT (S3, from any context through the package's DeviceReportBox or from the safety task) and DEVICE_FAULT (switching off, safety task only), context word safeSupervisor/DeviceReport.h with the bus id (F5). No device driver uses it yet; faults still end in the driver's own latch, the log, and — for the gate driver only — the RTE port gd.<device>.faults, whose qualifier now carries the supervisor's bus verdict package → application the device's measured values with a qualifier (the RTE signal qualifier, SM-30), so that a value from a faulty part is marked, not silently used partly: gd.<device>.faults exists; bcc.<device>.faults and qualifiers for cell values do not base software → package the safe state reaches the part: an output the part needs to be de-energised is declared safe_off (stage 1, SM-23); an actuator that is switched by a bus command rather than a pin (balancing) needs a base-software permission that S1 revokes and that the package must hold before commanding safe_off exists; the permission for bus-commanded actuators does not (gap G4) base software → package a time budget: the package's supervision cycle runs as a runnable with an RTE deadline (SM-05) exists through the RTE

The base-software side of this interface — the event, the context format, the permission and its revocation by S1 — is a stage-1 mechanism and is proposed as a task of its own (gap G5, section 10.9). The device-side use of it is a separate task.

docs.title: 13.2 What the manufacturer documents are needed for
docs.text:
This was section 6.8 in issue 1. The content is unchanged in substance; what changed is its standing: none of it is credited in stage 1, and does not analyse it does.

The open item, stated plainly. For none of the four parts do we have the manufacturer's safety manual or safety application note. The safety manager was asked for them (raised before this task started, as requires) and the answer is still outstanding. Without those documents we can describe what the driver does with the diagnostic features the data sheet documents, but we cannot state:

  • which diagnostics the manufacturer requires to be enabled and evaluated for a safety-related use;
  • which fault modes the part's internal diagnostics do not cover, and what external measure is expected instead;
  • the diagnostic coverage the manufacturer claims, and under which conditions;
  • the required test intervals of the part's own self-tests;
  • the part's assumptions of use towards us.

Therefore each part below carries an explicit gap entry. No diagnostic coverage is claimed for any device driver in this concept, and none may be claimed in a separate task until the documents are on the table. Everything in the tables below is read from the data sheets already used by the drivers and from the driver code; it is the floor of what the part offers, not a statement of sufficiency.

docs.text:

The item table of SM-41 (supervision cycle, what the part and the driver detect, reaction, times, evidence today, the open points that need the manufacturer's safety documentation) is the field STATEMENT of the node SM-41 in mechanisms.sdoc (stage 2).

docs.title: 13.7 Cross-cutting for all four
docs.text: Item Content SPI as the common path all four are on SPI. A failure of the SPI master or of the bus is a common cause for the gate-driver, cell-monitor and SBC diagnostics at once. Each driver detects its own communication failure and latches, but nothing today detects "the SPI bus is gone" as one event with one reaction. Finding F5 Polling, not interrupts none of the four uses its interrupt or FAULT line as an interrupt; all are polled at 10–20 ms. The parts themselves react in microseconds; the software knows one cycle later No RTE ports for the fault words gd.<device>.faults is implemented; bcc.<device>.faults is proposed but not implemented. Until an application can read them, the driver diagnostics end at the console and the log

docs.title: 14. History of issue 2 and its updates
docs.text: Kept unchanged from issue 2 as the record of how the concept developed (decision ZI of CM-07): the changes of issue 2 against issue 1 and every "Update after issue 2" block up to a separate task, in the order they were written. Their content is part of the body of issue 3; where a block says "announced", "follow-up", "not credited yet" or "proposed", the body states what holds now. Section numbers in the blocks are those of issue 2, which issue 3 keeps.

docs.title: Changes in issue 2
docs.text:
The safety manager's decision of 2026-09-21, verbatim: "ASIL B für die erste Umsetzung bestätigt; ASIL C und D werden später betrachtet. Festlegung zu den angenommenen Sicherheitszielen: strikte Trennung zwischen Sicherheitsmechanismen der Gerätetreiber und Sicherheitsmechanismen von neXtBSW. Jetzt werden alle notwendigen Sicherheitsmechanismen der Basissoftware selbst umgesetzt, um ASIL B (oder höher) erreichen zu können. Sicherheitsmechanismen der Gerätetreiber (z. B. Gate-Treiber TMC6200, MC33771C) kommen später, gekapselt." The rest of issue 1 (safe states, reaction times, the 21 AoUs, findings F1–F8) was accepted and stays; below is everything that changed, by section.

Section Change 0 Device-driver coverage now belongs to the later stage no longer waits for the manufacturer documents 1.2 Scope stays "everything", but in two stages: stage 1 (now) argues ASIL B with mechanisms of the base software only; stage 2 (later, encapsulated) adds the device drivers' own mechanisms. New subsection 1.4 defines the split 2.1 ASIL C and D are to be considered later instead of "not offered"; independence, decomposition and the MC/DC path are kept as a later stage, not dropped 2.2 Every assumed safety goal is argued with base-software mechanisms only. New columns: coverage at stage 1 and the later device contribution (not credited). ASG-03 and ASG-04 are not covered by the base software, ASG-01 and ASG-07 only partly — stated as gaps G1–G6 (new section 9.5). The mechanism references in the table were corrected (issue 1 cited SM-20/21/22, SM-13 and SM-11 for mechanisms whose catalogue numbers are SM-23/SM-17/SM-06, SM-21/SM-22 and SM-14) 3 New reaction S1 held (safe state held without reset until power cycle), introduced by an earlier change for two events; decided by the safety manager on 2026-09-21 (option a) 4 AoU-03 (ASIL C/D later), AoU-04 (held safe state), AoU-08 (watchdog values are code constants, not derived project values) and AoU-21 (device drivers belong to stage 2) reworded; AoU-22 (the integrator runs the static analysis on his own code and configuration, proposed by an earlier change) and AoU-23 (no stage-1 claim for ASG-03/ASG-04) added 5 Reaction level lists S1 held 6.1 SM-07: reaction is now S1 held 6.2 SM-14: the ROM check is not active today (no caller of RomCheck::idle(), .checksum removed from the HEX); reaction would be S1 held 6.4 Note on SM-22 adjusted: two more events enter S1 without reset now, but hold it 6.6, 6.7 SM-33 and SM-52 marked as device-dependent: described, not credited for stage 1 6.8 Content moved to the new section 13 (later stage); SM-40 … SM-43 keep their numbers 7.1, 7.2 Watchdog values: all three are code constants, the relation is checked by nxconfig moves them into a configuration level; the device row points to section 13; new row for S1 held 8.4 Static analysis listed as an existing safeguard 9.1 Status column: F1 and F2 addressed by an earlier change, F7 by an earlier change (both still without board proof), F3 extended by the inactive ROM check 9.2 safeSupervisor has its own host test since an earlier change 9.3, 9.5 An earlier change delivered listed; new section 9.5 lists the coverage gaps G1–G6 that the separation made visible 10 A related task analyses stage 1 only and is no longer blocked by the manufacturer documents carries the C/D items as a later stage takes 23 AoUs and the per-goal coverage; new 10.9 proposes tasks for G1–G6 11, 12 Review questions and sources extended for issue 2 13 New: later stage — encapsulated safety packages of the device drivers (SM-40 … SM-43) and their interface to the base software

docs.title: Update after issue 2: ROM check, 2026-09-21
docs.text: Board finding of session d3 (image c9a4f31): __checksum_list_start (0x7DFC0) and __checksum_result were not in the flashed image (0xFF), no build step computed the reference, and nothing called RomCheck::idle(). A related task makes SM-14 active: the build writes the checksum list and the reference CRC into every application image of the family (post-link step, build error instead of a missing list), RomCheck refuses an implausible list with ROM_CHECK_FAILURE instead of walking invalid addresses, and the board port starts the check once per start. Updated: sections 2.2 (ASG-07), 6.2 (SM-14 and its notes), 7 (reaction table), 9.1 (F1, F3) and 9.5 (G6). Still open: the bounded run time in slices and a re-check period (F3), and the board proof.

docs.title: Update after issue 2: failure analysis, 2026-09-21
docs.text: The failure analysis of the stage-1 mechanisms is fmea.md: per mechanism the faults considered, detection, reaction, detection and reaction time, a diagnostic-coverage class with its justification (no percentages) and the evidence. It confirms the verdicts of section 2.2, decides F3 and F5, scopes F4 for a separate task, and adds the findings F9–F16 (section 9.1 below). Its most important correction to section 7.2: the "10 ms" of the safety-task checks is nominal; the guaranteed bound is 31.25 ms until the safety task's own period is supervised (F9). Only the section 9.1 table was changed here; the rest of this issue stands.

docs.title: Update after issue 2: requirements and traceability, 2026-09-21
docs.text: The software safety requirements are ssr.sdoc (IDs SSR-nnn, stable), each derived from an ASG-* or AoU-* of this concept and linked to its mechanisms SM-*, findings, code (file and symbol, later nx-req tags) and tests (field requirements in tools/test/tests.yaml). python tools/trace check checks the chain in the CI (test safety-trace) and reports mechanisms without a test and AoUs without a place in the safety manual (section 10.3); the generated matrix is traceability.md (not published, available on request). Finding F2 is SSR-011, the ROM-check context of fmea.md section 5.1 is SSR-025. No other part of this document was changed.

docs.title: Update after issue 2: tool classification, 2026-09-21
docs.text: The classification of the tools and the safeguards of the generated code are tool-classification.md: per tool and use case the tool impact, the error detection and the resulting confidence level, the safety-relevant generated items with their safeguards, eight proposed tasks, the proposed assumptions of use AoU-26 … AoU-28 and the open requirements SSR-080 … SSR-084. It corrects three statements of section 8.4 and 10.5: there is no checked-in reference output of any generator (the tests assert derived expectations, finding TF1), the MPU descriptors are computed at run time and only the region count and the RAM layout are generated (TF2), and tools/intgen does not exist (TF3). The rest of this document was not changed.

docs.title: Update after issue 2: safety task period, 2026-09-22
docs.text: Finding F9 is addressed by a period check that extends SM-04 (section 6.1): every safety cycle first compares its distance to the previous cycle with the LPTMR, a free-running counter on the 1 kHz LPO clock that neither the scheduler nor the OpenBSW system time uses, and raises SAFETY_CYCLE_PERIOD_VIOLATION (S1 + S2) for an interval of 17 ms or more, for a window of 7 cycles (8 before a later change) that is too short, and for a deviating timer configuration. The analysis is fmea.md SM-04 (period part); the SM-04 row of section 6.1, the first row of section 7.2 and the F9 row of section 9.1 were updated. Nothing else was changed.

docs.title: Update after issue 2: ROM re-check, 2026-09-22
docs.text: Task T5 of fmea.md (rest of F3 and G6): SM-14 is repeated during operation with a period set as a module parameter of the project (modules.safeMemory.rom_check_period_ms, manifest platforms/s32k1xx/port/safety/safeMemory/module.yaml, default 60 000 ms, 0 = once per start as before). Every pass starts with a known-answer test of the CRC unit; no pass starts while a flash write is open (every NvM write is bracketed) or a flash command runs, and a pass during which one began is discarded, never reported. A due pass that could not run for longer than one period is reported as ROM_CHECK_FAILURE. The pass runs in the idle context without a lock, so slicing is not needed (fmea.md 5.1). Host verified with mutants; the duration of one pass and the re-check on the target are board checks (fmea.md B1, B9). Updated: sections 2.2 (ASG-06, ASG-07), 6.2 (SM-14 and its notes), 7.2 (row "faults a reset cannot remove"), 9.1 (F3), 9.5 (G6) and 10.9 (G6).

docs.title: Update after issue 2: device reports to the safe supervisor, gap G5, 2026-09-22
docs.text: Gap G5 is closed on the base-software side by the new mechanism SM-34 (proposed number; its catalogue row for section 6.6 is entered together with the revised SSR-064, because the trace check requires both at once): a context word for device reports (bus id, device instance, fault class, detail; safeSupervisor/DeviceReport.h), two events of the supervisor split by reaction, not by source — DEVICE_REPORT (S3 by construction, from any context through a per-package event box or from the safety task) and DEVICE_FAULT (switching-off reaction per fault class, safety context only) — the correlation of communication faults per bus (finding F5 of fmea.md) and the supervisor's bus verdict in the qualifier of the device values in the RTE. The split follows the safety manager's decision of 2026-09-21: the event box of a separate task only carries reports without a switching-off reaction; a fault that must switch off is detected in the safety task itself. No driver logic was added; whether the device packages of a separate task report through the box, through checks in the safety task, or both, stays open for a separate task — both paths exist and use the same word. Updated: the G5 rows of sections 9.5 and 10.9 and the first row of section 13.1. Nothing else was changed.

docs.title: Update after issue 2: the three safety role pins, 2026-09-25
docs.text: An earlier change found that nothing stated how the three pins of the safety section may be used: the indicator of the safe state (safe_state_output) is disabled in S1 and switched back with the application's last level when S1 is left, so an actuator there would float and then restart without an enable — the case SSR-004 excludes. The maintainer decided on 2026-09-25 (variant A): an assumption of use, a warning of nxconfig and an explicit, reasoned confirmation in the project. New: AoU-30 in section 4.2 (next free number after AoU-24/25 proposed in fmea.md and AoU-26 … AoU-29 proposed in tool-classification.md); SSR-004 now names AoU-30 in derived_from (its text is unchanged); the note on S1 in section 3; the residual row of SM-22 in fmea.md. Nothing else was changed. AoU-30 accepted by the safety manager on 2026-09-30 (safety review, without independence, T-11).

docs.title: Update after issue 2: degraded reaction SD, 2026-09-30
docs.text: Until now every reaction of neXtBSW ended in switching everything off or in a reset (finding PD-4 of partner-and-degraded.md); an ECU with two redundant drives, one of which must keep braking when the other fails, could not be built on it. The safety manager decided on 2026-09-29 all recommendations of that concept; part B is implemented by an earlier change: a fifth reaction SD — degraded (B1), only for the events on a closed list of the supervisor (B2; today DEVICE_FAULT, never a fault of the MCU itself), switching named safe-output groups of the one safe outputs table (B3), latched in no-init RAM until the power cycle, applied again after every safety reset, reported to the application and through it to the error memory (B4), escalating to S1 without a reset when the last group is degraded (B5), and with no return within the power cycle (B6). Changed: the last paragraph of section 2.2, section 3 (SD), AoU-04 and the new AoU-32 (section 4.1), level 2 of section 5, a row of section 7.2. Requirements SSR-001 (b), SSR-087, SSR-088. What SD does not do yet (the gate-driver enable joins a group with a separate task; the active short of a separate task; the partner events of a separate task) is listed in fmea.md under SM-23. Nothing else was changed.

docs.title: Update after issue 2: gate-driver enable in its safe-output group, 2026-09-30
docs.text: The binding "gate driver ↔ PWM group" is the board value pwm[].gate_driver. With a separate task the safe_off output of a device bound to a PWM group - the enable of its gate driver - is part of the safe-output group of that PWM group (decision C2 (a) of partner-and-degraded.md, in its freewheel form is not implemented): SD pulls it low together with the channels, and the driver of that enable is locked while its group is degraded, the same way as in S1 (enable refused, no mismatch fault). An enable of a device bound to no PWM group keeps going off with S1 only (nxconfig warning). Changed: AoU-32 (last sentence), the SM-40 table in section 13.3 (the enable rule of the driver - now one common state of the three phases - takes effect on the target), SM-23 residual (1) in fmea.md. Nothing else was changed.

docs.title: Update after issue 2: per-group lock in the drivers, 2026-09-30
docs.text: An earlier change left a window: after a safety reset or through the debug halt guard a degraded group could run again for at most one safety cycle, a deviation from partner-and-degraded.md 4.1 step 1 ("the drivers of those groups refuse on"). A related task closes it in the family port: the PWM driver keeps a locked group forced (at its initialisation before the pins reach the timer, at every duty write), the debug halt guard does not release it, and the degraded groups are walked again right after the BSP start. The lock is the supervisor's latch of a separate task, read per entry of the safe outputs table; no second latch. Only projects with a degraded mapping compile it (the object code of the demo is unchanged). Changed: SM-23 residual (2) and (3) in fmea.md. Nothing else was changed.

docs.title: Update after issue 2: hardware threshold, 2026-09-30
docs.text: A first mechanism that acts without software: a project may name a threshold on a board signal at an input of the MCU's comparator; the family port routes the comparator output to a fault input of the PWM timer, which forces the group's outputs to their inactive level in hardware and holds them until a reset (hardware-mechanisms.md 2.4). Added: the catalogue row SM-58 in section 6.5 and its analysis in fmea.md. It is optional, used by no checked-in project, verified on the host and in a target build only, and not credited: whether a hardware path counts for stage 1 stays the decision of a separate task (hardware-mechanisms.md section 3). Nothing else was changed.

docs.title: Update after issue 2: decisions of the safety responsible, 2026-09-30
docs.text:
The safety responsible decided on 2026-09-30 in the safety reviews of separate tasks and released this document (document register, anomaly-register.md section 6):

  • Released texts (review, R8): AoU-04, AoU-32, the last paragraph of section 2.2 and the paragraph on SD in section 3, as written by an earlier change (and AoU-32 as completed by an earlier change), stand as they are.
  • SM-58 stays not credited (review, H3): the row in section 6.5 keeps the mark not credited; the trace check treats such a row as described without a claim (no requirement needed, none may credit it).
  • Assumptions of use carried over from the safety manual (review, D2): AoU-26 … AoU-29 (proposed in tool-classification.md section 6) and AoU-34 … AoU-36 (numbered in safety-manual.md section 7) are now entries of section 4, so tools/trace checks them: AoU-35 in 4.1, AoU-34 and AoU-36 in 4.3, AoU-26 … AoU-29 in the new 4.5.
  • Stale places corrected (review, D6): AoU-08 (the watchdog values are project values since an earlier change, the service interval is derived), AoU-16 (the halt deadman is SM-06, not SM-22), AoU-19 (an error memory exists since an earlier change; which events reach it).

Nothing else was changed.

docs.title: Update after issue 2: selectable safe state of a PWM group, 2026-09-30
docs.text:
A motor inverter without a mechanical brake needs a second safe state: above the speed at which the induced voltage exceeds the DC link, freewheel brakes uncontrolled through the body diodes and charges the DC link, while an active short (every low-side or every high-side switch on) does not (finding PD-1 of partner-and-degraded.md). Part C of that concept, decisions C1-C6 (each the recommended variant), is implemented in the base software and the tools: per PWM group the project lists the allowed states (pwm.<group>.safe_states), the application selects the one in force through a validating service, and every walk of the one safe outputs table - fault handlers, halt deadman, S1, S1 held, SD - applies the selection with one read of an encoded selection word per entry; anything that is not exactly an allowed pattern, and a gated timer clock, gives freewheel (C1). The gate-driver enable bound to the group is left as it is in a short (C2). A register-level start-up test of the short exists as a building block (C5). Configuration checks with YAML path (tools/nxconfig/safestate.py). New: catalogue rows SM-26 and SM-27 (section 6.5), a paragraph in section 3, a row in section 7.2; requirements SSR-089 and SSR-090 (review status proposed). AoU-33 (the integrator confirms the choice of the state, the board reset state of the bridge and the standstill of the start test) stays announced in partner-and-degraded.md 7.1 and takes effect with the follow-ups - an obligation for a function no project can use yet would be none.

Not usable in a project yet. Two parts lie outside the paths of a separate task and are follow-ups; until they exist nxconfig refuses every active short, read as code facts of the tree: the safe supervisor's rule that a bridge fault forces freewheel (C4, NX_SAFE_BRIDGE_FAULT_CLASSES), and the family port's integration that keeps a shorted group's enable on in S1 and in the halt deadman's guard and keeps the short in the PWM group lock (C2, NX_SAFE_STATE_SHORT_HOLD). Without the second, the drivers of the family port would switch the enable off within their next cycle and the short would end in freewheel; without the first, a short could be applied onto a broken switch. Also open: the RTE port of the selection (C6), the call of the start test with phase voltages, the board proof (motor, 24 V power stage, with the maintainer). The object code of every project without a short is unchanged. Limits and residuals: fmea.md SM-26, SM-27.

(C4, 2026-09-30): the safe supervisor now withdraws the active short of a group before any walk of its reaction when a device bound to the group reports a DEVICE_FAULT of the classes OUTPUT, SUPPLY or INTERNAL (NX_SAFE_BRIDGE_FAULT_CLASSES in safeSupervisor/Degraded.h), and of every group for a malformed report; the bound devices are derived by nxconfig (requirement SSR-091, review status proposed; host verified, board open). (C2, 2026-09-30): the S32K1 family port keeps the short - the enable of a bound, enabled gate driver stays on in S1, in a degraded group and after a debug halt, and the PWM inhibit and the group lock write the selected output control (NX_SAFE_STATE_SHORT_HOLD, SSR-092, proposed; host verified, board open). With both code facts in the tree nxconfig accepts an active short; AoU-33 takes effect with the first project that uses one.

docs.title: Update after issue 2: read-back of the safe state, gap G1, 2026-09-30
docs.text: Gap G1 (section 9.5): until now nothing confirmed that S1 took effect. The generated safe outputs table now carries a read-back entry per entry (NX_SAFE_OUTPUT_READBACKS: for a PWM group its software output control - every channel forced, none to its active level; for a safe_off output the pin level of its port, not the data register, so a pin held by something else is seen), and SafeIo reads them in every safety cycle while S1 is latched. An entry that does not show its safe state is S1 that did not take effect: LOCK_REGISTER_ERROR with the context class SAFE_OUTPUT and the entry, reaction S1 + S2 - the reset is the one reaction left that puts the pins into their reset state; the reset-loop limit ends a loop in S1 held. Reported once, latched until the next init(). With an active short selected the short is a safe state as well. Not covered yet: S1 held (no task runs), the groups of SD and the fault handlers' path; board proof open. Changed: SSR-060 (open → partial), the G1 rows of sections 9.5 and 10.9, fmea.md SM-23 and B15.

docs.title: Update after issue 2: hardware shut-off path degrades only its group, 2026-09-30
docs.text: Decision of the safety responsible in the safety review of the point C1: the latched fault of a hardware shut-off path (SM-58, report HW_SHUTOFF of a separate task) need not hold S1 for the whole ECU. A project may map it to the degraded reaction SD (section 3): safety.degraded: [{event: HW_SHUTOFF, groups: [<group>]}] names exactly the safe-output group of the PWM group the path switches off, and a trip then degrades only that group - no reset (the path stays latched until reset, H1), the rest of the ECU keeps running, the last group escalates to S1 without a reset (review R2). The report is on a second closed list of the supervisor (NX_SAFE_DEGRADABLE_REPORTS in safeSupervisor/Degraded.h), because it is no event of SafeSupervisor::Event. Only "tripped and nothing else" is degraded: the findings of the path (switched off, reconfigured, stuck, not latched), a report without context, an unmapped timer and an implausible record keep S1 held as before - they may stem from a fault of the MCU, which is never degraded. Without the mapping nothing changes. The released paragraphs of sections 2.2 and 3 and AoU-04/AoU-32 (review, R8) are not edited: where they say "faults of one attached device", the trip of a hardware shut-off path is the second case the supervisor now allows (proposal for the review). New: AoU-37 in section 4.3 (point C3 of the same review: the start test of the path needs the input below VDDA by more than offset plus hysteresis). Limits and evidence: fmea.md SM-58, hardware-mechanisms.md 2.6.

docs.title: Update after issue 2: start test of the active short: power-on only, bounded, enable read back, 2026-09-30
docs.text:
Decisions E2-E4 of the safety responsible in the safety review of separate tasks (2026-09-30). A related task calls the register-level start test of the short (SM-27, partner-and-degraded.md 5.10) in RteSystem::init(), before the init runnables changes that call (ecu/application/src/systems/safeState/ SafeStateRte.h, startTests):

  • E4 - power-on only. The shorts are built only when the MCU reports a power-on reset (ecustate:: mcuStartReasons(), wake-up bit POWER). After any other reset (watchdog, pin, software, debugger) the machine may still turn, so nothing is built; the outcome of the power-on test is kept over resets in a record in no-init RAM (.noinit.safeStateTest, passed groups plus a check word, written before it is read after power-on, like the records of separate tasks). A group keeps its shorts after such a reset only if the record is intact and says it passed; otherwise its shorts are removed until the next power-on (log line of the SAFETY component, qualifier safety.qlf.safe_state.<GROUP> ERROR). A low-voltage reset (RAM content lost) and a start whose reason the MCU cannot tell count as "no record": freewheel only until power-on. Before a later change the removal of a failed test lived in .bss of the service and a warm reset gave the short back without a test.
  • E3 - enable read back. The test stays register level (5.10 step 3 b) and never reaches the bridge: the gate-driver enable bound to the group (board pwm[].gate_driver, a module with RTE access gate_driver) must read off before the short is built and after it is taken back, read through the driver (readGateDriver_<device> of the family integration; the TMC6200 driver verifies DRV_EN against its IOIN register, ENABLE_MISMATCH). An enable that reads on is no passed test (ENABLE_ON), the shorts are removed. The phase voltages stay with a separate task; standstill and the enable of a group without a bound gate driver are AoU-38.
  • E2 - budget. The hold is a busy wait in the first application task before any application task runs. The task that serves the MCU watchdog is above every application task (tasks.yaml above_application) and is not delayed; tasks below it (on the S32K1 port TASK_BSP with the SBC watchdog trigger, the device drivers' supervision and the halt guard's poll, and TASK_BACKGROUND) wait for the sum of all holds. tools/rtegen derives rte::SAFE_STATE_TEST_BUDGET_US = a third of modules.safeLifecycle.watchdog_timeout_ms (the three service opportunities of section 7.1; demo value 250 ms gives 83 333 us) and refuses a larger sum at pwm.<group>.safe_state_test_us; RteSystem.cpp asserts it again at compile time. A microsecond clock that stands still ends the hold after 100 000 reads (CLOCK_STUCK, no passed test) instead of holding the short for ever. The CPU time of the test is the sum of the holds plus a few register accesses per short, once per power-on.

Evidence: host only (tools/rtegen/test_rtegen_safe_state.py, the glue on the real selection service of the S32K1 port with 11 further mutants; generator tests of the reader and the budget); target build of the synthetic copy with a short (target-active-short); the object code of every project without a short is unchanged. Board proof open with the rest of part C (review E7). Changed: fmea.md SM-27, partner-and-degraded.md 5.10, AoU-38 (section 4.3, proposed).

docs.title: Update after issue 2: read-back in S1 held, for SD and before the reset, gap G1, 2026-09-30
docs.text: Decision of the safety responsible in the safety review of the point K6: close the gaps left; K5: the reaction stays the reset through LOCK_REGISTER_ERROR; an active short is a safe state. The read-back of a separate task is now one function of the family port (safeSupervisor/SafeStateReadback.h, S32K1: SafeIo) that the safe supervisor uses in three more places: S1 held reads back in every round of the hold loop before its walk - the loop is the only code that runs, with every interrupt suspended, so neither the halt deadman nor the idle context could carry it; the groups of SD are read back in every safety cycle before their walk; the S1 + S2 sequence of every resetting event and of the fault reactions in ecu/safety (kernel faults, ETL_ASSERT, ECC error) reads back after its walk and, if S1 did not take effect, resets at once without the console line. Not confirmed in the hold or for SD: LOCK_REGISTER_ERROR (class SAFE_OUTPUT, entry), S1 + S2. An entry whose clock is gated is not confirmed any more (it was not judged): a gated timer keeps its outputs frozen, and the register list expects every such gate on. Nothing is judged before SafeIo::init() (reset configuration of the pins). Open: the hard fault and watchdog handlers and the halt deadman of the family port (outside the task's paths), board check B16. Nothing else in this document was changed; limits and evidence: fmea.md SM-23.

docs.title: Update after issue 2: low-voltage detect reset in the family port, 2026-09-30
docs.text: Decision of the safety responsible on 2026-09-30 (anomaly AN-066, finding H9 of hsi-s32k1xx.md): the family port s32k1xx switches the MCU's low-voltage detect reset on instead of leaving the gap to the integrator (AoU-09). Before, a VDD falling below the detect threshold VLVD (2.80 … 3.00 V) was only flagged; the MCU kept running down to the low-voltage reset VLVR (2.50 … 2.70 V), below the specified supply range, and only SM-20 could see the drift of the internal supplies at safety-task speed. Now boardInit() writes PMC_LVDSC1[LVDRE] = 1 in every start, and the hardware resets and holds the MCU until VDD is back above VLVD plus its hysteresis. Added: the catalogue row SM-59 in section 6.4 (a hardware mechanism configured by the base software; not credited until the safety responsible decides, like SM-58), its analysis in fmea.md, the proposed AoU-39 in section 4.3 (supply margin of a 3.3 V board), and the note under SM-20. Effect per board: a 5 V board (the eval board) runs 2 V above the threshold and sees no difference in normal operation; a 3.3 V board keeps a margin of at least 0.3 V only (AoU-39); in the low-power modes VLPR/VLPS the LVD is off and only the LVR acts. Not changed: the reset-loop limit still clears on POR/LVD (a brown-out loop is not counted, SM-59 in fmea.md), the bootloader does not set the bit (after power-on it runs with the reset default until the application starts), and the bit is not re-checked cyclically (rest of H9). Host verified with a register model and the ELF of the demo; board proof open.

docs.title: Update after issue 2: TMC6200 without supply at the start, 2026-10-01
docs.text: Stage-2 driver rule, not credited for stage 1: the SM-40 table in section 13.3 names the new driver fault NO_SUPPLY (an all-zero IOIN answer: no supply or SDO held low) and when it is latched. Evidence: host test tmc6200 and tmc6200-io67-mutations (10 built-in faults, all detected); board proof open. Nothing else in this document was changed.

docs.title: Update after issue 2: safety catalogue in StrictDoc, 2026-10-01
docs.text: User decision Q5 of a separate task (2026-09-22): the assumed safety goals, the assumptions of use and the safety mechanisms are StrictDoc nodes, so that the software safety requirements name them with checked relations. docs.title: neXtBSW — argument over the admissible configuration range (N3)
docs.text:
Baseline: v0.2.0

Status: 2026-09-30, issue 1 (proposal N3 of safety-plan.md), written against dev at 65f3dc9. Readers: the safety manager, the author of a module manifest or of a check in tools/nxconfig, the integrator who configures neXtBSW for his ECU, and the author of the safety manual. Language: English, like the rest of doc/.

What this document is. neXtBSW is configurable software: the stage-1 safety mechanisms take times, counts, tables and memory layouts from the three configuration levels (derivative, board, project). For such software the standard leaves two routes (6-C.4.5, read through iso26262-gap.md (not published, available on request) rows 6-36 and 6-38): verify the configured software for the data set actually used, or verify it for the admissible range of the configuration data. This document states, for every configuration value the stage-1 mechanisms depend on, which route neXtBSW takes, what range the project has verified and with which evidence, and which verification the integrator owes for his own data set. It is the argument the tailoring T-10 of the safety plan promises and the input for the configuration chapter of the safety manual.

Licence rule. ISO 26262 is cited by part and clause only.

docs.title: 0. Result in one page
docs.text: Question Answer Values the stage-1 mechanisms depend on (section 2) 19 configuration values or value groups: 2 derivative, 2 board, 15 project level (module parameters, safety, interrupts, memory, task set, RTE periods, E2E); plus one code constant that behaves like one (CV-20, deadman time-out) Route chosen (section 1) combined: the relations the mechanisms need are verified for the whole declared range by checks that run on every configuration (tools/nxconfig with YAML path, static_assert on the generated values, generator refusals); the behaviour of the built software is verified per data set — for the project's own profiles by the project, for the integrator's data set by the integrator Range argument holds for 11 of 19 values: every value whose safety property is a relation that a check enforces (e.g. three watchdog services before the shortest time-out, bounds of the period check, interrupt level of the deadman, safe outputs of every safe_off connection) Data-set argument only 8 of 19 values: the property depends on the integrator's hardware or application (ADC tolerance against the needed accuracy, ROM-check period against the longest flash write, lateness of the safety task under his load, E2E choice per signal, task set) What the project verified beyond the demo configuration-level tests with own profiles for every timing relation (nxconfig-watchdog: other periods, time-outs, LPO range, supervisor values); host tests with own stub profiles (safety-cycle 270 ms / 8 cycles, ROM check 2500 ms); target builds of five projects on three derivatives — all with the default safety values. On the board only the demo values run Findings (section 4) G1 no target build with non-default safety values; G2 ROM-check period not checked against the longest flash write; G3 deadman time-out is a code constant; G4 device-bus window only warned; G5 no checked-in project uses a calibration segment Integrator's verification (section 5) 7 assumptions of use AoU-CFG-1 … AoU-CFG-7 proposed for the safety manual: run the checks and the reference outputs on his data set, repeat the board checks that depend on his values, measure the lateness under his load, choose data-set-dependent values with a rationale, keep the ROM check active behind the neXtBSW bootloader (AoU-CFG-7) New tasks proposed (section 7) C1 target test profile with non-default safety values, C2 check of the ROM-check period against the flash write time, C3 deadman time-out into the configuration, C4 configuration chapter of the safety manual Verification mock/host: doc/safety/test/test_config_range.py checks the value register against the module manifests (every module parameter of the stage-1 safety modules is listed, declared ranges agree), every named check, test and path exists, counts agree; counter-checks with broken copies. No board run for this document

docs.title: 1. The route and why
docs.text:
Range where a check can carry it. A safety mechanism of stage 1 rarely depends on a single value; it depends on a relation between values (time-out ≥ three service intervals at the fastest LPO; one interval shorter than a window; deadman level above the RTOS boundary). Such a relation is decidable from the configuration alone. neXtBSW decides it in two independent places — tools/nxconfig (with the YAML path of the value, the configure step stops on an error) and a static_assert on the generated macros in the code that uses them — so every configuration that builds satisfies it. For these values the verification is valid for the admissible range, and the admissible range is defined as: declared range of the manifest ∩ every relation the checks enforce.

Data set where the property is outside the configuration. Some properties depend on facts the configuration does not contain: the accuracy the integrator's function needs, the longest flash write of his application, the interrupt load of his software. For these the checks can only enforce the declared range; whether a value in that range is right is verified for the data set — by the project for its own profiles, by the integrator for his.

Why not the range route for everything. Target tests over the full range would need hardware per value combination, and the properties of the second kind cannot be judged without the integrator's facts. Why not the data-set route for everything: then every change of a value would invalidate the element's evidence; the checks make most of it re-usable.

Precondition of the argument. The checks run on the integrator's configuration: the image is built only through the build, which runs nxconfig and the generators (AoU-26 of tool-classification.md), and nxconfig and the generators are classified and qualified as there. The configuration files are safety-related data under change control (AoU-10).

Remarks:

  • CV-20 is not a configuration value; it is listed because the deadman's reaction time depends on it and on the clock plan (NX_CLOCK_LPIT_HZ, derived), and a project might need another value (finding G3). It is not counted among the 19 values of section 0.
  • The ROM-check areas are not a configuration value: they come from the linker template and the image check; the calibration region is excluded and checked by its own record.
  • safeLifecycle, safeSupervisor, safeSystem and safeMemory are the stage-1 modules with project parameters; the test checks that every one of their parameters is a row here with the declared range of its manifest.

docs.title: 3. The argument per route
docs.text:
Range (11 values: CV-01, CV-02, CV-04, CV-05, CV-06, CV-10, CV-12 … CV-16, and CV-20 as code constant). For each of them: the safety property is a relation; a check enforces it on every configuration with the YAML path, and a second check in the code (static_assert, #error, image check) enforces it on the generated values; the configuration-level tests exercise values across the declared range including both sides of every limit (nxconfig-watchdog tests 228/229 ms against the shortest time-out, 511/512 ms against the counter). Conclusion: a configuration inside the admissible range keeps the property; one outside it does not build. What the range argument does not cover: that the software behaves as designed at every value — the host tests exercise the mechanisms at the demo values and at one or two stub profiles (G1), and the board only at the demo values. Behaviour that scales with a value (a longer period means a longer detection time) is computed in concept.md section 7 as a formula of the values, not measured per value.

Data set (8 values: CV-03, CV-07, CV-08, CV-09, CV-11, CV-17, CV-18, CV-19). The project verifies its own data sets (demo, charge, buildtest, S32K116 minimal) and states the rationale of the defaults in the manifests. For the integrator's data set the verification is his (section 5); the checks only guarantee the declared range and, where it exists, a warning (CV-07).

docs.title: 4. Findings
docs.text: ID Finding Consequence Proposal G1 No target build and no generator reference profile uses safety values other than the defaults (10/250/2 ms, 3/60 000/200 ms, 60 000 ms); non-default values exist only in configuration-level tests and host stubs the range argument rests on the checks; that the generated code builds and runs at other values is shown only for the stubs C1 G2 rom_check_period_ms must be longer than the longest flash write of the ECU (manifest text), but no check enforces it a too-short period turns a long EEPROM write into ROM_CHECK_FAILURE (S1 held) — availability, not safety; the integrator must know it C2, AoU-CFG-4 G3 the halt-deadman time-out is a code constant (10 ms) a project whose fault tolerance time needs a shorter or allows a longer standstill cannot configure it C3 G4 the device-bus window is only warned about when it is shorter than two supervision cycles a configuration with a too-short window builds; the correlation then misses faults AoU-CFG-5 G5 no checked-in project has a calibration segment; the production profile runs only in target-calibration the calibration route is verified by derived profiles, not by a maintained project C1

docs.title: 5. Verification the integrator owes for his data set
docs.text:
Proposed for the safety manual; numbered AoU-CFG-n so that they do not collide with numbers proposed in parallel. They refine AoU-10 and AoU-26.

ID Assumption of use Values AoU-CFG-1 The integrator builds his image only through the build (so every check of section 2 runs on his configuration), treats every warning of nxconfig on a value of section 2 as a finding he resolves or justifies in writing, and keeps his configuration files under change control (AoU-10, AoU-26). all AoU-CFG-2 For every value of section 2 that differs from the defaults he repeats, on his ECU, the board checks of fmea.md section 8 that depend on it (watchdog reset, period violation, reset-loop limit, ROM check, safe outputs) and records the result with the configuration it was run with. CV-01 … CV-06, CV-11, CV-12 AoU-CFG-3 He measures the start distance of the safety cycle under his worst-case load (as board check B4) and sets cycle_lateness_ms from that measurement with margin; the default 2 ms is the demo's measured value, not a property of neXtBSW. CV-03, CV-18 AoU-CFG-4 He sets rom_check_period_ms longer than the longest flash write of his application (EEPROM emulation, NvM), and not longer than the latent-fault interval his analysis allows (AoU-25). CV-11 AoU-CFG-5 He chooses the data-set values from the needs of his function and records the rationale: ADC reference tolerance against the needed accuracy (AoU-24), read-error limit and device-bus window against his fault tolerance time, E2E profile and data ID per signal (AoU-11). CV-07, CV-08, CV-09, CV-17 AoU-CFG-6 He confirms that the halt-deadman time-out of 10 ms and the other fixed times of stage 1 fit his fault tolerance times (AoU-05), or requests a change (C3). CV-20 AoU-CFG-7 If the neXtBSW bootloader starts his application image, he keeps the ROM check (SM-14) active in that image: built only through the build, so that the reference CRC is written and the check is compiled in (AoU-CFG-1), and with a re-check period (CV-11, AoU-CFG-4) or a restart interval (AoU-25) that covers his latent-fault interval. Reason (safety review, 2026-10-03, F5): since earlier changes the bootloader checks the image again immediately before the jump without a second full CRC, so an image byte that changes between the CRC at start and the jump without a flash command (debugger, bit fault; with a held extended session the window can last minutes) is left to the flash ECC and SM-14. CV-11

docs.title: 6. Result for the safety manual
docs.text: The safety manual does not exist yet. Proposal C4: its configuration chapter states the route of section 1 in two sentences, carries the value register of section 2 (or references it), and carries AoU-CFG-1 … AoU-CFG-6 with their final numbers. The consistency test checks the reference as soon as the safety manual exists.

docs.title: 8. Review questions of the architecture (section 11)
docs.text: This task changes no code, generator or configuration. Board without an SBC: no value of section 2 assumes an SBC. Different crystal: the timing values run on the LPO or are relations to the safety task, whose own clock is what the period check measures; CV-20 depends on the LPIT clock through a derived value. Other derivative, S32K3/STM32/Cortex-R: CV-04 and CV-16 are derivative level; CV-02's upper bound is the family's watchdog counter, which nxconfig takes per family; the register is the list another family has to fill. Several CAN buses: CV-17 per signal and bus. Several tasks: CV-18. Exactly one level per value: every row names one level; none is set in two. Host test with own profile: test_config_range.py checks this document against the manifests. Qt, YAML paths: every check named reports with the YAML path. Driver granularity, platform rule: not applicable.

docs.title: neXtBSW development environment: languages, guidelines, tools, build and test flow
docs.text:
Status: 2026-09-28, issue 1, draft for acceptance by the safety manager. Baseline: v0.2.0 Readers: the safety manager, the maintainer, every contributor that writes C, C++ or a generator, and an integrator or reviewer who wants to know with what and under which rules neXtBSW is made. Language: English, like the rest of doc/.

What this document is. The one place that names the software development environment of neXtBSW, as asked by 6-5.5.1 and found missing by iso26262-gap.md (not published, available on request) (rows 6-01 and 6-02, section 6 task 21; safety plan row P6-01, safety case row EW-14). It states which languages are used and why (6-5.4.2), which coding guidelines cover the topics the standard lists for them (6-5.4.3), the neXtBSW C++ subset NXCPP (section 4), the tools with their pinned versions and tool confidence levels, and the build and test flow per lifecycle phase. It does not repeat what other documents own; it points to them.

Decision behind section 4. User decision (2026-09-28): neXtBSW defines its own C++ subset and enforces it with the tools it already has (cppcheck, clang-tidy, the compiler, the test runner); deviations are justified; no commercial MISRA C++ tool is bought. MISRA C++:2023 therefore stays not claimed (it is named only as the reference the subset was compared against, section 4.5).

Licence rule. ISO 26262 is cited by part and clause only (for example "6-5.4.3" = ISO 26262-6:2018, clause 5.4.3); no text, table or figure of it is reproduced. MISRA guidelines are named by number with a short description in our own words, never with their text.

Consistency test. test/test_dev_environment.py checks this document against the repository: every version of section 5 against the file that pins it, every tool-enforced NXCPP rule against the active compiler options and analysis checks, and the code-scan rules of section 4.3 against the code itself.

docs.title: 0. Result in one page
docs.text: Question Answer Languages C99 (bootloader, E2E library, startup, newlib hooks), C++17 (application frame, drivers, platform port, safety mechanisms), ARM assembly (startup, context switch), GNU linker scripts (generated from templates), Python 3.12 (configuration check, generators, verifiers, test runner), YAML (configuration), Jinja2 (generator templates), CMake. Simulink/Embedded Coder only for the application example (out of the element's scope) Guidelines C: MISRA C:2012 with the re-categorisation and deviations (static-analysis.md). C++: NXCPP — 27 rules (section 4), of them 20 enforced by a tool (compiler and build settings, clang-tidy, cppcheck add-on, the code scan of the consistency test or elfcheck; 3 of them with a review part), 7 by review with a named tool proposal each. Naming and layout: the OpenBSW conventions, adopted by reference Guideline topics of 6-5.4.3 9 topics; covered for C and C++: language subset, strong typing, defensive implementation, well-trusted principles, naming, concurrency (C++ by review); not covered by any tool: complexity limit (both languages) and style/format check (section 3.2) Tools 22 rows with version, where it is pinned and the TCL of tool-classification.md (section 5). Everything that builds or verifies the image is pinned once (tools/ci/versions.toml, tools/ci/constraints.txt, tools/misra/requirements.txt, the submodule gitlink); not pinned: MATLAB, J-Link software, Vector driver (bench and application tools, section 5.3) Build flow 7 steps from project.yaml to the checked image (section 6), one command per step, all run by cmake --build and tools/test Test flow per lifecycle phase (section 7): host unit tests (zig), generator tests with own profiles, target builds warning-free with -Werror, static analysis gating, coverage measured (not enforced), mutation runs, image checks (elfcheck), board runs outside CI Findings DE1–DE7 (section 8). Most important: DE5 — the demo image contained newlib's allocator (malloc, free, _sbrk, 488 bytes), pulled in by the sized operator delete that a virtual deleting destructor references; our code never calls it (scan: 0 heap uses), but nothing prevents it. Further: the tool classification names GCC 11.4 although 11.3.1 is pinned (DE1), GNU extensions on by default (DE2), no complexity limit (DE3), no format check of our own code (DE4), NXCPP review rules have no record (DE6), MATLAB and bench software not pinned (DE7) Verification mock/host: the document test runs against the repository at 6f868b5, with counter-checks on broken copies; the demo target build was repeated warning-free with the pinned GCC 11.3.1 in a Linux container and its image read with arm-none-eabi-nm and the linker map (DE5). No hardware

docs.title: 1. Scope and phases
docs.text:
The environment covers the software lifecycle of part 6 as tailored by safety-plan.md for a software SEooC, and the supporting processes of part 8 that need a tool (configuration management cm-plan.md, verification, tool confidence). One environment serves all phases (6-5.4.1 asks for consistency across them): the same pinned toolchain builds, analyses and tests, on the workstation and in CI.

Phase (clause of part 6) Environment element Where Software safety requirements (6-6) StrictDoc in doc/requirements/safety/ssr.sdoc (YAML in doc/safety/requirements.yaml until step 3), tools/trace traceability.md (not published, available on request) Architectural design (6-7) natural language and informal notations, module manifests, tools/schedana doc/architecture/README.md Unit design and implementation (6-8) C99, C++17 with NXCPP, generators with Jinja2 templates sections 2–4 of this document Unit verification (6-9) host tests (zig c++/zig cc), static analysis, coverage, mutation runs section 7 Integration and verification (6-10) target build (arm-none-eabi-gcc), image checks (elfcheck, disassembly tests) sections 6, 7 Testing of the embedded software (6-11) eval board, J-Link, Vector VN1610, tools/boardtest section 7.3 Configuration data (6-C) three-level YAML, tools/nxconfig checks config-range.md

The workstation is Windows (repository .venv, PYTHONUTF8=1); the CI runs the same pipeline (python -m tools.ci run --strict) on windows-latest by default (.github/workflows/ci.yml); tools/ci fetches the same archives for Linux, which the contributor sessions use. A difference between the three is a tool change in the sense of section 5.4.

docs.title: 2. Languages
docs.text:
6-5.4.2 asks that the language is chosen by criteria such as an unambiguous definition, support for embedded real-time software and for modularity, abstraction and structured constructs. The choice below was made by OpenBSW, which neXtBSW builds on; the table records the reasons as they apply to neXtBSW.

Language Standard / dialect Used for Compiler Why this language C ISO C99 (CMAKE_C_STANDARD 99), ISO mode -std=c99 (CMAKE_C_EXTENSIONS OFF; DE2 closed) bootloader and updater, E2E library, startup and newlib hooks, C parts of the platform, the C component interface of the RTE arm-none-eabi-gcc small runtime, direct register access, the language of the vendor headers; MISRA C:2012 exists as a mature subset with a free checker C++ ISO C++17 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17), ISO mode -std=c++17 (CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF; DE2 closed) application frame, RTE runtime, drivers, platform port, safety mechanisms (supervisor, watchdog, safe I/O, MPU, ROM check) arm-none-eabi-g++ the language of OpenBSW; classes and interfaces carry the layer and role model of the architecture, templates and constexpr move checks to compile time (static_assert on generated tables); used as the subset of section 4 ARM assembly GNU as, unified syntax startup, FreeRTOS port, context switch of the fault handler arm-none-eabi-gcc the few places C cannot express (stack switch, exception entry) Linker script GNU ld memory layout, generated from bl_memory.ld.j2 by blgen arm-none-eabi-ld layout is data of the derivative (mcudb), not code Python 3.12 (tools/ci/.python-version) configuration check, generators, verifiers, test runner, Studio CPython the tools run on the host only; their output is checked (tool confidence, section 5), not their source against a coding standard YAML, Jinja2, CMake — configuration levels, generator templates, build description — declarative; checked by nxconfig with YAML paths, templates by reference outputs Simulink MATLAB R2024a, Embedded Coder, AUTOSAR Blockset the example application swc/DemoSwc — out of the element's scope (concept 1.2); the integrator's language and code generator

What a language leaves undefined or weak is covered by the guidelines of section 3: undefined and implementation-defined behaviour of C by MISRA C:2012, of C++ by NXCPP; the target's implementation-defined choices (int 32 bit, little endian, wchar_t 4 byte, plain char unsigned, bit-fields unsigned) are fixed by the toolchain file and given to cppcheck as --platform=arm32-wchar_t4 (tools/misra/rules.yaml).

docs.text:

docs.title: 4.1 Basis
docs.text:
NXCPP is a positive list of restrictions on C++17 for neXtBSW's own C++ code (ecu, libs, platforms outside 3rdparty, the C++ parts of bootloader), in the order of the enforcement strength. It starts from the OpenBSW "disallowed features" (no dynamic memory, no RTTI, no exceptions), adds the checks that already runs, and names each rule's enforcement. It is not a MISRA C++:2023 compliance statement (section 4.5).

Scope rules:

  • Host tests and mocks (**/test/**) are not product code; NXCPP-05, NXCPP-19 and NXCPP-20 do not apply there.
  • OpenBSW copies (tools/openbswsync/copies.yaml) are checked by the tools like our code but reported separately (static-analysis.md section 2); the code scan of section 4.3 includes them, because an OpenBSW construct in the image is in the image.
  • Generated code (board headers, RTE, CAN database, UDS tables) follows NXCPP through its templates; a finding in it is a generator finding.

docs.title: 4.2 Rules
docs.text:
Enforcement: tool — a tool rejects a violation (build fails with -Werror, or the static analysis or the consistency test turns red); tool + review — a tool catches part of the rule, the rest is reviewed; review — only a review catches it, and the rule names a proposal (section 4.6) that would make it a tool rule. "State" is the measurement at 6f868b5.

ID Rule (own words) Topic Enforcement Enforced by State 2026-09-28 NXCPP-01 C++17 is the language level of all product code subset tool cmake: CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17 set in the root CMakeLists.txt NXCPP-02 No GNU language extension outside platform code; in platform code only attributes (section, used, naked, always_inline) and inline assembly subset tool + review cmake: CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF, cmake: CMAKE_C_EXTENSIONS OFF (P2) ISO mode since an earlier change: an extension that conflicts with ISO (typeof, asm without underscores) does not compile;
