docs.title: 4.3 The code scan (scan: rules)
docs.text:
Four NXCPP rules have no clang-tidy or cppcheck check among the active ones, but can be checked with certainty by reading the source: the constructs are keywords or #include lines. The consistency test test/test_dev_environment.py scans bootloader, ecu, libs and platforms (C++ files .cpp, .h, .hpp; without test, tests, 3rdparty, generated; 357 files at 6f868b5), after removing comments and string literals:

Scan Rejects exceptions the keywords throw, try, catch rtti dynamic_cast, typeid heap a call of malloc, calloc, realloc, free; a new expression that is not a placement new (new ( …)); a delete expression (= delete of a special member is allowed) goto the keyword goto headers an #include <…> of a standard C++ header that is not on the allow-list

Allow-list of standard headers (freestanding or without allocation; each one used today):

algorithm, array, atomic, cinttypes, cstdarg, cstddef, cstdint, cstdio, cstring, initializer_list, iterator, new, numeric, tuple

A header outside the list (for example vector, string, map, memory, functional, iostream, thread, mutex) needs either an entry here with the reason (it allocates nothing and needs no OS support) or a deviation (section 4.4). cstdio is on the list for snprintf-style formatting only; file and stream functions are covered by NXCPP-05 (they allocate) and by the newlib stubs, which return errors. new only declares the platform's own operator delete and placement new; it allocates nothing, and elfcheck rejects an image that links operator new or the allocator. Headers of C (stdint.h …) and of the vendor, ETL, estd and OpenBSW are not standard C++ headers and are not scanned.

The scan is a heuristic reader, not a compiler. It is exact for the keywords and includes it looks for; it cannot see a heap call hidden behind a macro or a library function. That is why P5 adds the check that closes it: the linked image must not contain the allocator. Since an earlier change (2026-10-01) elfcheck rejects every image that defines it (code heap-symbol), so NXCPP-05 is a tool rule (DE5 closed).

docs.title: 4.4 Deviations
docs.text:
A deviation from an NXCPP rule is written, justified and approved like a MISRA deviation, in the same process (static-analysis.md section 4):

  1. Tool rule, finding of clang-tidy or cppcheck → an entry in tools/misra/deviations.yaml (DEV-nnn, rule, files, source-line pattern or symbol, reason in own words, raised by, approved_by). This exists today; the entries DEV-001 … DEV-014 already cover the register access of NXCPP-11.
  2. Tool rule, finding of the code scan → a comment on the same line, // NXCPP-nn deviation: <DEV-nnn>, and an entry DEV-nnn in tools/misra/deviations.yaml with rule NXCPP-nn ([Proposal] — the misra checker accepts only the rule names of its tools today; until it accepts NXCPP-nn, the test honours the comment only when the DEV-nnn it names exists in the file).
  3. Review rule → the reviewer records the deviation in the task's changelog fragment ("Abweichung NXCPP-nn: Grund") and, if it stays in the code, the comment of item 2.

Approval is the safety manager's, as for every deviation; an open approval belongs. No NXCPP deviation exists today beyond the approved DEV-002/DEV-003 (register and fixed-location access, NXCPP-11) and the baseline entry of cert-dcl50-cpp (NXCPP-18), which is a baseline finding, not a deviation; it needs a decision (DE6).

docs.title: 4.5 What NXCPP does not cover, compared with MISRA C++:2023
docs.text:
The subset was compared topic by topic with the rule groups of MISRA C++:2023 (by group, not by rule text). It covers the groups on exceptions, dynamic memory, RTTI, recursion, initialisation, casts, virtual functions and destructors, switch and statement structure, and part of the integral-conversion and concurrency groups. Not covered, and therefore not claimed:

  • the full essential-type model of integral and floating arithmetic (only narrowing, signed bit operations and signed/ unsigned comparison are checked);
  • rules on templates, lambdas and constexpr beyond what the compiler rejects;
  • lifetime rules on references and pointers to temporaries beyond clang-analyzer-cplusplus.* and core.*;
  • the rules on the preprocessor for C++ units (the add-on's C view of C++ gives notices only, static-analysis.md 1);
  • the resource and library rules outside the allow-list of section 4.3.

An integrator whose process requires MISRA C++:2023 runs a qualified tool on neXtBSW's C++ code himself; this is a proposed assumption of use for a separate task (next to the one of static-analysis.md section 6).

docs.title: 4.6 Proposals that turn review rules into tool rules
docs.text:
Each proposal changes a file outside this task's path and is therefore not done here; it is listed for the maintainer (section 9).

Proposal Rules Change File P1 NXCPP-26 enable readability-function-cognitive-complexity (threshold 25 as a start), first as a report, then gating with the baseline mechanism tools/misra/rules.yaml P2 NXCPP-02 set CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF and CMAKE_C_EXTENSIONS OFF, build every profile, keep the attributes that need GNU mode behind the OpenBSW compiler macros root CMakeLists.txt. Done by an earlier change (2026-10-01): both set OFF, -ffp-contract=fast kept explicit (ISO mode would switch it off and change the object code), no source change, test cmake-iso-mode P3 NXCPP-19 replace the scan by the clang-tidy check cppcoreguidelines-avoid-goto (same result, one mechanism) tools/misra/rules.yaml P4 NXCPP-25, NXCPP-27 a check clang-format --dry-run with OpenBSW's .clang-format over the changed own files (the clang-format wheel is available like clang-tidy), and readability-identifier-naming with the OpenBSW options (their .clang-tidy carries them commented out) tools/misra/rules.yaml, tools/misra/requirements.txt P5 NXCPP-05 (a) the platform defines operator delete(void*) and operator delete(void*, unsigned int) itself, as a call that never returns into the fault reaction (a deleting destructor is never run, because no delete expression exists), so libstdc++'s version and with it newlib's allocator are no longer linked (DE5); (b) elfcheck then requires that the linked image contains none of malloc, _malloc_r, free, _sbrk, operator new platforms/*/port (or libs/bsp), tools/elfcheck P6 NXCPP-21 … NXCPP-24 a review checklist with these four rules in the task template (tools/todo/todoplan.py brief), answered in the changelog fragment tools/todo

docs.title: 5.4 Changing a tool
docs.text: A new version of a pinned tool is a change under cm-plan.md: version, URL and SHA-256 are changed together in the one file of the table, then python -m tools.ci setup and a full python -m tools.ci run --clean; a new ARM GCC must build every target profile warning-free with -Werror; a new cppcheck or clang-tidy needs a new baseline, reviewed finding by finding (tools/misra/requirements.txt header). The TCL argument of the tool is re-read for the new version (tool-classification.md section 3). This document's table is then updated; its consistency test fails until it is.

docs.title: 6. Build flow
docs.text:
One command (cmake --preset <profile> and cmake --build --preset <profile>) runs all steps; the preset base is cmake/NxPresets.json (Ninja Multi-Config, default RelWithDebInfo with -O2 -g3 -DNDEBUG, CMAKE_COMPILE_WARNING_AS_ERROR ON, C -Wall -Wextra, C++ -Wall -Wextra -Wvla). The toolchain file cmake/toolchains/NxArmNoneEabi-gcc.cmake adds the core options from the derivative and the C++ options of NXCPP-03, NXCPP-04 and NXCPP-21 (-fno-exceptions -fno-rtti -fno-threadsafe-statics), plus -fstack-usage, -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections, -fno-common, -fshort-enums, -mno-unaligned-access.

Step What Tool Check that follows 1 read and check the three configuration levels, derive values (clock plan, CAN timing, memory layout) nxconfig messages with YAML path; nxconfig check 2 generate board headers, memory layout and linker script, bootloader configuration bswgen, blgen reference outputs (bswgen-reference), static_assert in generated headers 3 generate RTE, CAN database, UDS tables rtegen, dbcgen, diaggen reference outputs (rtegen-reference), static_assert 4 compile and link bootloader, updater and application arm-none-eabi-gcc, CMake, Ninja warning-free with -Werror 5 post-link: calibration header, ROM check references, validity record calseg, romCheckImage, canflash record CRC over the real image (rom-check-image) 6 A2L for calibration a2lgen a2lgen, xcp-host 7 check the linked image against the configuration elfcheck (sections, core attributes, timing tables, priorities) elfcheck* entries of tools/test/tests.yaml

A build directory belongs to one compiler; a moved compiler needs --fresh (cmake/NxBuildDirCheck.cmake).

docs.text:
Findings of this document, proposed for the anomaly register (anomaly-register.md, not entered here, section 9).

ID Finding Effect Proposal DE1 tool-classification.md names the compiler GCC 11.4 (inventory row, heading 3.14, TCL argument); the pinned and used compiler is xPack GCC 11.3.1 (tools/ci/versions.toml; S32DS with 11.4 is uninstalled) the TCL 3 argument and proposal L (known wrong-code faults) refer to a version that no longer builds the image tool-classification.md: 11.4 → 11.3.1 in section 2 and 3.14, proposal L against 11.3.1 DE2 CMAKE_C_EXTENSIONS/CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS are not set, so C and C++ are compiled as gnu99/gnu++17 a GNU extension is accepted silently; the language of section 2 is not exactly ISO P2. Closed by an earlier change (2026-10-01): the root build compiles C and C++ in ISO mode (CMAKE_C_EXTENSIONS OFF, CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF, -ffp-contract=fast explicit), test cmake-iso-mode DE3 no complexity limit for C or C++ 6-5.4.3 topic "low complexity" not covered by a tool P1 DE4 OpenBSW's .clang-format is not applied to neXtBSW code; no format check style guide only by review P4 DE5 the demo image contains newlib's allocator. Measured on the demo build (xPack GCC 11.3.1, RelWithDebInfo, arm-none-eabi-nm and the linker map application.map): app.cpp.obj references the sized operator delete(void*, unsigned int) (the deleting destructors of classes with a virtual destructor, which their vtables name — for example that of the OpenBSW class lifecycle::LifecycleManager::ComponentTransitionExecutor, emitted in app.cpp); libstdc++ del_ops.o → del_op.o → free → newlib nano malloc.o, mallocr.o, freer.o, sbrkr.o → libnosys sbrk.o. Linked: malloc 16, _malloc_r 236, free 16, _free_r 152, _sbrk_r 32, _sbrk 28 and the two operator delete 4 + 4 bytes = 488 bytes. The bootloader image contains none of them. No code of ours calls it (scan heap: 0), so it is dead at run time; but a future delete, a library function that allocates, or a call through strdup/printf paths would link and run silently, and libnosys _sbrk grows from the end of .bss without a limit NXCPP-05 is only true in the source; the image carries an unbounded allocator; SM-10 (MPU) would catch a heap growing into a protected region, not one growing within the task's RAM P5 (a) and (b). docs.title: neXtBSW dependent failure analysis of the stage-1 mechanisms
docs.text:
Baseline: v0.2.0

Status: 2026-09-28, issue 1, written against dev at ae92e89. Update 2026-10-03 (implementation of the findings): DFA-1, DFA-2, DFA-3, DFA-4 (a) and DFA-6 are implemented in the family port and host verified, DFA-5 and AoU-DFA-a … AoU-DFA-c are in the safety manual; the rows DF-05, DF-14, DF-36, DF-46 and DF-47 changed their status, section 0 counts them, section 8.1 says what was done and what stays open, and the consistency script of section 10.2 is checked in as test/test_dfa.py. Update 2026-10-04 (board results of a separate task of 2026-10-03/04 and their safety review of 2026-10-04, all points as recommended): DF-05 from covered (host) to partial - a gated LPIT clock is a bus fault caught by SM-17, a slow LPIT clock is caught by DFA-2 on the board, a lost SIRC is a residual risk carried by an earlier change; DFA-6 and section 8.1 corrected: a stopped system time is not kind 4 (SM-06 and SM-01 react), kind 4/5 see a slow or fast one. Readers: the architect and safety owner, the maintainer, the contributors of a separate task (freedom from interference), device packages, hardware-software interface, ECC latent test and MCU safety manual (safety manual). Language: English, like the rest of doc/.

What this document is. The dependent failure analysis (DFA) that the gap analysis iso26262-gap.md (not published, available on request) section 6 no. 15 asks for (rows 9-03, 9-04, 9-05, 9-11, 6-16, 10-07 and 11-02 there): the stage-1 safety mechanisms of neXtBSW run on one MCU, one core, one supply and one die together with the software they supervise. This document asks, systematically and per topic, which single cause can make a mechanism fail together with the element it supervises or together with another mechanism that is supposed to catch the same fault (common cause), and which failure of one element can propagate into a mechanism (cascading failure). For every potential dependent failure it states whether it is plausible, which measure exists or is proposed, and why that measure is adequate. The SPI common cause (finding F5 of fmea.md) is analysed explicitly (section 6).

Licence rules followed here. ISO 26262 is not in the repository and was not available to this analysis (contributor session, doc/confidential/ does not exist in the remote repository). The standard is cited by part and clause only, as the gap analysis does, and no text or table of it is reproduced. The topic list of section 3 is the grouping the gap analysis gives for 9-7 (row 9-03), completed with the software topics that 6-7.4.11 and the freedom-from-interference annex of part 6 name, all in our own words. Whether the list is complete against the clause and its informative annex is open point O1 (section 10): it needs a reader of the licensed copy.

What it is not. Not a quantitative analysis (no beta factors, no failure rates — those are the integrator's, AoU-09), not the DFA of the device packages, and not the freedom-from-interference design itself. It is the list that tells which dependent failures they have to close or to accept, and why the ones that are already closed are.

docs.title: 0. Result in one page
docs.text: Question Answer Scope the 29 stage-1 mechanisms of fmea.md section 3 plus the period part of SM-04, the reset-loop limit of SM-50 and the kernel-fault reactions of a separate task; the SPI common cause (F5); one MCU (s32k1xx) as the only family with a safety port (concept 1.3) Independence the argument relies on 14 pairs (section 2): who supervises whom, who covers whose latent faults, and which reaction path must survive the fault it reacts to Shared resources found 22 (section 4), from the supply to the developer; every stage-1 mechanism of fmea.md section 3 is assigned to at least one Potential dependent failures analysed 47 (section 5): 11 random hardware, 8 systematic, 7 installation and maintenance, 4 environmental, 5 shared external resources, 5 stress, 7 cascading inside the element Result 18 covered by an existing measure (5 of them covered (host) only, board proof open), 14 partial, 8 open, 3 AoU, 1 residual, 3 not plausible (with the reason). Since an earlier change: the 5 open rows that led to the findings DFA-1 … DFA-5 are closed or narrowed (DF-36 covered (host), DF-05, DF-46 and DF-47 partial, DF-14 AoU; section 8.1; DF-05 partial since the board results of 2026-10-03/04: a lost SIRC stays a residual risk); a sixth finding, DFA-6, comes from the time-out analysis of DF-32 and SPI-3 and is implemented too. The 8 open ones are carried by existing tasks (twice, twice, N4). Section 7 adds the DFA view to separate tasks; section 9 proposes 3 assumptions of use The load-bearing measure diverse time bases. The core runs on the system clock (SOSC/SPLL), the watchdog SM-01 and the period check SM-04 on the LPO, the halt deadman SM-06 on the LPIT's own functional clock. A fault of the system clock or of the LPO is seen by a mechanism on another clock (DF-02, DF-03) — with one exception: a stopped LPIT clock stops SM-06 unseen (DF-05, DFA-2). Since an earlier change and the board of 2026-10-03/04: a slow LPIT clock is seen by DFA-2, a gated one is a bus fault (SM-17); a lost SIRC stops SM-06 and leaves only the hardware reset of SM-01 (residual risk). This is the one place where the stage-1 argument has real independence on one die The load-bearing limitation one core, one supply, one die. A core logic fault that keeps servicing the watchdog but computes wrongly (DF-06) and a supply fault outside what the MCU's own low-voltage reset catches (DF-01) have no stage-1 measure; both need the MCU manufacturer's safety manual (N2) or external hardware (AoU-13) New findings DFA-1 the run-time ROM re-check (SM-14) stops silently when the idle context is starved — nothing outside the idle context watches it · DFA-2 a stopped LPIT functional clock stops the halt deadman (SM-06) silently; the configuration re-check sees registers, not a counter that stands still · DFA-3 a stuck ADC converter that returns a plausible code blinds SM-18, SM-19, SM-20 and SM-30 together · DFA-4 a clock-gate fault of a PWM timer is detected (CLOCK_GATE class of SM-22) but also disables the PWM part of the reaction it triggers · DFA-5 expected values and configured values come from the same generated data, so a design fault in the configuration or a generator fault is masked by every run-time comparison · DFA-6 the SPI time-out and the CAN time-outs count on the OpenBSW system time — a stopped system time makes them unbounded (section 8) SPI common cause (F5) confirmed: no stage-1 mechanism depends on SPI, and no SPI failure can switch an output on that S1 switched off (the enable is a GPIO in the safe outputs table). SPI is a common cause for the stage-2 device diagnostics and a shared resource between partitions; a bus arbitration is missing if a board puts two devices on one SPI master (section 6) Coordination with a separate task A related task is open; its contributor has not started. Section 7 is the hand-over: 9 potential dependent failures whose measure belongs to a separate task, each with what must show. The DFA is verified against the repository and the other safety documents (section 10), but not reviewed by a second person (I1) and not yet acknowledged by an earlier change Verification analysis only (mock). Code and documents read at ae92e89; the consistency script test/test_dfa.py (section 10.2, checked in by an earlier change) checks every mechanism, task and test ID cited here and the counts of this page. The measures of a separate task are host verified (mock); on the board (2026-10-03/04, eval board) B3 and B4 passed, DFA-2 is proven with a slowed LPIT clock, and B2/B5 showed safe reactions through SM-17, SM-06 and SM-01 instead of the new checks (section 8.1; safety review board 2026-10-04)

docs.title: 1.1 Terms
docs.text:
In our own words:

  • Dependent failure — two or more failures whose probability of occurring together is higher than the product of their single probabilities. Two kinds:
  • Common cause failure (CCF) — one root cause makes several elements fail, directly, through a coupling factor they share (the same clock, the same supply, the same code origin, the same person);
  • Cascading failure (CF) — the failure of one element causes the failure of another (a runaway task corrupts the supervisor's data; a stuck SPI transfer stalls a task).
  • Initiator — the event or fault that starts the dependent failure.
  • Coupling factor — the shared property or resource through which it spreads.
  • Independence vs. freedom from interference. Freedom from interference (FFI) is the absence of cascading failures from a lower-rated element into a higher-rated one. Independence additionally excludes common causes. At ASIL B neXtBSW does not use decomposition (gap 9-01), so it needs independence only where the argument relies on it: where a mechanism is claimed to detect a fault of the element it supervises, or to cover the latent faults of another mechanism. That is the list of section 2.

docs.title: 1.2 Steps
docs.text:
1. What must be independent (section 2): from fmea.md section 3 and concept.md section 6, every pair "supervised element ↔ mechanism", "mechanism ↔ mechanism that covers its latent faults" and "detection ↔ reaction path" that the stage-1 argument relies on.
  2. Shared resources (section 4): for every mechanism, what it needs to work — hardware on the die, execution context, code and data, tools, people. A resource used by both sides of a pair of section 2 is a coupling factor.
  3. Topics (section 3): each topic is walked against the shared resources to find initiators.
  4. Per potential dependent failure (section 5): kind (CCF/CF), plausibility with reason, measure, rationale, status, evidence. A measure is one of three types, in the order of preference the gap analysis gives for 9-7:
  5. P — prevents the root cause (for example the CRC unit reserved for one user);
  6. D — detects or controls the effect (for example a check on an independent clock);
  7. R — reduces the coupling (for example a separate time base, a separate execution context).
  8. Findings and hand-over (sections 7 and 8): what is not closed becomes a finding, an addition to an existing task, or an assumption of use.

docs.title: 1.3 Status words
docs.text: Status Meaning covered a measure exists in the code and is verified (host tests with built-in faults and/or board, as named) covered (host) the measure exists and is host verified; the board proof is open (named) partial a measure exists but leaves a named gap open no measure yet; a finding DFA-n (section 8) or an addition to a named task AoU the element cannot close it; the integrator's duty, as a proposed assumption of use (section 9) residual accepted, with the reason and who accepted it not plausible the dependent failure cannot occur in the stage-1 design, with the reason

docs.title: 1.4 Plausibility
docs.text: A potential dependent failure is plausible if the initiator can occur in the target environment of the element (an S32K1 ECU in a vehicle, concept 1.2) and the coupling factor exists in the code at ae92e89. It is not plausible if the coupling factor does not exist (for example no second user of a resource) or if the initiator is excluded by construction (for example a build error). Rates are not estimated (concept section 0, AoU-09).

docs.title: 3. Topics walked
docs.text:
Own words; the grouping follows the gap analysis row 9-03 and the software topics of 6-7.4.11.

# Topic What it means for software mechanisms on one MCU Section 5 T1 Random hardware faults of shared on-chip resources supply, clocks, core, memories, interrupt and reset logic used by the supervised element and the mechanism 5.1 T2 Systematic development faults with a common origin same specification, same code origin (OpenBSW demonstration), same compiler, same generator and configuration data, same people 5.2 T3 Production faults end-of-line programming, MCU manufacturing faults (the latter AoU-09) 5.3 T4 Installation, repair, maintenance flashing, bootloader update, debug access, calibration, test commands left in the image 5.3 T5 Environmental conditions temperature, electromagnetic disturbance, humidity and vibration acting on the whole die at once 5.4 T6 Failure of shared external resources external supply, crystal, CAN bus, SPI buses and the devices on them, debug probe 5.5 and 6 T7 Stress from specific situations CPU and interrupt load, long operation without restart, repeated resets, flash writes 5.6 T8 Software shared resources (6-7.4.11, FFI annex of part 6) memory, execution and timing, exchange of information between elements of one image — the cascading failures inside the element 5.7

docs.text: Columns: Kind CCF / CF. P? plausible (yes / no). Measure with its type P / D / R (section 1.2).

docs.title: 5.1 T1 — random hardware faults of shared on-chip resources
docs.text: ID Initiator → coupling Fails together Kind P? Measure Rationale Status / evidence DF-01 Supply of the MCU out of range (R-01) every mechanism and everything it supervises; SM-20 measures the supply with the same die it supervises CCF yes D hardware power-on and low-voltage reset of the MCU (PMC); since an earlier change also the low-voltage detect reset, switched on by the family port (SM-59, not credited); D SM-20 for a drift inside the working range; R an external supply supervisor / SBC (stage 2, AoU-09) software on the die cannot be credited for an under-voltage that makes the die itself unreliable; it is credited only for a drift while the die still works correctly. docs.title: 6. SPI as a common cause (F5)
docs.text:
fmea.md section 5.3 decided that the SPI master is not a stage-1 problem. This analysis confirms the decision with the dependent-failure view and names what stays open for the other tasks.

Stage 1 does not depend on SPI. None of the mechanisms of section 4 uses R-19. The safe outputs walk writes port and FTM registers; the gate-driver enable is a GPIO declared safe_off (TMC6200 drv_en), so S1 takes effect without any SPI transfer. The only SPI-dependent function near a stage-1 mechanism is the SBC watchdog trigger, and its failure ends in an SBC reset — a safe direction (stage 2, SM-42).

No SPI failure can undo S1. A wrong command to the gate driver (wrong chip select, corrupted frame, a QM task writing the device) cannot energise the bridge while DRV_EN is held inactive by the table walk, because the enable does not go over SPI. That is the property that makes the SPI a stage-2 common cause and not a stage-1 one; it holds as long as every power stage has a safe_off enable outside the bus (AoU-06, and DFA-4 for the PWM side).

What SPI couples in stage 2.

ID Initiator Fails together Measure today For whom SPI-1 one LPSPI instance or its bus fails the diagnostics of every device on that bus SM-34 correlates communication faults of two devices on one bus within 20 safety cycles into one "bus lost" and sets QLF_ERROR on their values A related task per package: the reaction to a lost bus (a package that needs a switching-off reaction detects it in the safety task) SPI-2 all LPSPI instances fail together device diagnostics on every bus none beyond SPI-1 per bus The common causes of the instances — same driver code (platforms/s32k1xx/bsp/bspLpspi), same functional clock source, same system time for the transfer time-out, supply of the pin ports SPI-3 the OpenBSW system time stops every SPI transfer waits without bound (Lpspi.cpp times out on getSystemTimeUs32Bit()) the calling task stalls → SM-06 (BSP task) or SM-01 DFA-6 SPI-4 two tasks use one SPI master frames interleave no bus arbitration exists; the board model names one device per spi[] entry (eval board: three instances, one device each), so it does not occur today An arbitration (or a rule in nxconfig that refuses two users of one master from different tasks) before a board puts two devices on one bus SPI-5 the SPI master is a resource of a QM partition and of a safety-related one a QM driver reconfigures or blocks the master none (one address space, AoU-17) Shared resource between partitions

Result. No measure is needed in stage 1. The proposed additions go to a separate task (SPI-1 and SPI-2) (SPI-4, SPI-5); SPI-3 is part of DFA-6.

docs.title: 7.2 Clock plan
docs.text: DF-02: SM-04 detects large clock errors on the independent LPO; the band it cannot see (about −17 % … +32 % of the system clock) needs the register-level comparison of the clock plan. Addition: class SYSTEM_CLOCK (SCG CSR against the plan and valid flags of the planned sources every safety cycle) (reaction at start instead of a report). With DFA-2 the class should also carry SIRCVLD (or the LPIT's source) — the clock of SM-06.

docs.title: 7.3 ECC latent test and the MCU safety manual
docs.text: DF-10 (ECC blind) is already its scope. Addition from DF-01 and DF-06: when the S32K1 safety manual is available, its list of required software measures is to be checked in particular for (a) a software test of the core (DF-06) and (b) the configuration of the low-voltage detection and reset (DF-01). Both are the only dependent failures of stage 1 for which the element has no measure of its own.

docs.title: 7.4 Hardware-software interface
docs.text: Entries the HSI should carry because the DFA relies on them: the clock source of every supervision peripheral (LPO for WDOG and LPTMR0, the LPIT functional clock of mcudb clock.pcc.LPIT), the clock monitors with reset (SOSCCMRE, SPLLCMRE), the PMC low-voltage configuration (reset values, not written by neXtBSW), FTM CONF.BDMMODE, the debug behaviour of WDOG, LPTMR and LPIT, and the data-sheet LPO range with its source (DF-15).

docs.title: 7.5 Further items
docs.text:
• SPI-1 and SPI-2 (section 6); the DFA of each device package continues this document's method.
  • DF-23 is one more reason for the product build without test commands.
  • The claim limit of DFA-5 and the proposed AoUs of section 9 belong into the safety manual.

docs.title: 8. New findings of this analysis
docs.text: ID Finding Why it matters Proposed measure Proposed task (for the maintainer) DFA-1 The run-time re-check of the ROM check (SM-14) is only watched from inside the idle context: RomCheck::idle() computes ROMCHECK_OVERDUE only for a pass postponed by flash writes. If the idle context does not run (CPU overload, a task that never blocks), no pass is started and nothing reports it (DF-36) ASG-07 at run time silently falls back to SM-16 alone; the overload itself is only an S3 log (SM-05) the safety task checks that the pass counter advanced within a deadline derived from the period (for example two periods plus the longest pass), and raises ROM_CHECK_FAILURE with context "overdue, not called" (S1 held like the other ROM-check events, or S1 + S2 — reaction to decide); period 0 excluded. Host test with built-in faults (idle never called) P2 — platforms/s32k1xx/port/safety/safeMemory, platforms/s32k1xx/port/safety/safeLifecycle, ecu/safety/safeSupervisor (context) DFA-2 A stopped LPIT functional clock (source switched off, PCC gate) stops the halt deadman SM-06 without any event: the configuration re-check compares registers, not whether the counter moves. On ARMv7-M nothing else notices (DF-05) SM-06 becomes latent until the next stall, which it then misses (ASG-01 termination path, halt case) the safety cycle reads CVAL1 twice with the retrigger in between, or compares it with the previous cycle's value, and raises DEADMAN_CONFIGURATION_ERROR with a new field "counter stands still"; alternatively the valid flag of the LPIT's clock source in the SYSTEM_CLOCK class P2 — platforms/s32k1xx/port/safety/safeSupervisionCheck, platforms/s32k1xx/port/main/src/integration DFA-3 A stuck ADC converter that returns one plausible code for every channel blinds SM-18, SM-19, SM-20 and SM-30 together (DF-46); the bandgap reading alone cannot tell a stuck converter from a good one the reference and supply supervision and every analogue safety input fail together, silently (ASG-03 frame, 11-05 of the gap analysis) read a second internal channel with a clearly different expected code in the same safety cycle (for example the high or low reference of the converter — which internal channels the S32K1 ADC offers is to be confirmed in the reference manual by the HSI) and require both codes in their bands; a result that does not change between two different channels is a converter fault (context 3 of ADC_REFERENCE_ERROR). Host test with a converter model that sticks P2 — platforms/s32k1xx/port/safety/safeSystem; with a separate task DFA-4 The SM-23 walk skips a peripheral whose clock is gated. The class CLOCK_GATE detects a gated PWM timer and raises S1 — whose PWM part then does nothing for that timer, because the same fault gates it (DF-47) a PWM group without an enable on another peripheral stays at whatever level the timer froze; ASG-01 two parts: (a) a nxconfig warning with the YAML path of the PWM group when no safe_off output on another peripheral de-energises its power stage (the stage-1 argument then rests on AoU-07 alone for that group); (b) for a separate task: decide whether the walk re-enables the clock gate before writing SWOCTRL (needs the question whether an FTM output follows SWOCTRL immediately after the gate is opened, reference manual) or switches the pins to GPIO inactive — the PCR lock of SM-21 would forbid the latter, so (b) is the gate (a) P2 — tools/nxconfig/checks.py; (b) addition to a separate task DFA-5 Every run-time comparison of stage 1 (SM-13 MPU descriptors, SM-21/SM-22 register list, the safe outputs table of SM-23) takes its expected values from the same generated data that configured the hardware (DF-14). A wrong design value, a generator fault or a wrong derivative fact is configured and expected alike the claim of these mechanisms is "detects a change after start", not "detects a wrong configuration"; without saying so, a reader could credit them for the second no code change. State the claim limit in the safety manual and in fmea.md (with a separate task step 3); the design side is covered by tool confidence, generator tests with own profiles and mutants, and board tests of the generated result per project; proposed AoU-DFA-c (section 9) Addition DFA-6 The time-outs of the SPI transfers (Lpspi.cpp) and of the CAN reception supervision count on the OpenBSW system time. If the system time stops (for example DEMCR.TRCENA cleared, or DFA-2 on ARMv6-M), every such wait is unbounded and every reception time-out stays silent (SPI-3) a single initiator removes all time-outs of the communication layer at once; the stall that follows is caught only by SM-06/SM-01 if the waiting task is one they supervise (a) a supervision of the system time from the safety cycle: the system time must advance by about one period per cycle, measured against the SM-04 LPTMR (the check would reuse the SM-04 time base, no new peripheral); (b) SPI waits additionally bounded by a poll budget like the clock driver of a separate task P2 — platforms/s32k1xx/port/safety/safeLifecycle (a), platforms/s32k1xx/bsp/bspLpspi (b)

docs.title: 8.1 Implementation status
docs.text: Finding Status What was done Evidence (mock/host) Open DFA-1 implemented platforms/s32k1xx/port/safety/safeLifecycle ProgressSupervision.cpp: the safety cycle samples the pass counter of the ROM check (RomCheck::statistics().passes) in every cycle; when it stood still for more than three re-check periods in safety cycles (one until the pass is due, one that RomCheck itself grants flash writes before ROMCHECK_OVERDUE, one for the pass and the idle context) it raises ROM_CHECK_FAILURE with context 7 "not called" - S1 held like every other ROM-check event. Only in an image that runs the re-check (NX_ROM_CHECK_IMAGE) and with a period other than 0; not after the ROM check reported itself. The counting is hardware independent (ecu/safety/safeWatchdog ProgressChecks.h, ProgressDeadline) progress-checks, safety-progress board; with period 0 the first pass is not watched (AoU-25 unchanged) DFA-2 implemented safeSupervisionCheck LpitDeadmanProgress.cpp: with the channel enabled the counter of the deadman must change within a budget of polls that spans two LPIT ticks at the core clock of the project (derived from the clock plan, 22 polls on the eval board); a counter that stands still is DEADMAN_CONFIGURATION_ERROR with the new field 0x100 (S1 + S2). A channel disabled by the retrigger or by an expiry gives no verdict in that cycle lpit-deadman-progress, safety-progress board 2026-10-04: proven with a slowed LPIT clock (SIRCDIV2 /64, field 0x100) - the check also sees an LPIT clock that is too slow; a gated clock is a bus fault caught by SM-17 (board 2026-10-03); a lost SIRC is a residual risk (DF-05); O4 answered: CVAL is readable with the clock stopped (core halted). The alternative of the finding (SIRCVLD in the SYSTEM_CLOCK class) stays with a separate task DFA-3 implemented, partial safeSystem SafeSystem.cpp checkConverterSeparation(): the second internal channel is the internal supply channel the cycle reads anyway (INTERNAL0), not VREFSH/VREFSL - those would need a new adc_internal entry in every project and in the port manifest (port.yaml), outside this task. The two raw codes of one cycle must stand on the expected side of twice the bandgap code: above it for the 3.3 V supplies, below it for the 1.2 V core; otherwise ADC_REFERENCE_ERROR context 3 (S1 + S2). A converter that answers both channels alike is reported within three cycles, one that stopped converting at the core step safe-system board (no false alarm over the supply steps); the core step cannot tell one code from the other; a second converter with safety inputs (ADC1) is unchecked - proposal DFA-4 (a) implemented, (b) open tools/nxconfig/pwmgate.py: a used PWM group without a bound safe_off output (board pwm[].gate_driver and a safe_off connection of its module) is a warning with the YAML path pwm.<group> that names AoU-07. Six test profiles of the tree get the warning, the eval board demo does not nxconfig-pwmgate (b) whether the walk opens the clock gate before it writes SWOCTRL - decision for the proposal DFA-5 done (no code) the claim limit is stated in the safety manual 10.2; AoU-DFA-a … AoU-DFA-c are rows of its section 7 (status proposed) and test_safety_manual.py requires them from section 9 of this document safety-manual, safety-dfa acceptance of the three AoUs (safety review); fmea.md keeps its wording (step 3 owns the catalogue) DFA-6 implemented (a) ProgressSupervision.cpp: over the window of the period check the OpenBSW system time must advance like the LPTMR on LPO1K within the LPO range of the derivative, with a slack of one period plus the lateness for the one-off loss after a debugger exit; a slow system time is SAFETY_CYCLE_PERIOD_VIOLATION kind 4, a fast one kind 5 (S1 + S2), at the end of a window (eval board: 7 cycles, 70 ms). Corrected after the board (safety review board 2026-10-04): a stopped system time is not kind 4 - the safety task is scheduled through exactly this time base and does not run any more; the halt deadman SM-06 walks the table after about 10 ms and the watchdog SM-01 resets after about 160 … 283 ms, or, once the system time runs again (debugger halt and resume), the period check resets. (b) bspLpspi Lpspi.cpp: every wait is bounded by a poll budget as well (112 polls per µs of the time-out, the fastest core of the family), so a transfer ends also when the system time stands still progress-checks, safety-progress, lpspi board passed (no false alarm, also across a J-Link exit) (DWT CYCCNT stopped): safe reaction, not by kind 4 - 2026-10-03 WATCHDOG RESET: outputs off, 2026-10-04 SM-06 expired (_expired = 1, T_EN = 0, CYCCNT standing), the reset then came as kind 1 because the debugger's halt and resume restarted the system time; a wake-up of the safety task independent of the system time is for after release R1. The CAN reception time-outs stay on the system time and are supervised through (a) for a slow or fast one

docs.title: 9. Proposed assumptions of use
docs.text:
Numbers are assigned by the maintainer (AoU-24/25 are proposed in fmea.md, AoU-26 … AoU-29 in tool-classification.md, AoU-30 is in the concept; other tasks of the same wave may propose more).

ID Assumption AoU-DFA-a The integrator confirms that the MCU's own power-on and low-voltage reset (or an external supply supervisor) brings the MCU into reset before its supply leaves the range in which the MCU manufacturer guarantees correct operation. neXtBSW's supply check (SM-20) runs on the same die and is credited only for a drift while the die still works correctly (DF-01). AoU-DFA-b The stage-1 mechanisms detect faults that stop, divert or delay the program flow, or raise an exception, on an independent time base. They do not detect a core fault that computes wrong results on a correct program flow (DF-06). If the integrator's hardware metrics need that coverage, he provides it — a core self-test required by the MCU manufacturer's safety manual, an external challenge-response watchdog (AoU-13) or a second channel. AoU-DFA-c The run-time register, MPU and safe-outputs checks compare with the configured values: they detect a change after start, not a wrong configuration (DFA-5). The integrator verifies the configuration itself — inactive levels, safe_off declarations, dead times, MPU regions — against his design and on his hardware (AoU-06, AoU-07, AoU-10).

docs.title: 11. Review questions of the architecture (section 11)
docs.text:
This task changed no code, no generator, no configuration and no bootloader: one new document. The questions are answered for the analysis and for the proposed measures.

  1. Board without an SBC? Yes. No stage-1 measure relies on the SBC (DF-35); the independence the analysis credits comes from three on-chip clocks. The loss of independence from the die without an external watchdog is stated (AoU-13, AoU-DFA-b).
  2. Different crystal and system clock? Yes. The clock-error band of DF-02 is stated relative to the nominal period, not to 80 MHz; DFA-6 (a) and DFA-2 compare against the LPO, not against a frequency constant.
  3. Different derivative, S32K3 / STM32 / Cortex-R? Yes. The analysis is by resource class (supply, clocks, memories, timers); the S32K1 registers are named as the instance of the family port. Another family repeats the resource list of section 4 with its own peripherals; DFA-2 and DFA-3 are family-port measures.
  4. Two or more CAN buses? Yes. DF-32 and SPI-1 are per bus; SM-32 and SM-34 are per bus instance.
  5. Several tasks and free priorities? Yes; DF-36, DF-37, DF-43 and DFA-1 are exactly about what a task set can do to the mechanisms. The only fixed rule used is above_application for the safety task, which the configuration already checks.
  6. Every new value in one configuration level? No new value. DFA-1's deadline is derived from the existing module parameter modules.safeMemory.rom_check_period_ms; DFA-6 (a) derives its bound from the safety task period and the LPO range already in the configuration.
  7. Host test with its own test profile? Each proposed measure names its host test with built-in faults. The document itself is checked by the consistency script (section 10.2).
  8. Tool core free of Qt, messages with a YAML path? DFA-4 (a) is an nxconfig warning with the YAML path of the PWM group.
  9. Device driver granularity? Not applicable — no driver changed; the SPI part only hands SPI-1/SPI-2 to a separate task.
  10. Placement under platforms/? Not applicable — no new file there.

docs.text:
Title Failure analysis of the stage-1 mechanisms Issue 2, 2026-10-04 (issue 1: 2026-09-21, written against dev at 63ea900, with its update blocks up to 2026-10-03) Author issue 1 and the tasks of the update blocks (section 12.1) (issue 2) — author side Approver the safety manager: issue 1 accepted in a separate task, released with its updates up to a separate task on 2026-09-30; the state at dev aaa22c86 reviewed in the confirmation review CM-02 (record reviews/records/CR-02-1.md (not published, available on request), the safety manager under D-01, 2026-10-04, accepted with conditions); issue 2 released on 2026-10-04 in the re-check of the findings F-01 … F-11 in CR-02-1 (steps 6 and 7 at dev efc474ea: all closed, verdict accepted, CM-02 closed; D-01, without independence) Status issue 2 accepted (released 2026-10-04 in the re-check of CM-02, record CR-02-1); update after it, as the reviewer decided there (BRD a): captures of B2 and B15 in the repository, B16 (a), (c), (d) and the LVD reset with separate tasks at a separate task, the caveat of B17 in SM-10, SM-13 and N3; update: upkeep after the re-check (finding RN, open point N7, in review); update (section 1.3: a clause reference instead of the usual figures for the classes) accepted by the safety manager in the re-check of 2026-10-08 (C8, record CR-02-1; D-01, without independence) Change history section 12 (the update blocks of issue 1 unchanged in 12.1, the issues in 12.2)

Working state: dev at c0928380 (after v1.0.0-rc1) Readers: the maintainer as architect, the integrator, and the contributors of separate tasks. Language: English, like the rest of doc/. Licence rule: the standard is licensed to the maintainer since 2026-09-22 and compared in iso26262-gap.md (not published, available on request); this document cites it by part and clause only and restates nothing of its text (issue 1 said it was not available).

This document is the failure analysis that the safety concept concept.md hands to a separate task (concept section 10.1). It uses the concept's identifiers unchanged: ASG-* (assumed safety goals), AoU-* (assumptions of use), SM-* (mechanisms), F1–F8 (findings) and G1–G6 (coverage gaps). New findings of this analysis continue the concept's numbering as F9–F16; they are listed in section 6 and referenced from concept section 9.1.

Scope: stage 1 only (maintainer, 2026-09-21: strict separation). Analysed are the mechanisms of the base software whose detection runs on the MCU and uses only the MCU, its peripherals and the configuration (concept section 1.4). Not analysed, and not credited: the device-dependent mechanisms SM-33 (transceiver status through the SBC) and SM-52 (SBC reset counter), and the device packages SM-40 … SM-43 — they are the concept section 13. Where a stage-1 mechanism would be weakened by the absence of a stage-2 mechanism, this document says so instead of counting the stage-2 one.

docs.text: Question of the task Answer Mechanisms analysed 36 blocks in section 3: the 31 credited stage-1 mechanisms - the 29 of issue 1 (SM-01 … SM-07, SM-10 … SM-17, SM-18 … SM-22, SM-23 … SM-25, SM-30 … SM-32, SM-50, SM-51, SM-53) and since then SM-34 and SM-55 - and 5 not credited: SM-26, SM-27 (active short), SM-58 (hardware threshold), SM-59 (low-voltage reset), SM-60 (FlexNVM lock) Scope for Release R1 (v1.0.0-rc1) credited for Release R1 are the 31 mechanisms above, with the classes of section 3; SM-26, SM-27, SM-58, SM-59 and SM-60 are analysed but not claimed (most of them host verified only, as their blocks say) and carry no class. F4 stays open until the class SYSTEM_CLOCK exists (AN-004) F5 (SPI as common cause) decided: not a stage-1 problem — no credited mechanism uses SPI. Assigned to G5 (bus instance in the device context word, correlation in handle()) and dependent-failure analysis (shared resource); no separate SPI supervision in stage 1 (section 5.3) New findings F9 safety-task period unsupervised · F10 RTE task activation unsupervised · F11 ECC poll incomplete · F12 watchdog configuration check incomplete · F13 no reset-loop limit in stage 1 · F14 internal-supply read failures unlimited · F15 safety modules without host test · F16 ADC reference tolerance is a silent gain error (section 6) Proposed tasks six (section 7), plus additions to separate tasks and G5 Status after a later change F9 addressed by the period part of SM-04 (section 3.1): every safety cycle compares its distance to the previous one with the LPTMR, a free-running counter on the 1 kHz LPO clock that the scheduler does not use. The guaranteed detection time of a check in the safety task is 17 ms (nominal 10 ms) as long as the task runs; a cycle that comes later reports itself before its checks, a task that stops stays SM-01's (section 2). Host verified with mutants; board checks B4 and B7 passed 2026-09-22 (section 8.1) Status after a later change T2 done: F11 closed (ECC flags cleared, source in the event context), F12 closed for the watchdog, F14 closed (read-failure limit of SM-20), SM-04 with six checkpoints; F12 for the deadman: host verified, target binding pending - issue 2: bound by an earlier change and proven on the board by the fault injection of a separate task (F12 closed, AN-012). Board check B6 passed 2026-09-22; B5 run 2026-09-24 (shows only that no flag survives a reset, 8.1) Status after a later change T3 done, F15 closed: safety-gate (SM-11: real SafetyManager::cyclic, gate and supervisor on an MPU register model) and safe-io (SM-21/SM-22: real SafeIo, bspIo driver and supervisor on a PORT/GPIO register model with the PCR lock), each with 9 built-in faults that are all detected. docs.title: 1.1 What is analysed per mechanism
docs.text:
For each mechanism, one table with the fields the task asks for:

Field Content Faults considered the failures of the element the mechanism is meant to catch (fault model of the concept, made concrete), and the failures it explicitly does not catch Detection what the code reads or compares, where, and how often Reaction safe state per concept section 3: S1, S1 held, S1 + S2, S3; who decides (always SafeSupervisor::handle() unless stated) Times detection time (fault present → event raised), reaction time (event → reaction in effect), and the minimum FTTI served: the shortest fault tolerance time for which the mechanism can be relied on today (section 1.2) Diagnostic coverage class and justification (section 1.3) Latent faults of the mechanism how a failure of the mechanism itself is noticed, and after how long Evidence test IDs from tools/test/tests.yaml (run with .venv/Scripts/python tools/test -k <id>), target-artefact tests, and board runs recorded in CHANGELOG.md with their date Residual / action what remains, with the finding or task that carries it

A mechanism is a software safety mechanism: the analysis asks what the software detects and how fast it reacts, not how often the hardware fails. Failure rates, the single-point and latent-fault metrics, and the manufacturer's coverage claims for the MCU's own hardware features (ECC, watchdog, MPU, CRC unit) are the integrator's (AoU-09); the MCU manufacturer's safety manual for the S32K1 family is not available to this project, so every hardware coverage claim below is a claim about how neXtBSW uses the feature, not about the feature itself.

docs.title: 1.2 Time terms
docs.text:
These are the usual terms of the field, explained in our own words (issue 1 said the standard was not consulted; issue 2: the terms agree with the fault tolerant time interval and the fault handling time interval that concept 7.2 issue 3 uses, proposal C7 of the gap analysis; the standard is cited by part and clause only):

  • Detection time — from the moment the fault is present to the moment a mechanism raises its event.
  • Reaction time — from the event to the moment the reaction has taken effect (outputs de-energised for S1; the MCU in reset for S2).
  • Fault tolerance time (FTT) — the time the item tolerates the fault before a hazard can occur. It belongs to the integrator's item (AoU-01), not to neXtBSW.
  • Minimum FTTI served — detection time + reaction time, worst case, as this analysis can bound it today. An integrator may rely on the mechanism for a goal only if his FTT is longer (AoU-05).

Times are given in two forms where they differ:

  • nominal — with the demo's constants and the safety task running at its period (the concept's section 7.2 values);
  • guaranteed — what the element itself detects if the timing assumption breaks. Today these differ for every check in the safety task (F9, section 2).

Reaction times: S1 (safe outputs walk) is computed at well under 1 µs at 80 MHz; on the board the walk from the timer to the gate-driver enable is bounded at ≤ 21 µs (B3, oscilloscope 2026-09-22; a tighter bound of ≤ 2 µs of 2026-09-28 has its captures outside the repository, AN-008), so the computed value stays computed (F8). S2 brings the MCU into reset within the reset sequence of the core; the restart time afterwards is measured (B2, section 8.1: up to 1 077 ms through the watchdog path, 858 ms through a fault handler, the stated values) and does not add to the time to de-energise, but it is the time the ECU is out of service.

docs.title: 1.3 Diagnostic coverage: classes, not percentages
docs.text:
The concept forbids invented numbers (concept section 0), and the manufacturer data that a quantitative figure would rest on is not available. The coverage of each mechanism is therefore given as an ordinal class with the justification written out, so that a reader can disagree with the reasoning rather than with a number:

Class Meaning in this document high the mechanism checks the whole property it guards, by comparison with a reference that is independent of the fault, at a fixed interval (or on every access), and a failure of the mechanism itself is either detected or ends in a safe reaction medium the whole property is checked, but with a known blind spot that a realistic fault can fall into: sampling instead of continuous checking, a tolerance band, a reference that shares a cause with the checked value, or a part of the fault modes excluded low only a small part of the elements or fault modes is checked (demonstration scope, one pin, one path) reaction the mechanism does not detect anything; it is judged by whether it takes effect when called (SM-23 … SM-25, SM-53) none the fault is not covered by any stage-1 mechanism

The standard rates the diagnostic coverage of safety mechanisms per hardware element and technique in its informative annex 5-Annex D (with 11-5.1.12 for memories and 11-5.2.4 for analogue parts); the reader finds those ratings in his own copy of the standard. This document does not map its classes to them: the class is an engineering judgement about neXtBSW's use of a feature. Issue 2 (N1 closed, CM-02 decision Z2, measure M3): the gap analysis iso26262-gap.md (not published, available on request) section 3 answers the question - there is no direct mapping of these classes to the figures expected for the hardware metrics; a figure needs each mechanism re-based on the hardware element it diagnoses, the technique and its test interval (measure M2). The classes therefore stay as they are for Release R1, which makes no safety claim, and the hardware metrics stay with the integrator (AoU-09, N2). M2 is task, after Release R1 and before the first ASIL B release.

docs.title: 1.4 Evidence notation
docs.text:
• test-id — a test entry in tools/test/tests.yaml. host tests run the real production file against a model or stubs; target tests inspect the built ELF.
  • board YYYY-MM-DD — a board run recorded in CHANGELOG.md under that date.
  • review — the claim rests on reading the code at 63ea900 only; there is no test that would fail if the code broke. These are the weak spots of the evidence and are collected in F15.

docs.title: 2. The timing basis, corrected (F9)
docs.text:
The concept (section 7.2) gives 10 ms as the detection latency of every check in the safety task. That is the nominal value. The analysis looked for what guarantees it and found nothing below the watchdog:

  • The safety task is scheduled with scheduleAtFixedRate(…, SYSTEM_CYCLE_TIME = 10, …) (ecu/application/src/systems/SafetySystem.cpp; project value modules.safeLifecycle.task_period_ms since an earlier change). No code compares the distance between two safety cycles with a time base.
  • The watchdog is serviced every WATCHDOG_CYCLIC_COUNTER = 8 safety cycles (derived from modules.safeLifecycle.watchdog_timeout_ms and the period since an earlier change) and fires after 250 ms. It therefore fires only when 8 × (actual cycle) > 250 ms, i.e. when the actual cycle exceeds 31.25 ms.
  • The watchdog runs in timeout mode (Watchdog::enableWatchdog sets no WIN), so a safety task that runs too fast is not caught by the hardware either; SM-03 only counts calls of the service function.

Consequence: a safety task that runs at any period between 10 and 31.25 ms — through a wrong period, a starving higher-priority interrupt load, a clock plan error that slows the OS tick, or a timer fault — is not detected, and every "10 ms" latency in section 3 becomes up to 31.25 ms plus the reaction. The table below uses both values.

Quantity Nominal Guaranteed today detection latency of a check in the safety task 10 ms 31.25 ms SM-19 (10 consecutive failures) 100 ms 312.5 ms SM-20 (full multiplexer round, 6 cycles) 60 ms 187.5 ms SM-03 / SM-02 (every 8 cycles) 80 ms 250 ms SM-01 watchdog 250 ms 250 ms (hardware counter on the LPO clock) SM-06 deadman 10 ms 10 ms (hardware counter, LPIT)

The two hardware counters (SM-01, SM-06) are the only times that do not depend on the safety task keeping its period. Closing F9 — a check of the safety task's own period against a free-running hardware timer, or the watchdog's window mode — turns every "guaranteed" value back into the nominal one (proposed task T1, section 7).

Since an earlier change (period part of SM-04, section 3.1). Every safety cycle starts with a comparison of its distance to the previous cycle start against the LPTMR, counting on the LPO clock (the watchdog's oscillator, independent of the core clock, the OS tick and the OpenBSW system time). The bound is derived from the nominal period (10 ms), the tolerated lateness of a cycle start (2 ms, an assumption until B4) and the data-sheet range of the LPO: an interval of 17 ms or more is always reported, one of 12 ms or less never. Over each window of 7 cycles (the watchdog service interval, 8 before a later change) the sum must reach 59 ticks (68 before a later change), so a task that runs too fast, or a timer that runs too slow or stopped, is reported as well. What "guaranteed" means now:

  • while the safety task runs, two consecutive runs of every check are at most 17 ms apart, or the late cycle raises SAFETY_CYCLE_PERIOD_VIOLATION (S1 + S2) at its own start, before its checks run;
  • a task that stops is still detected by SM-01 only (250 ms). A stall that ends before the watchdog fires is reported when it ends, not after 17 ms: the check has no interrupt of its own (a hardware deadline needs a vector in the family's start-up code, proposed task T1b, section 7). SM-06 covers a stall of the whole software > 10 ms on boards with a power stage.
Quantity Nominal Guaranteed before a later change Guaranteed since an earlier change (task running) detection latency of a check in the safety task 10 ms 31.25 ms 17 ms SM-19 (10 consecutive failures) 100 ms 312.5 ms 170 ms SM-20 (full multiplexer round, 6 cycles) 60 ms 187.5 ms 102 ms SM-03 / SM-02 (every 7 cycles since an earlier change, 8 before) 70 ms (80 ms before a later change) 250 ms 119 ms (136 ms before a later change) SM-01 watchdog 250 ms 250 ms 250 ms (unchanged: the stop case) SM-06 deadman 10 ms 10 ms 10 ms

The sections of section 3 keep their original "guaranteed" statements; section 3.7 gives the values since an earlier change.

SM-01 over the LPO range (issue 2). The 250 ms of the watchdog are the nominal LPO; over the LPO range of the derivative (mcudb clock.lpo, S32K1xx 113 … 139 kHz) the time-out lies between 230 and about 283 ms (derived from WDOG_TOVAL, hsi-s32k1xx.md). The service interval of 7 safety cycles is derived at the fastest LPO, so the watchdog never fires early; the worst case to the reset is about 283 ms (concept 7.2 issue 3).

docs.title: 2.1 Faults of the time bases of the supervision (issue 2)
docs.text:
The mechanisms of this section run on three time bases: the safety task on the OpenBSW system time (DWT on ARMv7-M), SM-01 and the period part of SM-04 on the LPO, SM-06 on the LPIT's functional clock (SIRC). Issue 1 assumed these clocks; the dependent failure analysis (dfa.md DF-05, DFA-2, DFA-6) and the board of 2026-10-03/04 give what happens when one of them fails. The rows are those of concept 7.2 issue 3; every time says whether it is a constant, derived or measured.

Fault of a time base What reacts Detection Outputs de-energised Evidence OpenBSW system time stops (for example DEMCR.TRCENA cleared) SM-06, then SM-01 - not the period check of SM-04 (kind 4): the safety task is scheduled on this time base and does not run any more (DFA-6, corrected by the board) SM-06 after its 10 ms (constant of the family port), independent of the system time after about 10 ms (SM-06 walks the table); the reset follows through SM-01 after about 160 … 283 ms (derived: the watchdog time-out over the LPO range minus at most one service interval of 70 ms) board 2026-10-03/04 (B5: WATCHDOG RESET: outputs off, SM-06 expired, CYCCNT standing); progress-checks, safety-progress OpenBSW system time slow or fast while it runs SM-04, kinds 4 and 5 (DFA-6 (a)) at the end of a window of the period check (eval board: 7 cycles, 70 ms), against the LPTMR on the LPO as SM-04: S1 + S2 host (progress-checks, safety-progress); board: no false alarm, also across a J-Link exit LPIT functional clock gated (PCC) SM-17 the next access to the LPIT is a bus fault, within one poll of the halt guard, about 1 ms (derived from the poll period) about 1 ms plus the walk (derived) board 2026-10-03 (B2: HARD FAULT RESET: outputs off) LPIT functional clock too slow SM-06 progress check (DFA-2) the deadman's counter must change within a budget of two LPIT ticks per safety cycle (derived from the clock plan, 22 polls on the eval board); a counter that stands still or moves too slowly is DEADMAN_CONFIGURATION_ERROR field 0x100 within a few safety cycles plus the walk (S1 + S2) board 2026-10-04 (SIRCDIV2 /64, deadman 640 ms instead of 10 ms: SAFETY RESET (DEADMAN_CONFIGURATION_ERROR, fields 0x100)); lpit-deadman-progress, safety-progress SIRC lost while the core runs - residual risk DF-05 none in time; SM-01 by its hardware reset SM-06 runs on the same clock and stops; no log line and no walk were observed not shown before the watchdog reset, at most about 283 ms (derived from the watchdog time-out); then the pins in their reset state (AoU-07) board 2026-10-03 (B2b: hardware reset of the watchdog, RCM_SRS 0x20, no line, no walk); dfa.md DF-05, safety case D-16; investigation and architecture with a separate task after Release R1

The integrator takes the last row's time for his FTTI or provides an independent shut-off path (AoU-13, concept 7.2). SM-01 and SM-06 carry these faults in their blocks (latent faults, residual) since issue 2.

docs.title: SM-01 — MCU watchdog
docs.text: Field Content Faults considered the safety task stops: endless loop or deadlock at equal or higher priority, scheduler or OS tick dead, interrupt storm, core clock lost (the watchdog counts on the LPO clock, CS[CLK] = 1, independent of the core clock). Not considered by this mechanism: a slowed safety task (F9), a wrong flow inside the task that still reaches the service (SM-04), a service from the wrong place (SM-03), a service that comes too early (no window mode) Detection hardware time-out 250 ms at the nominal LPO (230.2 ms at the fastest, about 283 ms at the slowest LPO of the derivative; derived, section 2); serviced from the safety task every 7 cycles (derived at the fastest LPO; 8 before) Reaction watchdog warning interrupt (CS[INT] = 1, IRQ 22) → its handler walks the safe outputs table as its first action (SM-17), then the watchdog reset (S2). If interrupts are masked when it expires (a stuck critical section), only the reset de-energises: the pins return to their reset state, which is safe only under AoU-07 Times detection ≤ 250 ms after the last service at the nominal LPO, ≤ about 283 ms over the LPO range (derived, concept 7.2 issue 3); reaction < 1 µs (walk, computed; board bound ≤ 21 µs, B3) or the reset. Minimum FTTI served: > 283 ms (issue 1: > 250 ms, the nominal LPO only) Diagnostic coverage medium. Loss of execution of the safety task is detected completely and independently of the core clock. Blind spots: the task slowed below the 31.25 ms bound (F9; since an earlier change covered by SM-04 against the same LPO), too-early service (no window; since an earlier change the SM-04 window covers a service interval that is too short, against an independent clock, as an event instead of a reset), and a common cause on the chip (same supply, same die; AoU-13). SM-04 also covers a stopped LPO, which would stop the watchdog silently Latent faults of the mechanism watchdog unable to reset: SM-07 at every start. Configuration drift: SM-02 every 70 ms (nominal, 80 ms before a later change), since an earlier change including INT, WIN, PRES and UPDATE — a cleared CS[INT] is now SAFE_WATCHDOG_CONFIGURATION_ERROR (context bit 2) instead of silently removing the de-energising before the reset (F12 closed for the watchdog) Evidence nxconfig-watchdog (relation 3 × service ≤ time-out); safe-supervisor (the hold services the watchdog); safe-watchdog (real SafeWatchdog.cpp and family check on a WDOG register model, every field falsified singly, service bracket); board 2026-09-18 (halt > 250 ms: watchdog warning handler walked the table, EXC_RETURN 0xffffffed, DRV_EN off); board 2026-09-21 (safety wdg endless loop → watchdog reset, wake-up source 0x00000006) Residual / action F9 → SM-04; board check B6 passed 2026-09-22 (8.1). Residual risk DF-05 (issue 2, CM-02 decision Z3): after a loss of the SIRC the halt deadman SM-06 stands with its clock, nothing walks the table, and SM-01's hardware reset after up to about 283 ms (derived) is the only reaction - the outputs are not shown to be de-energised before it (board 2026-10-03, B2b; section 2.1). Carried by dfa.md DF-05 and safety case D-16 (after Release R1); the integrator takes this time or provides an independent shut-off path (AoU-13). A stopped system time (section 2.1) also ends in SM-01's reset after about 160 … 283 ms, but SM-06 has de-energised after about 10 ms

docs.title: SM-02 — Watchdog configuration check
docs.text: Field Content Faults considered the watchdog is disabled, switched to another clock, or its time-out changed after start Detection checkWatchdogConfiguration(250 ms) in SafeWatchdog::cyclic(), every 7 safety cycles (8 before a later change): CS[EN], CS[CLK] and TOVAL against the expected values; since an earlier change in the same call the family check checkWatchdogControl() (platforms/s32k1xx/port/safety/safeSupervisionCheck): CS[INT] against the requested value, CS[WIN] = 0, CS[PRES] = 0, CS[UPDATE] = 1 (as enableWatchdog() writes it) Reaction SAFE_WATCHDOG_CONFIGURATION_ERROR → S1 + S2, since an earlier change with the differing fields in the context word (1 driver check, 2 INT, 4 WIN, 8 PRES, 16 UPDATE; ValueMonitor with a uint32_t context). The reset reconfigures the watchdog, so a transient corruption is healed; a permanent one loops (F13) Times nominal 70 ms (80 ms before a later change), guaranteed 250 ms; reaction < 1 µs. Minimum FTTI served: > 250 ms (but the watchdog itself still covers the stop case) Diagnostic coverage medium. Since an earlier change every configuration field that changes the watchdog's effect is checked: disable, clock, time-out, warning interrupt, window, prescaler, update. Remaining blind spots: the check is sampled every 7 safety cycles, and CS[UPDATE] stays 1, so the watchdog remains reconfigurable at run time — a change is detected, not prevented Latent faults of the mechanism a check that is skipped is seen by the watchdog service bracket of SM-04 only if the service is skipped with it Evidence safe-watchdog (real SafeWatchdog.cpp with the family check and the real SafeSupervisor on a WDOG register model — the configuration of enableWatchdog passes, each field falsified singly is the event with that field in the context; mutants: family check not called, INT not compared, PRES left out, context dropped). Reaction: safe-supervisor. The OpenBSW driver in external/openbsw/platforms/s32k1xx/safety/safeBspMcuWatchdog stays outside our tests Residual / action F12 closed for the watchdog by an earlier change (T2). Open: whether UPDATE = 0 after start is wanted (needs a neXtBSW copy of the OpenBSW driver, which is never changed in the submodule); board check B6

docs.title: SM-03 — Watchdog over-service check
docs.text: Field Content Faults considered the watchdog is serviced by something other than the safety task (a runaway loop that calls the service function) Detection the service counter of bsp::Watchdog must advance by exactly one between two checks (every 7 cycles, 8 before a later change) Reaction SAFE_WATCHDOG_SERVICE_DEVIATION → S1 + S2 Times nominal 70 ms (80 ms before a later change), guaranteed 250 ms. Minimum FTTI served: > 250 ms Diagnostic coverage low. Only services through Watchdog::serviceWatchdog() are counted; a runaway that writes the refresh word to WDOG->CNT directly is invisible. There is no window, so timing of the service is not checked at all Latent faults of the mechanism none Evidence safe-watchdog (over-service is SAFE_WATCHDOG_SERVICE_DEVIATION); reaction safe-supervisor Residual / action the window mode (T1 alternative) would replace most of this check; F15 closed for safeWatchdog (T3)

docs.title: SM-04 — Safety manager sequence monitor
docs.text:
Field Content Faults considered control flow through the safety cycle is not the intended one: the cycle is entered twice without being left, or left without being entered; the same for the watchdog service bracket Detection safetyManagerSequenceMonitor (OpenBSW safeMonitor::Sequence) with, since an earlier change, six checkpoints per safety cycle: ENTER, MEMORY_CHECKED (after safe_memory::cyclic), SYSTEM_CHECKED (safeSystem.cyclic), IO_CHECKED (safeIo.cyclic), PERIPHERALS_CHECKED (deadman configuration, SM-06), LEAVE; safeWatchdogSequenceMonitor around the service Reaction SAFETY_MANAGER_SEQUENCE_DEVIATION / SAFE_WATCHDOG_SEQUENCE_DEVIATION → S1 + S2 Times a checkpoint out of order is seen at the next hit, a missing LEAVE at the next ENTER: nominal 10 ms, guaranteed 31.25 ms (17 ms since an earlier change). Since an earlier change a seventh checkpoint PERIOD_CHECKED follows the period check (period part below) directly after ENTER Diagnostic coverage medium (was low before a later change). A cycle that returns early or skips one of the sub-checks hits the next checkpoint out of order. Blind spots: a sub-check that returns early inside itself still reaches its checkpoint; the watchdog service (every 7 cycles) has only its own bracket. A cycle that never starts is SM-01's Latent faults of the mechanism none Evidence safety-cycle (real SafetyManager and SafeSupervisor, 24 cycles without event, early end and a skipped sub-check are deviations; mutant: IO checkpoint removed); reaction safe-supervisor; the service bracket safe-watchdog Residual / action closed by an earlier change (T2)

SM-04, period part (finding F9). The sequence monitor answers "in which order"; since an earlier change the same mechanism also answers "at which period" for the safety cycle. Both parts share the reaction (S1 + S2) and the place in the cycle; the period part has its own event, time base and evidence:

Field Content Faults considered the safety task runs at a period other than its nominal one while it still runs: a wrong period in the code, starvation by interrupt load or long critical sections, a clock plan error or a fault of the OS tick (SysTick) or of the OpenBSW system time that stretches or compresses it; too fast as well as too slow. Latent faults of the mechanism: the timer stopped, re-clocked, switched to another mode, its clock gate or the LPO1K clock off (F9) Detection SafetyManager::checkCyclePeriod() as the first step of every safety cycle, directly after ENTER: the family's timer configuration is checked (checkCycleTimer(): PCC clock gate, CSR[TEN], time counter / free running / no interrupt / no DMA, PSR = LPO1K with prescaler bypass, SIM_LPOCLKS[LPO1KCLKEN]), then the LPTMR counter is read and handed to the hardware-independent CyclePeriodCheck (ecu/safety/safeWatchdog): interval to the previous cycle start > 14 ticks → kind 1; window of 7 intervals (the watchdog service interval; 8 intervals and 68 ticks before a later change) < 59 ticks → kind 2; deviating timer configuration → kind 3 (the timer is not read then). Bounds derived in SafetyManager.cpp from the period (10 ms), the tolerated lateness of a cycle start (2 ms, CYCLE_LATENESS_MS) and the LPO range of the derivative (mcudb clock.lpo, S32K1xx 113 … 139 kHz, i.e. 0.882 … 1.086 ticks per ms; 141 kHz / 1.102 before); a counter difference misses the true time by less than one tick Time base LPTMR0, 16-bit time counter, free running, on LPO1K_CLK (PSR[PCS] = 01, prescaler bypassed): 1 tick = 1 ms nominal, wrap after 65 s. The LPO is the watchdog's oscillator: always on, no SCG divider, no PCC clock select, never the core clock, so it does not depend on the project's clock plan. In time counter mode the LPTMR stops while the core is halted — a debugger halt is no period violation, like for the watchdog. Not the OS tick, not the OpenBSW system time (DWT, on ARMv6-M LPIT channel 0) and not LPIT channel 1 (SM-06) Reaction SAFETY_CYCLE_PERIOD_VIOLATION (appended to the event list) → S1 + S2, context: kind in bits 31..24, ticks resp. deviating fields in bits 23..0. The late cycle reacts before its own checks run Times an interval of 17 ms or more is always reported (17 ms at the slowest LPO of the data sheet are 15.008 ticks), one of 12 ms or less (period + lateness) never, at any LPO; detection at the start of the late cycle. A window is always reported below a mean period of 7.6 ms; a stopped timer is reported at the end of the first window (≤ 7 cycles). Minimum FTTI served for the checks of the safety task: > 17 ms plus reaction while the task runs; a task that stops is SM-01's (250 ms) Diagnostic coverage medium. A slowed or accelerated safety task is detected against an independent oscillator at every cycle, including faults of the mechanism's own timer (configuration re-checked at every cycle, a stopped counter seen by the window). Blind spots: detection only when the late cycle runs (no interrupt of its own, so a stall that ends before the watchdog fires is reported at its end, not after 17 ms — T1b); the tolerance band between 12 and 17 ms, which is wide because of the LPO's data-sheet range; a common drift of LPO and core clock in the same direction; the LPTMR shares the die (AoU-13). On ARMv6-M with the deadman (MCR[DBG_EN] = 1) the OpenBSW system time keeps counting through a debugger halt, so the scheduler catches up with a burst after the halt, which ends in a window report and a reset — a debugging restriction of S32K11x projects with a power stage, not a safety gap Latent faults of the mechanism the timer's configuration and clock enables are re-checked in every cycle (kind 3); a counter that stops without a configuration change is seen by the window (kind 2, value 0). The derived bounds are static assertions of the build (window longer than one interval, window within one wrap) and are recomputed independently by cycle-period-constants Evidence cycle-period-check (hardware-independent part with two own test profiles: 32-bit counter at 5 ms and 16-bit; reference sample, bounds, wrap-around, window, catch-up, stopped counter; five mutants); lptmr-cycle-timer (start sequence of [RM13] 49.5.1, latched read, each configuration field falsified singly, clock gate off without LPTMR access; five mutants); safety-cycle (real SafetyManager with the real check: 60 runs of 400 cycles with LPO 0.883 … 1.102 kHz, every phase and random lateness up to 2 ms without a report; 17 ms after the previous cycle reported before the memory check at every LPO; a task at 20 ms reported at its first slow cycle; 5 ms and 7 ms at the fastest LPO reported at the end of the first window; stopped timer; configuration deviation without read; five mutants); cycle-period-constants (values from the configuration, no literal in the code; bounds recomputed); reaction safe-supervisor. Board: B4 and B7 passed 2026-09-22 (issue 1 said "no board run yet"; 8.1) Residual / action since an earlier change the reset of a period violation writes one synchronous console line; a stopped system time (debugger cleared DEMCR.TRCENA) stops the safety task itself and is SM-01's (watchdog). Board checks B4 (cycle distance under load, confirms the 2 ms lateness; passed 2026-09-22 without GPIO measurement) and B7 (provoked violation; (a) to be repeated after a later change); T1b hardware deadline: the LPTMR compare interrupt as a deadman of the safety task (walk of the safe outputs table at the bound, independent of whether the task comes back) — needs the LPTMR vector in platforms/s32k1xx/port/main/src/bsp/startUp.S and in tools/bswgen (FAMILY_IRQ_HANDLERS), outside 's paths; the constants (period, lateness, LPO range) into their configuration levels: done with separate tasks. Issue 2: B4 and B7 (a) … (c) passed on the board 2026-09-22 (8.1; B7 (a) repeated with SetSkipDebugDeInit), B4 again 2026-10-03 for 32 min under UDS load without a report

SM-04, progress of the system time (finding DFA-6 of dfa.md, issue 2). Since an earlier change the period part has two more kinds: over the window of the period check the OpenBSW system time must advance like the LPTMR on LPO1K within the LPO range of the derivative, with a slack of one period plus the lateness (the one-off loss after a debugger exit). A system time that runs too slow is SAFETY_CYCLE_PERIOD_VIOLATION kind 4, one that runs too fast kind 5 (S1 + S2), at the end of a window (eval board: 7 cycles, 70 ms; ProgressSupervision.cpp). Not covered by these kinds: a system time that stops - the safety task is scheduled on it and does not run any more; SM-06 de-energises after about 10 ms and SM-01 resets after about 160 … 283 ms (section 2.1; board 2026-10-03/04, B5). Evidence: progress-checks, safety-progress (host, with mutants); board (no false alarm, also across a J-Link exit). A wake-up of the safety task that does not depend on the system time is for after Release R1 (dfa.md DFA-6).

docs.title: SM-05 — RTE run-time supervision
docs.text: Field Content Faults considered a task cycle takes longer than the task period, or a runnable longer than its own period. Not considered: a task that is not activated at all or activated late (starvation by higher priorities) — the RTE measures durations from the start of a cycle, and records the activation distance only as a statistic (RteSystem.cpp, "activation jitter"), without an event (F10) Detection measured per cycle in the generated RTE; latched once per measurement window; reported through the event mailbox to the safety task Reaction S3 (log only), by a project decision Times detection at the end of the offending cycle; delivery up to one safety cycle later. No de-energising reaction, so no FTTI is served Diagnostic coverage medium for overruns of activated tasks and runnables (every cycle, deadline from the configuration); none for missing or late activation Latent faults of the mechanism mailbox corruption and overflow are reported as own contexts Evidence rte-deadline (with mutants: >= instead of >, no latch, deadline from task period), safe-supervisor-mpu, safety-context, safety-context-elf; board 2026-09-21 (eighth part): load-test build reports RTE_TIMING_VIOLATION per window, no bus fault Residual / action F10 → (temporal freedom from interference). Whether S3 is admissible for a violation was open point 6 of concept section 9.4 (issue 2); concept issue 3 gives the answer of the gap analysis: S3 only where the condition cannot violate a safety requirement within the FTTI or the reaction is allocated to another element - here the application, AoU-18 (C18)

docs.title: SM-06 — Debug-halt / stall deadman
