docs.title: Hardware safety mechanisms
docs.text:
Baseline: v0.2.0

Standing. This document describes safety mechanisms that act without software — paths inside the MCU (or between a device and the MCU) that reach a safe condition even when no instruction is executed. It is a catalogue and an analysis, not a specification of what neXtBSW does today: at the time of writing none of the mechanisms below is used, and the document exists to say what is available, what it would cost and what it would buy.

Update (2026-09-30). The comparator path of section 2.2 is now configurable (section 2.4): a project can name a hardware threshold on a board signal, and the family port routes CMP0 to a fault input of the PWM timer. It is optional; no checked-in project uses it (the eval board has no meaningful signal at a comparator input, section 4), it is verified on the host and in a target build only, and nothing in this document credits it — the catalogue entry is SM-58 in concept.md 6.5, analysed in fmea.md, with no coverage claimed. The pin sources of section 2.1 (gate driver fault, SBC interrupt) are still.

Update (2026-09-30). The comparator path detects its own loss (section 2.5): a start test of the comparator output before the route exists, and a check of every register of the path plus the consistency of the output with the timer's fault latch in the 1 ms poll of the power stage; a finding forces the group inactive. Host verified only; still nothing credited.

Update (2026-09-30). A second hardware mechanism is now in use, and unlike the comparator path it is not optional: the family port s32k1xx switches the MCU's low-voltage detect reset on in every start (PMC_LVDSC1[LVDRE] = 1, decision of the safety responsible, anomaly AN-066). A VDD below VLVD (2.80 … 3.00 V) resets the MCU in hardware and holds it in reset until the supply is back; no instruction is involved. Catalogue entry SM-59 in concept.md 6.4, analysed in fmea.md, not credited; the supply margin a 3.3 V board has to keep is AoU-39. Register facts and what is not re-checked: hsi-s32k1xx.md 4.8 and H9.

Update (2026-09-30). The latched fault (FMS[FAULTF]) and the findings of section 2.5 reach the safe supervisor from the safety task through the narrow interface safeSupervisor/HwShutoff.h; the supervisor holds S1 until reset (no reset). The reader for the application exists; the RTE signal and the DTC need the generator and the application (section 2.6).

Update (2026-10-01, safety review H6). The path behind the comparator is no longer untested: once per start, with the timer running, every output masked and no pin muxed, the route is selected without its lock, the fault is tripped through the comparator forced by its DAC and cleared again (section 2.7). A failure is a finding of section 2.5 (group forced, reported as in section 2.6). Host verified only; still nothing credited.

Why it is separate from concept.md and fmea.md: those two argue the stage 1 safety element, whose mechanisms all share one property — they detect and react in software, from the safety task or a fault handler, and they therefore all depend on the assumption that code still runs (SM-01 covers the case where it does not). The mechanisms here break that dependency. They belong to a different argument and mixing them into the stage-1 tables would blur exactly the line that makes the stage-1 argument honest.

Board neutrality. The catalogue is written for the MCU family, not for one board. The eval board appears only as a worked example, in its own clearly marked section. A mechanism that exists only because of one board's wiring is a board fact, not an architecture decision.

docs.title: 1. Why a hardware path is worth having
docs.text:
Every switch-off path in stage 1 today ends in software:

Path Needs safe outputs table (SM-23) the safety task or a caller of enterSafeState() runs fault handlers (SM-17) the exception is taken and its handler runs halt deadman (SM-06) the LPIT interrupt is serviced gate driver reaction (SM-40, stage 2) the driver's cycle runs and an SPI transfer completes

All four fail together in the same class of fault: the core stops executing useful instructions (a lock-up, a runaway loop with interrupts masked, a clock loss on the core domain, a debugger halt). SM-01 — the external watchdog — is the only stage-1 answer, and it answers by resetting, which takes a reset time plus a restart before outputs are defined again.

A hardware path answers in nanoseconds, needs no code, and is unaffected by what the software is doing. It does not replace the software paths (it detects nothing by itself — something must assert it) but it removes the shared dependency that all of them have.

Two gaps in concept.md name this directly: G1 ("nothing reads back that S1 took effect") and the coverage note on ASG-01 ("no base-software mechanism compares what is commanded with what happens").

docs.title: 2.1 FTM fault inputs — PWM channels forced to a safe level in hardware
docs.text:
What it does. Each FlexTimer has fault inputs. An asserted fault input puts the PWM channels of that FTM into the state defined by FTM_POL and FTM_OUTINIT, in hardware, within the timer's clock domain. No software runs. This is the mechanism AN5303 §4.2 describes.

What it costs. One pin per fault source, and the pin loses whatever other function it had.

Configuration, from [RM13]:

Item Register Note Which channels react FTM_FLTCTRL[FAULTM] all channels, or only the even ones Enable per channel pair FTM_FLTCTRL[FAULTENx] per pair, not per channel Polarity of each input FTM_FLTPOL which level means "fault" Recovery FTM_MODE[FAULTM] automatic (fault gone → PWM returns) or manual (software must clear) Filter FTM_FLTCTRL[FFVAL], FFLTRxEN a glitch filter per input

Source of each fault input — this is the part that is easy to get wrong. SIM_FTMOPT0.FTMxFLTxSEL selects it, and the reference manual is explicit that the choice is per input:

"Selects the source of the FTM0 fault. Every bit means one fault input, respectively." 000b – FTMx_FLTx pin · 001b – TRGMUX_FTMx out

So for fault inputs 0, 1 and 2 there are two possible sources, chosen independently per input:

  • the dedicated pin (FTMx_FLT0/1/2), or
  • the trigger multiplexer output (TRGMUX_FTMx SEL1/SEL2/SEL3 → fault input 0/1/2).

Fault input 3 has no bit in FTMxFLTxSEL and therefore only the pin route (FTMx_FLT3).

Why the TRGMUX route matters. It widens the set of usable pins enormously. A pin that is not a FTMx_FLTx pin but is a TRGMUX_INn pin can still reach a fault input. It also allows non-pin sources — a comparator output (CMP0_COUT), an LPIT channel, an ADC conversion-complete — to force the bridge off in hardware. The TRGMUX input list is in [RM13] ch. 19; every FTM (0–3) has three TRGMUX-driven fault inputs.

Locking. TRGMUX_FTMx[LK] locks the register until the next reset. A safety-relevant routing should set it, and the register-check mechanism (SM-21/SM-22) should cover the registers involved.

docs.title: 2.2 Comparator (CMP0) — a threshold without the core
docs.text:
CMP0 compares an input against an internal DAC reference and produces CMP0_COUT, which is a TRGMUX input (in14). Combined with §2.1 this gives a complete hardware loop: an over-current or over-voltage crosses a threshold, and the bridge is off before any interrupt is taken. The comparison itself is analogue and continuous; nothing polls it.

This is the most interesting unused capability on the part, because it turns a measurement into a reaction without the ADC, the RTE or the safety task being involved.

Facts from [RM13] and [DS13], checked for a separate task: CMP0 has its own 8-bit DAC whose ladder uses either VDDA or the internal 1 V bandgap (45.1.3; DAC output = V_in / 256 × (VOSEL + 1), 45.8.2), up to eight inputs from pins (which pins per package: pin multiplexing CMP0_IN0..7), and its output is TRGMUX source 0x0E (Table 19-1). The fault inputs 0..2 of FTM0..FTM3 are TRGMUX_FTMx SEL1..SEL3 (Figure 19-2), each switched from its pin to the TRGMUX separately (SIM_FTMOPT0, 11.3.1.3). Data sheet limits (Table 44, -40 … 125 °C, high-speed mode): input offset at most 25 mV, DAC non-linearity at most 0.75 LSB, propagation delay at most 500 ns (small overdrive; 300 ns with a large one), settling of comparator and DAC at most 30 µs; bandgap 0.97 … 1.03 V (Table 8).

docs.title: 2.4 The comparator path as configured by an earlier change
docs.text:
Configuration, one value per level (checked by tools/nxconfig/hwthreshold.py, messages with YAML path):

Level Value Example derivative (mcudb) comparators[]: DAC bits, references, the limits above, which timer fault inputs the output reaches S32K142/144/146/148: CMP0, FTM0..3 inputs 0..2. Not described for the S32K116: its FTM0 has one fault input and the manual does not say which, so nothing is claimed board comparators.inputs[]: which pin is which comparator input and which board ADC entry's circuit is in front of it (signal); comparators.supply: the voltage at VDDA a shunt amplifier also wired to CMP0_IN3 project hw_thresholds.<name>: threshold in the unit of the signal (mA, mV), above/below, reference supply/bandgap, the PWM group, an optional glitch filter in ns DC link current above 40 A switches BRIDGE off

Derived, not configured. The pin voltage of the threshold comes from the inverse of the signal's characteristic (linear characteristics only). The DAC level is rounded towards the safe side: an above threshold trips at or below the configured value, a below threshold at or above it — never later. A falling characteristic swaps the direction at the pin, and the comparator output is inverted where the pin trips below the DAC. The first free fault input of the group's timer is used. nxconfig check prints per threshold the DAC level, the realised threshold, its band (offset + non-linearity, plus the bandgap tolerance; with the supply reference the supply's own tolerance is not included and is said so) and the worst-case reaction time.

Reaction and recovery. On a fault the FTM forces every channel of the group's pairs to its POL value — the inactive level, freewheel (47.5.18; FSTATE = 0, never tri-state). The fault control comes after software output control, dead-time insertion and output mask in the FTM's feature order (Figure 47-86), so it overrides SWOCTRL: a group whose safe state is an active short ends in freewheel on this fault, as partner-and-degraded.md 5.6 and 5.9 require. Recovery is manual only (MODE[FAULTM] = 10b): the outputs stay forced until a reset, the latching behaviour of every software path (SM-40). There is no service that clears the fault at run time.

Time. Worst case from the crossing at the pin to the forced outputs: comparator propagation (500 ns) plus the fault path of the FTM — 3 FTM input clocks without filter, 4 + FFVAL with the filter (Table 47-15, FLTPS = 0). At 64 MHz and a 200 ns filter (13 clocks): 766 ns. Computed, not measured.

Start-up order (family code platforms/s32k1xx/bsp/bspHwThreshold, called from the PWM driver's init()): comparator and DAC configured and switched on, the fault input switched to the TRGMUX (which still delivers 0), then the FTM configuration with fault control, the counter started, 30 µs settling, then the TRGMUX selection written and locked until reset (LK), and only then the pins are switched to the FTM. A threshold that is already exceeded at that moment reaches the fault input as a rising edge and should latch the fault at once — the manual describes fault detection as an edge; this is not verified on a target (section 5, point 6).

Checked at run time. The registers of the path join the register list of SafeIo (SM-22, one check per safety cycle): the FTM's MODE[FAULTM], FLTCTRL, FLTPOL and the FAULTEN bits of COMBINE, the TRGMUX selection with its lock, the fault source bit of SIM_FTMOPT0 and the comparator's C0/C1/C2. This matters because a comparator switched off reads as its INVT bit: for an above threshold that is "not exceeded" — a silent loss of the path that only the register check sees. A comparator that is on but broken (output stuck) is not detected by anything; that is point 3 of section 5.

What the software does not see. The fault is latched in the FTM (FMS[FAULTF], readable through hwThreshold::faultDetected()), but no module reports it to the supervisor or the application yet. The software paths keep commanding duties while the hardware holds the outputs; the drivers do not know why the bridge does not respond. : the safety task now reports it to the safe supervisor, which holds S1 until reset; the reader for the application exists, its RTE signal and DTC are open (section 2.6).

docs.title: 2.5 Detection of a lost or stuck comparator path
docs.text:
Safety review, point H5: a comparator switched off or stuck is an accepted residual risk of a separate task, its detection a follow-up. Correction: a comparator switched off does not trip in either direction - in disabled mode CMPO, the signal to the trigger mux, is 0 ([RM13] 45.7.1); only the register bit C0[COUT] reads INVT. The loss is silent for above and below thresholds alike.

Family code hwThreshold/HwThresholdMonitor.h (header only), three parts:

Part When What Finds start test once per start, in ComplementaryPwm::init() before prepare(): trigger mux still 0, timer not configured, pins not muxed - nothing reaches the fault input, no pulse on a power output DAC at VDDA (VOSEL 255, VRSEL 0); pin (+) against VDDA (-) must read 0, VDDA (+) against the pin (-) must read 1; 30 µs settling each; the comparator is left off for prepare() output stuck at "above" or at "not above" register check every 1 ms poll of the power stage (integration/HwThresholdWatch.h, after the debug halt guard in DebugHaltGuardSystem) CMP0 C0 (configuration bits, not the flags), C1, C2 round robin, TRGMUX_FTMx selection and LK, SIM_FTMOPT0 bit, MODE[FAULTM], FLTCTRL, FLTPOL, FAULTEN of the pairs switched off or reconfigured - the same registers as SM-22, ten times as often consistency the same poll C0[COUT] "above" (comparator on) on two polls in a row while FMS[FAULTF] is clear the route or the fault logic after the comparator is broken

A finding is latched until reset (one word of ordinary RAM: findings and their complement, written in one store; a word that fails the check reads as a finding). Reaction: the channels of the group are forced inactive through the software output control - at once in init() after a failed start test (before the counter runs and before a pin is muxed), and in every poll while anything is latched; that is the state the tripped hardware path would leave. The route is armed anyway, so a comparator stuck at "above" still trips the timer. What the ECU does about it is the safe supervisor's decision (section 2.6). Only a project with a hardware threshold has any of this code.

Limits. A comparator output that sticks at "not above" between two starts is not detected at run time: without a second, independent measurement of the signal a stuck output cannot be told from a quiet signal (that is plausibility G2). The start test needs the input further below VDDA than the comparator's offset plus hysteresis (data sheet: offset at most 25 mV); a signal at the rail fails it (fail-safe) - an assumption of use of the board. It uses the VDDA ladder, not the configured reference: the bandgap reference of a threshold is covered by the register check (VRSEL), not by the forced comparisons.

docs.title: 2.6 Report of the latched fault to the supervisor and the application
docs.text:
Safety review, point H7: the latched fault (FMS[FAULTF]) was reported to nobody; the report is this follow-up. The supervisor is reached through a new narrow interface of its own library, safeSupervisor/HwShutoff.h (family neutral - a "hardware shut-off path of a PWM group", whatever the family builds it from); no class layout, no event number and no existing reaction of the supervisor changes.

Step Where What detection safety task, every cycle (SafetyManager::checkSupervisionPeripherals(), family port, hwThreshold::shutoffContext) FMS[FAULTF] of the group's timer, the registers of the path read again (independent of the power stage poll, whose task may have stopped), and the findings latch of §2.5 (start test, consistency) report hwShutoff::report(context), safety context only context word: bit 0 = tripped, bits 23..8 = findings of the path, bits 31..24 = timer; only bits not reported before react reaction (decided by the supervisor library) HwShutoff.cpp log line, S1 held until reset without a reset: every safe output off (the gate driver enable with it), the ECU keeps running for the application, the tester and the fault memory. No reset because the hardware path latches until reset (H1: manual recovery only) - a reset would re-arm the bridge by itself. The return path of the register check (CHECK_REGISTER_ERROR "ok") does not leave S1 while a report is latched record protected RAM of the supervisor, two copies a mismatch reads as "everything reported" (fail-safe) and is written back so at the next report application hwShutoff::read(context), read only from any task the bits reported so far and whether the record is plausible - the reader for an RTE signal and a DTC

Open for the application (outside 's paths). The reader exists; the generated RTE does not call it yet and no DTC samples it. Needed: an RTE signal safety.hw_shutoff (boolean, 1 while anything is reported or the record is implausible) and safety.qlf.hw_shutoff in tools/rtegen (like safety.degraded of a separate task); a BSW event safety.hw_shutoff with a fixed number in the safety block of the numbering plan (tools/nxconfig/bswdtc.py, e.g. +0x05FE next to +0x05FF, because the report is no event of SafeSupervisor::Event), its entry in DEM_BSW_REPORTERS and a logging reporter next to safety.device_fault in ecu/application (dem/SafetyFaultReport.h, RteSystem.cpp: FAILED while read() reports anything or is implausible).

Choice of the reaction (for the review): S1 held without reset. The alternatives were the existing interface DEVICE_FAULT (class OUTPUT: S1 + S2 - a reset re-arms the latched path, against H1; the degraded reaction SD only with a mapping of a device instance the hardware path does not have) and DEVICE_REPORT (S3 only: the other outputs and the gate driver enable would stay on). A reaction that degrades only the group (SD) would keep the rest of the ECU running; it needs the event on the closed list of Degraded.h and a mapping in tools/nxconfig/degraded.py.

Update (2026-09-30, safety review point C1). The safety responsible decided for that degraded reaction: a project may map the report to SD. HW_SHUTOFF stands on a second closed list of the supervisor, NX_SAFE_DEGRADABLE_REPORTS in safeSupervisor/Degraded.h (id 0xFE in the event field of a mapping word, above every event number), because it is no event of SafeSupervisor::Event.

Step Where What project safety.degraded: [{event: HW_SHUTOFF, groups: [<group>]}], checked by tools/nxconfig/degraded.py with the YAML path exactly one group, and it must be the group of a PWM group a hardware threshold switches off; refused as well: thresholds on more than one timer (the report record keeps all paths in one word, so a second path could add no new bit) and a timer without an instance number; derived 0xFE << 24 \| timer << 16 \| 0xFF << 8 \| group decision SafeSupervisor::degradeHwShutoff(context), called by hwShutoff::report() in the safety context with the interrupt lock degraded only if the context says "tripped" and nothing else (bit 0, no findings in bits 23..8) and the timer of bits 31..24 is mapped; then the ordinary SD sequence of a separate task (outputs of the group, latch, record in no-init RAM with 0xFE and the context, log), no reset, the last group escalates to S1 without a reset fail-safe HwShutoff.cpp findings of the path, a report without context, an unmapped timer and an implausible record hold S1 as in a separate task; latched() now means "S1 held by a report", so a degraded report does not keep the register check's return path closed - its group is held by the degraded walk of every safety cycle after a reset Degraded.h record the reset re-arms the path, but the group stays degraded until the power cycle (decision B4 (a) of a separate task)

A project without the mapping, and every project without a threshold, is unchanged. The start test of the path needs the input below VDDA by more than offset plus hysteresis: AoU-37 of the concept (point C3 of the same review).

docs.title: 2.7 Start test of the path behind the comparator
docs.text:
Safety review, point H6: the path was never exercised - a broken route, a fault input that does not see the comparator or a fault logic that does not latch stayed latent until a real over-current; the start test is this follow-up. The start test of §2.5 proves only that the comparator output can move. The open point 3 of section 5 named the obstacle: asserting the fault input from software costs a pulse on a power output. A related task avoids it by when it runs, not by what it asserts: the fault is real, but nothing behind the timer is connected yet.

Family code hwThreshold::pathTest() (HwThresholdMonitor.h), called once by ComplementaryPwm::init() after Ftm::start() and before the settling wait, route() (selection and LK) and the pin multiplexing:

Step State What Finding precondition timer configured with its fault control (MODE[FAULTM] 10b, FLTCTRL, FLTPOL 0, FAULTEN), counter clocked, OUTMASK = every channel, no pin of the group muxed to the timer, TRGMUX_FTMx not locked, fault source select on the trigger mux (prepare()); start test of §2.5 passed (otherwise skipped - the group is forced and reported already) - - A comparator forced "not above" (pin (+) against VDDA (-)), then TRGMUX_FTMx SEL(n+1) = CMP0_OUT without LK; two waits FMS[FAULTF], FAULTFn of the configured input and FAULTIN must be 0 PATH_FAULT_UNFORCED (0x0800): fault input active without the comparator - stuck, or another enabled input already latched B comparator forced "above" (VDDA (+) against the pin (-)); two waits FAULTF, FAULTFn and FAULTIN must be 1 PATH_NO_TRIP (0x1000): route, source select, fault input, its enable, the timer clock or the fault logic broken C comparator forced "not above" again; two waits; FMS read while set, then 0 written to FAULTFn of the configured input only (1 to FAULTF and the other flags - no effect, [RM13] 47.4.3.17); one wait FAULTF, FAULTFn and FAULTIN must be 0 PATH_NO_CLEAR (0x2000): the input stays asserted, or another input holds FAULTF - its flag is not cleared by the test D SEL(n+1) back to 0 (still unlocked) before the comparator changes; comparator configured as prepare() left it - -

Every wait is settleUs (30 µs): one for the comparator and its DAC ([DS13] Table 44), one for the synchronizer and the filter of the fault input - (4 + FFVAL) FTM input clocks ([RM13] Table 47-15); the driver checks by static_assert that this is shorter than one wait at the generated FTM clock, and that the fault input is active high (FLTPOL 0, as generated). The test costs seven waits, about 0.21 ms per start. After step D the driver goes on exactly as before: settling wait, route() with LK, pins.

Why there is no pulse on a power output. The forced fault exists for about 90 µs between steps B and C. During that time every channel is masked (OUTMASK, inactive level), the fault control forces the same inactive level, and the pins of the group are still in their reset state (not muxed to the timer) - the timer's outputs reach no pad. The argument does not rely on the gate driver enable (it rests on the pin multiplexing alone, which ComplementaryPwm already relies on for its safe start). After the clearing the outputs leave the fault control only at the start of the next PWM cycle ([RM13] 47.5.18.2) and are still masked.

Findings and reaction. A finding goes into the findings latch of §2.5 (bits 0x0800/0x1000/0x2000, in the report context bits 23..8) and the driver forces the group inactive through the software output control before any pin is muxed (freewheel, review C2); the route is still armed and locked. The first 1 ms poll of the power stage logs the finding and keeps the group forced, the safety cycle reports it (HW_SHUTOFF with findings: S1 held, never the degraded reaction of a separate task, which degrades only "tripped and nothing else"). If the test's fault cannot be cleared, FMS[FAULTF] stays set and the hardware keeps the group forced as well (fail-safe).

Not covered. The forcing of the channels by the fault control (FAULTEN → POL) is not observed: with every channel masked the outputs read inactive with and without the fault (CnSC[CHOV] would show the final value only with the mask open - a review point). FAULTEN, FAULTM and the polarity are covered by the register check of §2.5. Faults that appear between two starts stay with the register check and the consistency check of §2.5 (latent-fault interval = drive cycle). Same assumption of use as the start test (AoU-37): the input lies below VDDA by more than offset plus hysteresis.

docs.title: 2.3 What is not a hardware safety mechanism
docs.text:
Worth stating, because all three are easy to mistake for one:

  • The watchdog (WDOG) reacts by resetting. It is a hardware supervisor of software, not a hardware path to a safe output state, and it is already SM-01/SM-02.
  • The MPU prevents a write; it does not put an output anywhere.
  • A device's own protection (the TMC6200 switching its bridge off in < 2.2 µs) is a device mechanism, stage 2, SM-40 — outside the MCU and outside this document's scope except as a source for §2.1.

docs.title: 3. Where such a mechanism belongs in the safety argument
docs.text:
An honest placement matters, and it is not obvious, so it is written out here rather than assumed.

A hardware path has two halves, and they can belong to different stages:

Half Example Belongs to the reaction — PWM channels forced to a safe level by the FTM FTM_FLTCTRL, FTM_POL the MCU and its configuration → a stage-1 candidate, same class as SM-23 the detection — whatever asserts the fault input a gate driver's FAULT output depends: a comparator on the MCU is stage 1; a device reporting over its own pin is stage 2 (SM-40 …)

So a mechanism of this kind may be credited for its reaction while its detection is not credited — the same split that concept.md §2.2 already applies. Whether it is credited at all is a decision for a separate task (stage-1 analysis) (device packages), not for this document. What this document may state is what the hardware does.

Diagnostic coverage of the mechanism itself is not claimed anywhere here. A fault path that has never been asserted is a latent fault: nothing proves it still works. Any use of §2.1 needs a statement of how the path is tested — at start-up, at each power cycle, or never — and that statement is part of the task that introduces it, not of this catalogue.

docs.title: 4. Worked example: the eval board (boards/evalboard_s32k144)
docs.text:
This section is an example, not a requirement. The facts below were read from board.yaml and the pin multiplexing tables of the derivative; the routing has not been measured on hardware.

The motor bridge runs on FTM0 (pwm[].instance: FTM0, group MOT1, complementary mode). A hardware fault path must therefore reach a fault input of FTM0.

Two candidate sources exist on this board, and — because the source is selectable per fault input — both can be used at the same time:

Source Pin Route to FTM0 What it costs Gate driver FAULT (TMC6200) PTC10 not an FTM0_FLTx pin. But PTC10 alt 6 is TRGMUX_IN11 (in13) → TRGMUX_FTM0[SEL1] → fault input 0, with FTM0FLTxSEL bit 0 = 1 the pin stops being a GPIO input — see below SBC interrupt 1 (UJA1131) PTE12 PTE12 alt 2 is FTM0_FLT3 → fault input 3 directly, pin-only route, no SIM bit involved the pin stops being a GPIO input

What the gate driver path costs is close to nothing, and that is a real argument. established that the TMC6200 FAULT pin is the OR of the GSTAT bits and carries no information the SPI read does not already give — the driver classifies faults from GSTAT, not from the pin. Giving the pin to the TRGMUX therefore loses no diagnostic content while gaining a path that works when software does not. (One caveat from the same task: with faultdirect = 0 the pin does not follow shortdet, so the configuration of the device decides what the hardware path actually sees. That is a device parameter, and it would become safety-relevant the moment this path is used.)

What the SBC path costs is one console line: SBC_INTERRUPT1 is read only for the sbc status display (SbcSystem.cpp, SbcConsole.h). No safety function reads it today.

Not verified, and needed before any of this is designed in:

  • that PTC10 and PTE12 really carry these signals on the built board, and with which polarity and idle level;
  • whether the TMC6200 FAULT output is push-pull or open-drain on this board, and whether a pull is fitted — an open-drain output with no pull would make the fault input float;
  • what either pin does during reset and before the port is configured, since an asserted fault input at start-up and a floating one are very different failures.

The comparator path has no signal on this board. From board.yaml and the pin multiplexing of the S32K144 LQFP100, the eight CMP0 inputs carry: IN0 PTA0 = MOTOR_NTC (pull-up R148 not fitted, the pin floats), IN1 PTA1 = Hall signal HALL_UX, IN2 PTC4 = debug clock (JTAG_TCLK/SWD_CLK), IN3 PTE8 = PILOT_DUTY (input capture), IN4/IN5 PTC3/PTC2 = CAN0, IN6/IN7 PTD7/PTD6 = UART. None of the bridge's current or voltage signals (SENSE_TSCURRENT PTC15, ADC_CURRENT_U/V/W, BEMF_*, SENSE_TSVOLTAGE) reaches a comparator input. So the eval board gets no board fact and the demo no threshold. A board proof needs a signal wired to a free comparator input — the least intrusive candidate is PTA0 through J11 pin 5 (unused while R148 is not fitted), fed from a lab source; that is a change to the board setup the safety manager has to decide and make.

docs.title: 5. Open points
docs.text: # Point 1 The pin sources are not configurable. Since an earlier change the FTM fault control of a PWM group is generated when a project has a hardware threshold (comparator source, section 2.4); for everything else tools/bswgen still emits FLTCTRL and FLTPOL as a hard 0, and there is no board fact for a fault pin, no project value, no check. Task 2 Automatic or manual recovery is a safety decision, not a default. Automatic recovery means the bridge restarts by itself when the fault clears — which is the opposite of the latching behaviour every software path in neXtBSW has (SM-40: a shutdown fault latches, enable() is refused until cleared). Mixing the two silently would be a bad surprise. A related task offers manual recovery only for the comparator path (latched until reset) and proposes the same for a separate task 3 Testing the path. See §3: an untested fault path is a latent fault. A start-up self-test is possible in principle (assert the input from software, observe the channels) but costs a pulse on a power output, which is exactly what must not happen at start-up. : the comparator output alone is tested at every start before the route exists (no pulse, §2.5); a comparator output that sticks at "not above" between two starts stays undetected until an independent measurement of the signal exists (plausibility G2). The path behind the comparator (trigger mux, fault latch of the timer) stays untested:. : tested once per start after the timer runs and before any pin is muxed (§2.7) - a real fault, but no pad connected, so no pulse; the forcing of the channels themselves is not observed (masked), the board proof is open 4 Interaction with the safe outputs table. If hardware forces the channels off and SM-23 also walks them, two mechanisms write the same registers. Which one wins, and what the register check (SM-21/SM-22) expects to read, has to be decided rather than discovered. For the comparator path states it (§2.4): the fault control comes after SWOCTRL in the FTM ([RM13] Figure 47-86), so the fault wins; SM-22 expects the configured fault registers, which a fault does not change (FMS is not in the list). For the pin sources it stays with a separate task 5 CMP0 was completely unused (§2.2). A related task makes it configurable (§2.4), verified on the host (register model, fault path model, mutants) and in a target build; the board proof - approaching the threshold at a board with a signal at a comparator input - is open, and the eval board has no such signal (§4). : the detection of §2.5 is host verified as well; its board proof is part of the same run - the two forced comparisons of the start test read back, and a comparator switched off while running (J-Link write CMP0_C0[EN] = 0) forcing the group within one poll, time from the write to the forced pins measured 6 Start with the threshold already exceeded. The route is connected after the FTM runs, so an exceeded threshold reaches the fault input as a rising edge; the manual describes fault detection as an edge ([RM13] 47.5.18) and does not say what an input that is already asserted when fault control is enabled does. Not verified on a target; until then a start into an exceeded threshold is not claimed to be caught (board test with a separate task) 7 Output buffers under fault control. SIM_MISCTRL0.FTMx_OBE_CTRL (reset 0, [RM13] 11.1.1.2) describes the output buffer of an FTM channel in terms of fault control (FAULTM ≠ 0, FSTATE = 0) and PWM enable; with fault control enabled for the first time, that the channels drive the POL values (and are not tri-stated) has to be confirmed at the pins before the path is relied on (board test with a separate task) 8 SBC watchdog without software development mode (UJA113x SDMS 0). According to the public UJA113x data sheet (Rev. 2, Tables 7 and 8, 7.2.1) the SBC watchdog of a device without software development mode starts after an SBC reset already in Standby (time-out 128 ms). With bootloader.sbc_watchdog: leave (the default) the bootloader of v1.0.0-rc1 does not touch it: without a valid application the SBC resets the MCU in a loop (outputs de-energised, safe state, but the device cannot be updated), with an application it must trigger within about 256 ms after the SBC start. The eval board (SDMS 1) is not affected. Found by the safety review SBC watchdog of 2026-10-06 (decision SDMS0-2 a); correction with a separate task; until then use bootloader.sbc_watchdog: serve; board proof on the Longboard control unit after its return (SDMS0-3 a) ---

docs.title: neXtBSW hardware-software interface of the stage-1 safety mechanisms — s32k1xx
docs.text:
Working state: dev at 6812a0b4 (after v0.2.0)

Status: 2026-09-28, issue 1, written against dev at ae92e89. Task no. 8 of iso26262-gap.md (not published, available on request) section 6 (requirement 6-04 of its section 2.2: the hardware-software interface is refined and every safety-related dependency described). Readers: the integrator (safety manual), the contributors of the register list, ECC injection, hardware paths (freedom from interference), and whoever writes the HSI of the next family. Language: English, like the rest of doc/.

Update (2026-09-30, finding H9, anomaly AN-066). Decision of the safety responsible 2026-09-30: the family port switches the PMC low-voltage detect reset on instead of leaving the gap to AoU-09. boardInit() writes PMC_LVDSC1 = LVDRE (reset on, interrupt off, no acknowledge) in every start (platforms/s32k1xx/port/main/include/pmc/LowVoltageDetectReset.h); a VDD falling below VLVD (2.80 … 3.00 V) now resets the MCU instead of only a VDD below VLVR (2.50 … 2.70 V). Rows changed: section 2 (PMC), 4.8 (LVDSC1), 5 (LVD/LVW vector), 8 (H9, now partly closed) and 9; the mechanism is catalogued as SM-59 in concept.md 6.4 (not credited) and analysed in fmea.md. What remains of H9: the bit is written at each start but not re-checked cyclically (it is not in the SafeIo list, 4.9). Host verified with a register model; board proof open.

Update (2026-10-01, rest of H9). PMC_LVDSC1 is now an entry of the SafeIo list (4.9, class SUPERVISION, mask 0x30, expected 0x10, 8-bit access; the engine got an access width per entry). A cleared LVDRE or a set LVDIE is seen within one safety cycle (S1). H9 closed except VLPR/VLPS; the bootloader sets LVDRE itself since an earlier change. Host verified; board proof open.

Update (2026-10-02, safety review check point, findings SFP-F02 … SFP-F04 of reviews/code-inspection/INS-SFP-1.md (not published, available on request)). Section 4.4: RGD0_WORD2 is now really compared every cycle (it was claimed but never read), WORD2 of every descriptor is compared in all fields of the bus masters 0 … 3 (before only M0 … M2), the rows name descriptors 1 … 7 (guard, part of SFP-F12), and the statement that the descriptors keep M2/M3 out of the protected RAM is corrected: descriptor 0 grants them rwx (H10, section 8, section 0). Host verified with a register model and 15 mutants; board check B17 (fmea section 8) open.

Update (2026-10-04, re-check of CM-02, decision BRD a). Board check B17 (2026-10-02, fmea.md 8.2) reads RGD0_WORD3 = 0: the valid bit of descriptor 0 is not set after init(). Section 4.4 and H10 carry this as a caveat: the M2/M3 rights of descriptor 0 may not be in effect; until the reference manual settles it this document keeps the unfavourable reading, and the restriction of descriptor 0 stays.

This document lists, for the family s32k1xx, every peripheral, register class, clock, interrupt and pin that a stage-1 mechanism of concept.md / fmea.md depends on, with the configuration the mechanism expects, who writes that configuration, what re-checks it, and where each value comes from (derivative database mcudb, board, project, or a constant of the family port). It is derived from mcudb/s32k1xx/*.yaml, from fmea section 5.2 (register classes of SM-21/SM-22) and from the code of platforms/s32k1xx; register facts that the code relies on were read again in the S32K1xx Reference Manual Rev. 13 in the repository ([RM13], doc/hardware/s32k1xx/S32K-RM.pdf) where section 11 says so.

Scope. Stage 1 only, as in fmea.md: mechanisms whose detection runs on the MCU and uses only the MCU, its peripherals and the configuration. Device-dependent mechanisms (SM-33, SM-40 … SM-43, SM-52) have their HSI in the device packages. The hardware paths of hardware-mechanisms.md are not used today; section 9 lists them only so that their registers are not mistaken for unused.

Not a copy of the reference manual. The tables name registers and fields and the value neXtBSW expects; for the meaning of a field see [RM13]. Where a field is written by the OpenBSW driver in external/openbsw (never changed in the submodule), the table says so.

docs.title: 0. Result in one page
docs.text: Question Answer Peripherals the stage-1 mechanisms depend on 20: WDOG, LPTMR0, LPIT0, SIM, PCC, SCG, PMC (by its reset default), RCM, MPU, ERM, FTFC, CRC, ADC0, PORT, GPIO, FTM (of the PWM group), FlexCAN (per bus), NVIC, SCB (SHCSR, AIRCR, DFSR, DEMCR), SysTick / DWT (time bases of the OS and the system time) — section 2 Clocks LPO128K (WDOG), LPO1K (LPTMR0), LPIT functional clock (PCC_LPIT, demo SIRCDIV2 8 MHz), system/core clock (SCG → FTM counter, SysTick, DWT, CRC and the safety task itself), ADC clock (PCC_ADC0) — section 3 Interrupts and exceptions HardFault (exception 3, all faults escalate to it), WDOG warning (IRQ 22), LPIT0 channel 1 (IRQ 49 on S32K14x, the shared LPIT IRQ 20 on S32K11x), SysTick/PendSV/SVC of the RTOS; expected disabled: BusFault/UsageFault/MemManage enables, ERM and FTFC fault IRQs, LPTMR IRQ — section 5 Pins none of their own for the supervision peripherals; the pins of the safe outputs (PWM group, safe_off outputs), the role pins safety.locked_pin, safety.test_pin and safety.safe_state_output, all from the board and project — section 6 Where the values come from derivative (mcudb: MPU regions, LPO range, NVIC bits, ERM channels, ADC internal channels), board (pins, active level, adc_reference_mv, oscillator), project (clock plan, PWM group, safety roles, modules.safe* parameters), family constants (register masks, deadman channel, watchdog clock) — no board value lives in reusable code Re-checked at run time WDOG control, LPTMR0, LPIT channel 1 + its NVIC entry, MPU descriptors and enable, the register list of SafeIo (pin control, GPIO direction, clock gates, FTM configuration, PMC_LVDSC1 since an earlier change), CRC unit (known-answer test) Not re-checked, and relied on findings H1 … H10 (section 8): the NVIC entry of the watchdog warning IRQ (H1), the fault enables in SCB_SHCSR (H2), disabled ERM/FTFC fault interrupts (H3), the LPIT functional clock (H4), the system clock and with it the FTM dead time in nanoseconds (H5), FTM OUTMASK/SWOCTRL and GPIO PDOR (H6, known:), SIM_PLATCGC (H7), SIM_CHIPCTL (H8), PMC low-voltage detect reset (H9: since an earlier change switched on at every start and re-checked cyclically since an earlier change; remaining: LVD off in VLPR/VLPS), descriptor 0 of the MPU grants the DMA/ENET bus masters full access, so the MPU does not keep them out of the protected RAM (H10, open point N3; no such user today) Other derivatives of the family the table holds for S32K116 … S32K148; differences (core, NVIC bits, MPU regions, ERM channels, IRQ numbers, time base of the system time) are in section 7 and all come from mcudb or the device header, not from a board Review author review against code and [RM13] recorded in section 10; independent review (I1) open — it needs a second person (gap analysis Q1)

docs.title: 1.1 Columns
docs.text:
Each table in section 4 has one row per register or field group:

Column Meaning Register / field peripheral register and the fields that matter; x = instance or index from the configuration Expected the value or relation the mechanism assumes while the ECU runs Written by the code that sets it (file under platforms/s32k1xx unless stated), or "reset value" if nobody writes it Re-checked by the mechanism or check that detects a deviation at run time, and how often; "—" = nothing Value from family = constant of the family port (register facts, fixed choices of the mechanism); mcudb = derivative database; board = boards/<board>/board.yaml; project = projects/<project>/project.yaml (including module parameters); derived = computed by tools/bswgen or tools/nxconfig from those

docs.title: 1.2 Status words for the check
docs.text: Word Meaning cyclic compared with the expected value in every safety cycle (nominal 10 ms, guaranteed 17 ms while the task runs, fmea section 2) or at the stated period start compared once after it was written self-healing rewritten before each use, so a drifted value does not survive the next use fail-safe by access a drift makes the next access of the mechanism fault (bus fault → HardFault → SM-17), which is a safe reaction not checked a drift is not detected; the row names the consequence — these rows are the findings of section 8

Other bus masters (finding SFP-F03, open point N3 answered). The MPU master numbers of the S32K1 are M0 core, M1 debugger, M2 DMA, M3 ENET (S32K148 only); M4 … M7 are not implemented ([RM13] 15.1.2 Table 15-3). The system MPU grants an access when any valid descriptor grants it. Descriptor 0 covers the whole address space and grants M2 and M3 rwx, so the "no access" for M2/M3 in the locked gate word and in the guard has no effect as long as descriptor 0 is valid: the MPU does not protect the protected RAM, the safety stack or the guard against the DMA (or the ENET). Whether descriptor 0 is still valid after init() (its WORD2 write clears VLD per [RM13] 15.4.7, while the debug chapter says the debugger keeps its RGD0 access) read 0 on the board (B17, 2026-10-02: not valid), but the effect on the M2/M3 rights is not settled; this document assumes the unfavourable case. No neXtBSW driver enables the DMA or the ENET today (dfa DF-44, the ADC driver refuses DMAEN), so the gap has no coupling factor in the code; before the first such user, descriptor 0 must be restricted for M2/M3 and the master be granted only the regions it needs (H10).

docs.title: 4.13 SM-51 — image check by the bootloader
docs.text:
The bootloader uses a software CRC-32 (bootloader/src/core/crc32) and reads the program flash; the CRC unit is not used there. Its HSI is the flash read path (ECC, SM-16 of the application does not run yet) and the FTFC command interface for flashing, which belongs to the bootloader's own documentation. The integrity of the bootloader itself is open point N4.

What the bootloader configures and leaves behind (safety review 2026-10-02, finding BLI-F03 of INS-BLI-1):

Register / field Expected Written by Re-checked by Value from WDOG_CS, WDOG_TOVAL watchdog disabled (TOVAL 0xFFFF, EN 0, unlock sequence before the interrupts are on), WDOG_CS[TST] kept for the application's fast test bl_system_init() in the reset handler (bootloader/platforms/s32k1xx/hal_s32k1xx.c) not re-checked in the bootloader; the application configures the watchdog again in its own start-up and checks it (SM-07, section 4.1) family fault vectors every fault vector of the bootloader resets unconditionally (Fault_Handler: NVIC_SystemReset()), no output is touched bootloader vector table — family PMC_LVDSC1[LVDRE] 1 from the reset handler on (SM-59) bl_lvd_reset_enable() the application family SBC watchdog (board device UJA113x, register 0x00 WMC/NWP over SPI) SDMS 0 (no software development mode; with serve or leave) or serve with a watchdog that runs in Normal mode: set in Standby to autonomous, 1 024 ms (written twice, read back; an SBC found in Normal mode is put into Standby first), then Normal mode; triggered every 256 ms by bl_device_service() and once more right before the jump. Not taken (read back differs) → no Normal mode, stage 0xE5. SDMS 1 with leave: not touched, Normal mode as before. Forced Normal mode: not touched (off). Read only (bootloader.init without the SBC, sbc_init(false)): with SDMS 0 only the watchdog is set (same fixed setting, in Standby; an SBC found in Normal mode is put into Standby first) and triggered as above - the SBC stays in Standby, regulator (V2) and CAN control are not written, no Normal mode (autonomous runs in Standby as timeout while an interrupt is pending, INTN1 low, otherwise it is off; Table 8); not taken → stage 0xE5; with SDMS 1 read only, nothing written. Reason in bl_sbc_watchdog.reason (3 = read only with SDMS 0) sbc_init(), bl_device_service() (bootloader/devices/sbcUja113x/sbc_uja113x.c) read back after the setting; the application's SBC driver takes the running watchdog over (AoU-34) project (bootloader.sbc_watchdog), device state (SDMS, data sheet UJA113X_SER Table 7, 7.2.1, Table 8)

The bootloader phase is not supervised by the MCU watchdog. From the reset until the application has enabled the watchdog in its start-up, a hang (program flow, a peripheral that never answers) is not detected by any neXtBSW mechanism; it ends only by a reset from outside (power cycle, the SBC watchdog the bootloader serves — always with an SBC without software development mode (SDMS 0; since an earlier change also if the SBC is only read), with bootloader.sbc_watchdog: serve also with it; AoU-34 — or a tester's ECU reset). The SBC watchdog then supervises only the bootloader's main loop, not its program flow. Why SDMS 0 is always served (safety review SBC watchdog 2026-10-06, SDMS0-1 c): after an SBC reset without development mode the UJA113x watchdog is a timeout watchdog with 128 ms that already runs in Standby (public data sheet UJA113X_SER Rev. 2, Table 7 with 7.2.1 and Table 8). A bootloader that left it alone would be reset over and over without a valid application and would hand the application only the rest of 128 ms since the SBC reset; leave therefore takes effect only with SDMS 1. The same holds for an SBC that is only read (safety review bootloader 0.3.10 2026-10-07): the watchdog runs whether or not the bootloader needs the SBC as its transceiver, so the hook sets up the watchdog alone; it needs Standby for the setting (data sheet 7.2, 7.3.3) but not Normal mode for serving, so V2 and CAN stay as found. The updater is not changed: it still refuses to run unless the SBC watchdog is off (SDMS 1). This is acceptable because the bootloader configures no pin of a power output: all outputs keep their reset state while it runs (AoU-07, AoU-SEC-3), and a bootloader that stays is a state with de-energised outputs. The decision to start the application does not rest on RAM state of the past: since an earlier change the start is checked again immediately before hal_jump_to_app(), and a record without compatibility block is not started. Since an earlier change (bootloader 0.3.8) that second check reads record, compatibility block and entry again from flash and requires the record's size and CRC field to be the ones the single CRC-32 over the image of bl_init() was computed for and matched; it does not compute a second CRC over the image (0.3.7 did, about 160 ms per start after the start-up window). This is sufficient because the bootloader issues no flash command between the two checks: erase, download and the record write need the programming session, which keeps the bootloader from jumping. An image body changed without such a command (debugger, bit error) is not seen again before the jump; it is covered by the flash ECC and by the application's ROM check SM-14 at its start (bootloader README, "One CRC per start"). The flash read path of the checks is unchanged (ECC of the program flash; a non-correctable error during the check is a bus fault and resets, BLI-F02).

docs.title: 4.15 SM-34, SM-53 — no MCU hardware of their own
docs.text: SM-34 (device reports to the safe supervisor) is a software report path in RAM; its hardware interface is that of the reporting device package. SM-53 (defined run-down) drives the supply role through its driver; since an earlier change its last run-down step walks the safe outputs table (the registers of 4.10, the same walk as the fault handlers), and since an earlier change an overdue restart ends in the software reset of 4.7 after the same walk. The rest is device-dependent.

docs.text:

Priority rule that the safety argument relies on: the vectors that walk the safe outputs table (WDOG, LPIT channel 1) must not be delayed by an RTOS critical section. The deadman's level is chosen above the RTOS boundary and checked; the watchdog vector stays at the reset level 0, which is the most urgent — correct, but unchecked (H1).

docs.title: 8. Findings — configuration that is relied on but not re-checked
docs.text:
IDs H1 … H10 are local to this document. Proposals, not decisions; the maintainer assigns task IDs.

# Finding Consequence if the value drifts Proposal H1 NVIC enable and priority of the watchdog warning IRQ (WDOG_EWM_IRQn) are written once (enable by the OpenBSW driver, priority left at its reset value) and never read back. SM-02 checks WDOG_CS[INT] only with the IRQ disabled or delayed, the watchdog still resets, but the de-energising before the reset (SM-01 reaction, SM-17 walk) is lost; the pins go to their reset state (AoU-07) add NVIC enable and priority of the vector to checkWatchdogControl() (same pattern as checkLpitDeadman), expected values from the family port; or class SUPERVISION of the SafeIo list H2 SCB_SHCSR fault enables must stay 0: BusFault_Handler and UsageFault_Handler print and reset without the walk, MemManage is DefaultISR a set enable bit turns an MPU violation or an ECC read error into a handler that does not switch the outputs off before the reset either a start-up + cyclic check SHCSR & (MEMFAULTENA|BUSFAULTENA|USGFAULTENA) == 0 in the family safety port, or point all three vectors at customHardFaultHandler; the second removes the dependency H3 ERM (CR0) and FTFC (FERCNFG[DFDIE]) fault interrupts must stay disabled: their handlers (isr_erm.cpp, isr_ftfc.cpp) print and loop forever without the walk. Nobody sets their priority, so an enabled one would run at the reset level 0 like the watchdog vector, which then cannot preempt the loop an enabled ERM/FTFC IRQ turns SM-15/SM-16 into "stuck in an ISR until the watchdog resets" — 250 ms without de-energising, then the reset make the two handlers walk the table and reset (as HardFault_Handler_Final does), and add ERM_CR0 == 0, DFDIE == 0 to a cyclic check; alternatively state them as configuration rules in the safety manual H4 the LPIT functional clock (PCC_LPIT[PCS], SCG divider SIRCDIV2 in the demo) is not checked; TVAL1 is checked in ticks a slower LPIT clock stretches the deadman time-out beyond 10 ms (a faster one gives false trips, safe direction) include PCC_LPIT (CGC, PCS) and the source divider in the deadman check or in class SYSTEM_CLOCK H5 the system clock (SCG RCCR, dividers, source status) is not in the register list (class SYSTEM_CLOCK reserved). The FTM of a PWM group counts the system clock, so PAIRnDEADTIME (checked in ticks) means a different time at a different clock: a faster clock shortens the dead time — the hazard of ASG-01 that no other mechanism sees. SM-04 notices a changed clock only through the OS tick, i.e. only if SysTick runs on the same wrong clock and the change exceeds the period tolerance (12 … 17 ms band) shoot-through risk on a bridge with a clock that is too fast but inside SM-04's band SCG class with RCCR/CSR (source and dividers), SOSCCSR/SPLLCSR (CM, CMRE, VLD, LK — the lock is only a write guard, [RM13] 28.3.8); expected values derived from the clock plan H6 FTMx_OUTMASK, FTMx_SWOCTRL and GPIOx_PDOR are not read back (known, G1) the safe state is written but not confirmed (unchanged) H7 SIM_PLATCGC (clock gates of MPU, ERM, EIM, DMA, MSCM; reset value 0x1F) is not written and not checked; what a gated MPU or ERM does to SM-10…13 and SM-15 was not analysed here possibly a silently inactive MPU or ERM analyse against [RM13] ch. 11/15/22 and add CGCMPU, CGCERM to the cyclic check (class SUPERVISION) H8 SIM_CHIPCTL[ADC_SUPPLYEN] is written once at init and not checked assumed safe direction (the supply reading fails the band → SM-20) — not verified host test of that case in safe-system, or include the bit in the rotation write (self-healing) H9 PMC low-voltage detect reset is off: PMC_LVDSC1[LVDRE] = 0 after POR and nobody sets it ([RM13] 41.7.1.2); only the low-voltage reset (LVR) and POR act. Partly closed by an earlier change (decision of the safety responsible 2026-09-30, AN-066): boardInit() sets LVDRE in every start (SM-59). Closed by an earlier change (cyclic check and class SUPERVISION) (bootloader sets LVDRE); remaining: LVD off in VLPR/VLPS before a later change: a supply between LVD and LVR threshold was detected by SM-20 (1.2 V / 3.3 V band) only, at safety-task speed. Until a follow-up task: a bit flip that clears LVDRE went unnoticed until the next start (the LVR still acts); since an earlier change it is CHECK_REGISTER_ERROR within one safety cycle (S1 without reset) add PMC_LVDSC1 (mask 0x30, expected 0x10, 8-bit access) to the cyclic check — class SUPERVISION of the SafeIo list (generator collect_safe_io()) or a check next to checkWatchdogControl() - done by an earlier change in the SafeIo list; board proof open H10 descriptor 0 (whole address space) grants the bus masters M2 (DMA) and M3 (ENET, S32K148) rwx, so the locked gate word and the guard do not keep them out of the protected RAM, the safety stack and the guard; master assignment per [RM13] 15.1.2 Table 15-3 (M4 … M7 not implemented). Corrected by an earlier change (finding SFP-F03): this row said before that the descriptors give M2/M3 no access. Caveat of B17: the board reads RGD0_WORD3 = 0, the valid bit of descriptor 0 is not set after init(), so the M2/M3 rights may not be in effect; the unfavourable reading stays until a follow-up task settles it a DMA or ENET user could write the safety manager's data without detection (SM-10 void for it) — open point N3 of fmea SM-10 before the first DMA/ENET user: restrict descriptor 0 for M2/M3, grant the master only the regions it needs, and refuse such a configuration until then (dfa DF-44); until then AoU-41 (safety manual section 7.4) forbids any bus master other than the core, review

Observation without a finding: WDOG_CS[DBG] = 0 (the watchdog stops in a debugger halt) and FTMx_CONF[BDMMODE] = 01 (outputs safe in a halt) are consistent with the deadman design of SM-06; CS[STOP] = CS[WAIT] = 1 keep the watchdog running in the low-power modes neXtBSW does not use today.

docs.title: 9. Hardware functions that are deliberately not used in stage 1
docs.text: So that their registers are not mistaken for configured: FTM fault inputs (FLTCTRL, FLTPOL generated as 0, SIM_FTMOPT0, TRGMUX_FTMx), comparator CMP0, EWM (external watchdog monitor; PCC_EWM gate is enabled as infrastructure on derivatives that have it, the module itself is not configured), EIM (error injection), CMU0/CMU1 (clock monitor units where the derivative has them; gate enabled as infrastructure only), LPTMR compare interrupt (T1b), PMC LVD/LVW interrupts (H9; the LVD reset is used since an earlier change, SM-59), CSEc key storage (only with the maintainer).

docs.title: 11. Review questions of the architecture (section 11)
docs.text:
This task changes no code, generator or bootloader; the answers concern the document.

  1. Without an SBC: nothing in the table depends on an SBC; the SBC's watchdog and reset counter are stage 2.
  2. Different crystal / clock: the clock facts are project and derivative values (section 3); H4 and H5 name the two places where a changed clock is not seen.
  3. Other derivative / family: section 7; the way to S32K3, STM32 and RM4x is a separate HSI per family with the same structure.
  4. Several CAN buses: 4.11 is per bus instance.
  5. Several tasks: priorities are listed where a mechanism relies on them (section 5); nothing assumes a single task.
  6. One configuration level per value: column "value from"; no new value is introduced.
  7. Host test with own profile: not applicable (document only); proposed follow-up: a consistency test that every mechanism of fmea section 3 has a row here and that every expected value of 4.9 matches the bswgen reference outputs of several profiles (demo, testproject_safe_outputs, s32k116evb_minimal).
  8. Qt-free core: not applicable.
  9. Device driver granularity: not applicable.
  10. Platform rule: no file under platforms/ added.

docs.title: Partner MCU supervision, degraded reaction and active short circuit — concept
docs.text:
Baseline: v0.2.0

Status: 2026-09-29, issue 1, draft, checked against the state an integration branch at 7af5b7f — concept for a separate task together, written without the safety manager; every choice that is his is written as a numbered decision with options and a recommendation (section 6). No code, no schema and no other document was changed. The changes this concept proposes to concept.md, fmea.md and ssr.sdoc are listed in section 7, not made. Decisions and implementation (2026-09-30). The safety manager took all 18 recommendations on 2026-09-29 (decision log A1-A6, B1-B6, C1-C6 each in the recommended variant).

Implementation notes of parts B and C (not published, available on request)

Readers: the architect and safety owner, the maintainer, the contributors who implement after the decisions, and whoever works on separate tasks's follow-up tasks. Language: English, like the rest of doc/.

Occasion (maintainer, session a5, 2026-09-29): an ECU of two MCUs (master and slave; in the real motor hardware the slave has no system basis chip and no external watchdog, and the link is SPI), two redundant drives (one motor keeps braking when the other fails) and a motor inverter without a mechanical brake. neXtBSW today is fail-safe only (concept section 3, AoU-04), supervises exactly one MCU, and knows one safe state of a PWM group — all switches off (freewheel).

Rules kept. Board neutrality: the hardware of the maintainer's power unit stays outside neXtBSW; no value of it appears here, and the eval board is at most an example. No invented numbers (concept section 0): every time is a symbol, a configured value or a derived one; the one worked example in section 3.7 is labelled as hypothetical. No text or clause of a standard is cited. Stage separation (concept section 1.4): what is credited in stage 1 must detect and react with the MCU and its configuration; the partner MCU is an MCU running neXtBSW, not a device.

docs.title: 0. Result in one page
docs.text:
• Partner supervision. The master asks, the slave answers: a question-and-answer watchdog over the inter-MCU link. The answer is a function of the question and of the slave's own program-flow evidence (its safety cycle completed, its deadman armed and not expired, its fast loop alive), so a slave that is stuck, runs wild or skips its checks cannot produce it. Late, early, wrong or missing answers raise an error counter; at its threshold the master cuts a hardware shut-off line that disables the slave's power stage outside the slave (board fact), and raises an event with a project-chosen reaction. The slave supervises the master by the arrival of the questions and enters its own safe state when they stop. The shut-off line is a safe_off output of the master, so every switch-off path of the master (safe state, fault handlers, halt deadman, its reset) cuts it too.
  • Link neutral and bootloader compatible. The supervision is one short message class on whatever transport carries messages between the MCUs (the SPI link mcuLink today, CAN possible). A slave in its bootloader answers a question with the bootloader's ordinary "service not supported" — no byte of bootloader code is needed, and a bootloader can never produce a valid answer, so "partner in bootloader" is seen, and the line stays cut.
  • Proof against the fault tolerance time. Question period, answer window, error counter and the integrator's fault tolerance time are project values in milliseconds; nxconfig derives the worst-case detection and reaction time and refuses a configuration that does not fit (section 3.7).
  • Degraded reaction. A new reaction class SD — degraded: the affected safe-output group goes to its safe state, the event goes to the error memory and to the application as an RTE signal, the rest keeps running, no reset. Which events may be degraded is a closed list in the supervisor — faults of the MCU itself (ROM, RAM, ECC, MPU, watchdog, program flow, kernel, clock, supply) stay fail-safe; device faults, partner faults and fast-loop faults may be degraded. The mapping event → group is a project value; nxconfig refuses a mapping of a fail-safe event. The degraded state is latched until the power cycle and survives a safety reset.
  • Active short circuit. Per PWM group a project value lists the allowed safe states (freewheel, active_short_low, active_short_high); the application selects the currently valid one at run time (for example by speed); every switch-off path applies the selection. Anything that makes the selection untrustworthy or unavailable falls back to freewheel: an invalid selection word, a gated timer clock, a bridge fault, the hardware fault input (which forces freewheel in hardware), and the reset. The gate-driver enable of a group in active short stays on — the one real conflict with today's safe_off rule, resolved by binding enables to their PWM group. A start-up test builds the short at standstill and reads it back.
  • 18 decisions for the safety manager (section 6), each with a recommendation; proposed changes to concept, FMEA, requirements, DFA and the DTC plan (section 7); the implementation tasks (section 8).

docs.title: 1. Starting point
docs.text:
What exists, checked in the code at 7af5b7f:
