docs.title: 5. Design principles applied (6-7.4.3)
docs.text: Principle (own words) How the safety part meets it Gap hierarchical structure detection → reaction → recovery (concept section 5); family-neutral C-SUP/C-WDG over the family port — restricted size and complexity of components one mechanism per unit in the family port; the supervisor's handle() is the one large switch by design handle() has 23 cases; its cyclomatic complexity is not measured restricted size of interfaces monitor API with three calls and one context word — strong cohesion one component per protected resource (memory, system, I/O, supervision peripherals) — loose coupling mechanisms know only the monitor API, not each other the safety task hosts the console command safety (test functions; gap analysis task 19) appropriate scheduling safety task above every application task, fixed rate; tools/schedana for the application tasks the safety cycle's execution time is measured on the board only indirectly (period check) restricted use of interrupts two bypass paths (fault handlers, deadman) with no RTOS call and no stack beyond their frames the level-0 fault interrupts reach the logger and the ETL assert handler (section 7.3) appropriate management of shared resources MPU gate, deferred event box SPI shared with the SBC (fmea F5), DMA rights (N3)

docs.title: 6. Resource estimate (6-7.4.13)
docs.text: Resource Estimate Source Status execution time safety task period and lateness bound, watchdog relation (static_assert + nxconfig); application tasks by tools/schedana concept.md 7.1, tools/schedana analysed; measured WCET of the safety cycle open program memory 208 464 B .text + 1 024 B vectors + small sections of the demo image; layout against the derivative arm-none-eabi-size, tools/elfcheck (SSR-083) checked data memory .mpu_bss 576 B, .hot_bss 22 464 B, .bss 16 692 B, .data_general 496 B, .noinit 352 B, .heap 516 B, .stack (MSP) 1 024 B; : .stack 4 096 B and .stack_guard 1 024 B (+4 096 B RAM; demo image: guard 0x200045E0 … 0x200049E0, stack up to 0x200059E0, 4 640 B free up to the no-init area at 0x20006C00) arm-none-eabi-size -A, nm measured stack per context below (section 7) tools/stackuse new communication CAN bus load — open (no estimate; outside this task)

docs.title: 7.1 Method
docs.text:
tools/stackuse (README) combines the -fstack-usage output of the build with the call graph of the linked image. Frame of a function = the larger of its .su value and the sum of its stack decrements in the disassembly; call graph on the exact symbols; indirect calls only as far as the profile resolves them, otherwise the context is marked incomplete; recursion only as bounded where the profile says so, with the number of times a function can be on the stack. The facts the image does not contain (contexts, stacks, targets of indirect calls, interrupt levels) are in the profile profiles/evalboard_s32k144_demo.yaml, each with its source. The full report of the baseline build is reports/evalboard_s32k144_demo.md (not published, available on request).

Cross-check of the two frame sources in the demo image: 1 457 functions have both; 1 308 agree exactly, 14 have a larger sum in the disassembly (taken), the rest are template instances merged under one key (the larger .su value taken). 895 indirect call sites exist in the image (310 virtual); the profile resolves 51 callers.

Task stacks carry, in addition to the call tree, the exception frame of a preemption and the context FreeRTOS saves on a switch: 108 B + 100 B = 208 B (context_bytes). Interrupt handlers run on the MSP; per nesting level one exception frame of 108 B (Cortex-M4F, extended frame with lazy FP stacking, plus alignment).

docs.title: 7.2 Safety task
docs.text:
Context Stack Worst case Margin Complete safety task, all entries 2 048 B 1 200 B (59 %) 848 B yes — cyclic supervision only (SafetySystem::execute) 2 048 B 1 112 B (54 %) 936 B yes — console command safety only 2 048 B 1 200 B (59 %) 848 B yes

Update (the work step, 2026-09-29). The table above is measured again after a later change (lean ETL assert handler safety::etlAssertFailed, kernel faults without handle() and logger, ECC interrupts without printf); the report reports/evalboard_s32k144_demo.md (not published, available on request) is regenerated from the same build. The deepest console path now ends in Uart::getInstance → safety::etlAssertFailed → resetWithLine → safeConsoleWrite → Uart::write → Uart::init instead of formatting in etl_assert_function; the cyclic part grew by 16 B (frame of resetWithLine, no longer inlined). The paths described below are those of issue 1 and are kept for the history.

Deepest path (console): dispatch 176 B incl. context → AsyncCommandWrapper::execute → AsyncConsole::terminate → StringWriter::printf → PrintfFormatter → the stream chain (Tagged → NormalizeLf → Stdout) → Uart::getInstance → etl_assert_function (frame 200 B, counted twice as bounded recursion) → putByteToStdout → Uart::write. Deepest path (cyclic): SafetyManager::cyclic → SafeSystem::checkAdcReference → SafeSupervisor::handle (200 B) → handleDeviceReport → Logger::warn → BufferedLoggerOutput::logOutput (128 B entry buffer) → entry serializer. The graph merges all branches of handle(), so these are upper bounds: the device-report branch is not reachable from the ADC check in the real control flow.

Sensitivity: without the ETL assert handler on the paths (profile variant with ignore), the safety task needs 1 192 B.

The task stack overflow check of FreeRTOS (STACK_OVERFLOW, S1 + S2) catches an overflow of this stack at the next context switch; the 472 B margin makes it a second line, not the first.

docs.title: 7.3 Interrupt stack (MSP)
docs.text:
Level Deepest handler Worst case Complete fault (−1) HardFault/BusFault/UsageFault → HardFault_Handler_Final → safeConsoleWrite (no checkEccErrors) 96 B yes 0 Safe_ERM_double_fault_IRQHandler → reportEccError → resetWithLine → safeConsoleWrite (no printf) 288 B yes 4 LPIT0 ch 1 (deadman) 0 B yes 8 FlexCAN0 → receive/transmit → DoCAN transmitter callbacks ≥ 768 B no (DoCAN transmit path not resolved) 9 LPUART2 28 B yes 15 SysTick → xTaskIncrementTick → configASSERT → KernelFaultReaction → resetOnKernelFault → safeConsoleWrite 392 B yes all levels nested per level deepest + 108 B ≥ 2 220 B of 1 024 B (issue 1: ≥ 3 980 B) no

Without the ETL assert handler (sensitivity): level 0 needs 456 B, nested ≥ 3 404 B.

Update (2026-09-30, host). Budget and overflow detection of the MSP (findings STK-1, STK-2, STK-6; maintainer decision: shorten the deep paths first - then size the MSP to the tool value plus reserve, MPU guard below it, stackuse --strict in the CI). Report of the same build: reports/evalboard_s32k144_demo.md (not published, available on request).

Level / context Deepest path Worst case Complete fault (−1) HardFault → customHardFaultHandler → HardFault_Handler_Final (naked MSP check) → nxHardFaultFinal / nxIsrStackOverflowFinal → safeConsoleWrite 104 B yes 0 ERM/FTFC/WDOG_EWM, unchanged 288 B yes 4 LPIT0 ch 1 (deadman) 0 B yes 8 FlexCAN0 → transmitISR → canFrameSentCallback → async::execute (queues the completion for the CAN task) → xTaskGenericNotify → configASSERT → kernel fault reaction 400 B yes (AN-084) 9 LPUART2 28 B yes 15 SysTick/PendSV/SVC, unchanged 392 B yes all levels nested per level deepest + 108 B 1 860 B yes start-up on the MSP (main-before-scheduler) reset handler, static constructors (.init_array), main(), app::startApp in vTaskStartScheduler; interrupts are enabled, every level nests on top ≥ 928 B lower bound, accepted in the profile (reason there) MSP need start-up + nested ≥ 2 788 B of 4 096 B, margin 1 308 B levels complete
  • CAN level (AN-084, STK-6): had resolved the frame-sent delegate of FlexCANDevice::transmitISR to both canFrameSentCallback and canFrameSentAsyncCallback. The only construction of the device in the image (CanFlex2Transceiver) passes canFrameSentCallback, which only queues canFrameSentAsyncCallback for the CAN task (async::execute → RunnableExecutor::enqueue). The listeners and the DoCAN transmit path (DoCanPhysicalCanTransceiver::canFrameSent → DoCanTransmitter::dataFramesSent → sendNextFrames → ... → CanFlex2Transceiver::write) therefore run in the CAN task, not on the MSP. Their indirect calls are resolved in the profile all the same (tick generator, nowUs delegate, frame transmitter, transport listeners, frame size mapper), so a context that reaches them is not a lower bound; such a context would report the cycle write → notifySentListeners → canFrameSent → ... → write, bounded by the send lock of DoCanTransmitter (argument not made, no context reaches it today).
  • New interrupt paths (sample group "group complete", fast loop, pin events): none is linked into the demo image - their vectors are weak stubs to DefaultISR. The profile now checks the vector table: a handler that is linked later is UNCOVERED until it gets a context, the nested bound is then incomplete and stackuse --strict (CI) fails. A fast loop above the RTOS boundary adds one level (its depth + 108 B); the reserve of 1 308 B covers a few such levels, the tool says when it does not.
  • Guard: 1 KB below __StackLimit (linker section .stack_guard, __StackGuardStart/End, 32-byte aligned), own MPU descriptor (core read, no write), cut out of the full-access region that contains it. Size check of the tool: largest frame on the MSP plus the larger of that frame and an exception frame; because the start-up is only a lower bound, the largest frame of the whole image counts (432 B) → 864 B needed.

docs.title: 7.4 Findings of the stack analysis
docs.text: ID Finding Consequence Proposal STK-1 The interrupt stack (1 024 B) is not shown to be sufficient. The level-0 memory-fault handler alone reaches 1 032 B + 108 B frame on its deepest path; nested, the bound is ≥ 3 980 B. An overflow of the MSP is not detected (STK-2) and would overwrite .heap and then .bss. The bound is conservative (every level at its deepest at once, all branches of handle() merged), but even the single-handler case exceeds the stack. decide a stack budget: either enlarge STACK_SIZE to a value the tool proves, or cut the deep paths (STK-3, STK-4); then run stackuse --strict in the CI (proposed test entry below). Done by an earlier change (host): MSP 4 096 B against a need of ≥ 2 788 B (levels complete 1 860 B, start-up an accepted lower bound 928 B), stackuse --strict green in stackuse-demo; board counter-check with the fill pattern (inject mspuse) open STK-2 No overflow detection for the MSP (no MPU guard below __StackLimit, no stack limit register on ARMv7-M). a silent overwrite of general RAM; outside the MPU-protected safety data, but the RTE and the deferred event box live there MPU guard region below the MSP (SM-10 code, family port) or a watermark check in the safety cycle. Done by an earlier change (host): 1 KB guard, read-only for the core (MemoryProtection::STACK_GUARD_REGION, covered by the descriptor check SM-13); the hard fault moves an MSP below the limit back to the top before any C code and writes HARD FAULT RESET: interrupt stack overflow (guard), outputs off. Board proof (inject mspoverflow) open STK-3 etl_assert_function (frame 200 B) is reachable from every context through etl::singleton_base::instance() and Uart::getInstance; it formats with etl::print on the stack. +400 B on the deepest paths of the safety task and of the level-0 fault interrupt a lean assert handler (safe state + reset, a fixed string without formatting), as holdSafeState does with safeConsoleWrite. Done by an earlier change (host): safety::etlAssertFailed, event ETL_ASSERT (0x117); board proof lc assert open STK-4 Fault handlers and the kernel tick log through the buffered logger (128 B entry buffer) and printf: HardFault_Handler_Final → checkEccErrors → Logger::debug; ERM_double_fault_IRQHandler → debug_printf; SafeSupervisor::handle → Logger::warn from configASSERT in SysTick. QM code (logger, printf) on the stack of safety reactions; the logger takes a lock move the logging of fault paths behind the reaction or to the synchronous safeConsoleWrite. Done by an earlier change (host): kernel faults, ERM/FTFC and the hard fault reach no logger or printf (rule 5 of hold-console-elf); nested MSP ≥ 2 220 B, the rest is a separate task (CAN level, safeConsoleWrite → Uart::init) STK-5 The console command safety (test and fault-injection functions) runs in the safety task and determines its worst case (1 576 B against 1 096 B for the cyclic part). test code on the safety stack in the product covered by gap analysis task 19 (product build without test commands) STK-6 The CAN interrupt reaches DoCAN transmit callbacks from the ISR; the tool does not resolve them yet. level 8 is a lower bound resolve in the profile (outside the safety part). Done by an earlier change (host): the transmit interrupt only queues the completion for the CAN task; the DoCAN callbacks are not on the MSP, level 8 complete with 400 B (section 7.3)

docs.title: 7.5 Limits of the estimate
docs.text:
• The profile's resolutions of indirect calls are a review item: a wrong resolution hides a path. Each resolution names its source in the profile.
  • Merged branches over-estimate (see 7.2); nothing under-estimates as long as the resolutions are complete, no function uses alloca or a VLA (the image has none: all .su qualifiers are static) and the bounded cycles are bounded as stated.
  • Measured values are not available: a stack watermark on the board (FreeRTOS uxTaskGetStackHighWaterMark, MSP fill pattern) would give a lower bound to compare against — open, needs the board. : main() fills the free MSP with a pattern as its first statement; inject mspuse (test build with NX_SAFETY_FAULT_INJECTION_COMMAND) prints the high-water mark since then, which includes the start-up phase the tool only bounds from below. Board run open.

docs.title: 8. Architectural analysis hooks
docs.text: The safety-oriented analysis of the architecture (6-7.4.10) and the dependent-failure analysis (6-7.4.11) are separate work products (fmea.md, dfa.md; gap analysis task 16 for the failure propagation of RTE, ecuState, CAN, NvM and bootloader). This document provides their input: the components and interfaces of section 1, the contexts of section 2 and the shared stacks of section 7 (a shared stack is a coupling between components of different intent: STK-3 … STK-5).

docs.title: 9. Inspection record (6-7.4.14)
docs.text:
Object: this document, issue 1, against the code of the baseline. Method: inspection with a checklist derived from the verification methods the standard lists for the architectural design at ASIL B (in own words: walk-through or inspection of the design, control-flow and data-flow analysis, scheduling analysis; simulation and prototyping where useful), plus the architecture review questions (section 11 of the architecture). Inspector: the author (contributor, contributor session 2026-09-28). Independence: not met — the gap analysis (row 2-14, question Q1) requires a person other than the author for a confirmation; this record is the author's self-inspection and the input for that review.

# Check Result Evidence I1 every stage-1 SSR allocated to a component with ASIL pass (52 SSR; the 5 open ones with a proposed component) section 4, generated from requirements.yaml I2 every component of the safety part has a place in the repository and named units pass section 1 I3 interfaces between safety components named with their rule pass section 1.1 I4 global data of the safety part with writer and protection pass section 1.2, arm-none-eabi-size -A, nm I5 every safety mechanism assigned to a task or interrupt (control flow) pass section 2.1, 2.3 I6 data flow of events from detection to reaction without a bypass of handle() except the two named ones pass (code reading of SafeSupervisor.cpp handle(), 23 cases; the bypasses are the fault handlers and the deadman) section 2.4 I7 scheduling: safety task above application tasks; watchdog relation checked pass tasks.yaml, SafetyManager.cpp static_asserts I8 resource estimate complete (time, memory, stack, communication) fail in part: communication (bus load) not estimated; safety-cycle WCET not measured section 6 I9 stack of every safety context bounded and below its size fail: MSP (STK-1); safety task pass section 7 I10 freedom from interference: the three kinds addressed partial (memory: MSP unguarded; application unpartitioned) section 3 I11 QM code on safety paths identified pass (identified: console, logger, printf, ETL assert handler) STK-3 … STK-5 I12 review questions of the architecture answered pass section 11

Findings of the inspection: STK-1 … STK-6 (section 7.4), I8. None changes a requirement; STK-1 and STK-2 need a decision (budget, guard) before a release claim.

docs.title: 10. Other families
docs.text: The family-neutral components (C-SUP, C-WDG, C-RTE, C-E2E, C-CAN, C-ECU) carry over. The family port (C-LCY, C-MEM, C-SYS, C-SIO, C-SPC, C-HFH) exists only for s32k1xx (concept.md 1.3). The stack tool is family-neutral for Arm Thumb-2 images (Cortex-M and the Thumb state of Cortex-R); a new family needs its own profile with its exception frame size (Cortex-M0+: 32 B, no FP; Cortex-R4F: the port's own interrupt frame, no hardware stacking) and, on Cortex-R in ARM state, an extension of the instruction patterns in sp_decrement (stmfd, sub sp, sp, # are covered, push in ARM state is the same mnemonic).

docs.title: 11. Review questions of the architecture (section 11)
docs.text:
Changes: a new document and a new tool under tools/stackuse (host tool, not in the image).

  1. Without an SBC: the tool and the document are independent of the SBC; the MCU watchdog path is described.
  2. Other crystal / clock: no clock value in the tool; frames do not depend on the clock.
  3. Other derivative / S32K3, STM32, Cortex-R: the tool reads any Arm Thumb image; derivative facts (MSP size, exception frame, levels) are in the profile. Section 10 names what a Cortex-R profile needs.
  4. Two or more CAN buses: CAN handlers are contexts of the profile; a second bus is a second entry.
  5. Several tasks, free priorities: every task is a context of its own with its own stack; ISR levels come from the profile.
  6. One configuration level per value: the tool introduces no configuration value of the image; the profile only records image facts with their source (stack sizes, levels), it does not feed the build.
  7. Host test with its own profile: tools/stackuse/test/profile_test.yaml with a made-up image; the demo profile is tested against the real build only when one exists.
  8. Tools free of Qt, messages with YAML path: no Qt; profile errors name the YAML path (contexts[0].entries).
  9. Device drivers: not affected.
  10. Files under platforms/: none.

docs.title: neXtBSW tool classification and safeguards of the generated code
docs.text:
Baseline: v0.2.0

Status: 2026-09-21, issue 1, written against dev at f8ee573. Update 2026-09-22 (against dev at f2e2c43): proposals A and E are done; findings TF5 and TF8 are closed, SSR-080 and SSR-084 are implemented, and dbcgen moves from TD2 to TD1 (TCL 1). Update 2026-09-22: proposals B (reference output) and F (RTE timing and interrupt priorities of the linked image against the configuration, tools/elfcheck/timing.py) are done; findings TF1 and TF7 are closed and SSR-081 is implemented. D was done before; C (SSR-082) was the one proposal of the generated items still open and is implemented by an earlier change since 2026-10-01 (all of A to F are done). The image check elfcheck has its own row in section 3. Update 2026-09-22 (norm questions, against dev at 62a1b53): the open points TN1–TN5 are checked against ISO 26262 (mainly ISO 26262-8, clause 11) and answered in section 9.2; the tool impact classes are renamed to the standard's names (TI1 = no possibility of impact, TI2 = possibility), the planning data of the tool usage (section 1.4) and the norm-based content of the qualification record (section 5) are added, the host-test compiler moves from TD1 to TD2** (conservative estimation), StrictDoc gets its row, and proposals I–L are new. Readers: the safety manager as architect, the integrator who builds a safety-related ECU with the neXtBSW tools, and the contributors of the safety manual, requirements and the tasks proposed in section 7. Language: English, like the rest of doc/.

This document is the tool part that the safety concept concept.md hands to a separate task (concept sections 1.2, 8.3, 8.4 and 10.5). It classifies every tool that produces, transforms, transfers or checks a part of the ECU image, says how an error of the tool would be noticed, and names the safeguards that exist and the ones that are missing. It uses the concept's identifiers unchanged (ASG-*, AoU-*, SM-*, F*, G*) and those of the failure analysis fmea.md (F9 …, T*, N*).

ISO 26262 and this document. Issue 1 was written without the standard. Since 2026-09-22 the maintainer holds a licensed copy of ISO 26262 parts 1–12 (outside the repository). This document now follows ISO 26262-8, clause 11 (confidence in the use of software tools) and is meant as the software tool criteria evaluation report of neXtBSW's tools in the sense of ISO 26262-8, clause 11.5.1; the qualification reports of clause 11.5.2 are proposal G. Licence rule: the standard is cited only by part and clause ("ISO 26262-8, clause 11.4.5"); no sentence, table or figure of it is reproduced, everything is said in this document's own words, and the consistency test safety-tools refuses references to tables or figures of the standard. Where a decision is the safety manager's and not the standard's, it is recorded as such (section 9.2).

No invented numbers. No failure rates, no probabilities of tool errors, no coverage percentages. The detection levels are ordinal classes with the reasoning written out, like the diagnostic-coverage classes of fmea.md.

No board, no hardware

docs.title: 1.1 The three questions per tool and use case
docs.text:
A tool is classified per use case, not once for all: the same program can be harmless as a planning aid and relevant when its verdict is used as evidence. The standard asks for exactly this: the usage plan names the use cases, and impact and detection are determined from the intended usage (ISO 26262-8, clauses 11.4.4.1 and 11.4.5; ISO 26262-10, clause 13). A classification is valid only for the use cases it names; a new use case of a tool needs a new classification (impact analysis) before it is relied on.

  1. Tool impact (TI). Can a malfunction of the tool, in this use case, put an error into the product or let an error in the product go unnoticed? The class names are those of ISO 26262-8, clause 11.4.5.2 (issue 1 called them TI0 and TI1; the meaning is unchanged):
  2. TI1 — no: there is an argument that the output does not reach the image, and no verification result that the safety argument relies on depends on it.
  3. TI2 — yes, in all other cases. Every generator whose output is compiled into the image is TI2, and so is every verifier whose "pass" is used as evidence.
  4. Tool error detection (TD). If the tool does malfunction, how confident are we that the erroneous output is prevented or detected before it is used — by a check that does not trust the tool?
  5. TD1 — high: an independent check looks at exactly the erroneous item (an expectation derived without the generator's logic, a check in the linked image, a run-time mechanism that detects this very error class), and the check has been shown to fail on a broken generator or broken output (fault injection).
  6. TD2 — medium: the output is exercised and many errors would show (compiled and executed on the host, validated input, consistency between consumers), but an error that is consistent with itself could pass.
  7. TD3 — low or none.

Where the choice of TI or TD is doubtful, the more conservative class is taken (ISO 26262-8, clause 11.4.5.3). Our TD1 is deliberately stricter than the standard's wording: it also asks for fault injection that shows the check fires. 3. Tool confidence level (TCL), derived — never chosen (ISO 26262-8, clause 11.4.5.4). In this document's words: a use case without impact (TI1) or with high detection (TD1) is TCL 1; with impact (TI2), medium detection gives TCL 2 and low detection TCL 3. The consistency test applies exactly this rule to every row of section 3.

TCL 1 needs no qualification method; TCL 2 and TCL 3 need one (ISO 26262-8, clause 11.4.6.1). The standard offers four alternative methods — increased confidence from use (clause 11.4.7), evaluation of the tool's development process (clause 11.4.8), validation of the tool (clause 11.4.9) and development according to a safety standard — and grades them by ASIL. At ASIL B, for TCL 2 as for TCL 3, the first two are the highly recommended ones; validation and development according to a safety standard are only recommended. Because the methods are alternatives, a combination fitting the ASIL may be chosen, the higher-graded ones should be preferred, and the choice needs a written rationale (ISO 26262-8, clause 4.3). For a project whose generators change every week, increased confidence from use is not available (it needs an unchanged specification and holds only for the evaluated version, clauses 11.4.7.2 and 11.4.7.4), and no assessment of our development process exists; validation is therefore the realistic method, with a rationale (section 5, TN3). The standard itself points to the other way out: add checks of the tool output to the development process until TD1, so that no qualification is needed (ISO 26262-10, clause 13) — that is route 1.

A run-time mechanism (SM-*, K7) counts towards TD only under two conditions (TN1). First, it must detect the specific error class of the tool — SM-51 detects a wrong validity record because the bootloader recomputes it; a mechanism whose own configuration comes from the same generator does not count (a wrong safe outputs table is walked faithfully by SM-23; the standard asks for such interdependencies to be considered, ISO 26262-8, clause 11.4.5.2, note 3). Second, the error must show deterministically before release: the standard names measures of the development process — tests, reviews, checks in the tool — and detection only in the field is not among them (ISO 26262-8, clause 11.2). SM-51 and SM-14 qualify, because a wrong record or reference CRC stops every start of the image, so the integrator's first test on the target sees it (AoU-26). The watchdog behind schedana does not: a starved task shows only under the load that causes it, possibly first in the field — no TD credit.

docs.title: 1.2 Kinds of safeguard
docs.text:
Concept section 8.4 lists four safeguard kinds that already exist. They are refined here into eight, so that each tool can be credited precisely:

Kind Safeguard Independent of the generator? K1 Independent expectation: the expected content is derived from the configuration by another path — reference-manual register addresses, cantools for the bit layout, a Python reference model, the example values of a specification yes K2 Generated code compiled and executed on the host against the generators' own test profiles (not only the eval board) partly: it tests behaviour, but the expectation is often written by the same author as the generator K3 Validation before generation: a wrong or incomplete configuration is refused with a message carrying the YAML path, instead of being generated no (same tool) — it prevents configuration errors, not tool errors K4 Build-time enforcement in the target code: static_assert, #error, counts that must match (e.g. NX_SAFE_OFF_OUTPUT_COUNT, SM-24), derivative facts checked against the device header yes, if the checked fact comes from a different source than the generated value K5 Check in the target artefact: the linked ELF or HEX is inspected (disassembly, symbols, section placement, checksums) yes K6 Fault injection: a broken generator, generated file or production code must make the test fail (mutants) shows that K1/K2/K5 detect K7 Run-time mechanism that detects the error class of the tool in the product (e.g. SM-51, SM-14) yes, if not configured by the same generator; credited for TD only if the error shows at every start (section 1.1) K8 Controlled tool environment: pinned versions of Python packages (tools/ci/constraints.txt, checked by python -m tools.ci check), one interpreter per repository (.venv), generators run by the build only prevents, does not detect

docs.title: 1.3 What was looked at
docs.text: For every tool: where the build or the maintainer runs it (CMakeLists.txt, bootloader/CMakeLists.txt, bootloader/updater/CMakeLists.txt, ecu/application/CMakeLists.txt, ecu/uds/CMakeLists.txt, ecu/xcp/CMakeLists.txt, cmake/NxRomCheck.cmake, tools/studio/core/commands.py), which generated files it writes and which mechanism consumes them, and which entries of tools/test/tests.yaml test it and how (read in the test sources: expectation derived how, mutants yes or no, own profiles yes or no).

docs.title: 1.4 Planning data of the tool usage
docs.text:
The standard asks the usage of every tool to be planned with its identification and version, its configuration, its use cases, its execution environment, the maximum ASIL it can violate, and the qualification method where one is needed (ISO 26262-8, clause 11.4.4.1); it also asks for a description of the tool, its user guide, its behaviour under anomalous conditions, its known malfunctions and the measures against them (clause 11.4.4.2). The use cases and measures are section 3; the rest is here, per group of tools. What is marked missing is part of proposal G (neXtBSW's tools) or L (external tools).

Group Identification and version Configuration Environment Description, user guide Anomalous conditions, known malfunctions neXtBSW generators and checks (nxconfig, bswgen, blgen, rtegen, dbcgen, diaggen, a2lgen, schedana, romCheckImage, canflash, elfcheck, mcudb tools, swc tools, trace, test runner, boardtest) the repository commit; one version for all, no separate tool releases the project, board and derivative files are the tool input, not its configuration; command-line options as the build passes them (CMakeLists.txt, cmake/*.cmake) .venv with the packages of tools/ci/constraints.txt (checked by python -m tools.ci check), workstation and CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) README per tool, doc/reference pages refusal of wrong input with YAML path (K3) is tested; malfunction list missing (the fixes are in CHANGELOG.md, not collected) Studio version in tools/studio/version.py, packaged .exe user settings packaged interpreter with frozen copies of the tool packages (TF9) tools/studio/README.md a packaged Studio older than the repository (AoU-27) arm-none-eabi-gcc, binutils 11.4, NXP S32DS build (NX_ARM_GCC_BIN) compile and link options of the toolchain files in cmake/toolchains and the family ports; -Werror Windows workstation; the version is not checked by the build (missing: proposal J) vendor manuals missing: no review of the known wrong-code faults of this version (proposal L) zig cc (host tests) ziglang package, clang 21.1.0, pinned in constraints.txt options of tools/test .venv vendor documentation missing (proposal L) cppcheck, clang-tidy cppcheck 2.17.1 (wheel 1.5.1) and clang-tidy 22.1.8, pinned in tools/misra/requirements.txt tools/misra/rules.yaml, baseline.yaml, deviations.yaml CI and workstation doc/safety/static-analysis.md partly: misra runs synthetic violations (proposal H) StrictDoc pinned in tools/ci/constraints-docs.txt doc/requirements/strictdoc_config.py, grammar nextbsw.sgra own venv (NX_STRICTDOC_VENV, python -m tools.ci setup --tool strictdoc) doc/requirements/migration-plan.md UID cross-check in tools/trace CMake, Ninja versions of the workstation, not pinned CMakePresets.json workstation, CI vendor documentation build-attribute check of the image (proposal D, done)

Maximum ASIL. Every TI2 use case of this document is classified for ASIL B, the target of the element (concept section 2.1). For an element out of context this is a predetermined ASIL, which the standard allows but asks to be verified for the actual item (ISO 26262-8, clause 11.4.4.1, note 3, and clause 11.4.2) — that is the integrator's step in AoU-26. For ASIL C or D the classification stays valid, but the qualification methods of the TCL 2 and TCL 3 tools would have to be chosen again, because the grading of the methods shifts towards validation at those levels (clause 11.4.6.1).

docs.title: 3.1 nxconfig
docs.text: Use cases (a) validator of project, board and derivative before every build; (b) writer of the build settings (nxconfig cmake: family, core, -mcpu/-mfpu, derivative, debug probe); (c) library of derived values used by bswgen, blgen, rtegen and diaggen (clock plan, CAN bit timing, memory partitioning, target ID, sensor conversion, watchdog timing relation) Impact TI2 in all three. (a) a check that does not fire lets a wrong configuration through; (b) wrong core flags compile the image for the wrong core; (c) a wrong derived value is wrong in every generated file that uses it — the clock plan sets every time in the image Detection today 236 unit tests with synthetic profiles in nxconfig, each check with a deliberately broken input and the YAML path compared (K3, K6); the watchdog relation with counter-examples (nxconfig-watchdog); generated build settings and generated files of every project configured (nxconfig-build); clock and bit timing compiled and run at four system clocks (system-timer-80mhz and siblings, can-bit-timing, K2); versions pinned (K8) Why TD2 the expectations of the derived values are written by the same author and mostly from the same formulas; a consistent error in the clock plan or the memory model would pass the host tests. The board runs of the changelog are the only independent check of the clock plan, and they exist for the eval board only To reach TCL 1 derived values that set safety-relevant times and addresses are checked in the image or by a second path: the memory layout (proposal D), the configuration identity so a reviewed configuration can be recognised in the image (C). The rest stays TCL 2 with the validation record (G)

docs.title: 3.2 bswgen
docs.text: Use cases generator of the board headers at configure time (also stm32gen.py for the stm32 family, modules.py for the module composition) Impact TI2. Safety-relevant outputs: the safe outputs table (SM-23, used by three switch-off paths), the safe_off count (SM-24), the MPU region count (SM-12, SM-13), the interrupt priorities, the ADC reference band (SM-18), the pin functions of safe outputs and PWM pins (SM-21/SM-22 lock and check them only at demo scope, F4) Detection today safe outputs table: the strongest safeguard in the repository — BswGenSafeOutputsHostTest (in bswgen) compiles the real table definition of the port on the host and compares it with an expectation read from board.yaml, the project's use and the module manifests, with register addresses taken from the reference manual, not from the generator (K1), over five profiles including a board without power outputs, with mutants (PCOR/PSOR swapped and others, K6); the safe_off count is enforced by the build (K4, SM-24, target-demo); safe-outputs-order checks in the linked image that the table is read-only, is the project's strong table, has as many entries as NX_SAFE_OUTPUT_COUNT and ends with the end entry (K5). Since an earlier change (proposal A): safe-outputs-table reads every entry (address, value, gate register, gate mask, order) from the linked image and compares it with the bswgen-independent expectation tools/bswgen/test/safe_outputs_expectation.py (reference-manual addresses, cross-checked against the NXP device headers), for two own profiles (one of them S32K116, Cortex-M0+), the demo, charge, S32K148 and S32K116 profiles with the target compiler, and for the application ELFs of the demo, charge and S32K148 builds (safe-outputs-table-charge, safe-outputs-table-bt148); generator, generat and image mutants turn it red (K1, K5, K6). Since an earlier change BswGenSafeOutputsHostTest uses the same expectation instead of its own copy of the rules. MPU region count: encoded for 8/12/16 regions, a derivative with an unknown count is refused, the MPU header does not compile without the facts and a device header with too few descriptors does not compile (K4, bswgen-mpu). Interrupt priorities: ranks in order, a rank beyond the derivative's priority bits does not compile (K4, bswgen-interrupts); since an earlier change (proposal F) the ranks, the syscall level and the NVIC priority bits the application image was compiled with are read from its debugging information (.debug_macro) and compared with the project's ranks and mcudb, and the NVIC level of every rank is evaluated by the target compiler from the generated headers (probe) and compared with max_syscall_level + rank — by tools/elfcheck/timing.py, which imports no generator; own profiles (two UART ranks, S32K116 with 2 bits and syscall level 0), the S32K148 build test and the demo; generat, template and configuration mutants turn it red (K1, K5, K6; elfcheck-timing-host, elfcheck-timing-demo). Reference output of the safety-relevant headers per profile since an earlier change (proposal B, bswgen-reference). ADC reference band: against the headers of an own profile and the demo, with mutants of SafeSystem.cpp (K2, K6). 194 unit tests in bswgen over own profiles in tools/bswgen/test/profiles Why TD2 the safe outputs table is TD1 since an earlier change (finding TF5 closed: its content is checked in the linked image) and the interrupt priorities since an earlier change (finding TF7 closed: rank, syscall level and bits of the image and the level of every rank against the configuration); a changed header is noticed since an earlier change (finding TF1 closed). Still TD2: the pin functions of the safe outputs have no independent check beyond the generator's own validation against the pinmux data, and nothing ties an image to the configuration it was generated from (C) To reach TCL 1 A (done), B (done), F (done), C (configuration identity, open); the pin functions of the safe outputs with a separate task. Everything else stays TCL 2 with G

docs.title: 3.3 blgen
docs.text: Use cases generator of the bootloader's board part and of the memory layout that bootloader, application linker script, updater and canflash all read Impact TI2. A wrong layout places the application, the validity record or the checksum list wrongly; the bootloader could erase or start the wrong area. SM-51 checks the image against the record — but at the addresses the same layout names Detection today 22 unit tests in blgen (own profiles, target ID as CRC-32 of the identifying string), blgen-stm32 links a stm32 bootloader; application-linker runs the real arm-none-eabi-ld over the template with one to four RAM regions (K5); bootloader-host, bl-update-host and the mutation run bl-update-mutations exercise the bootloader with the generated layout (K2, K6); canflash compat compares the tool's layout with the running target (K7, board). nxconfig validates the partitioning against the derivative's flash map (K3) Why TD2 one generated source feeds all consumers (finding TF6): they are consistent by construction, so a layout that is wrong for the derivative is wrong in the bootloader, the application and the tool alike, and every consumer test passes. The only independent source is the derivative's flash map, and it is checked by nxconfig, which is part of the same chain To reach TCL 1 D (linked bootloader, application and updater ELFs checked against the derivative map from mcudb and against each other), B, C

docs.title: 3.4 rtegen
docs.text: Use cases generator of the RTE from rte.yaml, the component descriptions and the DBC (through dbcgen) Impact TI2. Safety-relevant outputs: the task list with priorities and periods; the SM-05 deadlines, which are the configured periods; the qualifier computation of SM-30 (converter limits, amplifier range, breakpoints); the E2E configuration of each protected signal (SM-31); the copies at task boundaries Detection today 206 unit tests in rtegen that compile and run the generated RTE on the host in 14 host-test programs over own profiles (K2) — PWM, CAN, qualifier and qualifier stall, types, parameters, sensors, ECU state, multitask, BSW services, modes, implicit access, communication control; the sensor values the host test expects are those of the independent Python reference tools/nxconfig/sensor.py, with mutants of the generated RteConfig.cpp (K1, K6); the E2E library is checked against the example values of the specification through the reference model (e2e-ref, e2e-host, e2e-mutations); the demo task list (order, hence priorities) is pinned by a test (test_demo_task_list_is_unchanged); rte-deadline runs the real RteSystem.cpp against a virtual clock with an own two-task profile and mutants; demoswc-sil runs model code and RTE together; safety-context-elf checks the event mailbox placement in the linked image (K5). Since an earlier change (proposal B) RteTasks.h, Config.h, RteConfig.cpp and CanDb.c/h of four profiles are compared with a reviewed reference (rtegen-reference). Since an earlier change (proposal F) tools/elfcheck/timing.py reads rte::TASKS, rte::RUNNABLES and rte::MODE_RUNNABLES from the linked image (names, called functions, periods = SM-05 deadlines, offsets, task index, tick counts) and the context number (FreeRTOS priority) of every task, BSW tasks included, from the TASK_* enumerators of its debugging information, and compares them with an expectation derived without rtegen from rte.yaml, tasks.yaml, the component ARXML and, since an earlier change, the swc.yaml of hand-written C components (own reader, not rtegen's or swc_yaml.py); the expectation itself agrees with the reviewed reference output of six profiles (two with C components); demo and S32K148 images, the firmware of test/c_swc (C component next to a Simulink one) and the own profiles test/multitask and test/c_swc built with the target compiler for Cortex-M4 and M0+; image, generat, template and configuration mutants turn it red (K1, K5, K6; elfcheck-timing*) Why TD2 the task list, the priorities, the periods and the SM-05 deadlines are TD1 since an earlier change (finding TF7 closed for the RTE part), and a change of any generated RTE file is noticed since an earlier change (TF1 closed). Still TD2: the E2E configuration (which signal, which data ID, which profile) and the qualifier limits are exercised and guarded against change by the reference, but not compared with an independent source; nothing ties an image to its configuration (C) To reach TCL 1 B (done), F (done), C (open); an independent check of the E2E configuration — today it is checked at run time by the partner ECU (a mismatched data ID or counter makes the E2E check fail there), which is independent but only at integration

docs.title: 3.5 dbcgen
docs.text: Use cases generator of pack and unpack code for every CAN signal a project uses Impact TI2. A wrong bit position, byte order, sign or scaling delivers a wrong value with a good qualifier; E2E (SM-31) protects the bytes, not their interpretation, so it does not detect this error class Detection today the generated code is compiled and run with ziglang and compared with the exact Python model, and the model is compared with cantools as independent reference for the bit layout (K1, K2, dbcgen); rtegen's CAN host tests use it (rtegen). Since an earlier change (proposal E): dbcgen-projects finds every DBC under projects/ and tools/ and every ECU description with can: dbc:, and packs and unpacks every signal of the messages the node sends or receives with the generated code and with cantools (limits of the bit field, DBC minimum and maximum, raw and physical zero, random values with a fixed seed per DBC; raw bytes and physical values, E2E signals and the bit offset rtegen hands to the E2E library included); eight mutants of the generat of the demo DBC turn it red (K1, K2, K6) Why TD1 an independent decoder checks exactly the erroneous item (the bit layout and scaling of every used signal) for the DBC of every project and test profile, and the check is shown to fail on broken output (finding TF8 closed). Remaining limits: messages dbcgen cannot generate (multiplexed, IEEE float) are skipped and listed, and a description that uses one turns the test red; a new project DBC is covered automatically, but only once it is in the repository (AoU-26) To reach TCL 1 reached with E; B (reference output of CanDb.c/h) remains as a guard against unasserted changes

docs.title: 3.6 diaggen
docs.text: Use cases generator of the UDS job tables of the application (read and write data identifiers, routines, security access masks) Impact TI2 if a routine or a write reaches a safety-relevant output or value: a wrong session or security mask would allow it where it should not be allowed Detection today 22 unit tests with an own profile, every check with a deliberately broken input and its YAML path (K3, K6, diaggen); the description itself validated by nxconfig-diag; the RTE side of the jobs compiled and called on the host (rtegen-diag, K2) Why TD2 the masks are exercised with the author's expectation; nothing independent says which job may run in which session Target stays TCL 2 (validation record, G). Proposed AoU-28: a diagnostic job must not be the only barrier in front of a safety-relevant output — the application or the safe supervisor interlocks it. With AoU-28 met, the use case becomes TI1

docs.title: 3.7 a2lgen
docs.text: Use cases writer of the A2L after link; a calibration tool uses it to write calibration parameters over XCP Impact TI2 when a safety-relevant parameter is calibrated with it: a wrong conversion (COMPU_METHOD) makes the tool write a wrong stored value while showing the right physical one Detection today addresses and tables come from the linked ELF itself (K5), for little and big endian images of an own profile (a2lgen); since an earlier change also the calibration objects (curves, maps, axes, limits, value tables) of the profile test/calib, every A2L through the formal check tools/a2lgen/a2lcheck.py and read back from the image; the XCP slave refuses writes outside its writable regions and writes of partial elements (xcp-host, K7 for wrong addresses) Why TD2 a wrong conversion is consistent with itself and is not detected by the slave Target TCL 2, or TI1 under the proposed AoU-28: XCP is disabled in the product, or a safety-relevant parameter is verified after calibration by reading it back through a path that does not use the A2L conversion (since an earlier change the console command cal values, which prints every stored value as it is in memory; and the production profile of memory.calibration has no XCP at all)

docs.title: 3.8 schedana
docs.text: Use cases (a) planning aid while the task set is designed; (b) evidence that the safety task and the other tasks meet their periods under load (AoU-08) Impact (a) TI1. (b) TI2: a "schedulable" verdict that is wrong lets a task set pass whose safety task can starve Detection today 63 tests with mutants of the analysis itself (K6, schedana), a measurement path that compares computed with measured run times (K2); in the product the watchdog (SM-01) detects a starved safety task and SM-05 reports overruns — detection in the field, fail-safe, but after release, and only under the load that causes it; per section 1.1 (TN1) this is no TD credit, it only limits the consequence Target TCL 2 for use (b) with the validation record (G); TCL 1 when the integrator's AoU-08 evidence is a measurement under worst-case load on his board and schedana only plans it. The measurement path of schedana makes that easy should say so

docs.title: 3.9 Studio
docs.text: Use cases (a) editor of the configuration files; (b) launcher of the same generator, build and test commands as CMake and the command line (tools/studio/core/commands.py builds the same nxconfig, bswgen, rtegen calls); (c) display of validation messages, step state and test results Impact (a) TI2: a wrong write (wrong key, wrong element of a list) is a configuration error. (b) TI1 beyond the generators themselves: the build re-runs every generator at configure time, so what the Studio generated is overwritten. (c) TI1 if its display is not used as evidence Detection today (a) every write is validated live with the same functions as the command line (K3) and, independently, again by the build's nxconfig run; AoU-10 requires the change control of source code for the configuration files, and the Studio's own git page shows each change by role — a reviewed diff of the YAML is an independent check of what the Studio wrote. (c) The packaged application imports frozen copies of nxconfig, rtegen, bswgen and the other tool packages for its live validation (tools/studio/build_exe.py, TOOL_PACKAGES), while generators and builds run with the repository's interpreter: its live messages can differ from the build's (finding TF9) Classification TD1 for (a) under AoU-10 (reviewed diff of every configuration change) → TCL 1; (c) excluded from the evidence by the proposed AoU-27

docs.title: 3.10 romCheckImage (post-link step of SM-14)
docs.text: TI2: it writes the reference CRC and the list of areas into the image. TD1: the CRC is checked against a known vector and a register model of the CRC unit, the rules (gaps, content outside the areas, missing or implausible list → build error, changed byte → mismatch) are tested on synthetic images and on the real linker template (rom-check-image, K1, K5, K6); on the target, SM-14 recomputes the CRC at every start and a wrong reference leads to ROM_CHECK_FAILURE and S1 held (rom-check, K7) — fail-safe. An area missing from the list would weaken SM-14 silently, and exactly that is a build error ("does not cover every flash byte"). The K7 credit meets both conditions of section 1.1: SM-14 checks exactly the reference the tool wrote, with its own CRC computation, and a wrong reference stops every start, so it cannot survive the integrator's first run on the target. The only content the tool accepts outside the list is the area with its own reference, which the linker template defines around the calibration segment; the tool refuses it if an area of the list overlaps it, and SM-14 checks it at run time against its own header, not against the tool's reference. TCL 1.

docs.title: 3.11 canflash (validity record and transfer)
docs.text: TI2: canflash record computes the validity record that SM-51 checks, and the download writes the image. TD1: the bootloader recomputes the CRC over the image and compares the identifier and version field at every start (SM-51, K7), which a wrong record or an interrupted download cannot pass; the bootloader and updater host tests and their mutation run show that a broken check is detected (bootloader-host, bl-update-host, bl-update-mutations, K6). canflash certifies whatever image it is given — a wrong image is the compiler's or a generator's error, not canflash's. The K7 credit meets both conditions of section 1.1 (a wrong record stops every start, so the first run on the target shows it). TCL 1. Key provisioning (provision.py, keygen, unlock) is security, not safety, and is not classified here.

docs.title: 3.12 mcudb tools
docs.text: TI2: the derivative data is safety-related configuration data (AoU-10) — flash and RAM map, pin functions, MPU region count, peripheral instances. TD2: the derivative data carries a source per value for RM46L852 (mcudb-rm4x), the generated device header is compared with the vendor header where the SVD collection is available (mcudb-svd2header, K1 — skipped without it), and the pinmux importers are tested against their sources. The derivative facts are also checked at compile time against the device header (K4, device-header, bswgen-mpu). Stays TCL 2: a new derivative's data is reviewed value by value with its source (validation record, G).

docs.title: 3.13 swc tools
docs.text:
TI2 through rtegen: the component description sets ports and the qualifier constants. TD2: schema and messages with YAML path, the demo component against its ARXML, the QLF constants against rtegen (swc-yaml), model code and RTE run together (demoswc-sil). TCL 2. The MATLAB/Simulink code generation of the component itself is the integrator's (section 2).

A second use case came up with TN5: tools/swc/swc_create.m sets the Embedded Coder configuration of every component it creates (system target file, production hardware type, fixed-step discrete solver, export-function model, non-finite numbers off, file logging off, identifier length, code generation only). That is part of the configuration of the integrator's code generator, which the standard asks him to fix in his tool usage plan (ISO 26262-8, clause 11.4.4.1). A wrong setting written by the script is an error in his tool configuration, which his own classification of Embedded Coder has to cover — neXtBSW's part is to state which settings the script applies and that he owns them from then on (AoU-29). No change to the classification of the swc tools.

docs.title: 3.14 Compiler, assembler, linker (arm-none-eabi-gcc 11.4, binutils)
docs.text:
The options of qualification are described in concept section 8.3; the norm answer is TN2 (section 9.2). TI2. TD3 for the image in general: the host tests are built with a different compiler (zig cc / clang), so they prove the logic, not the emitted target code; the checks that do look at the target code cover selected mechanisms only — the disassembly of the fault handlers and the halt deadman (safe-outputs-order), section placement (safety-context-elf), the real linker over the template (application-linker), the CRC over the real hex (rom-check-image), the safe outputs table, the RTE tables and the priorities in the image (safe-outputs-table, elfcheck-timing*) — plus the board runs. The standard asks that tests which do not run in the target environment have their differences to it analysed and covered by later tests in the target environment (ISO 26262-6, clauses 9.4.5 and 10.4.7); today no such analysis exists, which is a gap of the element, not only of the tool argument.

TCL 3 today. At ASIL B a TCL 3 tool needs one or a combination of the qualification methods, and the highly recommended ones are increased confidence from use and evaluation of the tool's development process; validation is only recommended and then needs a rationale (ISO 26262-8, clauses 11.4.6.1 and 4.3). For GCC 11.4 in our configuration neither highly recommended method is within reach of the project today: confidence from use needs recorded use of this version with this configuration and a systematic record of its malfunctions (clauses 11.4.7.2 and 11.4.7.3), and a process evaluation of GCC would have to be done against a recognised standard (clause 11.4.8). Target TCL 2, not TCL 1: proposal I runs the host tests of the safety modules also as target code (compiled by this compiler with the product options, executed on the target core or its simulator) and compares the results with the host run; proposal J makes the compiler version and options that built an image checkable; proposal L collects the known wrong-code faults of GCC 11.4 for the used options. Together they give TD2 — many miscompilations of safety code would show, but not every construct of the whole image is exercised — and the remaining TCL 2 needs a qualification method with rationale. The decision between (1) a commercial toolchain with a qualification kit, whose predetermined classification must then be checked against our use cases (clause 11.4.2), (2) validation of GCC 11.4 with a test suite for the language subset and options we use, with rationale, and (3) the TD2 route with I, J, L plus validation is the maintainer's (TN2).

docs.title: 3.15 CMake and Ninja
docs.text: TI2: they decide which files and flags make the image. TD2 today: a missing generated file is found per project (nxconfig-build), a missing module adapter breaks the build (SM-24, K4), and the demo build is warning-free with -Werror (target-demo). Proposal D (done) checks the build attributes of the linked ELF (Tag_CPU_arch, FP ABI) against the derivative's core; the other options (optimisation, language standard, warnings) are still not checked in the image, so TD2 stays until proposal J compares the options recorded in the image with the pinned configuration. TCL 1 after J.

docs.title: 3.16 Verifiers
docs.text:
• zig cc for the host tests — TI2 (a miscompilation could make a test pass). Issue 1 claimed TD1 on the argument that a miscompilation hiding exactly the fault under test while the tests still fail on their mutants is implausible. The norm check (TN4) keeps the argument but not its reach: a mutation run shows that this test, compiled by this compiler, fails on these mutants — it says nothing about modules without a mutation run, and the mutation runs exist per task (safe-io-mutations, safety-gate-mutations, rom-check-mutations, e2e-mutations, bl-update-mutations and others), not systematically for every safety module. Where the choice is doubtful the conservative class applies (ISO 26262-8, clause 11.4.5.3), and the interdependency between the compiler and the verdicts it produces has to be considered (clause 11.4.5.2, note 3). Hence two use cases: (a) verdict of a test of a module with its own mutation run — TD1; (b) any other host-test verdict — TD2. The row takes the worse, TCL 2. Target TCL 1 with proposal K (a mutation run for every safety module, checked for completeness) and proposal I (the same tests as target code: a second, diverse compiler on the same test).
  • cppcheck and clang-tidy — TI2 when the static analysis is credited (concept 8.4, AoU-22). TD2: misra runs the real add-on over synthetic code with known violations, which is a partial validation of the tool; nothing independent notices a violation the tool misses in the real code. TCL 2, qualification by validation: proposal H, with the rationale and record of proposal G; the standard's own example rates a static checker at medium detection only when testing also covers the same property (ISO 26262-8, clause 11.4.5.2, example 3), which fits the combination with the test suites here.
  • Test runner and coverage — TI2 (a false "green"). TD1: inventory check (a test file that no entry covers turns the run red), skips reported as skips, own tests of the runner and of the coverage measurement with invented groups and a never-called probe function (run-tests-selbst, coverage-selbst). TCL 1.
  • elfcheck (tools/elfcheck) — TI2 where its "pass" is evidence for SSR-081 and SSR-083. TD1: its expectations come from mcudb, the project, rte.yaml, tasks.yaml, the ARXML and the swc.yaml of C components (own reader), not from the generators; its ELF, HEX and DWARF readers are its own and are compared with arm-none-eabi-readelf on the demo images (elfcheck-demo, elfcheck-timing-demo); its timing expectation agrees with the reviewed reference output of rtegen (elfcheck-timing); image, derivative, generat, template and configuration mutants show that every check fires. TCL 1.
  • trace — TI2 for the argument (a missing test would be hidden). TD1: a synthetic repository with one broken input per rule (trace-tool), and the generated matrix is reviewed. TCL 1.
  • StrictDoc (strictdoc, pinned in tools/ci/constraints-docs.txt; row taken over from doc/requirements/migration-plan.md section 9) — two use cases. (a) Parser and validator whose JSON export tools/trace checks — TI2: a requirement or field lost in the export would hide a missing test or a dead reference. TD1: tools/trace counts the UID: lines of every .sdoc file with its own expression and compares the set with the export, and every rule has a fault injection in trace-tool, including an export with a missing node and a missing field; the version is pinned (K8). Because tools/trace checks StrictDoc's output, the interdependency of the two (ISO 26262-8, clause 11.4.5.2, note 3) is covered by that independent count. (b) HTML export for reading — TI1, not evidence (like the Studio display, AoU-27). TCL 1. An update of StrictDoc is a tool change: full trace-tool run and equality of the export before and after.
  • E2E reference model — TI2 (it is the expectation of the E2E library). TD1: checked against the example values of the specification (e2e-ref); the library is checked against it with mutants (e2e-host, e2e-mutations). TCL 1.
  • boardtest — TI2 where it is named as evidence (SSR-040). TD2: parsers and checks against recorded console and CAN captures and the format strings of the firmware; the expectations are the author's. TCL 2 (G).

docs.title: 4. Safety-relevant generated items
docs.text:
Concept sections 8.4 and 10.5 name the items whose generation is a direct fault mode of the element. Per item: who generates it, which mechanism consumes it, which safeguard kinds apply today, and what is missing.

Item Generated by, file Consumed by Safeguards today Missing Safe outputs table bswgen, safeOutputsConfiguration.h SM-23 (three paths), SM-25 K1 host and image (reference-manual addresses, one shared expectation), K4 count (SM-24), K5 image: read-only, strong table, count, end entry, handler order and, since an earlier change, the content of every entry (A done); K6; reference output (B done) pin function of the safe_off outputs (GPIO mux, direction) is checked by the generator only safe_off output count bswgen, NX_SAFE_OFF_OUTPUT_COUNT SM-24 K4 build error, K2 - MPU region count bswgen from mcudb, derivativeFacts.h SM-12, SM-13 K4 against the device header, encoding tested for 8/12/16 regions - MPU descriptors not generated: computed at run time in MemoryProtection::init() from linker symbols (TF2) SM-10, SM-13 K5 placement of the protected data between __MPU_BSS_START and __MPU_BSS_END (safety-context-elf) the RAM layout they derive from is generated (see memory layout) Interrupt priorities bswgen, interruptPriorities.h every ISR; timing of the safety task K4 range against the derivative's priority bits, K2 compiled for the cores; since an earlier change (F done) K1/K5: ranks, syscall level and bits as compiled into the image, and the level of every rank through the target compiler, against the project and mcudb; K6; reference output (B done) the NVIC registers in a running device (board check TB4) ADC reference band bswgen, adcReferenceConfiguration.h SM-18 K2 with own profile, K6 mutants of SafeSystem.cpp; reference output (B done) - Task list, priorities, periods rtegen, RteTasks.h, Config.h scheduling; SM-01 relation via nxconfig-watchdog K2 own profiles, demo list pinned by a test; reference output (B done); since an earlier change (F done) K1/K5: rte::TASKS and the context number of every task in the linked image against rte.yaml and tasks.yaml, K6 the running task list (board check TB3) SM-05 deadlines rtegen (= the periods) SM-05 K2 rte-deadline with an own profile and mutants; since an earlier change (F done) K1/K5: periods and offsets of rte::RUNNABLES in the linked image against the ARXML (C components: swc.yaml, own reader) and rte.yaml, K6 as above (TB3) Signal qualifier limits rtegen, RteConfig.cpp SM-30 K1 Python reference for sensor values, K6 mutants of the generat; reference output (B done) - E2E configuration rtegen with dbcgen SM-31 K2; K1 for the library; partner ECU at integration; reference output (B done) an independent source for data ID and profile per signal CAN pack/unpack dbcgen, CanDb.c/h every CAN value K1 cantools on the test DBC and, since an earlier change, on every project and profile DBC (E done); K6 mutants; reference output (B done) - Memory layout, target ID blgen / nxconfig memory.py, memoryLayout.h, bl_memory.* SM-51, SM-14, both linker scripts, canflash K3 against the derivative map, K5 real ld run, K6 bootloader mutants, K7 canflash compat at the board independent check of the linked images against the derivative map (D) ROM-check list and reference CRC romCheckImage SM-14 K1, K5, K6, K7 - Validity record canflash record SM-51 K7, K6 - Clock plan nxconfig timing.py, bswgen boardClock.h every time in the image, watchdog relation K2 at four system clocks, board runs (eval board only) configuration identity (C); a run-time clock check is a separate task's register class "system clock" (fmea 5.2) Watchdog times code constants, not generated (concept 7.1, AoU-08) SM-01 relation checked by nxconfig (nxconfig-watchdog) moves into a configuration level with a separate task; then B applies

docs.title: 5. Two routes, and which one is taken where
docs.text:
Route 1 — raise detection until TD1. A check of the output that does not use the generator's logic. Its value is independent of how the generator is written, it keeps working when the generator is refactored, and it is visible to the integrator: he can run it on his own project (AoU-26). It is the route for the items of section 4, because there a wrong output is a direct fault mode of the element (concept 10.5). The standard backs this route explicitly: its tool clause applies only where a tool's relevant output is not examined or verified (ISO 26262-8, clause 11.4.1); a code generator whose generated code is verified is its own example of high detection (clause 11.4.5.2, example 1); and the guidance calls adding checks of the tool output to the development process the alternative to qualification, valid independently of the tool version as long as the use cases stay the same (ISO 26262-10, clause 13). Its advantage here is decisive: the generators change every week, and a qualification would have to be repeated for each version.

Route 2 — qualify the tool (TCL 2) by validation. For everything else a generator writes (UART, pin names, console strings, most of the RTE plumbing) a check per item would be out of proportion. The existing test suites already are a validation in substance: own profiles, a deliberately broken input per check, mutants of the output. What the standard asks of it (TN3):

  • Admissible, with rationale. At ASIL B validation is only a recommended method for TCL 2; the highly recommended ones (increased confidence from use, evaluation of the tool development process) are not available for tools that change every week (section 1.1). Choosing validation alone is allowed because the methods are alternatives, but the record must say why it is sufficient (ISO 26262-8, clause 4.3). The rationale proposed here: the tools are in-house and fully visible, their requirements are written, the validation runs on every commit (so it always matches the version used, which confidence from use never could), it includes fault injection, and the safety-relevant items are additionally covered by route 1.
  • What the validation must show (ISO 26262-8, clause 11.4.9.2): that the tool meets the requirements of its classified purpose; that every malfunction found during validation is analysed with its possible consequence and a measure against it; and how the tool reacts to anomalous conditions — wrong or incomplete input (K3 covers this for the configuration), forbidden option combinations, and an incomplete update of the tool (for us: a package version differing from constraints.txt, a stale generated file, a packaged Studio with older tool copies, TF9).
  • What the record must contain (ISO 26262-8, clause 11.4.6.2, in our words): the tool's identification and exact version; its TCL with a pointer to this document; the maximum ASIL of the requirements it could violate, per use case; the configuration and environment the qualification holds for; who qualified it; the method chosen and its rationale; the results; and the usage constraints and malfunctions found. The planning data of section 1.4 and the information of ISO 26262-8, clause 11.4.4.2 (description, user guide, behaviour under anomalous conditions, known malfunctions with work-arounds) go with it. The work product is the software tool qualification report (ISO 26262-8, clause 11.5.2). That is proposal G.
  • Per version. A qualification holds for the qualified version and environment only (ISO 26262-10, clause 13); a change of the tool or of its environment (Python, a package) needs the validation again. For our tools this is cheap if the record is produced by the CI run of the released commit — proposal G asks for exactly that.

Common to both routes: the checks run on our test profiles and on the demo. An integrator's project is a different configuration; the safeguards only protect him if they run on his project too. That is the reason for the proposed AoU-26 and for proposal C, which makes the configuration that was checked recognisable in the image. The standard says the same from two sides: a classification made independently of the item must be checked for validity before the tool is used for that item, and the tool must then be used in the version, configuration and conditions the classification assumed (ISO 26262-8, clauses 11.4.2 and 11.4.3); and configurable software must be verified for the configuration data set actually used (ISO 26262-6, Annex C, clause C.4.4).

docs.title: 6. Proposed assumptions of use
docs.text:
Numbered after AoU-24 and AoU-25 proposed in fmea.md; to be taken into concept section 4 and the safety manual by the maintainer.

ID Assumption (proposed) AoU-26 The integrator generates the image only through the build (CMake runs nxconfig, bswgen, blgen, rtegen, diaggen, the post-link steps), with the tool versions pinned by tools/ci/constraints.txt, never edits a generated file, and runs the tool checks named in section 4 on his own project configuration — not only on the neXtBSW test profiles — after every change of configuration or tool version. Without that, the TD1 classifications of section 3 do not apply to his project. Added after the norm check: he verifies the validity of this predetermined classification (use cases, maximum ASIL, tool versions and environment of section 1.4) for his item before relying on it, uses the tools only in the versions and configuration it names, and runs every image at least once on the target before release, because the K7 credit of romCheckImage and canflash rests on that first start (ISO 26262-8, clauses 11.4.2 and 11.4.3; section 1.1). AoU-27 The Studio's display (validation messages, step state, test results, schedule analysis) is not evidence. Evidence is the output of the command-line tools and of tools/test from the repository's interpreter, as recorded by the CI. The packaged Studio may carry older copies of the tool packages. AoU-28 Calibration and diagnostic write access to safety-relevant values: either XCP calibration and the diagnostic write jobs and routines that reach a safety-relevant output or parameter are disabled in the product, or each such write is interlocked by the application or the safe supervisor, and a calibrated safety-relevant parameter is verified by reading back its stored value through a path that does not use the A2L conversion. neXtBSW offers both since an earlier change: memory.calibration.profile: production (no XCP, values read from the flash segment) and the console command cal values (stored values without conversion); the integrator applies them. Since an earlier change an XCP write to a safety-relevant parameter is also interlocked in the ECU itself: the generated plausibility check (limits, ascending axes) refuses it before it takes effect, and cal check shows the result; this does not replace the read-back, because a plausible value can still be the wrong one. Since an earlier change a dataset flashed on its own reaches this start-up check (the segment is no longer covered by the build reference of the ROM check, but re-checked against its own header in every ROM check pass), so the integrator's dataset release is decided by on_invalid and the plausibility checks, not by a safe-state hold. AoU-29 Code generator of the application (Embedded Coder). Its classification and qualification are the integrator's, for his use cases and his maximum ASIL. neXtBSW supplies for it: (1) the interface description of the RTE (ports, types, runnables and their calling contract); (2) the list of Embedded Coder settings that tools/swc/swc_create.m applies to every component it creates, which become part of his tool configuration and which he owns from then on; (3) the statement that no neXtBSW check verifies the behaviour of the generated model code — rtegen checks only the interface against the ARXML, and demoswc-sil runs the demo component only — so his tool error detection for Embedded Coder cannot rest on neXtBSW's checks; he verifies the generated code himself, for example by back-to-back tests of model and object code (ISO 26262-6, clause 9.4.5).
