docs.title: 8. Requirements added to the SSR (ssr.sdoc, was requirements.yaml)
docs.text:
The missing safeguards of section 4 that protect a mechanism of stage 1 are entered as open requirements, derived from AoU-10 (configuration is safety-related data) and the goals whose mechanisms consume the generated item. They carry no code link and no test until the proposed task is done; tools/trace reports them as open. When a proposal is done, its requirement becomes implemented with code links and test entries (update: A and E; D; B and F). The column "Status" must equal the status in ssr.sdoc; safety-tools checks it, and that every implemented one is named by at least one entry of tools/test/tests.yaml.

ID Title Derived from Mechanisms Proposal Status SSR-080 Safe outputs table checked in the linked image against an independent expectation ASG-01, ASG-02, AoU-06, AoU-10 SM-23 A implemented SSR-081 Change of a safety-relevant generated file detected ASG-06, AoU-10 SM-05, SM-18, SM-23, SM-30 B, F implemented SSR-082 Configuration and generator identity recognisable in the image ASG-07, AoU-10 SM-51 C implemented SSR-083 Memory layout of the linked images checked against the derivative ASG-07, AoU-10 SM-14, SM-51 D implemented SSR-084 CAN signal layout of every project checked against an independent decoder ASG-05, AoU-10 SM-30 E implemented

The existing safeguards are already traced through their mechanisms (SSR-005, SSR-007, SSR-022, SSR-024, SSR-040, SSR-041, SSR-051 with the test entries bswgen, bswgen-mpu, safe-outputs-order, rom-check-image, rtegen, e2e-ref, bootloader-host); this document adds no second requirement for them.

docs.title: 9.1 Findings
docs.text: ID Finding Consequence TF1 Concept 8.4 counts "generated output compared against checked-in reference output". There is no checked-in expected output of any generator (no expected, golden or reference files under tools/*/test); the tests assert expectations and properties, and compile and run the generated code parts of a generated file that no test asserts can change unnoticed when a generator is refactored. Proposal B — closed by an earlier change (bswgen-reference, rtegen-reference: the safety-relevant generated files of every profile against a reviewed reference) TF2 Concept 8.4 and 10.5 say the MPU descriptors are generated. Only the region count (derivativeFacts.h) and the RAM layout they are computed from (memoryLayout.h → application linker script) are; the descriptors are computed at run time in MemoryProtection::init() from __MPU_BSS_START, __MPU_BSS_END and the safety stack the descriptor contents are code, covered by SM-13 and safety-context-elf; the generated part is covered by bswgen-mpu and proposal D TF3 Concept 1.2 and 8.4 list tools/intgen. It does not exist; the module composition is Integration.cpp (hand-written, X-macros) plus modules.cmake from bswgen nothing to classify; when intgen is written it joins section 3 and proposal B TF4 No generated file carries the generator's version or a fingerprint of its inputs, and the image carries no configuration identity AoU-10's change control cannot tell from an image which configuration and which generator produced it. Proposal C TF5 safe-outputs-order checks in the linked image the count, the end entry, the read-only placement and the handler order, not the entries' content; the content is checked independently only in a host build of the definition a difference between host build and target build of the table (compiler, preprocessor, linker) would not be noticed. Proposal A — closed by an earlier change (safe-outputs-table, every entry of the linked image against the independent expectation) TF6 One generated memory layout feeds the bootloader, the application linker script, the updater and canflash consistent by construction, wrong everywhere at once; SM-51 checks at the addresses the same layout names. Proposal D — closed by an earlier change (elfcheck, images against mcudb and the core) TF7 Interrupt priorities are checked for range at compile time, not for the assignment to the configured rank in the image or at run time a swapped priority would pass every test. Proposal F — closed by an earlier change (elfcheck-timing*: task contexts, periods, deadlines and the interrupt ranks, syscall level and NVIC bits of the linked image, and the level of every rank through the target compiler, against the configuration; the NVIC registers of a running device stay board check TB4) TF8 dbcgen's independent reference (cantools) runs on the test DBC only a layout error that appears only with a project's DBC passes. Proposal E — closed by an earlier change (dbcgen-projects, every DBC of the repository against cantools, eight mutants) TF9 The packaged Studio imports frozen copies of the tool packages for its live validation, while the generators run with the repository's interpreter its messages can differ from the build's; AoU-27

docs.title: 9.2 Norm questions TN1–TN5 (record)
docs.text:
Raised in issue 1 because the standard was not available; answered on 2026-09-22 from ISO 26262-8, clause 11, with ISO 26262-6 and ISO 26262-10 where they add to it. The table is kept as the record: status, answer in this document's own words, where the answer changed the document. "Answered" means the standard gives the answer; "decision open" means the standard leaves a choice that belongs to the maintainer.

ID Question Status Answer (own words, with clause) Changed in this document TN1 Is the classification per use case, with credit for run-time mechanisms (K7), what the standard intends? answered Per use case: yes. Use cases are part of the usage plan and impact and detection are determined from the intended usage (ISO 26262-8, clauses 11.4.4.1 and 11.4.5.2; ISO 26262-10, clause 13); a classification holds only as long as the use cases do. Run-time mechanisms: only with two conditions. Detection is credited to measures of the development process — tests, reviews, checks inside the tool (ISO 26262-8, clause 11.2 and clause 11.4.5.2, note 1) — and interdependencies between a tool and whatever checks it must be considered (clause 11.4.5.2, note 3). A product mechanism therefore counts only when it checks exactly the tool's error class independently of that tool and the error shows deterministically in the integrator's own tests before release (SM-51, SM-14: every start fails). Detection that depends on the operating situation (watchdog behind schedana) is not credited. The class names are the standard's: TI1 = no impact, TI2 = impact (clause 11.4.5.2); doubtful cases are estimated conservatively (clause 11.4.5.3) section 1.1 (names, conditions for K7, conservative rule), 3.8, 3.10, 3.11, summary table (TI0/TI1 → TI1/TI2), AoU-26 (first start on target) TN2 Which qualification does the compiler need at ASIL B? answered, decision open With TD3 the compiler is TCL 3; at ASIL B the highly recommended qualification methods are increased confidence from use and evaluation of the tool's development process, validation and development according to a safety standard are only recommended; the methods are alternatives, and a combination with rationale is required (ISO 26262-8, clauses 11.4.6.1 and 4.3). Neither highly recommended method is within reach for GCC 11.4 in our configuration (clauses 11.4.7 and 11.4.8). The standard also allows lowering TD by process measures instead of qualifying (ISO 26262-10, clause 13), and independently asks that host tests be complemented by tests in the target environment (ISO 26262-6, clauses 9.4.5 and 10.4.7). Route: proposals I, J, L give TD2 → TCL 2, which still needs a qualification method with rationale. The choice between a commercial toolchain with a qualification kit (its classification then checked against our use cases, ISO 26262-8, clause 11.4.2), validation of GCC 11.4 for our language subset and options, and the TD2 route with validation is the safety manager's — decision log section 3.14, summary table (target TCL 2, proposals D, I, J, L), section 1.4 (compiler identification and configuration), proposals I, J, L TN3 Is validation (route 2) enough for TCL 2 generators at ASIL B, and what must the record contain? answered Admissible, but not the preferred method, so only with a written rationale: at ASIL B validation is a recommended, not a highly recommended method for TCL 2 (ISO 26262-8, clauses 11.4.6.1 and 4.3); the highly recommended ones are not available for tools that change every week (clauses 11.4.7.2 and 11.4.7.4). The validation must show conformance to the tool's written requirements, analyse every malfunction found, and examine the reaction to anomalous conditions including an incomplete tool update (clause 11.4.9.2). The record must hold identification and version, TCL with its analysis, maximum ASIL per use case, configuration and environment, who qualified, method, results, and usage constraints and malfunctions found (clause 11.4.6.2), together with the tool information of clause 11.4.4.2; it is the qualification report of clause 11.5.2 and holds per version (ISO 26262-10, clause 13). Route 1 remains the preferred way for the safety-relevant items (ISO 26262-8, clause 11.4.1) section 1.1 (methods), 1.4 (planning data), section 5 (rationale, validation criteria, record content, per version), proposal G (content, P2) TN4 May the TD1 of the host compiler rest on the mutation runs? answered Not for all host tests. A mutation run shows that one test, compiled by this compiler, fails on its mutants; it covers the modules that have one. For the rest the choice is doubtful, and doubtful cases are classified conservatively (ISO 26262-8, clause 11.4.5.3), with the interdependency between compiler and verdict considered (clause 11.4.5.2, note 3). zig cc is therefore TD2 → TCL 2 today, TD1 only for tests with their own mutation run; TCL 1 for all after proposals K (a mutation run per safety module) and I (the same tests as target code by a second compiler) section 3.16, summary table (zig cc TD1 → TD2, TCL 1 → TCL 2, target TCL 1, proposals I, K, L), proposal K TN5 What must the integrator get for his Embedded Coder classification? answered His code generator is his tool: he classifies it for his use cases and maximum ASIL (ISO 26262-8, clause 11.4.4.1), and as integrator of an element out of context he checks every assumption the element makes (ISO 26262-10, clause 9.2.4.5). neXtBSW must give him what his classification depends on: the RTE interface description; the Embedded Coder settings that tools/swc/swc_create.m applies, because they are part of his tool configuration (ISO 26262-8, clause 11.4.4.1); and the statement that no neXtBSW check verifies the behaviour of the generated model code, so his detection must come from his own verification of that code (ISO 26262-6, clause 9.4.5). Nothing beyond that is needed from neXtBSW; the swc tools themselves stay classified here section 3.13 (second use case of the swc tools), AoU-29 (new) addition

Consequences for the concept (to be taken over by the maintainer; this task does not edit concept.md): section 0 and 9.4 no longer need to say that the standard is unavailable for the tool part; concept 9.4 point 2 (evidence expected for the tool confidence level) and point 4 (compiler) are answered by TN3 and TN2; concept 8.3 should name the target-environment tests (proposal I) as part of the compiler path and the decision of TN2 as the safety manager's; concept 8.4 should say that the tool classification is the software tool criteria evaluation report and that the TCL 2 tools need qualification reports (G).

# Check How Expected TB1 Safe outputs table in the flashed image J-Link: read nxSafeOutputs from flash and compare with the ELF and with the expectation safe_outputs_expectation.expected (used by safe-outputs-table and BswGenSafeOutputsHostTest) for the demo identical, ends with address 0 TB2 Memory layout seen by the tool and the target canflash compat against the running demo board, derivative, layout and addresses agree TB3 Task list and deadlines in the running image console commands rte runnables and rte json, compared with rte.yaml and tasks.yaml identical periods and priorities TB4 Interrupt priorities in the running image J-Link: read the NVIC IPR registers of the configured interrupts after start-up the levels of interruptPriorities.h for the demo (CAN 8, UART-RX 9 as recorded)

docs.title: 11. Review questions of the architecture (section 11)
docs.text:
This task changed no reusable code, no generator and no bootloader; it added this document, a consistency test under doc/safety/test/, a test entry, five open requirements with the regenerated matrix, and a pointer in concept.md.

  1. Board without an SBC? Yes. No tool classification depends on the SBC; the safe outputs table and its checks include a board without power outputs (S32K116 profile), and proposal A keeps that profile.
  2. Different crystal and system clock? Yes. The clock plan is classified as a derived value of nxconfig (section 3.1); its check today runs at four system clocks, and proposal C makes the configured clock plan recognisable in the image.
  3. Different derivative, S32K3 / STM32 / Cortex-R? Yes. The classification is per tool, not per family; the stm32 generator is part of bswgen's row, and proposal D is explicitly required to run for S32K116, S32K148 and a stm32 profile, and to take its expectation from mcudb, which also holds RM46L852.
  4. Two or more CAN buses and different IDs? Yes. dbcgen's proposal E covers every signal of every DBC of every project; nothing assumes one bus.
  5. Several tasks and freely chosen priorities? Yes. Proposal F compares the task list and priorities of the project with its configuration, whatever they are; the schedana classification distinguishes planning from evidence (AoU-08).
  6. Every new value in exactly one configuration level? No new configuration value. Proposal C adds a derived value (the configuration identity), computed by the generator, not configured.
  7. Host test with its own test profile? The new test doc/safety/test/test_tool_classification.py checks the document against the repository (every build-run tool classified, every test named exists, TCL derived by the table, every proposal has a "done when") with deliberately broken copies of the document; it needs no board profile. Every proposal of section 7 requires own profiles besides the demo.
  8. Tool core free of Qt, messages with a YAML path? Not applicable — no tool changed. K3 (messages with a YAML path) is credited where it exists; AoU-27 records that the Studio's display is not evidence.
  9. Device driver granularity? Not applicable — no driver changed.
  10. Placement under platforms/? Not applicable — no new file there.

Board peculiarity forced into the architecture? None.

Norm follow-up (2026-09-22). Again no code, generator or bootloader changed; only this document and its consistency test. The answers are per tool and use case, not per board: proposal I runs for Cortex-M4 and Cortex-M0+, proposal J for the demo, S32K116 and S32K148 builds, and nothing in TN1–TN5 depends on the eval board, the SBC, the crystal or the number of CAN buses.

docs.title: neXtBSW — software unit design: watchdog handling, fault handlers, safety task (N2)
docs.text:
Baseline: v0.2.0

Status: 2026-09-30, issue 1 (proposal N2 of safety-plan.md), written against dev at 65f3dc9. Readers: the author of a change to one of the units below, the code inspector, the confirmation reviewer, and an integrator who ports the safety part to another family. Language: English, like the rest of doc/.

What this document is. The software unit design (activity P6-12 of the safety plan, 6-8.4.2 … 6-8.4.4 read through iso26262-gap.md (not published, available on request) row 6-20) of the three parts of the safety software that had no design description: the watchdog handling (SafeWatchdog, its configuration check and its service), the fault handlers (hard fault, bus and usage fault, watchdog warning interrupt) and the safety task (SafetySystem, SafetyManager, the period check and the safe ISR hooks). It sits one level below the architecture sw-architecture.md (components C-WDG, C-LCY, C-HFH, C-SPC, C-INT) and uses the register view of hsi-s32k1xx.md; it does not repeat what those say, it says how each unit does it.

Section 1 is the unit register: every translation unit of the safety part with the document that describes its design. The register is checked against the source tree and against the list of safety units of a separate task by test/test_unit_design.py.

Licence rule. ISO 26262 is cited by part and clause only, as in the safety plan.

docs.title: 1. Unit register
docs.text:
A unit is a translation unit (.c, .cpp, .S), the level at which the host tests build and the coverage measures (definition of sw-architecture.md section 1). Headers belong to the unit that implements them; a header-only unit (e.g. the table walk of safeOutputs.h) is described with the unit that owns it.

Scope. Every translation unit below the source paths of the safety units decided for a separate task (safety manager: E2E + ecu/safety + platforms/*/port/safety, bootloader later), plus the units outside those paths that the architecture counts as the safety part and that N2 names (fault handlers, their vectors, the scheduling of the safety task). Test sources (test/) are not units of the product.

docs.title: 2. Design rules common to the three designs
docs.text:
These rules follow from the architecture (sections 1.1, 5) and hold for every unit of sections 3 to 5; a unit section only names a deviation.

Rule How the units keep it Detection raises, the supervisor reacts (SSR-001) a unit never resets, never switches an output and never logs a fault as reaction; it calls trigger(), check() or hit() of a monitor of SafeSupervisor::getInstance(), whose handle() decides. Exception by design: the fault handlers (UD-HFH) act before the supervisor can run — they walk the safe outputs table and reset themselves (bypass reaction, architecture section 2.4) Static memory only no heap, no RTOS object created at run time; every state variable is a namespace-scope object or member, zero initialised (.bss) where it lies in the MPU protected RAM of a libsafe* archive (architecture section 1.2) Constants from the configuration times, counts and table contents come from generated macros (NX_MODULE_SAFELIFECYCLE_*, bsp/safeOutputs/safeOutputsConfiguration.h); relations between them are checked twice — by tools/nxconfig with the YAML path and by static_assert on the generated values Family interface by header a family-neutral unit (ecu/safety/safeWatchdog) reaches the hardware only through safety::bsp::Watchdog (OpenBSW driver) and the family headers of safeSupervisionCheck; another family provides the same headers (see section 8) Single exit MISRA C:2012 rule 15.5 is re-enabled for the safety units by an earlier change. The units of this document are written with one return per function except CyclePeriodCheck::sample() (two early returns) and SafetyManager::checkSupervisionPeripherals() (none) decides the rework

docs.text:
Unit Responsibility Mechanisms (concept) Requirements SafeWatchdog (ecu/safety/safeWatchdog) enable the MCU watchdog with the project time-out; at every service: re-check its configuration, detect over-service, service it, close the service bracket SM-01, SM-02, SM-03 SSR-010, SSR-012, SSR-013 WatchdogControlCheck (safeSupervisionCheck, family S32K1) compare the WDOG control fields that the OpenBSW driver's own check leaves out SM-02 SSR-012, SSR-066 CyclePeriodCheck (ecu/safety/safeWatchdog) compare the safety task's cycle distance with an independent counter: one interval too long, a window too short SM-04 (period part) SSR-018 LptmrCycleTimer (safeSupervisionCheck, family S32K1) provide that counter (LPTMR0 on LPO1K) and re-check its configuration SM-04 (period part) SSR-018, SSR-066 main (watchdog part only, platforms/s32k1xx/port/main/src/main.cpp) run the watchdog fast test once per start and enable the watchdog before the BSP and the application SM-07 SSR-017

The driver safety::bsp::Watchdog (OpenBSW safeBspMcuWatchdog, submodule, unchanged) is pre-existing software: its qualification is a separate task (P6-07, P8-09), not part of this design.

docs.title: 3.4 Behaviour — start-up and service
docs.text:
Start-up (main(), before the scheduler). Inside one SafetyShell: the supervisor is constructed and set to limp home; executeFastTest(6000 µs) runs the WDOG fast test (two test resets with CS[TST] 2 and 3; the reset reason code of the start tells them from real watchdog resets). On success limp home is left; on failure the monitor watchdogStartupCheckMonitor raises WATCHDOG_STARTUP_CHECK_FAILURE, whose reaction is S1 held without reset (holdSafeState()). In both cases enableMcuWatchdog() follows, so from here on the watchdog runs until the next reset — including through a held safe state, which services it from its hold loop. The time from this enable to the first service of the safety task must stay below the shortest time-out (observation D1, proposal U3).

Service (SafeWatchdog::cyclic()), in this order:

  1. fields = checkWatchdogControl(true); if Watchdog::checkWatchdogConfiguration(WATCHDOG_TIMEOUT_MS) fails, fields |= WATCHDOG_FIELD_DRIVER_CHECK. safeWatchdogConfigMonitor.check(fields == 0, fields) — a deviation is SAFE_WATCHDOG_CONFIGURATION_ERROR with the fields as context (S1 + S2).
  2. current = Watchdog::getWatchdogServiceCounter(). If current > _serviceCounter + 1 (unsigned), somebody else serviced the watchdog since the last service of the safety task: serviceWatchdogMonitor.trigger() → SAFE_WATCHDOG_SERVICE_DEVIATION (S1 + S2). The initial value 0xFFFFFFFF makes _serviceCounter + 1 wrap to 0, so the first service after init() already requires that nobody serviced the watchdog since it was enabled. _serviceCounter = current.
  3. Watchdog::serviceWatchdog() (refresh sequence of the driver).
  4. safeWatchdogSequenceMonitor.hit(LEAVE). A service path that returned early or was entered without ENTER (made by the caller) is SAFE_WATCHDOG_SEQUENCE_DEVIATION (S1 + S2).

Without PLATFORM_SUPPORT_WATCHDOG (a family without the driver) steps 1–3 are compiled out and only the bracket remains; such a family has no MCU watchdog supervision from this unit and must say so in its port (section 8).

Detection of a missing service is the watchdog hardware itself (SM-01): the warning interrupt WDOG_EWM_IRQHandler enters the fault handler (UD-HFH), which switches the outputs off; the watchdog reset follows. Over-service by the safety task itself (too many services) is not possible by construction (one call site, every WATCHDOG_CYCLIC_COUNTER cycles); a safety task that runs too fast is the window part of SM-04 (section 3.5).

docs.title: 3.5 Behaviour — period check (CyclePeriodCheck::sample)
docs.text:
State machine with two states: unstarted (_started == 0) and running.

  • unstarted: the sample becomes the reference (_last), window sum and count are cleared, state → running, return 0. Entered after construction and after restart().
  • running: interval = (now − _last) & counterMask (correct across one wrap-around of the counter); _last = now; the interval is added to the window sum (saturating at 0xFFFFFFFF) and the window count incremented. When the count reaches windowCycles, the window is evaluated — a sum below minWindowTicks gives WINDOW_TOO_SHORT with the sum — and cleared. Then, independent of the window: an interval above maxIntervalTicks returns INTERVAL_TOO_LONG with the interval; otherwise the window result (0 or WINDOW_TOO_SHORT) is returned. A too-long interval is therefore reported by the first late cycle, before any other check of that cycle.

The context word packs the kind into bits 31..24 and the value (saturated to 24 bit) into bits 23..0; the kind TIMER_CONFIGURATION (3) carries the deviating fields of checkCycleTimer() instead of a time. All three kinds are one event, SAFETY_CYCLE_PERIOD_VIOLATION (S1 + S2).

Why a window and not a per-interval lower bound: the task is scheduled at a fixed rate; after one late cycle the scheduler catches up with a short interval. One short interval is legitimate, a whole window of them is not — the task runs too fast, or the counter runs too slow or stopped (which would otherwise switch the check off silently).

docs.title: 3.6 Timing and derived values
docs.text:
Quantity Formula (source) Demo value service interval in cycles WATCHDOG_CYCLIC_COUNTER floor(watchdog_timeout_ms × 1000 / (3 × task_period_ms × LPO_max‰)) (tools/nxconfig, generated NX_MODULE_SAFELIFECYCLE_DERIVED_WATCHDOG_SERVICE_CYCLES) 7 → service every 70 ms shortest real time-out watchdog_timeout_ms × 1000 / LPO_max‰ 250 ms → 230.2 ms three services before that time-out 3 × 7 × 10 ms = 210 ms ≤ 230.2 ms (static_assert in SafetyManager.cpp, checks.py safety_timing) holds maxIntervalTicks floor((P + D) × 1 kHz × LPO_max‰ / 10⁶) + 1 14 ticks: 17 ms always reported, 12 ms never minWindowTicks floor((W × P − D) × 1 kHz × LPO_min‰ / 10⁶), W = service interval 59 ticks: a mean period below about 7.6 ms is reported wrap-around of the counter 16 bit at 1 kHz 65.5 s ≫ one window (static_assert)

P = task_period_ms, D = cycle_lateness_ms; LPO‰ are the per-mille limits derived from mcudb clock.lpo.

docs.title: 3.7 Configuration
docs.text: Project values (modules.safeLifecycle): task_period_ms, watchdog_timeout_ms, cycle_lateness_ms. Derivative value: clock.lpo (min/max/nominal). Everything else is derived (section 3.6). Ranges and checks are in the module manifest and in safeLifecycle.md; the admissible configuration range of these values is argued in config-range.md (N3).

docs.text: WDOG fields, expected values and the re-check per field: HSI section 4.1. LPTMR0, LPO1K and the clock gate: HSI sections 3 and 4.2. The unit design adds no register the HSI does not list.

docs.title: 4.3 Behaviour — customHardFaultHandler
docs.text:
Both architecture variants follow the same sequence; the ARMv6-M variant uses only low registers and 8-bit immediates, the ARMv7-M variant adds the fault status registers and the FP extended frame.

  1. R12 = xPSR (exception number for the dump).
  2. Safe outputs first: for every entry of nxSafeOutputs until address 0: if a gate address is given and (*gate & mask) == 0, skip (the peripheral's clock is off — an access would fault again); else store value to address. Then dsb. Only R0–R3 are used; they were stacked by the exception entry.
  3. Clear the whole dump region including the magic word (a partly written dump is never valid).
  4. Store handler xPSR and EXC_RETURN, then R4–R11 (not stacked by the hardware).
  5. ARMv7-M: store CFSR, HFSR, MMFAR, BFAR (lost on the reset).
  6. Select MSP or PSP by EXC_RETURN bit 2. If the stack pointer is not inside [__hard_fault_ram_start, __hard_fault_ram_end − frame size], store it raw and skip 7–8 (a corrupt stack pointer is a frequent fault cause; reading through it would fault inside the handler → lockup).
  7. Set DUMP_FLAG_FRAME_VALID; copy the stacked R0–R3, R12, LR, PC, xPSR; compute the SP before the exception (frame size, FP extended frame by EXC_RETURN bit 4, alignment padding by stacked xPSR bit 9).
  8. Copy stack words while they lie inside the RAM, up to the dump's stack area.
  9. Checksum over all words before the checksum field; store it; store the magic last.
  10. Branch to HardFault_Handler_Final.

Why this order. De-energising is the safety reaction; everything after step 2 is diagnosis. A handler that printed first would leave a bridge switching for milliseconds (board finding 2026-09-18); a handler that called a function first would lose EXC_RETURN and read the wrong frame.

docs.title: 4.4 Behaviour — after the handler
docs.text: HardFault_Handler_Final writes HARD FAULT RESET: outputs off, dump saved (WATCHDOG RESET: outputs off, dump saved when the valid dump carries the watchdog's vector, WDOG_EWM_IRQn + 16) between two flushes of the safe console (polling, bounded — the fault may have hit the UART driver, the logger or the RTOS), checks the ECC error flags once more (checkEccErrors(): an ECC error that caused the fault is reported, not lost) and requests the system reset. At the next start main() counts a present dump (or a lockup) as a fault exception for the reset-loop limit (SSR-065) and prints the dump once (reportAndClearDump()).

docs.title: 5.3 Behaviour — one cycle (SafetyManager::cyclic)
docs.text:
1. Read the gate state (fusaGateIsLocked()), then open it for the scope of the cycle (ProtectedRamScopedUnlock, restored at scope exit). mpuStatusCheckOnEnterMonitor.check(locked): the gate must have been closed on entry (MPU_UNLOCKED_ON_SAFETY_MANAGER_ENTRY otherwise).
  2. hit(SAFETY_MANAGER_ENTER).
  3. checkCyclePeriod(): checkCycleTimer(); if the timer deviates, context = TIMER_CONFIGURATION + fields (the counter is not read — with the clock gate off the read would bus fault); else sample(readCycleTimer(), CYCLE_PERIOD_LIMITS). A non-zero context → safetyCyclePeriodMonitor.trigger(). First, so that a late cycle reports itself before the results of its checks are used.
  4. hit(SAFETY_MANAGER_PERIOD_CHECKED).
  5. ++_counter; when it reaches WATCHDOG_CYCLIC_COUNTER: safeWatchdogSequenceMonitor.hit(ENTER), safeWatchdog.cyclic() (section 3.4, ends with hit(LEAVE)), _counter = 0.
  6. safe_memory::cyclic() (MPU descriptors, ECC status) → hit(MEMORY_CHECKED).
  7. safeSystem.cyclic() (ADC reference, supplies) → hit(SYSTEM_CHECKED).
  8. safeIo.cyclic() (register check) → hit(IO_CHECKED).
  9. checkSupervisionPeripherals(): if the project has a halt deadman, checkLpitDeadman(expected); deviations → deadmanConfigMonitor.trigger(fields) → hit(PERIPHERALS_CHECKED).
  10. deliverDeferredEvents() (reports of tasks without write access, e.g. RTE deadlines); with I/O support the pending safeadc reset request of the console task is carried out here.
  11. hit(SAFETY_MANAGER_LEAVE); read the gate state again and mpuStatusCheckOnLeaveMonitor.check(locked): it must still be open here (closed would mean something inside the cycle closed it); the scope then restores it.

Every checkpoint is a hit() of one sequence monitor: a cycle that returns early, skips or reorders a step is SAFETY_MANAGER_SEQUENCE_DEVIATION at the next hit, one that never reaches LEAVE is seen by the next ENTER. The reactions of every event raised in the cycle are S1 + S2 (architecture section 2.4); the supervisor's handle() runs synchronously in the cycle, so a fault found in step n stops the cycle there.

docs.title: 5.4 Behaviour — safe ISR hooks
docs.text:
counterSafeIsrHook (protected .bss) counts nesting. Pre hook: with all interrupts suspended; if the counter is above 0 (a safe ISR is already active) it is incremented under a short unlock; else, if the gate is open (the interrupt preempted the safety cycle), counter = 1, the safety stack region is closed for the ISR and the gate closed. If the gate was closed (the interrupt preempted a normal task) nothing is done. Post hook: mirror image; at counter 1 the stack region and the gate are reopened and the counter cleared. The safety cycle continues with the gate state it had.

Which vectors run through the hooks (finding SFP-F01). Up to a separate task only FTFC fault, ERM double fault and the CAN message-buffer vectors had a wrapper, so UART, pin-event, LPIT and SysTick handlers that preempted the cycle ran with write access to the protected RAM. Since an earlier change the vector table of both startups is the generated list of the derivative (startup/nxIrqVectors.inc, tools/bswgen) and every entry points at Safe_<handler>: for every external vector except the safety handlers, and for SysTick, Safe_<handler> is a SAFE_ISR wrapper (IsrWrapper.cpp, list interrupts/nxSafeIsrVectors.h), whether the integration uses the vector or not (an unused one reaches DefaultISR with the gate closed). So an interrupt handler that returns to the interrupted code never runs with write access to the safety RAM.

Not wrapped, each on purpose:

Vector Why watchdog/EWM (Safe_WDOG_EWM_IRQHandler) naked branch into the fault handler, outputs off first, never returns (section 4.2, K10) halt deadman, LPIT0 channel 1 (Safe_LPIT0_Ch1_IRQHandler = alias of LPIT0_Ch1_IRQHandler) a safety path itself: its first action is the safe outputs walk with no call before it (checked by disassembly, test_safe_outputs_order.py); it stores only LPIT registers and a flag outside the protected RAM. Without the debug halt guard the vector is DefaultISR (weak). The other LPIT channels are wrapped HardFault, BusFault, UsageFault never return; the fault path must reach the safe outputs without C code first (section 4) PendSV, SVC RTOS context switch: PendSV stacks the outgoing task's registers onto its process stack, which the pre hook makes read-only for the safety task, and a post hook after a switch would open the gate for the incoming task. The safety task has the highest priority and never blocks inside the cycle (section 5.2), so no switch away from it happens while the gate is open NMI, MemManage, DebugMon, reserved numbers DefaultISR (unused, the S32K1 NMI pin is not configured)

Assumption (review point): interrupt handlers use no floating point. The core stacks the FP context of an interrupted task lazily: the exception entry only reserves the space on that task's stack, the first FP instruction of the handler writes it there. If the interrupted task is the safety task with an active FP context, the pre hook has just made that stack read-only, and the deferred write would be a bus fault (fault reaction, reset). So nothing a wrapped handler or the hooks reach may contain a VFP instruction; tools/elfcheck checks it on the image (code isr-fpu, every function reached through bl/b.w; calls through a register and DefaultISR - an unexpected interrupt that never returns - are not followed). Eval board image: 63 functions, none with FP.

The rule is checked on the linked image by tools/elfcheck (code isr-unwrapped): every vector from SysTick on points at DefaultISR, the watchdog path, the halt deadman or a function whose first call is SafePreIsrHook and which calls SafePostIsrHook — recognised by its code, not by its name.

docs.title: 6. Consistency with the architecture and the HSI
docs.text:
Each statement of the architecture or the HSI about these units, compared with the code at 65f3dc9.

# Statement Source Code Result K1 the watchdog is serviced from the safety task only sw-architecture.md 1.1, SSR-010 one call site of serviceWatchdog() in the running system (SafeWatchdog::cyclic), plus the hold loop of the supervisor, which never returns agrees K2 service every 7th cycle, three services before the shortest time-out sw-architecture.md 2.1, 2.3 WATCHDOG_CYCLIC_COUNTER from the generated macro, static_assert on the relation agrees K3 configuration re-check at every service covers EN, CLK, TOVAL, INT, WIN, PRES, UPDATE hsi-s32k1xx.md 4.1 driver check + checkWatchdogControl() agrees; CMD32EN, STOP, WAIT, DBG not checked, as the HSI says K4 the period check comes first in the cycle sw-architecture.md 2.3 step 3 of section 5.3 agrees K5 the period check is measured against LPTMR0 on LPO1K, independent of the scheduler hsi-s32k1xx.md 4.2 startCycleTimer(): PSR[PCS] = 1, prescaler bypassed agrees K6 a timer with gated clock is reported without a counter read hsi-s32k1xx.md 3 checkCycleTimer() returns at the gate before any LPTMR access agrees K7 every checkpoint of the cycle is a hit of the sequence monitor sw-architecture.md 2.3 seven hits, ENTER … LEAVE agrees K8 gate closed on entry, open on exit of the cycle sw-architecture.md 1.1 (SSR-021) mpuStatusCheckOnEnter/OnLeaveMonitor agrees K9 the fault handlers walk the table before anything else sw-architecture.md 2.4, hsi-s32k1xx.md 4.7 step 2 of section 4.3, checked by disassembly agrees K10 the watchdog warning vector branches into the fault handler without a wrapper sw-architecture.md 2.1 isr_wdg.cpp, IsrWrapper.cpp comment agrees K11 BusFault and UsageFault print and reset without the walk hsi-s32k1xx.md 4.7 isr_sys.cpp agrees (finding H2 stands) K12 the dump lies in no-init RAM and is cleared after POR/LVD before its first read hsi-s32k1xx.md 4.7 prepareDump() in main() agrees K13 SafetySystem::shutdown cancels the cycle and disables the watchdog sw-architecture.md 2.2 SafetySystem.cpp agrees (observation D2) K14 state of the safety components lies in the protected .bss of the libsafe* archives sw-architecture.md 1.2 watchdog, period check, hook counter: yes; safetyManager._counter: no agrees for the components the architecture lists; see D3

Design observations for the code inspection. None contradicts a document; each is a property the design relies on without a check of its own.

  • D1 — start-up budget of the watchdog. The watchdog is enabled in main() before the BSP, the scheduler and lifecycle run level 1; its first service is WATCHDOG_CYCLIC_COUNTER cycles after SafetySystem::run(). The time in between must stay below the shortest time-out (230 ms for the demo). It holds on the eval board (no watchdog reset in any run), but no tool checks it; a project with more or slower run-level-1 components (e.g. SBC initialisation over SPI) moves it. Proposal U3.
  • D2 — watchdog off during the run-down. SafetySystem::shutdown() disables the MCU watchdog. During the remaining run-down the steps are supervised by their own time-outs (SM-53), not by the watchdog. That is the inherited OpenBSW behaviour; whether the run-down should keep the watchdog running (and service it from the run-down) is a question for a separate task and the FMEA. Update (2026-10-02): SafetySystem::shutdown() runs only on the way to level 0 (restart); the sleep path stays at level 1 with the watchdog on. The restart itself is now supervised by the ECU state management (direct reset after shutdown_timeout_ms) as long as level 1 is not taken down. Replacing the disable by "stop servicing" (finding WDG-F03) was examined and not done: after the last service at most about 160 ms of the watchdog remain (250 ms nominal, 230 ms at the fastest LPO, service every 7 cycles = 70 ms), while the orderly reset of the IdleHandler (lowest priority) first drains the logger - up to 8 KiB at 115 200 Bd, about 5.7 s. Every orderly restart would turn into a watchdog reset (start reason WATCHDOG, counted by the reset-loop limit). Open as check point of the safety review.
  • D3 — cycle counter outside the protected RAM. safetyManager is defined in SafetySystem.cpp (ecu/application), so _counter lies in the general .bss. A wild write can at worst delay the watchdog service by up to 65 535 cycles — which the watchdog itself then detects (reset) — or bring it forward, which the over-service check does not see because the service stays in the safety task. Effect: availability, not a missed detection. Moving the object into libsafeLifecycle is a small change for separate tasks.
  • D4 — first service after init(). The over-service check of the first service requires that nobody serviced the watchdog between enableMcuWatchdog() and it (section 3.4, step 2). No code does so today; a future service during a long start-up (a remedy for D1) must go through SafeWatchdog or re-initialise its counter.

docs.title: 8. Review questions of the architecture (section 11)
docs.text: This task changes no code, no generator and no configuration: one document and one consistency test. Board without an SBC: the designs use the MCU watchdog only; the SBC watchdog is a device driver (stage 2). Different crystal / system clock: the watchdog and the period check run on the LPO, not on the system clock; the only clock dependency is the safety task itself, which is what the period check measures. Other derivative of the family: the LPO range comes from mcudb; ARMv6-M (S32K11x) has its own handler variant. S32K3, STM32, Cortex-R: SafeWatchdog and CyclePeriodCheck are family-neutral; a new family provides safety::bsp::Watchdog, the headers of safeSupervisionCheck (watchdog control fields, a free-running counter on an independent clock) and a fault handler with the same contract (walk first, dump, reset). On Cortex-R the exception model differs (no EXC_RETURN, separate abort modes) — the contract stays, the handler is new code; nothing in this design blocks that. Several CAN buses: not affected (the CAN message-buffer vectors are wrapped per generated bus). Several tasks, free priorities: the design assumes the safety task is the highest application task (above_application: true), which tasks.yaml enforces. New values: none. Host test with own profile: test_unit_design.py checks the document against the tree; the designs cite the unit tests with their own profiles. Qt, YAML paths: not affected. Driver granularity, platform rule: not applicable.

docs.title: neXtBSW verification plan and archived reports per baseline
docs.text:
Title Verification plan and archived reports per baseline Issue 2, 2026-10-04 (issue 1: 2026-10-01, written against an integration branch at baa1d837) Author issue 1, update 2026-10-02 (issue 2) — author side Approver the safety manager: issue 1 judged in the safety review of 2026-10-02 (VP-1 … VP-11, decisions in section 11) and in the confirmation review CM-04 (record reviews/records/CR-04-1.md (not published, available on request), the safety manager under D-01, 2026-10-04, accepted with conditions); issue 2 released on 2026-10-04 in the re-check of the findings F-01 … F-09 in CR-04-1 (steps 6 and 7 at dev efc474ea: all closed, verdict accepted, CM-04 closed; D-01, without independence) Status issue 2 accepted (released 2026-10-04 in the re-check of CM-04, record CR-04-1); update after it, as the reviewer decided there: VP-10 open (Z7), T-VP8 = (T8), finding VF-1 (RN, section 10.1) Change history section 15

Working state: dev at 6812a0b4 (after v0.2.0) Readers: the safety manager and release authority, the maintainer who merges, runs the release CI and tags, the contributors who write tests, and the reviewer of confirmation measure CM-04 (integration and test strategy). Language: English, like the rest of doc/.

Terms. "Release R1" is the first release the safety manager wants to be releasable, tagged v1.0.0-rc1 — a development release without a safety claim (safety plan section 5, deviation for release R1); this plan writes it as "Release R1 (v1.0.0-rc1)". The release preconditions of safety plan section 6 are always written "precondition R1" … "precondition R6"; they are a different thing (CM-04 finding F-05).

What this document is. The verification plan that iso26262-gap.md (not published, available on request) found missing (rows 8-20 to 8-22, 6-22 to 6-36; section 6 task 9) and that the safety plan names as work product of P6-14, P6-16, P6-17, P6-20 and P8-06. It says, per verification level, which methods neXtBSW uses and how they are rated at ASIL B, what passes and what fails, in which environment and with which tool versions, how test cases are derived, what runs on every merge and what per baseline, and how the report of a baseline is bound to its tag and archived. It closes the gaps G1 and G2 of cm-plan.md section 10 together with two small tool changes in tools/ci (section 7).

What it is not. Not the configuration management plan (cm-plan.md owns baselines, tags and the release steps; this plan defines what "green" means for them), not the description of the tools (dev-environment.md section 7 lists the test flow and the pinned tools; this plan does not repeat it), not a test specification per case (the cases live in the test code, section 5).

Licence rule. ISO 26262 is cited by part and clause only (for example "6-9.4.3" = ISO 26262-6:2018, clause 9.4.3). Methods are named in our own words; the rating at ASIL B is given as HR (highly recommended) or R (recommended) for the methods this project uses, never as a copy of a table. The ratings are our reading and are a review point (VP-10): open, checked by the safety manager against the licensed standard before the first safety release (CM-04 re-check Z7; not needed for Release R1 without a safety claim).

Consistency test. tools/ci/test_verification_plan.py checks this document against the repository: every group of tools/test/tests.yaml has a level in section 2, every pinned version of section 4 equals its pin file, every switch of section 3.2 equals pipeline.toml/coverage.yaml, every derivation value in tests.yaml is one of section 5, every provenance field of section 7.1 is written by tools/ci, the counts of section 3.6 equal tests.yaml and traceability.md, and the list of section 3.5 is exactly the safety entries without fault-injection (both since issue 2). Each rule has a counter-check on a broken copy. Numbers in the running text are taken from the table of section 3.6 at the working state.

docs.title: 1. Scope and interfaces
docs.text:
The plan covers the verification of the neXtBSW element (SEooC, claim of the safety plan section 1.2) in this repository: own code, generated code, the modified OpenBSW copies, the configuration data of the project's own profiles, and the own tools whose output reaches the image (tool confidence in tool-classification.md). The verification of a customer's configuration and integration is the integrator's; tools/ci run --workspace gives him the same pipeline. The assumptions of use that hand it over (safety manual sections 1.3 and 7, assumptions.sdoc):

What the integrator verifies Assumption of use his configuration data under change control, re-verified after every change AoU-10, AoU-CFG-1 the configuration itself on his hardware (the run-time checks detect a change, not a wrong value) AoU-DFA-c, AoU-CFG-2 the board checks of fmea.md section 8 that depend on a value he changed, his schedule and restart time AoU-CFG-2, AoU-CFG-3, AoU-08 his application and its generated model code AoU-29 the parts of the assumed goals the element does not cover AoU-23 the integration test of his ECU and the test in the vehicle (section 2.3, tailored) the safety manual section 1.3 row "verification of the integration and of the item", with AoU-10 and AoU-CFG-2 Interface Document What it takes from here What this plan takes from it Configuration management cm-plan.md what a green report is, the report files, the binding rule (section 7) the baseline, the release steps 1-9, the preconditions P1-P9 Safety plan safety-plan.md the work product of P6-14, P6-16, P6-17, P6-20, P8-06; evidence for precondition R2 (section 6 of the safety plan) the activities and their status Development environment dev-environment.md the host/target difference analysis it leaves open (its 7.1) the list of pinned tools and the test flow Traceability traceability.md (generated) the rule that every SSR has a verification (section 3.3) the requirement coverage per SSR Reviews reviews/ the review packages of CM-04 and the inspections the record template Anomalies anomaly-register.md failures of verification that are not fixed in the same task become anomalies the register Safety case safety-case.md EW-26 (this plan), ER-02 (archived report) the deficits D-12, D-21

docs.title: 2. Levels and methods
docs.text:
The levels follow part 6: unit verification (6-9), software integration and its verification (6-10), testing of the embedded software (6-11). Every automated verification is an entry of tools/test/tests.yaml; its group says how it runs, the table says which level a group serves. One group can serve two levels, because a group is a way of running (Python, C/C++ via zig, target build), not a level.

Level tests.yaml groups What is verified Environment Unit host C/C++ units of the element (safety mechanisms, drivers, BSW services) with the real unit code against register models and stubs, own test profiles host, zig c++/zig cc Unit python own tools and generators (nxconfig, bswgen, rtegen, dbcgen, …), Python wrappers that build C/C++ host tests, mutation runs, document consistency tests host, pinned Python Unit pytest neXtBSW Studio (tool, not part of the image) host, offscreen Qt Integration target every visible build profile built warning-free with the pinned ARM GCC; checks of the linked image (sections, safe outputs table, disassembly of the fault paths, timing tables, stack use, ROM check list) host with ARM GCC, no board Integration build host builds of the bootloader core as DLL and of the STM32 build test host Integration matlab model tests of the component generator (tools/swc), outside the CI workstation with MATLAB Embedded software — (no entry in the list) board runs with tools/boardtest, board checklists of fmea.md section 8 and of the task records, captures in tools/boardtest/captures eval board, J-Link, VN1610, lab devices; only the maintainer

The board level is the weakest: it is run by the maintainer only and so far per task image, not per baseline. Since an earlier change the cases are specified per SSR and repeatable (tools/boardtest suite); the board state for Release R1 was taken from 2026-10-02 to 2026-10-04 at integration states (captures tools/boardtest/captures/evalboard_s32k144_demo/2026-10-02_board, 2026-10-03_board and the suite runs 2026-10-02_suite-integ12*), not at a tag. Section 9 (VP-6) defines what a safety release needs, section 9.1 what Release R1 needs on its tagged image.

docs.title: 2.4 Reviews and document checks
docs.text: Inspections and confirmation reviews are planned by the safety plan (sections 4 and 5) and recorded in doc/safety/reviews. Every safety document that makes a checkable statement has a consistency test in doc/safety/test or next to its tool; these tests are part of the unit level of the CI and fail when a document and the repository disagree.

docs.title: 3.1 Per level
docs.text:
Level Pass Fail Unit, entry the runner's verdict pass (exit 0 and the expected summary line, tools/test) fail, timeout, or a test file no entry covers ("NICHT IN tools/test/tests.yaml") Unit, static analysis no finding outside baseline and deviation list (tools/misra) a new finding; with --strict a missing tool Unit, coverage reported per module against coverage.yaml today never red (VP-1) Unit, mutation run every inserted fault is found a surviving fault Integration, build configure and build with -Werror any warning or error Integration, image check the check's own expectation, independent of the generator where stated any deviation Integration, profiles every visible preset is built or listed with a reason under presets.not_built a profile without a decision Embedded software the expected console lines and measured values of the checklist, recorded as capture with image CRC any deviation; a deviation is an anomaly until explained Whole run (tools/ci run --strict) verdict pass: every stage ok, no fail finding, every skip listed in allowed_skips anything else

A run that is not --strict is a trial; it never counts as evidence of a baseline (section 7.2).

docs.title: 3.3 Requirement coverage
docs.text:
Every SSR names its verification methods (VERIFICATION in doc/requirements/safety/ssr.sdoc), and every test entry that verifies one names it in requirements:. tools/trace (entry safety-trace) fails on a dead reference and regenerates traceability.md; the counts at the working state are in section 3.6 (59 SSR, 57 with at least one test entry, 2 open). A test entry is evidence of a defined test, not of a passed one: the passed state comes from the archived report of the baseline (section 7).

  • Board verification per SSR. Every SSR whose VERIFICATION names "board" is covered per clause by the cases of board-test-spec.md (section 5 there: 91 board items by 31 cases, of which 3 cases are for projects with features the demo does not configure, and 7 items without a board case, each with its reason). The board level of a baseline is the run of those cases on its image (section 9, VP-6; for Release R1 section 9.1).
  • Open SSR. An SSR with status open is not implemented; it has no test entry and carries no claim. At the working state these are SSR-061 (plausibility between two measurement paths, gap G2) and SSR-063 (safe state of bus-commanded actuators, gap G4). They are a limit of Release R1: the safety manual hands the missing coverage to the integrator (AoU-23); their verification is planned with the stage-2 work that implements them.

docs.title: 3.4 Structural coverage
docs.text:
Level Measure Target State Unit statement and branch coverage of the C/C++ host tests (tools/test/coverage.py, gcov counting) safety modules 95 % statements / 70 % branches, others 80 / 50 (coverage.yaml) measured in every full run, not enforced; the safety modules miss the branch proposal in part (gap row 6-24) Unit MC/DC not targeted at B (recommended only); the way to it is noted in a change-log fragment — Architecture function and call coverage not measured (recommended at B, gap row 6-30) argued in VP-2

Decision VP-1 a (safety review 2026-10-02): the gate is switched on for the safety modules before the first safety release; the other modules stay reported. Until then coverage.enforce and enforce stay false (section 3.2) and the gate is a limit of Release R1 (section 9.1). Today coverage.yaml records per module the measured value and its cause (reason); several safety modules are below the branch proposal of 70 %. That is a measurement, not yet an argument: the argument per module — which branches are not reached, and why their behaviour is shown otherwise (by a board case, an image check, or because the branch is defensive and cannot be reached) — is part of switching the gate on and is required for the first safety release, not for Release R1, which makes no safety claim (CM-04 finding F-08).

docs.title: 3.5 Effectiveness of the tests
docs.text:
A test of a safety mechanism has a counter-check: a mutation run (*-mutations), a built-in broken copy in the test itself ("Gegenprobe"), or a reference against an independent expectation. A safety test entry without one of these is a weakness. The derivation value fault-injection marks the entries that insert faults (mutation runs, register model faults, broken copies); the safety entries without it are the candidates and are listed below (CM-04 finding F-09; the consistency test keeps the list equal to tests.yaml). The column "Marker" says whether a text search of the entry's test files finds a counter-check marker ("Gegenprobe", "counter-check", "broken copy"); it is a search, not a judgement. An entry with "none found" may still compare against an independent expectation (for example a reference model or a hand-written table) — sighting each one and adding or arguing its counter-check is T-VP8 (section 10), required before the first safety release.

The versions are pinned once in the files named; every report of tools/ci records them (stage "Werkzeuge pruefen", static_analysis.tool_versions) and, since this issue, the commit that pins them (section 7.1).

Tool Version Pinned in Used for ARM GCC (xPack) 11.3.1 tools/ci/versions.toml target builds, image CMake 4.4.3 tools/ci/versions.toml target and host builds Ninja 1.13.2 tools/ci/versions.toml target and host builds Python 3.12.10 tools/ci/.python-version all tools and Python tests ziglang (zig cc/c++, clang) 0.16.0 tools/ci/constraints.txt C/C++ host tests, coverage cppcheck (pip wheel) 1.5.1 tools/misra/requirements.txt static analysis clang-tidy (pip wheel) 22.1.8 tools/misra/requirements.txt static analysis

docs.title: 4.2 Host and target: the differences and what bridges them (6-9.4.5, 6-10.4.7)
docs.text:
The unit level runs on the host with zig c++/zig cc (clang) for x86-64; the image is built by ARM GCC 11.3.1 for Cortex-M4F (S32K14x) or Cortex-M0+ (S32K11x). A host result carries over to the target only where the difference does not matter or a target check bridges it.

# Difference Consequence for a host result Bridge on the target Remaining HT-1 Compiler and optimiser (clang vs GCC, other flags) undefined or implementation-defined behaviour can differ; code generation differs static analysis over the target compile database; target build with -Werror; disassembly checks of the fault paths (safe-outputs-order, hold-console-elf, freertos-config-elf) units without an ELF check rely on the static analysis HT-2 Pointer and long width (host 64-bit pointers; long 32-bit on Windows, 64-bit on Linux; target 32/32) arithmetic on long, casts between pointers and integers, structure layout NXCPP/MISRA rules on fixed-width types (uint32 = uint32_t since an earlier change); layout of records checked in the ELF where it matters (safety-context-elf, hard-fault dump layout) no general check that host and target layouts agree (VP-3) HT-3 Signedness of plain char (signed on x86-64, unsigned with ARM GCC) comparisons and shifts on char can differ MISRA essential-type rules in the static analysis host tests are not built with -funsigned-char (VP-3) HT-4 Floating point (target single-precision FPU, double in software; host hardware double) rounding of double paths, timing safety mechanisms use integer arithmetic; FPU and ABI attributes checked by elfcheck — HT-5 Hardware registers the host sees a register model, not the silicon register models follow the reference manual and are named per test; the HSI (hsi-s32k1xx.md) lists every register a mechanism uses; board checks per mechanism a model can share an error with the code (same reader of the manual): board checks B1-B11 HT-6 Interrupts and concurrency host tests are single-threaded with simulated interrupts and a virtual clock MPU placement and priorities checked in the ELF (safety-context-elf, elfcheck-timing*), safe-supervisor-mpu with the host MMU; board runs under load (B4) races are argued, not tested exhaustively HT-7 Start-up code, linker script, memory map not executed on the host application-linker, elfcheck* (sections, overlap, records), rom-check-image, safe-memory-ecc-latent-elf, stackuse-demo start-up timing only on the board HT-8 Timing and clock virtual time on the host elfcheck-timing* (periods and offsets as configured), cycle-period-constants, board B2, B4, B7 measured WCET open (N10) HT-9 RTOS (FreeRTOS on the target, stubs on the host) scheduling and kernel hooks only in the image freertos-config-elf, kernel-fault-reaction with the real hooks, board runs FreeRTOS qualification is O2 of the safety plan

docs.title: 5.1 Methods
docs.text: Value Method (own words) Rating at B Typical evidence in a test requirements-analysis cases taken from the requirement text, one or more per statement HR a case per sentence of the SSR or mechanism equivalence-classes inputs split into classes that the unit treats alike, one case per class HR every register value, state or event class once boundary-values cases at, just inside and just outside each limit HR limit, limit plus one tick, zero, counter overflow error-guessing cases from experience and earlier findings (board findings, review findings) R a case named after a finding (Fn, SR-…, board session) fault-injection faults inserted into the unit, its inputs or its registers; the test must notice R a mutation run, register-model faults operational-use-cases cases from the way the element is used in a vehicle (start, sleep/wake, flashing, load) HR at target level board sessions, SIL of the demo component functional-dependencies cases from the dependencies between functions (order, shared resources) R at target level order checks in the ELF, lock and bracket tests

docs.title: 5.2 Where the derivation is recorded
docs.text:
• Per safety test entry (an entry with requirements:) the field derivation: in tools/test/tests.yaml lists the methods used, values from 5.1. The field is optional for the runner (it ignores it) and checked by the consistency test (only known values, only on entries with requirements:).
  • Per case the test code says which class, limit or finding it covers, in the name or the comment of the case; that is the test specification of 8-9.4.2 (ID = entry name plus case name, version = commit, expected result = assertion). A separate specification document is not written (VP-8, decided in CM-04, Z5).
  • At target level the board checklist of the task names its cases with the expected result; the capture is the record. Since an earlier change the cases per SSR and operational use case are specified in board-test-spec.md and run with tools/boardtest suite; the record of a run is its capture folder with suite-run.json (image, baseline, result and values per case).

docs.title: 6. Regression strategy
docs.text:
Ring When What Who Gate R-A Task before the contributor commits the entries of the contributor's own files, at most one small group (tools/test -k), target build of the touched profile contributor the maintainer does not merge red R-B Merge after every merge into the integration branch tools/test --since <merge base> --jobs 4: every entry whose covers, watch, imports or own entry the merge touched, plus the groups the changelog names maintainer red → fix-up before the next merge R-C Integration at least once per integration branch before it goes to dev, and after a tool pin changes the full list tools/test --clean (all groups, without --slow) maintainer red → the branch does not go to dev R-D Baseline per release candidate pre-flight of section 8, then python -m tools.ci run --strict --clean [--slow] on the frozen candidate; board regression for a safety release (section 9); for Release R1 the strict, slow, bound run and the board points of section 9.1 maintainer, maintainer for the board cm-plan.md P2

A change of a tool pin (CI-06), of pipeline.toml or of coverage.yaml always goes through R-C. The mutation runs (--slow) are part of R-D for a safety release and of R-B when the merge touches the unit they mutate (--since selects them only with --slow).

docs.title: 7.1 Content and provenance (G1)
docs.text:
python -m tools.ci run --out <dir> writes ci-result.json, summary.md, tests.json, tests.log, the coverage report (coverage.json, coverage.md, coverage.log), the static analysis under misra/ and the artefacts with sizes. Since this issue ci-result.json also records which state it judged:

Field of provenance Content commit full commit of HEAD at the start of the run tree tree hash of that commit (equal for the candidate on dev and the release merge on master) describe git describe --tags --always --dirty, for the reader openbsw gitlink of the OpenBSW submodule in that commit version content of VERSION dirty whether the working tree had tracked or untracked changes (ignored files such as build/ do not count) changes the first 20 changed paths, changes_total their number end commit, tree, dirty, changes_total at the end of the run

workspace_provenance holds the same for a customer workspace run, slow and release the flags of the run. The summary prints the line Stand <describe>: Commit …, Baum …. A HEAD that moved during the run is a Herkunft finding, red with --strict: a report of hours must not mix two states. Changes that appear during the run (a test writing into the tree, someone working in it) are a warning.

docs.title: 7.2 Binding and archiving (G2)
docs.text:
A report is bound to a baseline when (tools/ci/release.py: report_binding):

  1. ci-result.json exists, verdict pass, the run was --strict, a run of the tree (not of a workspace);
  2. it records its provenance (reports written before this issue do not - v0.2.0 is such a case);
  3. the working tree was clean at the start and HEAD did not move;
  4. its tree hash equals HEAD^{tree} of the checkout that is tagged, and its VERSION the release version.

Procedure, after step 5 of cm-plan.md 5.2 (merge on master) and before the tag (step 6):

python -m tools.ci release --report-dir build/ci-out-vX.Y.Z --strict [--profile open --archive]

It copies the report to <archive>/vX.Y.Z/ (NX_RELEASE_ARCHIVE, else %LOCALAPPDATA%/nextbsw/release-archive), writes <archive>/ci-out-vX.Y.Z.zip and ci-out-vX.Y.Z.zip.sha256, and prints in release-plan.md the tag message line CI report: sha256 <hash> (ci-out-vX.Y.Z.zip) and the command for the GitHub release asset (gh release create vX.Y.Z <zip> <zip>.sha256 …), which the integrator runs after the tag is pushed (step 9). The tool never tags and never pushes. --strict stops at an unbound report and names every reason; without --strict the plan says "Bound to this tree: no" with the reasons, which a development release may accept and name in its tag message.

Copy Where Retention Release asset GitHub release vX.Y.Z on origin (zip + .sha256) permanent (Q-CM3) Local archive <archive>/vX.Y.Z/ and the zip, on the workstation; a second medium is the maintainer's backup permanent Binding SHA-256 in the tag message; tree in the report permanent with the tag Other CI runs GitHub Actions artefacts 14 days, working records only

For a safety release the archives of ARM GCC, CMake and Ninja go next to the report (Q-CM3); tools.ci release does not copy them yet (open, section 10).

docs.title: 8. Finding faults before the release CI
8.1 What the first release run showed
docs.text:
The release procedure for v0.2.0 (maintainer, 2026-10-01) needed three runs of tools/ci run --strict of about 5 h each. The faults that turned them red were found only there, in calgen, mcudb, stackuse, safe-outputs-table and in the classification of the static analysis (files under a build/ folder inside the tree). The detailed causes are the maintainer's record of the release — CHANGELOG.md section "0.2.0 – 2026-10-01" and the entry REL-020-FIX4; the duration of about 5 h per run is the maintainer's account of 2026-10-01, not a recorded measurement. This plan uses only their pattern:

Pattern Why the earlier rings missed it Pre-flight step that finds it A merge changes an input of an entry that is not in the contributor's group (generated reports such as the stack-use report, tables checked against an independent expectation, mcudb data) R-A runs only the contributor's group, R-B was run per group, not per touched input PF-3 A stage that runs only in the full CI (coverage, static analysis) meets something new tools/test alone never runs them PF-4 The environment of the run differs (folders inside the tree, a dirty working copy, tools of the workstation) the release run was the first strict run in that checkout PF-1, PF-2 A fix-up between two runs breaks something else each fix-up was followed by another full run PF-3 on the fix-up, then one full run

docs.title: 8.2 Pre-flight (about one hour, then the release CI once)
docs.text:
Step Command Finds Time (order) PF-1 Freeze a separate clean worktree of the candidate commit: git worktree add <dir> <commit>; nothing else works in it; build root and output folder outside the tree changes during the run, folders in the tree minutes PF-2 Tools and profiles python -m tools.ci check --strict pin deviations, profiles without a decision seconds PF-3 Increment python -m tools.test --since v<previous> --list, then the same with --jobs 4 (with --slow for a safety release) every entry whose inputs changed since the last baseline most of the hour PF-4 CI-only stages python -m tools.test -k target-demo (writes the compile database), then python -m tools.misra run --compile-db <build root>/demo/compile_commands.json and python tools/test/coverage.py --jobs 4 new static-analysis findings, classification of generated files, coverage measurement failures 20-30 min PF-5 Document state tools/test -k safety (document tests, safety-trace) on the candidate after release step 1 (Baseline: lines) state lines, tables of the safety documents minutes

Only when PF-1 to PF-5 are green does the release CI start. A fault found by the release CI anyway is recorded with the pattern it belongs to, and this section gets a new row; the goal is one release CI run per baseline.

Tool (in review since 2026-10-02): python -m tools.ci preflight --since v<previous> runs PF-2 to PF-5 in this order and writes a short report (task proposal T-VP3 of issue 1). Its first real run on a release candidate is the one before the release CI of Release R1 (section 9.1, CM-04 Z3).

docs.title: 9.1 Release R1 (v1.0.0-rc1)
docs.text:
Release R1 is the first release the safety manager wants to be releasable (Freigabeumfang R1). By the safety plan (section 5, deviation for release R1) it is a development release without a safety claim (D-01, precondition R5 not met). It is not judged against the development column of the matrix alone: the safety manager decided in CM-04 (2026-10-04) what it needs on top. Release R1 = development release plus:

  1. Release CI as for a safety release (CM-04 Z3): python -m tools.ci run --strict --clean --slow on the frozen candidate — the mutation runs included — and the report bound with python -m tools.ci release --strict (section 7.2); v1.0.0-rc1 is the first bound report. Before it the pre-flight python -m tools.ci preflight (section 8.2) — its first real run on a candidate, which also completes.
  2. Board list before the tag (CM-04 Z4): a related task delivers the board regression list (T-VP2) before the tag is set. The list contains BT-S1-03 (S1 confirmed by read-back, fmea.md B15; decision BRD a of the re-check of CM-02, 2026-10-04).
  3. Board run on the tagged image (CM-04 Z4): a suite run of the demo cases of board-test-spec.md with tools/boardtest suite on the tagged rc1 image, plus the restart-time measurement F4 (review F4 a: at least four runs with the oscilloscope); records with image CRC and the tag. The board state of 2026-10-02 … 2026-10-04 (section 2.3) was taken at integration states and does not replace this run.
  4. Requirement coverage, derivation and the automated rows as in the development column; safety-trace green; CM-04 performed (record CR-04-1).

docs.text:
%%{init: {'theme':'base','flowchart':{'curve':'basis'},'themeVariables':{'fontFamily':'Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif','fontSize':'14px','background':'#ffffff','primaryColor':'#ffffff','primaryBorderColor':'#64748b','primaryTextColor':'#0f172a','lineColor':'#475569','edgeLabelBackground':'#ffffff','tertiaryColor':'#f8fafc','clusterBkg':'#f8fafc','clusterBorder':'#cbd5e1'}}}%%
stateDiagram-v2
    state "normal operation" as RUN
    S3: S3 log and continue
    SD: SD mapped groups degraded
    S1: S1 outputs off
    HELD: S1 held
    S1S2: S1 + S2

    [*] --> RUN
    RUN --> S3: SM-05, SM-34 report
    S3 --> RUN
    RUN --> SD: degradable event, mapped
    SD --> SD: more groups
    SD --> S1: last working group
    RUN --> S1: SM-22
    S1 --> RUN: leaveSafeState, indicator only
    RUN --> HELD: SM-07, SM-14, SM-50, SM-34
    RUN --> S1S2: most events
    S1S2 --> RUN: reset, restart
    S1S2 --> HELD: reset-loop limit
    HELD --> [*]: power cycle
    SD --> [*]: power cycle

Legende

  • Eine Stelle entscheidet: SafeSupervisor::handle(). Ein Mechanismus meldet nur.
  • S1 ist eine Einbahnstraße nach oben: leaveSafeState() gibt nur die Anzeige frei, eine Leistungsstufe kommt nur über ein ausdrückliches enable() ihres Treibers zurück.
  • S1 held: alle Interrupts gesperrt, Tabelle zyklisch neu geschrieben, MCU-Watchdog bedient; Ende nur durch Aus- und Einschalten oder Reset von außen.
  • SD: nur Ereignisse der geschlossenen Liste (DEVICE_FAULT außer IDENTITY, Auslösung eines Hardware-Abschaltpfads HW_SHUTOFF), nur wenn das Projekt sie abbildet; Fehler der MCU selbst nie. Gruppen sammeln sich, nur Aus- und Einschalten beendet SD.
  • S3 ist nur zulässig, wo die Analyse zeigt, dass innerhalb der FTTI kein Sicherheitsziel verletzt wird (SM-05: Reaktion bei der Anwendung, AoU-18).

Quelle: Konzept Ausgabe 3, Abschnitt 3.

    FHTI("FHTI of the element<br/>concept 7.2")

Legende

  • Balken: garantierte Werte der Tabelle 7.2 bis „Ausgänge stromlos“, jeweils zuzüglich des Tabellendurchlaufs (< 1 µs gerechnet, am Board ≤ 21 µs begrenzt). Nominal sind die Prüfungen im Safety-Task 10 ms, SM-19 100 ms, SM-20 60 ms; SM-01 sind 250 ms bei nominalem LPO, bis etwa 283 ms über den LPO-Bereich.
  • Nicht im Balken: Restrisiko DF-05 (SIRC verloren): kein Tabellendurchlauf vor dem Watchdog-Reset nachgewiesen, höchstens etwa 283 ms. SM-05 schaltet nichts ab (nur Log).
  • Grundwerte (Demo-Projekt): Safety-Task 10 ms, Watchdog-Bedienung alle 70 ms, Watchdog-Zeitablauf 250 ms; geprüft wird 3 × 70 ms = 210 ms ≤ 230,2 ms (Zeitablauf beim schnellsten LPO).
  • Ein Reset ist nicht sofort: der Neustart dauert am Eval Board bis 1 077 ms (Watchdog-Weg) bzw. 858 ms (MPU-Fehler).
  • Das Element legt keine FTTI fest; der Integrator vergleicht je Ziel (AoU-05).

docs.text:
R1 (v1.0.0-rc1) is a development release and makes no safety claim. Die Safety-Dokumente beschreiben das Ziel (Software-SEooC, ASIL B) und den Stand der Nachweise, keine Zusicherung. Maßgeblich ist der Safety Case, Abschnitt 0.

Legende

  • Von links nach rechts: Die angenommenen Sicherheitsziele (ASG) werden zu Sicherheitsanforderungen (SSR), diese durch Mechanismen (SM) umgesetzt; die Mechanismen werden durch Tests, Boardaufzeichnungen und Arbeitsprodukte belegt, und der Safety Case bündelt die Nachweise mit den offenen Lücken.
  • Gestrichelt: Was neXtBSW nicht selbst leistet, steht als Annahme (AoU) an den Integrator im Sicherheitshandbuch; auch sie werden belegt, soweit sie neXtBSW betreffen.
  • Türkis = eigener Code (die Mechanismen), hellgrau = Dokumente und Daten, rot = Ergebnis mit Urteil und Lücken.
  • Die Kataloge stehen im offenen Baum: Ziele, Anforderungen, Mechanismen, Annahmen.

docs.title: Hauptpfad
docs.text:
1. Sicherheitshandbuch: was ein Integrator beachten muss, mit den Annahmen (AoU) an seine Umgebung und Konfiguration.
  2. Sicherheitskonzept: angenommene Sicherheitsziele, Mechanismen der Stufe 1, Reaktionen und sichere Zustände, Grenzen des Anspruchs.
  3. Anomalie-Register: bekannte Abweichungen und offene Befunde, die ein Anwender kennen muss.

Bilder zu Konzept und FMEA (ergänzende Darstellung ohne inhaltliche Änderung): Bilder zum Sicherheitskonzept, Bilder zur Fehleranalyse. Die Safety-Kette im Überblick: Bild 6.

docs.text:
Nachweise und Hintergrund für Assessoren; für das Verständnis des Hauptpfads sind sie nicht nötig.
