There is no option to pass the key on the command line (shell history); the key is never printed. Instead of --key-file, --project <project.yaml> or --key-name <name> read the key from the key store of the workstation (%LOCALAPPDATA%/neXtBSW/keys/csec/<name>.key, name from project.yaml security.master_ecu_key, default the board name; created once with python tools/nxconfig csec-key new <project>; see doc/architecture/csec-concept.md section 6.5). The same file format applies to --key-file (# comments allowed; the empty slot, all zeros and public test values are refused).

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: she.py: AES-128 (encryption only), AES-CBC, AES-CMAC, Miyaguchi-Preneel compression, KDF, memory update protocol, debug authorisation – pure Python on purpose (a few blocks per run; a crypto package would be a new pinned dependency of the shared environment). cli.py: the command line.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
test_she.py (tools/test csec-host), published vectors only: FIPS-197 Appendix B and C.1 (AES), NIST SP 800-38A F.2.1 (CBC), RFC 4493 section 4 (CMAC), and the HIS SHE Functional Specification v1.1 example of the memory update protocol (K1, K2, M1..M5). The debug authorisation has no published vector and is tested by construction from the checked KDF and CMAC. The test also checks that the constant of the device (FIRST_LOAD_M2_BLOCK0) and the vectors of its host test are what this tool computes.

Sources: HIS SHE Functional Specification v1.1; NXP AN5401 Rev. 1 Appendix A and section 4.5 (doc/hardware/s32k1xx/AN5401.pdf); S32K1xx Reference Manual Rev. 13, 36.5.13.

docs.title: distcheck – distribution check and export of the open tree
docs.text:
tools/distcheck checks a tree before anything is exported and writes the open source line as a fresh tree without git history. The concept is doc/architecture/lizenz-und-release.md, section 5.3; the decisions of 2026-09-17 behind the rules are listed at the top of distribution.yaml. Core logic without Qt (distcheck.py, exporter.py), command line in __main__.py, host tests in test_distcheck.py.

python tools/distcheck check --profile open --references           # exit 1 on errors
python tools/distcheck check --references --json > report.json      # machine readable (severity, rule, path, line)
python tools/distcheck report --format markdown                      # which rule classified how many files
python tools/distcheck export --out %TEMP%/s32k/export --verify --openbsw external/openbsw
python tools/distcheck verify --tree %TEMP%/s32k/export --openbsw external/openbsw
python tools/distcheck export --out C:/nx --verify --verify-timeout 0 --verify-jobs 6 --openbsw external/openbsw
python tools/distcheck patterns --out doc/confidential/distcheck-patterns.yaml

Nothing here publishes anything. export writes a directory; what happens with it is decided by the maintainer.

docs.title: Classification
docs.text: Every file gets one class: open < licensed < nda < private < workstation. The class comes from a module manifest with distribution: if there is one, otherwise from the path table distribution.yaml (most specific glob wins). The catch-all ** makes an unknown file private (fail closed) and reports it (R1 warning), so every file needs an entry of its own. A profile (open, licensed, nda) contains the files whose class is not higher.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
Rule Error if R1 a file has no class of its own, or no class at all R2 an SPDX header names a licence outside the profile's allowlist, or LicenseRef-* in open; warning if a source file has no header and the licence only comes from the table R3 text matches a content pattern: the public base list in distribution.yaml, plus the private list (below); the base list includes simulink_generated, the header lines Simulink Coder writes into generated C code and ARXML (below) R4 a binary or document file (PDF, SVD, ...) has no explicit binary_ok entry; PDFs are text-scanned (first four and last page) R5 (--references) a file of the profile points out of it: #include, add_subdirectory, target_link_libraries, python import, board:/derivative: of a project; a target that any file of the profile also defines counts as present, and external_targets of the rules lists targets that come from Eclipse OpenBSW in the real build (stand-ins in the build tests of private families) R6 a .sha256 file does not match; a third party folder lacks its README/LICENSE (warning) R7 key material (BL_SECURITY_CONSTANT with a value, private keys, tokens), the address of a private repository (development neXtBSW_development, Studio neXtBSW-Studio; the open repository neXtBSW may be named), the decision log; workstation paths (warning) R8 (--history <range>) a path that ever held a blob in the range is not in the profile; more than one commit (warning) R9 verify: host tests and the target preset verify_preset run in the exported tree; skipped steps are named. Each step is limited to 5400 s by default; the full host suite takes longer on a loaded workstation, so a release export passes --verify-timeout 0 (no limit) or a larger value, and --verify-jobs (verify: --timeout, --jobs). Keep --out short: deep paths break the target build R10 the export lacks LICENSE, NOTICE or CONTRIBUTING.md, or NOTICE misses a licence in use R11 a value of the derivative database cites a non-public source ([S32DS], decision of 2026-09-17) R12 the markers of a private section (below) are unbalanced, nested, unreadable or end inside a fenced code block; the export refuses to run R13 an entry of export.overlay (below) cannot be applied: its source is not in the profile, its target is already a file of the profile, or the path it replaces does not exist; in an exported tree: a target is missing or differs from its source. The export refuses to run

Every finding carries rule, severity, tree relative path and – where the rule works on text – the line.

docs.title: The private pattern list
docs.text: Patterns that name documents under NDA reveal those documents, so the list is not part of the repository. Its path is pattern_file in distribution.yaml (default doc/confidential/distcheck-patterns.yaml; doc/confidential/ is in .gitignore). patterns.example.yaml is a template without real document numbers. Without the list the check still runs and says so on every run: UEBERSPRUNGEN: R3: private Musterliste ... fehlt.

docs.title: Code generated with MATLAB/Simulink
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    gen["swc/*/generated/**<br/>TypeSwc/generated/**<br/>(class private)"] -. "stays in the development repository" .-> dev["development repository"]
    sub["swc/DemoSwcSubstitute/<br/>swc.yaml, src/DemoSwc.c"] -- "export.overlay" --> dst["swc/DemoSwc/swc.yaml<br/>swc/DemoSwc/src/DemoSwc.c"]
    dst --> out["exported tree"]
    r3["R3 simulink_generated"] -. "stops a copy in an open file" .-> out

The C code and ARXML of the Simulink components were generated with Simulink Coder R2024a under a MATLAB student licence, which does not allow commercial use; Apache-2.0 does. Decision F9 A of 2026-10-06: the generated output is not published, the models (.slx), their data files and the build scripts are.

  • Classification: swc/*/generated/**, tools/rtegen/test/types/TypeSwc/generated/** and the ARXML copy TypeSink_datatype.arxml are private; so are the three host tests that include the generated TypeSwc.h (R5).
  • Detection: the content pattern simulink_generated (R3) matches the header lines Simulink Coder writes (Code generated for Simulink model, Simulink Coder version :, Embedded Coder version :, Auto generated XML Component Description for model). A copy of generated code or ARXML in an open file is an error, and the export refuses to run. Only this folder may name the lines (allow).
  • Substitute: export.overlay names files the export writes in place of a path the profile lacks. Today one entry: when swc/DemoSwc/generated is not exported, swc/DemoSwcSubstitute/swc.yaml and src/DemoSwc.c are copied into swc/DemoSwc, which makes DemoSwc a hand-written C component with the same RTE interface. The projects and their rte.yaml stay unchanged, so the open demo projects build without MATLAB. Whoever has a MATLAB licence generates the original with swc_build and removes the two files again - see swc/DemoSwcSubstitute/README.md. R13 checks the entry before the export and the copies in the exported tree; the tests of the substitute assemble the folder from the same entry.
  • Tests of the export: entries whose files are no longer exported drop out of tools/test/tests.yaml as usual (demoswc-sil, the NvM suites on the test model TypeSwc); rtegen keeps running in the export without the cases that need the generated code (clean rule narrow, which now runs before the drop, so it can also take a private file out of covers); the same holds for rtegen-c-swc, rtegen-device-values, rtegen-disabled, swc-yaml, elfcheck-timing and a2lgen, target-c-swc drops out (reads). An export.substitute renames the runnables of DemoSwc in the rtegen reference outputs to the C names of the substitute, so rtegen-reference stays green.

docs.title: Export
docs.text:
export copies the files of the profile, writes the cleaned forms of CHANGELOG.md (replaced), the project rules (internal sections and bullets removed) (only tasks on open paths, public fields), tools/test/tests.yaml (entries on non-exported files and their dependants removed) and CMakePresets.json (presets of private projects and their heirs removed), and generates LICENSE. NOTICE and SECURITY.md are kept by hand in the repository; R10 checks that NOTICE names every licence in use. export.substitute replaces single texts inside otherwise unchanged files (glob, regex, with) - today the link of the internal review page in the safety review records (doc/**/*.md), which stays in the development repository as evidence; check scans those files as the export writes them, so it reports only what would remain.

Links to unpublished files (decision K1 of 2026-10-04): review records, gap analysis, migration plan, RTOS comparison, traceability matrix and the stack report of the private demo project stay in the development repository, and the published documents keep linking to them there. In the export every Markdown link of an exported .md file to a file or folder of the tree that is not exported (and not written by a clean rule or generated) is replaced by its link text plus (not published, available on request) - inline links with or without anchor, images, reference links and their definitions; links in fenced code blocks, web addresses and unknown paths stay. The source text is unchanged; check scans the replaced text and names the number (EXPORT:). The export writes the list of all its replacements - per file the number of replaced links and export.substitute texts, then every replaced link with line and target - next to the tree as <out>.replacements.md (never into it) and prints the summary. In tools/test/tests.yaml the clean rule drops entries that read an unpublished file without naming it (reads) and narrows the selection of an entry where only single cases need such a file (narrow, e.g. a -k pattern). The cleaner is lenient, because it also runs on an exported tree; the repository test (tests_yaml_rule_problems) checks in the development tree that every named entry, path and narrow text still exists.

Private sections of published documents (decision K1 of 2026-10-04; today parts B and C of doc/safety/partner-and-degraded.md): a block between <!-- export:private-begin [label] --> and <!-- export:private-end --> (own lines, outside fenced code blocks) stays in the development repository, and the export replaces it by one line *label (not published, available on request)*. The anchors of the headings and of <a id/name> inside a block do not exist in the export; every link to them - from any published Markdown file, also a pure #anchor of the same file - is replaced like a link to an unpublished file, with the target file#anchor in the list. So the documents that cite a section by link stay unchanged and the export has no dead anchor. check scans the cut text and names the number of sections (EXPORT:); <out>.replacements.md lists every cut section with the lines of its markers in the source and the number of anchors it held.

The list of what the export leaves out on purpose: the consistency tests of the safety documents check them against each other (anomaly register against the gap analysis and the review records, document register against the traceability matrix, DFA against the test list and the tasks). In the exported tree such a source may be absent on purpose, and the check must neither fail nor disappear. So the export writes doc/unpublished.yaml (export.unpublished, format and reader in unpublished.py): the private files of the scope export.unpublished.files (today doc/safety/**, doc/requirements/**; NDA and workstation material is never named), the folders of export.unpublished.folders as a whole (board captures, Studio, planning tool - each must be wholly private, else the export stops), the files written only in cleaned form (a text of the original need not be in them), the entries the clean rule removed from tools/test/tests.yaml, and the tasks the public the task list lacks, with their status. The tests in doc/safety/test accept an absent source only when it is listed and check everything else as in the development repository; a public file that is missing from the export stays an error. The development repository has no list (the repository test makes sure it never tracks one).

The export refuses to run while check reports errors (--allow-findings only for trial runs), writes no .git (--git-init creates a repository with exactly one commit), and checks the result again as an exported tree.

Submodule link. .gitmodules alone gives a clone no OpenBSW: git submodule update --init (README, CONTRIBUTING) needs the gitlink (mode 160000) of external/openbsw with the commit the source tree pins. A plain folder cannot hold a gitlink, so the export reads it from the source tree (git ls-files -s, only for submodule paths that are exported) and records it as <out>.gitlinks next to the tree (the input format of git update-index --index-info; the note of the export says so). With --git-init it goes into the index before the one commit, and the export stops with an error if .gitmodules and the commit disagree (a submodule without gitlink, or a gitlink without entry). A release that commits the folder by other means must run git update-index --index-info < <out>.gitlinks before the commit. The check for a release export, to be run before anything is pushed:

git clone <export> %TEMP%/s32k/clone && cd %TEMP%/s32k/clone && git submodule update --init
git -C external/openbsw rev-parse HEAD     # must equal the commit in <out>.gitlinks

GitlinkExportTest in test_distcheck.py does this with a local upstream repository (no network, not the real external/openbsw), and its counter-check shows that an export without the gitlink is detected.

docs.title: Release publication (doc/architecture/customer-project.md gap N15)
docs.text: A release exports one or more profiles for a tagged baseline, plus the tag, the CI report and the release notes - that whole local plan is python -m tools.ci release in tools/ci, which calls export() here per profile. release-targets.yaml next to this README names the repository each profile would be pushed to (doc/architecture/customer-project.md Abschnitt 7 Q2). Since an earlier change (repositories created by the maintainer on 2026-10-02) the open profile has its repository; licensed and NDA stay null, and the plan carries them as undecided instead of a guessed address. The Studio's repository is recorded beside the profiles (studio:), never as one - the Studio is no part of any export (F12). Neither this tool nor tools/ci release ever pushes anything - the target is only a value in the plan; a push into a release repository needs the maintainer's yes.

docs.title: Build checks without the Studio
docs.text: Open tests must not import tools/studio (R5): the Studio is not distributed. The target build checks that copy a project and build it the way the Studio builds use the open helper tools/nxconfig/projectbuild.py; the configure arguments come from tools/nxconfig/presets.py, which the Studio re-exports and uses itself. The MATLAB tests that drive the Studio's import and model flow (tools/swc/test/studio_flow.py and the four Swc*Test.m that call it) are classified private with the Studio, and the export removes their entries from tools/test/tests.yaml.

docs.title: docgen - generated reference documentation
docs.text:
Writes the configuration reference in doc/reference/ from the pydantic schema in tools/nxconfig/model.py: one page per configuration level (derivative, board, project, ECU description) with every key, its type, unit, required/optional, default, allowed values and description. The pages are checked in; a host test fails when schema and pages disagree.

It also writes the module catalogue doc/reference/modules.md: one entry per directory in libs/bsw and libs/bsp, and one per module with a manifest in a port (platforms/<family>/port, ecu/platforms/<board> - the places tools/nxconfig reads port modules from), collected from the module manifest (module.yaml, or a parked module.yaml.pending), the module documentation doc/<module>.md, the public headers and tools/test/tests.yaml: an entry is a host test of a module if one of its covers lies in the module directory or if it names the module in its optional field modules (for tests outside the module directory, such as the generator host tests of the port modules). The state of verification is only taken from the manifest fields verification and verification_note; without them the page says not stated. The counts in the introduction and in README.md and the section Gaps (modules without manifest, verification, documentation or host test) are computed from the same data, so no sentence goes stale.

And it writes the console reference doc/reference/console.md: every console command group the application can register, collected from the registration in the C++ sources (DEFINE_COMMAND_GROUP_GET_INFO_BEGIN/COMMAND_GROUP_COMMAND, the PlainCommandInfo tables of per-device groups, ParentCommand/SimpleCommand members, OpenBSW testers that a neXtBSW source declares, and help). Parameters come from the help text (param: ..., Usage: ...); availability from #ifdefs around the registration, the CMake conditions of the source file (IN_LIST NX_MODULES, option(NX_...), PLATFORM_SUPPORT_* of the board port), the module and family directory; per-device group names from the manifests and, per project, from tools/nxconfig; board rules from the help text (console.MARKERS) and from the list "Only with a person at the board:" in boards/<board>/README.md. It needs external/openbsw checked out (exit code 2 otherwise).

Outside doc/reference it writes the module map doc/figures/07-modulkarte.md from the same module list as modules.md, a Mermaid figure with one node per module (grouped by layer or port and by kind, colour = verification) and a status table with a symbol per verification, legend in German. --check compares it like the reference pages; --figures <dir> writes it elsewhere (with another --out it follows --out).

.venv/Scripts/python tools/docgen            # rewrite doc/reference and the module map (only files that changed)
.venv/Scripts/python tools/docgen --check    # exit 1 with a diff if a page is stale
.venv/Scripts/python tools/docgen --gaps     # schema fields without description or unit, and module gaps
.venv/Scripts/python tools/docgen/test_docgen.py
.venv/Scripts/python tools/docgen/test_console.py

After changing the schema - including a comment in model.py, because comments are where most descriptions come from today - run the first command and commit the changed pages together with the schema.

File Content schema.py model → sections and fields (data classes, no Qt, no file access; usable from neXtBSW Studio) render.py Markdown tables, contents, escaping reference.py the pages of doc/reference, write, check, gap list modules.py module catalogue: collect libs/bsw, libs/bsp, the port modules and the test list, render modules.md with its section Gaps, module gaps console.py console reference: scan the command registration, CMake conditions, projects, board rules; render console.md, console gaps modulemap.py module map doc/figures/07-modulkarte.md: Mermaid figure and status table from the module catalogue __main__.py command line test_docgen.py host test with its own small schema, plus the check against the real one test_console.py host test of the console reference with its own small source tree, plus the real sources site.py, mkdocs_hooks.py documentation website: pages of the open profile staged for MkDocs, build from the export (website.md) test_site.py strict build of the website from the export, with counter-tests (tests.yaml docgen-site)

Short forms on the pages (all anchors stay valid): an object whose table and subtree equal an earlier one is written as a pointer (render.signature, reference.layout); a description of 15 words or more that repeats on a page is written once and then pointed to (render.REPEAT_WORDS); the objects of the power stage and motor control (reference.AFTER_R1, per page and path) and the modules gdTmc6200, bccMc33771, mcuLink (modules.AFTER_R1) get a short entry marked after R1. To bring one back, remove it from that list. modules.md leaves out what its overview table already says (host test lists, documentation link, empty configuration lines).

Descriptions are taken from Field(description=...), else the field's comment in the model source, else the first paragraph of the docstring of its object type. Units come from Field(json_schema_extra={"unit": ...}) or the naming convention <name>_<unit> (UNIT_SUFFIXES in schema.py). Nothing is filled in by hand: where the schema says nothing, the page shows the gap.

docs.title: Documentation website
docs.text: site.py, mkdocs_hooks.py and test_site.py build the same sources into a website with MkDocs Material (configuration mkdocs.yml). How it works, how to build it and what the test checks: website.md (German, like all new texts until a follow-up task).

docs.title: Doku-Website
docs.text:
Aus denselben Markdown- und Mermaid-Quellen, die im Repository liegen, entsteht eine Website mit MkDocs Material: Suche, Sprachumschalter Deutsch/Englisch, Mermaid direkt im Browser gezeichnet und nach der Veröffentlichung eine Dokuversion je Release (mike). Die Konfiguration ist mkdocs.yml in der Wurzel, die Pakete stehen in tools/requirements-site.txt – getrennt von tools/requirements.txt, damit sich die Bau- und Testpakete nicht ändern.

pip install -r tools/requirements-site.txt
.venv/Scripts/python -m tools.docgen.site build --out %TEMP%/nx-site     # exportieren, dort bauen, strict
.venv/Scripts/python -m tools.docgen.site build --tree <export> --out <dir>   # einen schon exportierten Baum bauen
.venv/Scripts/python -m tools.docgen.site pages                          # welche Seiten und Dateien bereitgestellt würden
.venv/Scripts/python tools/docgen/test_site.py                           # Eintrag docgen-site in tools/test/tests.yaml

docs.title: Welche Seiten
docs.text:
Nicht nur doc/: auch README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, SECURITY.md, die Moduldokus neben dem Code (libs/**/doc, bootloader/doc, Port-Module) und die READMEs der Werkzeuge sind Seiten. MkDocs braucht genau einen docs_dir. Deshalb stellt der Hook tools/docgen/mkdocs_hooks.py die veröffentlichten Seiten mit ihren Repository-Pfaden in einen Temp-Ordner und macht diesen zum docs_dir; jeder relative Link funktioniert dort wie auf dem Code-Host.

Was veröffentlicht wird, entscheidet nicht die Website, sondern die Export-Klassifizierung (tools/distcheck/distribution.yaml, Profil open). Was nicht ausdrücklich offen ist, kommt nicht hinein, und doc/confidential ist zusätzlich ausdrücklich ausgeschlossen. Dateien ohne Markdown, auf die eine Seite verweist (NOTICE, eine YAML- oder Quelldatei), werden als einfache Datei mitkopiert.

docs.title: Gebaut wird im Export
docs.text:
Die öffentliche Website entsteht im exportierten Baum; site.py build exportiert dafür zuerst in einen Temp-Ordner. Begründung: Nur dort sind Verweise auf nicht veröffentlichte Seiten durch not published, available on request ersetzt, private Abschnitte herausgeschnitten und interne Review-Links ersetzt. Die Website zeigt damit genau den Text, der veröffentlicht wird, und es gibt nur eine Stelle, die über „öffentlich“ entscheidet. Eine zweite Ausschlussliste in mkdocs.yml (exclude_docs) müsste dieselbe Entscheidung nachbauen, würde die Verweise auf ausgeschlossene Seiten tot lassen und die privaten Abschnitte nicht schneiden.

Ein Bau des Entwicklungsbaums geht als Vorschau (mkdocs serve), scheitert mit --strict aber an seinen Links auf private Seiten – mit Absicht.

Nicht als Seite, Navigationseintrag oder Suchtreffer erscheinen außerdem (SITE_EXCLUDE in site.py, gespiegelt durch exclude_docs in mkdocs.yml): CHANGELOG.md (bleiben bereinigt im Release-Repository) sowie die STM32-Detailseiten (platforms/stm32, mcudb/stm32, boards/nucleo_f446re). Von STM32 bleibt nur die Kurzseite stm32-nucleo.md mit dem Status planned. Ein Link auf diese Dateien wird wie jeder Link ins Repository zu Text plus Pfad.

docs.title: Links ohne Seite
docs.text:
• Ein Link auf einen Ordner geht auf dessen README.md, wenn der Ordner eine hat.
  • Jeder andere Link in den veröffentlichten Baum, der keine Seite ist (ein Code-Ordner, external/openbsw/...), zeigt seinen Text mit dem Repository-Pfad. Sobald die Website veröffentlicht wird, verweist er stattdessen auf extra.nextbsw.source_url in mkdocs.yml (Baum-Adresse des Release-Tags).
  • Ein Link auf einen Pfad, den es nicht gibt, bleibt stehen; der strikte Bau meldet ihn.

docs.title: Navigation und Sprachen
docs.text:
Die Navigation folgt den Lesepfaden aus doc/README.md: Integrator, Safety-Assessor, Contributor. Seiten außerhalb der Navigation werden trotzdem gebaut und sind über Links erreichbar. Jede Seite steht nur einmal in der Navigation; der Integrator-Pfad endet im Sicherheitshandbuch unter Safety-Assessor.

mkdocs-static-i18n mit Suffix-Struktur: Heute gibt es jede Seite in einer Sprache, beide Bäume (/ deutsch, /en/ englisch) zeigen sie. Eine Übersetzung kommt mit einer eigenen Aufgabe als <name>.en.md bzw. <name>.de.md neben die Seite. Die generierte Referenz bleibt in beiden Bäumen englisch.

docs.title: Veröffentlichung
docs.text:
Der Workflow .github/workflows/docs.yml (Name Docs) läuft nur von Hand (workflow_dispatch, wie CI) und nur auf dem Zweig main des Release-Repositorys; im Entwicklungsbaum bricht er ab, denn die Website entsteht nur aus dem Export. Der Ablauf:

  1. Job build (Recht contents: read): Checkout mit external/openbsw, pip install -r tools/requirements-site.txt, python -m tools.docgen.site build --out site (strict, Profil open der Export-Klassifizierung – anderes Profil gibt es nicht).
  2. Job publish (nur er hat contents: write, mike schreibt ausschließlich den Zweig gh-pages): mike deploy --push --update-aliases <Version> latest mit der Version aus der Datei VERSION, danach mike set-default --push latest. Eine Dokuversion je Release; ein weiterer Lauf mit derselben Version ersetzt sie, latest zeigt auf die neueste.
  3. Nach F15/F16 schaltet der Maintainer GitHub Pages frei (Einstellung Pages, Quelle: Zweig gh-pages) und trägt in mkdocs.yml extra.nextbsw.source_url (Baum-Adresse des Release-Tags) ein. Vorher läuft der Workflow nicht.

Der Workflow gehört mit Klasse open (Apache-2.0) in den Export (tools/distcheck/distribution.yaml, Test test_docs_workflow_is_exported_in_the_open_profile). Er wurde nicht auf GitHub ausgeführt.

docs.title: Mermaid
docs.text: pymdownx.superfences mit dem Custom Fence mermaid: Ein Block kommt als <pre class="mermaid"> samt B1-Kopfzeile (%%{init: ...}%%) im HTML an, Material lädt Mermaid im Browser. Ob die Rundung der Gruppen (rx/ry in classDef grp) greift, lässt sich nur im Browser sehen; der Test prüft das HTML.

docs.title: Prüfung
docs.text: tools/test -k docgen-site (übersprungen ohne die Pakete): Export in einen Temp-Ordner, dort mkdocs build --strict – kein toter Link, kein toter Anker, keine Warnung. Im HTML: Mermaid als pre.mermaid mit Kopfzeile, private Seiten und doc/confidential fehlen, Verweise darauf tragen den Sprachumschalter vorhanden, jede Seite der Navigation ist veröffentlicht und steht nur einmal darin. Gegenproben auf einem kleinen Baum mit derselben mkdocs.yml: kaputter Link, kaputter Anker, Link auf eine private Seite und ein Navigationseintrag einer unveröffentlichten Seite lassen den Bau scheitern. Dauer: etwa 1 min Export und 1–3 min Bau (zwei Sprachbäume).

docs.title: Werkzeuge und Lizenzen

docs.title: elfcheck – linked images against the derivative map and the core
docs.text:
Proposal D of doc/safety/tool-classification.md (finding TF6, requirement SSR-083), task.

One generated memory layout feeds the bootloader, the application linker script, the updater and canflash. They agree by construction, so a layout that is wrong for the derivative is wrong everywhere at once and every consumer test passes. elfcheck checks the linked images against an expectation that does not come from that chain:

Source What it gives mcudb/<family>/<derivative>.yaml code flash, RAM regions, sector geometry (equal or unequal sectors), program size, core and FPU project.yaml (read directly, not through tools/nxconfig) which flash, bootloader size and RAM, application RAM regions, board name the images sections, program headers, symbols, build attributes and the ten layout values the bootloader was compiled with (layoutValues, read out of the bootloader image)

It imports nothing from tools/nxconfig, tools/bswgen, tools/rtegen or tools/canflash; the ELF reader (elffile.py), the DWARF reader (dwarf.py), the Intel HEX reader (ihex.py) and the table of expected build attributes per core (cores.py) are its own. No Qt. The subcommand timing (below) checks the RTE timing and the interrupt priorities.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text: Code Check core-arch, core-profile, fp-arch, fp-precision, fp-abi Tag_CPU_arch, profile, Tag_FP_arch, Tag_ABI_HardFP_use, Tag_ABI_VFP_args of every image against derivative.core/fpu (hard float ABI with FPU, soft without) section-outside-memory, section-region-kind run address of every allocated section inside a code flash or RAM region of the derivative section-outside-flash, section-outside-area load address of every section with content inside the code flash and inside the image's area (bootloader area, application area) section-outside-ram RAM sections inside the regions the project gives the image (memory.bootloader.ram/ram_size, memory.application.ram) overlap no two sections on the same load or RAM bytes, no byte shared by bootloader and application or updater, application area outside the bootloader area layout-flash, layout-sector-size, layout-phrase, layout-ram the bootloader's layout values against the derivative (flash start and size, sector size or 0 for unequal sectors, program size, one block of RAM) sector-alignment application start and end, validity record and end of the bootloader area on sector boundaries of the derivative record-position record sector inside the flash, outside the application and the bootloader area; record file at the address the bootloader reads vector-table, vector-alignment, initial-sp, reset-vector Cortex-M: vector table at the start of the area, aligned for VTOR, stack pointer in the image's RAM, reset vector Thumb and inside the image boot-request boot request word inside bootloader and application RAM, not covered by a section a start-up code initialises rom-list-* ROM check list of SM-14 present, directly behind the last flash content, inside the application area, areas disjoint and covering every flash byte except the list record-missing, record-format, record-image, record-layout, record-target <stem>.record.hex exists, its fields are consistent, size and CRC-32 match the image (the .hex next to the ELF, itself compared with the ELF: hex-differs), layout identity and target identity (CRC-32("<board>/<derivative>")) match blob-* the bootloader embedded in the updater is this bootloader image and fits the bootloader area fcf-missing, fcf-secured, fcf-mass-erase, fcf-backdoor, fcf-protection, fcf-value An image that writes the first code flash sector (the bootloader) carries the family's flash configuration field complete and with the reference value, in the ELF and in the .hex next to it. s32k1xx: 0x400..0x40F, FSEC 0xFE (unsecured, mass erase enabled, backdoor key disabled), FOPT 0x7F, nothing protected - the only field the updater accepts. Missing or secured, the chip comes up secured after the next reset; once the CSEc took a key space, mass erase is locked too and the part is lost. Families without such a field (CONFIG_FIELDS in check.py) are not checked heap-symbol (NXCPP-05, finding DE5 of doc/safety/dev-environment.md): no image defines a symbol of a heap allocator - newlib/libnosys malloc, _malloc_r, calloc, realloc, free, _free_r, memalign, _sbrk, _sbrk_r,... (HEAP_SYMBOLS in check.py) or any operator new/new[] (_Znw*, _Zna*; placement new _ZnwjPv allocates nothing and stays allowed). The source scan sees only our calls; the image also shows what a library pulls in behind them. Before a later change the deleting destructors linked the allocator (488 bytes) through libstdc++'s operator delete; the family port now defines both forms itself (platforms/s32k1xx/port/main/src/cxxRuntime/NoHeapOperatorDelete.cpp, fault reaction, never returns) isr-unwrapped, isr-vector-table (finding SFP-F01): in an application with the safety shell (SafePreIsrHook defined) every vector from SysTick (15) on points at DefaultISR, at one of the safety paths without hook wrapper (Safe_WDOG_EWM_IRQHandler, the halt deadman Safe_LPIT0_Ch1_IRQHandler) or at a function whose first call (bl) is SafePreIsrHook and which calls or branches to SafePostIsrHook - recognised by its code, not by its name, so an interrupt that preempts the safety cycle never runs with the MPU gate of the protected RAM open. Reserved entries (0) and the S32K14x TRIM word are skipped; bootloader and updater have no safety shell and are not checked isr-fpu Review point (a): no function reached through bl/b.w from a handler such a wrapper calls (and from the hooks) holds a VFP/Advanced SIMD instruction (coprocessor 10/11; data marked $d skipped). With lazy FP stacking the first FP instruction of an interrupt writes the interrupted task's FP context onto that task's stack - for the safety task the stack the pre hook has just made read-only, a bus fault. Not followed: calls through a register (function pointers, virtual calls) and DefaultISR (unexpected interrupt, never returns; OpenBSW's vIllegalISR prints through code that uses d8/d9). Eval board image: 63 functions followed, 0 findings segment-extra-bytes (warning) a PT_LOAD segment carries file bytes of no section (ELF header) at an address outside the image's area

docs.title: Use
docs.text:
.venv/Scripts/python tools/elfcheck --project projects/evalboard_s32k144_demo/project.yaml --build build/evalboard-s32k144-demo
.venv/Scripts/python tools/elfcheck --mcudb mcudb/stm32/STM32F446RE.yaml --flash FLASH --bootloader bootloader.elf

Only the flash configuration field, the post-build step of the bootloader (bootloader/CMakeLists.txt, which turns the build red); --family ends with exit code 0 for a family without such a field:

.venv/Scripts/python tools/elfcheck fcf --family s32k1xx --project projects/evalboard_s32k144_demo/project.yaml bootloader.elf bootloader.hex

The bootloader linker script (bootloader/platforms/s32k1xx/linker.ld) also stops the link if .FlashConfig is not 16 bytes, and the application linker template refuses an application at the start of the code flash.

Messages: error: <file>: <section|symbol|record>: <text> [<code>]. Exit code 1 with errors, 2 for unusable input; --strict counts warnings as errors, --no-records and --no-rom-list switch those parts off.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: tools/elfcheck/test/test_elfcheck.py, entries elfcheck, elfcheck-stm32, elfcheck-demo, elfcheck-bt148 and elfcheck-s32k116 in tools/test/tests.yaml. The demo images must pass and 29 image mutants (one: a vector around its SAFE_ISR wrapper; four of them FSEC secured in ELF and hex or in the hex only, mass erase disabled, field missing; three: malloc and operator new in the application, _sbrk_r in the bootloader) and 7 derivative mutants must turn the check red; ReaderUnitTest.test_heap_symbols checks the allocator list without a build. elfcheck-isr (IsrWrapperUnitTest) checks the interrupt frame rule, the floating-point rule and the branch and VFP decoders on synthetic images. elfcheck-fcf checks the configuration field rule without a build (ten counter-checks). S32K116: bootloader and updater of the project plus an own small application linked with the real linker template (the application of the project does not link yet).

docs.title: Product image without test commands (product)
docs.text:
Task (iso26262-gap.md task 19, SG6). A build with -DNX_PRODUCT_BUILD=ON (cmake/NxProductBuild.cmake) leaves out the console commands that only test a safety mechanism by provoking a fault or its reaction. product.py holds their inventory (MARKERS: command, reason, symbols, console texts, test-build option) and reports each one it still finds in a linked application: a defined symbol, or a console text in the bytes that go into the ECU (sections with content; the debug information is ignored).

.venv/Scripts/python tools/elfcheck product --app <app.ecu.elf>                # product image: 0 findings
.venv/Scripts/python tools/elfcheck product --app <app.ecu.elf> --expect-all   # counter check: every command found

Tests: elfcheck-product (no build: text only in image bytes, mangled symbols, inventory against the test-build options of the family ports and NX_TEST_BUILD_OPTIONS, guards in the sources, built-in faults) and target-product (test/product_build.py: demo product image clean, build with every test option finds every command, product plus test option refused at configure time, standard demo keeps its development commands).

docs.title: Bootloader image changed → version changed (blversion)
docs.text:
A bootloader in the field is known only by BL_VERSION_NUMBER. blversion.py hashes the flash content of bootloader.hex (first to last written address, gaps 0xFF - no debug information, no paths) and compares it with the entry of the current number in bootloader/test/image_version.sha256 (reference preset evalboard-s32k144-demo, one line <version> <sha256> <gcc version> per number, append only):

.venv/Scripts/python tools/elfcheck blversion <bootloader.hex>          # 0 unchanged, 1 changed/entry missing
.venv/Scripts/python tools/elfcheck blversion --add <bootloader.hex>    # append the entry of a new number

Exit code 3: the entry was taken with another GCC version (other code, not comparable). --add never rewrites an existing entry - a changed image needs a new number. Test: bootloader/test/test_bl_image_version.py.

docs.title: RTE timing and interrupt priorities (timing)
docs.text:
Proposal F of the tool classification (finding TF7, requirement SSR-081), task. rtegen turns rte.yaml and the BSW task profile into the task list, the FreeRTOS priorities (context numbers of async/Config.h) and the periods and offsets of the runnables, which SM-05 uses as deadlines; bswgen turns the project's interrupt ranks into NVIC levels. timing.py compares the linked application with an expectation it derives itself:

Source What it gives project.yaml ECU description, board (derivative), interrupts.max_syscall_level and interrupts.ranks rte.yaml application tasks (period, priority key, runnables in call order with offsets), components <component>/generated/arxml/*.arxml Simulink component: runnables, their symbols, TIMING-EVENT periods, INIT-EVENTs, mode switch events <component>/swc.yaml with implementation: c hand-written C component: name, runnables and period_ms; <Swc>_Init first, C function <Swc>_<Runnable> ecu/asyncCoreConfiguration/tasks.yaml BSW tasks and keys, OS tick, default application task mcudb core and nvic_priority_bits

Rules applied (the documented ones): all tasks sorted by key and numbered 1..N (idle 0, timer N+1); deadline of a runnable = its period, of a task cycle = the task period; NVIC level = max_syscall_level + rank. The expectation of six profiles (two of them with C components: test_c_swc, test_calib) is compared with the reviewed reference output of rtegen - two independent paths that agree.

The swc.yaml of a C component is read by an own narrow reader in timing.py (PyYAML, only name, runnables and periods), not by rtegen or tools/swc/swc_yaml.py: SSR-081 (b) asks for a parser that uses no generator code, and a difference between this reader and rtegen's is exactly what the check is there to find (finding).

Code Check (image) task-count, task-name, task-priority, task-period, task-runnables, task-hyper rows of rte::TASKS (context = FreeRTOS priority, period = deadline of a cycle) runnable-count, runnable-name, runnable-function, runnable-period, runnable-offset, runnable-task, runnable-ticks rows of rte::RUNNABLES (called function resolved to its symbol, period = SM-05 deadline) mode-runnables rows of rte::MODE_RUNNABLES (task of every mode switch runnable) task-list, task-priority, task-count, task-context-units enumerators TASK_<NAME> and ASYNC_CONFIG_TASK_COUNT of every compilation unit (DWARF, dwarf.py): the priority of every task, BSW tasks included; units that disagree point to a stale object os-tick, irq-rank, irq-syscall, irq-bits ASYNC_CONFIG_TICK_IN_US, NX_IRQ_RANK_*, NX_IRQ_MAX_SYSCALL_LEVEL, NX_NVIC_PRIORITY_BITS as compiled (.debug_macro; the presets of CMakePresets.json build with -g3) irq-level, irq-level-missing, irq-level-extra, irq-probe-build probe: the generated interruptPriorities.h with the platform's nxInterruptPriority.h, compiled and linked by arm-none-eabi-gcc for the core; the NVIC level of every rank read back with the own ELF reader 
.venv/Scripts/python tools/elfcheck timing --project projects/evalboard_s32k144_demo/project.yaml --build build/demo
.venv/Scripts/python tools/elfcheck timing --project <project.yaml> --app app.elf --generated <build>/generated/board
.venv/Scripts/python tools/elfcheck timing --project <project.yaml> --rte <rte.yaml> --tasks <tasks.yaml> --app rte.elf

Tests: tools/elfcheck/test/test_timing.py, entries elfcheck-timing (expectation, no compiler), elfcheck-timing-host (own profile tools/rtegen/test/multitask built with the target compiler for Cortex-M4 and M0+; own profile tools/rtegen/test/c_swc with the C component LevelMonSwc next to the Simulink DemoSwc, class TimingCSwcHostBuildTest; interrupt probe for own and open profiles), elfcheck-timing-demo and elfcheck-timing-bt148 (linked applications) and the firmware of test/c_swc (class TimingCSwcImageTest, target build target-c-swc, NX_CSWC_BUILD_DIR). Image, generat, template and configuration mutants must turn it red; for the C component also a period that drifts apart between swc.yaml and the image, from both sides.

Limits of timing: an image without debugging information gets warnings instead of the BSW task and macro checks (the RTE tables are still checked); the NVIC registers of a running device are a board check (tool-classification.md TB4); Cortex-R (VIM channels) has no level check yet.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The expectation of the partition itself (where the bootloader ends, where the record lies) is only checked for consistency with the derivative (sector boundaries, disjoint areas) and with the project's bootloader size; the project decides the partition.
  • The key sector (BL_KEY_ADDR) is not among the bootloader's layout values and is not checked.
  • The check works on the files of the build, not on the flash of a device.

docs.title: tools/misra – static analysis
docs.text:
cppcheck with the MISRA C:2012 add-on and clang-tidy over neXtBSW's own code, with an inventory (baseline), a justified deviation list and a list of real faults. Any finding that is in neither the baseline nor the deviation list breaks the run. Rule set, scope and handling of deviations: doc/safety/static-analysis.md. The core (analysis.py) has no Qt and no CI provider; configuration errors are reported with their YAML path.

python -m tools.misra setup                  # pinned cppcheck + clang-tidy (pip wheels) into a venv of their own
python -m tools.misra run                    # analyse the demo build, compare, report (exit 1 on new findings)
python -m tools.misra baseline               # analyse and rewrite baseline.yaml (after fixing findings)
python -m tools.misra check                  # validate rules/deviations/defects/baseline.yaml only
python -m unittest tools/misra/test_misra.py # host test with a synthetic example (no tool needed)

run needs the compile database of a target build: by default that of the demo project (tools/test/build_dirs.py: NX_BUILD_DIR, <tools/test build root>/demo, then the preset directory), otherwise --compile-db <file>. In CI the stage "Statische Analyse" of python -m tools.ci run calls it after the target builds ([static_analysis] in tools/ci/pipeline.toml). Reports go to --out (default %TEMP%/nextbsw-misra): report.md, result.json and the raw output cppcheck.xml/clang-tidy.txt, which --from-raw <dir> evaluates again without running the tools.

A customer workspace (gap N19). run, baseline and check take --workspace <dir>: the files then come from <dir>/ci/misra/ (deviations.yaml required, baseline.yaml, optional defects.yaml and rules.yaml – without it the tree's rules.yaml applies), only files of the workspace are own code, and the pinned tree (also as a submodule inside the workspace), the build root and .venv are read as context and never judged. OpenBSW copies are not looked up – they are a matter of the tree. The compile database defaults to <dir>/build/nxtest/ plus [static_analysis] compile_db of <dir>/ci/pipeline.toml; --compile-db and the explicit file options still win. python -m tools.ci run --workspace calls it the same way.

python -m tools.misra run --workspace <dir>        # analyse the customer's own code
python -m tools.misra baseline --workspace <dir>   # writes <dir>/ci/misra/baseline.yaml
python -m tools.misra check --workspace <dir>      # validates the workspace's files

docs.title: Files
docs.text: File Content rules.yaml rule set: scope exclusions, cppcheck arguments, clang-tidy checks and options, tool notices, own short descriptions of every rule that occurs (no MISRA rule texts – copyright), and the guideline re-categorization plan (revised_category: stricter, or disapplied for advisory rules only – their findings are counted apart, neither new nor baseline) deviations.yaml justified deviations and proven false positives: rule, files, source-line pattern or symbol, optional limit, reason, who/when, approval defects.yaml findings that are real faults or safeguard gaps, with a proposed owner – listed separately, not suppressed baseline.yaml inventory of the known findings (generated, one line per entry, matched by file + rule + source line) requirements.txt the tool versions – the only place they are pinned

docs.title: Where the tools come from
docs.text:
1. --tool-dir <dir>,
  2. otherwise NX_MISRA_TOOLS (a directory holding cppcheck and clang-tidy),
  3. otherwise the venv of setup: NX_MISRA_VENV, else <CI tool cache>/misra-venv (NX_CI_CACHE or %LOCALAPPDATA%/nextbsw/ci-cache) – python -m tools.ci setup installs the same venv,
  4. otherwise PATH.

A tool that is not found is skipped with the list of places searched – never reported as clean. If no tool ran, run ends with exit code 3.

docs.title: What is analysed
docs.text: The units of the compile database, classified per file: own code (gating), OpenBSW copies from tools/openbswsync/copies.yaml (reported separately), the submodule (not analysed), generated code and host tests (read as context, findings dropped). A modified copy that matches scope.gating_copies in rules.yaml counts as own code and is gating: it is own development in an ASIL B module of doc/safety/coexistence.md, see doc/safety/component-qualification.md section 3. Identical copies and copies in QM modules stay separate. test_misra.py checks that the list hits exactly the modified copies of the ASIL B modules. To take a newly gated file into the baseline without taking in unrelated new findings: python -m tools.misra baseline --only <file> (repeatable) rewrites the entries of the matching files only. Include paths and defines come from the compile database; the target compiler's predefined macros (-dM) are given to cppcheck, its system include directories to clang-tidy. cppcheck 2.17 splits include paths of a compile database at blanks, so paths below the repository are passed relative to the unit.

docs.title: nxupdate — moving a workspace's pin
docs.text:
doc/architecture/customer-project.md gap N9, section 5.5. Qt-free, command line, no compile.

A customer workspace pins exactly one neXtBSW release in nextbsw.yaml (doc/architecture/customer-project.md section 3.1) and never updates it automatically. nxupdate is the one command that makes an update deliberate and traceable: it generates every project of the workspace with the old and the new tree, checks the target release's provenance (gap N10), runs the new tree's format migrations (gap N11), and writes a report of what changed - in particular the changes that decide whether a fielded ECU can take the new software without a bootloader update.

.venv/Scripts/python tools/nxupdate acme-bcm --to 1.5.0                    # dry run: report only, nothing changes
.venv/Scripts/python tools/nxupdate acme-bcm --to 1.5.0 --write            # moves the pin, writes the report
.venv/Scripts/python tools/nxupdate acme-bcm --to 1.5.0 --write --commit   # ... and commits it (never pushes)
.venv/Scripts/python tools/nxupdate acme-bcm --to 1.5.0 --release          # customer release: a development
                                                                           # target tag is an error, not a warning
.venv/Scripts/python tools/nxupdate acme-bcm --to v1.0.0-rc1               # a release candidate (TOOL-232)

Release candidates. --to also takes a release candidate tag vX.Y.Z-rcN (Release R1 is v1.0.0-rc1). It is used as the git ref of the target tree; the pin keeps X.Y.Z, because nextbsw.version has to equal the tree's VERSION, and the version part of the tag must be that VERSION - a candidate v1.0.1-rc1 on a tree with VERSION 1.0.0 is refused before anything moves, and so is any other spelling (v1.0.0-rc, v1.0.0-beta1). The release rule checks the candidate tag like a release tag: annotated, reachable from master, clean. Known limit until the rule moves into tools/nxconfig after R1: nxconfig pin on the updated workspace still looks for v<version> and reports the candidate checkout as a development pin.

The default is a dry run: the workspace, its pin and its pinned tree are left exactly as they are, and the full report goes to stdout. Nothing is written unless --write is given, and nothing is committed unless --commit is given (which implies --write) - nxupdate never pushes, in any mode. This mirrors the project rule that only an explicit switch commits or pushes on someone's behalf.

docs.title: What one run does (section 5.5)
docs.text:
1. Generate "before" every project.yaml of the workspace with the currently pinned tree (bswgen, rtegen; nothing is compiled).
  2. Move the pin. The target tree is checked against the release rule first (annotated tag v<version>, reachable from master, clean); a bad tag is refused before anything changes. A dry run uses a throwaway git worktree of the pinned tree at the target tag (no network, the real submodule is untouched); with --write the real submodule is checked out to the tag (git submodule update --recursive) and nextbsw.yaml is updated.
  3. Migrate. <target tree>/tools/nxconfig migrate <workspace>: the target release's own migration engine, dry run unless --write. A migration only changes how a value is written, not what is generated.
  4. Generate "after" with the target tree in a staged copy of the workspace: its own files with a pin naming the target version and the target tree where the pin points (a git worktree at the tag; with --tree a directory link), because every tool checks that the workspace pins exactly that tree. Paths are mapped back in the report.
  5. Report: the pin check's findings, skipped releases, a changelog excerpt, the migration's output, nxconfig check messages that appeared or disappeared, and the generated-file diff with the field-relevant files marked. With --write it is saved to doc/nextbsw-updates/v<old>-v<new>.md in the workspace (customer-project.md section 3.2); a dry run prints it (and writes --report <file> if given).
  6. Commit (--commit only): the pin, the submodule gitlink, the migration's changes and the report as one commit; never a push.

docs.title: Field-relevant changes
docs.text: Section 5.5 asks for a prominent list of field-relevant changes (memory layout, bootloader identity, CAN IDs, diagnostic addresses, record formats): those decide whether a fielded ECU can take the new software without a bootloader update. No registry says which generated file holds which of these, so field_relevance() in update.py is a deliberately over-inclusive heuristic: a path hint (memory/flash layout, bootloader, CAN, diagnostics, NVM) flags the whole file, a content hint (a changed line matches a CAN_ID_, DID_, FLASH_..., BOOTLOADER_... or NVM_... identifier) flags it even without a path clue. A false positive costs one look, a false negative could cost a bootloader update in the field. Extend FIELD_PATH_HINTS/FIELD_CONTENT_HINTS rather than special-casing a board or project.

docs.title: --tree: the source: archive fallback
docs.text: nxupdate does not download or unpack a release archive (nextbsw.yaml source: archive, customer-project.md 4.4) - that stays a manual step. --tree <path> uses an already-materialised tree as the target as it is, for either pin source. Without --tree and with source: submodule (the recommended variant), the target is resolved from the pinned tree's own git history at v<version>.

docs.title: Design notes (see update.py's module docstring)
docs.text:
• Generation and migration run as a subprocess against an explicit tree path (python <tree>/tools/bswgen/bswgen.py ...): a tool runs with the generator code of the release it is judging (customer-project.md 5.4, N7). Only the release rule (pincheck) is called in-process.
  • A dry run touches nothing; the "after" tree is a git worktree, not a clone.
  • On a refused tag with --write the submodule may already be at the new commit while nextbsw.yaml still names the old version; nxconfig pin/check report that mismatch and the report says so.

docs.title: Host tests
docs.text: tools/nxupdate/test_nxupdate.py (tools/test -k nxupdate) builds an invented upstream repository with invented releases and stub bswgen/rtegen scripts in %TEMP% (no network); one test points the real migration step at this repository's tools/nxconfig (read-only). tools/nxupdate/test_nxupdate_workspace.py (-k nxupdate-workspace) uses a local bare clone of this repository with two invented annotated releases, a customer repository with the tree as a submodule and a project with its own board outside the tree: a dry run from a relative path, a dry run with --tree and --write --commit with the real generators.

docs.title: Open points
docs.text:
• A Studio dialog around nxupdate (customer-project.md N9) is a later task.
  • The command stops at generation: no compile and no workspace tests (tools/ci run --workspace <dir>, does that; chaining it is a follow-up) and no ELF size change (the report says so).
  • The comparison of nxconfig check messages is skipped for a project when either tree has no tools/nxconfig.
  • Signed tags and a real release mirror are out of scope (N15, Q2).

docs.title: tools/schedana – analyse processor load, scheduling and data flow
docs.text:
Answers three questions about an ECU configuration:

  1. Does the schedule fit? Utilisation per task, response time with fixed priorities (all tasks including BSW, ISR groups as interferers), deadline violations, load peaks over the hyperperiod, suggestions for the offset of runnables.
  2. Are the priorities sensible? A warning with a reason if an application task lies above a safety- or communication-relevant BSW task. No lock – the choice stays free.
  3. Is the data flow right? Reader before writer in the same cycle, age and consistency of values across tasks, rate transitions, signals without writer or reader, cycles (control loops).

The core is without Qt and without hardware access (architecture section 10, review question 8). Report as text and as JSON; every message names task/runnable/signal and the YAML path, so that a user interface can attach it to the line that caused it.

docs.title: Invocations
docs.text:
# configuration only (structure, priorities, data flow; run times are missing)
.venv/Scripts/python tools/schedana analyse projects/evalboard_s32k144_demo

# with measured values from the target and assumptions for BSW tasks/ISR groups
.venv/Scripts/python tools/schedana analyse projects/evalboard_s32k144_demo \
    --measure console.txt --budget tools/schedana/test/budget_demo.yaml --json bericht.json

# constructed schedule without a project (test profile, estimate, what-if)
.venv/Scripts/python tools/schedana analyse --scenario tools/schedana/test/scenarios/overloaded.yaml

# only read in the console output (also from standard input: --input -)
.venv/Scripts/python tools/schedana measure --input console.txt --json

# look at the model or export it as a scenario (input for TOOL-10, for what-if)
.venv/Scripts/python tools/schedana show projects/evalboard_s32k144_demo
.venv/Scripts/python tools/schedana scenario projects/evalboard_s32k144_demo --measure console.txt -o modell.yaml

Return value: 0 without findings, 1 from one error on (--fail-on warning|error|none), 2 on faulty input.

docs.title: Where the values come from
docs.text:
Value Source application tasks, runnables, offset, order, connections projects/<project>/rte.yaml (via tools/rtegen, read only) BSW tasks, priorities, OS tick, ISR groups ecu/asyncCoreConfiguration/tasks.yaml board/derivative (signal names of the connections) tools/nxconfig run time and jitter per runnable, cycles and overruns per task console rte json (new) or rte runnables CPU load, runs, mean/minimum/maximum per task and ISR group console stats cpu (OpenBSW RuntimeMonitor) stack size and usage per task console stats stack period and run time of the BSW tasks/ISR groups without measurement, length of interrupt locks, deviating deadlines budget file (--budget, example test/budget_demo.yaml) roles (safety, communication) for the priority warning roles.yaml, replaceable with --roles

Periods from a measurement. A configured period is never changed by a measurement; the measurement only brings runtime and jitter (a remark names a run count that does not fit). A BSW task or ISR group without a configured period gets its period from the runs in the window, put on the OS tick grid: the nearest tick multiple if the deviation is within the measurement uncertainty (run count ±1, at least 1 %: 100 runs in 999 995 µs → 10 ms), otherwise (sporadic ISR, event-driven task) rounded down so its disturbance is not underestimated; a rate faster than one tick keeps its measured value.

Activation limit. The simulation over the hyperperiod handles at most MAX_JOBS (40 000) activations; above it the list stops at a release instant and the report sets hyperperiod.truncated, analysed_ms, activations, activations_analysed and the finding hyperperiod_truncated.

schedana opens no serial port: the console output comes as a file or via standard input (--measure -); recording is the caller's job (python tools/studio console --port COM9 > console.txt or the Studio). The parser works line by line; lost or garbled lines cost only that line and are counted in the report. rte json states the number of tasks and runnables in its header and closes with an end marker, which is how missing lines are detected. Echo of the command, prompt, the acknowledgement ok, OpenBSW logger lines and the ### <command> headings and # … comments of a capture recorded with tools/boardtest --record are expected noise, not unreadable.

docs.title: Assumptions of the response time analysis
docs.text: A1 Fixed priorities, preemptive, one core; every task has its own priority (OpenBSW: context number). A2 ISR groups lie above all tasks, modelled as periodic interferers with their shortest interval; nesting within a group is not modelled. A3 An application task is calculated with its longest cycle (the tick of the hyperperiod with the most runnables due, offset taken into account). This is an upper bound for all cycles and pessimistic for multi-rate tasks; the simulation over the hyperperiod shows the actual cycles. A4 Blocking = blocking_us of the task plus max_lock_us of the system, once per activation (interrupt locks of the BSW). Priority inheritance of mutexes is not modelled. A5 Deadline = period, unless deadline_ms says otherwise. A6 Run times are measured maxima or estimates, not a proven WCET. A7 All tasks start together (RteSystem::run() starts every task with scheduleAtFixedRate), so the critical instant really occurs. A phase per task cannot be configured today, only the offset of a runnable within its task. A8 Only for systems with mode switch runnables: they are event driven load of their task. The worst switch of a task – every runnable one change of the ECU mode runs: all exits of the old mode, the transitions old → new, all entries of the new mode; in the first cycle also the entry of the initial mode STARTUP – lies in the same cycle as its longest periodic cycle. A higher priority task disturbs with one switch per busy window (the ECU mode changes rarely compared to the task periods). Mode switch runnables have no period: they are not part of the long term utilisation and not of the simulation over the hyperperiod. Any pair of modes is considered, because a task sees a mode change only at its cycle start and skips a mode shorter than its cycle.

docs.title: Mode switch runnables
docs.text:
• Configuration: rteload takes them from tools/rtegen (mode_runnable_table, the rows of rte::MODE_RUNNABLES, one per event). Their accesses count in their task at the cycle start, not as init runnables; they have no rate.
  • Scenario: per application task mode_runnables: [{name, event: entry|exit|transition, mode, from, wcet_us, mean_us, min_us, reads, writes}] (from only for a transition; test profile test/scenarios/modes.yaml).
  • Measurement: rte runnables prints mode <Swc.Runnable> (task <task>): on entry RUN, calls 3, last 12 us, max 15 us; rte json one object {"t":"mode", ...} per event and "modes":<n> in the header. A runnable with calls 0 gets no runtime (remark); switch the ECU mode while measuring.
  • Report: mode_switches (JSON), the section "Moduswechsel je Task", mode_switch_us in utilisation and response_times, findings mode_switch_load and mode_runtime_missing, assumption A8. A system without such runnables gets exactly the report it got before.

docs.title: Implicit access
docs.text:
• Configuration: a runnable with DATA-READ-ACCESSS/DATA-WRITE-ACCESSS works on copies of its own (plan_implicit). rteload marks these accesses (Access.implicit) and gives each runnable the RAM of its copies (implicit_bytes) and the lock sections of its wrapper (implicit_locks; none for copies of task copies).
  • Data flow: order and age are unchanged; an implicit reader of an atomic signal keeps one value for its whole run (finding implicit_hand_over, info, instead of atomic_hand_over, warning).
  • Report: implicit_access (JSON) and the section "Implizite Zugriffe (Kopie je Runnable)". The time of the copies is part of the measured runtime. Scenario files do not describe implicit access yet.

docs.title: Measuring on the board and overrun test
docs.text:
1. Open the console, rte reset, wait (the CPU statistics cover the last second, the RTE statistics everything since rte reset), send rte json, rte runnables, stats cpu and stats stack and record them into a file.
  2. schedana analyse <project> --measure <file> --budget <file>; the finding load_measured_vs_analysed compares the measured CPU load (100 % − idle) with the analysed upper bound.
  3. Overrun test: the switch NX_RTE_LOAD_TEST_US (length of the busy loop) with NX_RTE_LOAD_TEST_INDEX (runnable, default 0) in ecu/application/src/systems/RteSystem.cpp; without it no code is generated, with it rte runnables and the header of rte json say so and the report warns (load_test_build). For the demo project: NX_RTE_LOAD_TEST_US=12000, NX_RTE_LOAD_TEST_INDEX=1 (DemoSwc.Run100ms): every tenth cycle of the 10 ms task exceeds its period, the board stays operable.

docs.title: Package structure
docs.text: File Content model.py data model (tasks, runnables, ISR groups, signals, accesses) without reference to any tool scenario.py self-contained analysis input (test profile, export), role table rteload.py model from a project (tools/nxconfig + tools/rtegen, read only), budget file measure.py parser for rte json, rte runnables, stats cpu, stats stack; measured values into the model scheduling.py utilisation, response time analysis, hyperperiod with simulation, offset suggestions priorities.py priority order and warning with a reason dataflow.py data flow analysis and cycle search report.py report (text and JSON), check of the measured values against the analysis findings.py finding as a data object (severity, code, message, target, YAML path) cli.py, __main__.py command line roles.yaml default roles per task/ISR group name (data, replaceable) test/scenarios, test/console, test/budget_demo.yaml test profiles and example measurements test_schedana.py host tests (python -m unittest tools/schedana/test_schedana.py)

docs.title: Connection to the Studio
docs.text:
tools/studio must not change anything here; the connection is prepared:

from schedana import rteload, measure, analyse
model = rteload.load(project.file)               # the same project model as studio.core.project
values = measure.parse(text, known_tasks=[t.name for t in model.tasks])
remarks = measure.apply_to(model, values)
report = analyse(model, values, remarks)         # report.to_dict() / to_text()
  • report.to_dict() is the complete, JSON-capable view (hyperperiod.windows, hyperperiod.simulation, utilisation, response_times), the basis of the timeline in a separate task.
  • Every finding has severity, code, message, target and where (YAML path such as tasks[1].runnables[0]); reader_before_writer names the entry of the reading runnable, the port is in detail.port.
  • scheduling.simulate(jobs, horizon_us, trace=True) additionally returns pieces, every execution slice in time order (the Studio timeline draws them); the aggregates are the same as without trace.
  • runtime_missing names every task/ISR group once (can (task and ISR group)); utilisation.without_runtime_by_kind keeps tasks and ISR groups apart. Recording the console belongs in the Studio, reading it in belongs here.
  • scenario.to_dict(model) / from_dict allow what-if calculations without writing rte.yaml.

docs.title: Open / suggestions to other tools
docs.text:
• The role of a task (safety, communication) belongs in the configuration. tasks.yaml and rte.yaml do not allow an additional key today (rtegen rejects unknown keys), so the default is in roles.yaml. Suggestion: optional roles: [...] per task in tasks.yaml/rte.yaml (rtegen).
  • Deadline and activation period of the BSW tasks are nowhere in the configuration; today they come from the measurement (runs in the measurement window) or from the budget file.
  • Event-triggered runnables other than the mode switch runnables (A8), queues between tasks and multi-core are not modelled (as in a separate task).
  • The analysis knows no priority inheritance; the mutex variant from a separate task is represented as blocking time.

docs.title: tools/setup – the Python environment of a workspace
docs.text:
A customer works in their own repository – the workspace – with neXtBSW as a submodule on a fixed tag (doc/architecture/customer-project.md, section 5.3, gap N8). The generators, the configuration check and the build of that workspace run with the workspace's own .venv, built from the requirements and the constraints of exactly that pinned tree. This is the one command that creates it:

nextbsw/.venv/Scripts/python -m tools.setup venv .              # from the workspace root, core packages
python -m tools.setup venv <workdir>/acme_bcm                     # or with the folder named
python -m tools.setup venv <workdir>/acme_bcm --studio            # plus PySide6 and the Studio test tools
python -m tools.setup check <workdir>/acme_bcm                    # report only, writes nothing

Without a folder the command walks up from the current one and takes the first folder holding nextbsw.yaml – the same rule tools/nxconfig/workspace.py uses, so both tools always mean the same workspace. It runs with any Python 3.12 (only the standard library), needs no Qt and does not import the Studio.

docs.title: Which packages
docs.text:
File Content Who needs it ../requirements.txt core: jinja2, jsonschema, PyYAML, pydantic, ruamel.yaml, python-can, udsoncan, can-isotp, intelhex, pyserial, ziglang, cantools generators, nxconfig, host tests, CI – everything that builds and checks ../requirements-studio.txt PySide6, pytest, pytest-qt, pyinstaller only tools/studio (GUI, its test suite, the .exe build) ../ci/constraints.txt the exact version of every package of both files the one place a version is written down

A workspace that only builds and checks installs the core list and stays free of Qt. --studio adds the second file; it never replaces the first.

docs.title: What the command decides
docs.text:
The state of <workspace>/.venv is read first, and only then is anything run. A second run therefore changes nothing, and a broken environment is named instead of being quietly overwritten:

State Meaning What happens missing no .venv create, install, write the marker current marker fits the tree, all packages at their pinned version nothing is run at all ("Nichts zu tun") stale the tree's requirements/constraints changed, or another profile is asked for install over it, marker rewritten incomplete marker fits, packages are missing or at the wrong version the missing ones are named and installed broken .venv without an interpreter, or an unreadable marker named, exit code 1 – --recreate rebuilds it unmarked an environment this command did not create named – --adopt checks and takes it over, --recreate replaces it other tree the marker names a different neXtBSW tree named, exit code 1 – --recreate

--adopt never installs: it compares what is installed with constraints.txt and only writes the marker when everything fits. That is how an environment somebody created by hand (pip install -r …) becomes a marked one.

docs.title: The marker
docs.text:
<workspace>/.venv/nextbsw-venv.json records the tree, its VERSION, the profile, the interpreter version and a SHA-256 over the requirement files, constraints.txt and .python-version. It is written last – an interrupted installation is never taken for a complete one (the same rule the tool cache of tools/ci follows).

After a pin move the hash no longer fits, and the tools say so instead of generating with the wrong packages:

  • python -m tools.setup check <workspace> – exit code 1 and the command that repairs it,
  • python -m tools.ci check – a finding "Umgebung" (a warning, never red; an environment without a marker stays silent),
  • the Studio's tool page (Werkzeuge) names the same command.

docs.title: Own tests
docs.text:
python -m unittest tools/setup/test_setup.py

A synthetic workspace and a synthetic tree in %TEMP% with a recorded pip: nothing is downloaded and no package is installed – what is tested is the decision, not the installation. One test creates a real, empty venv locally.

docs.title: stackuse – worst-case stack per execution context
docs.text:
Task (gap analysis doc/safety/iso26262-gap.md (not published, available on request) section 6 no. 7, row 6-18): an upper estimate of the stack of every execution context of an image, from the -fstack-usage output the toolchain already emits (cmake/toolchains/NxArmNoneEabi-gcc.cmake). The result for the demo image is part of the software architectural design specification of the safety part (doc/safety/sw-architecture.md, section 7).

python tools/stackuse --build build/evalboard-s32k144-demo \
    --elf build/evalboard-s32k144-demo/ecu/application/RelWithDebInfo/app.ecu.elf \
    --profile tools/stackuse/profiles/evalboard_s32k144_demo.yaml --out report.md
python tools/stackuse ... --strict          # incomplete contexts fail as well
python tools/stackuse ... --json            # machine-readable
python -m unittest tools/stackuse/test/test_stackuse.py

arm-none-eabi-objdump comes from NX_ARM_GCC_BIN or PATH. Exit code 0: every context fits its stack and the nested interrupt bound fits the interrupt stack; 1: something overflows (with --strict also: a context is incomplete or its margin is below --min-margin); 2: unusable input. No Qt; standard library plus PyYAML.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Input What it gives .su files below --build the frame of every compiled function (<file>:<line>:<col>:<name>\t<bytes>\t<qualifier>) disassembly of the image (objdump -d -C --no-show-raw-insn) function starts, direct calls (bl), tail calls (b/b.w/b.n to the start of another function), indirect calls (blx rN, bx rN with N ≠ lr), and every stack pointer decrement (push, vpush, stmdb sp!, sub sp, pre-indexed stores on sp) profile (YAML) the execution contexts, their stacks, the resolution of indirect calls, frames of functions nothing else bounds

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
• Frames. A function's frame is the larger of (a) the largest .su value under its key and (b) the sum of all stack pointer decrements in its disassembly. The key is the qualified name without return type, parameters, template arguments and clone suffix, because .su names (static void ns::C::f(uint8_t), [with T = ...]) and demangled symbols (ns::C::f(unsigned char), ns::C<int>::f) spell the same function differently; merging under the key can only raise a frame. Some .su names are unusable (GCC writes only ) for some template instances); (b) covers those, and it also covers newlib, libgcc and the assembly handlers, which have no .su at all. The report states how many functions have both values and how often they agree (demo: 1308 of 1457 equal, 14 with a larger disassembly sum). A frame the profile gives (frames:) overrides both.
  • Call graph. Nodes are the exact symbols of the image, so template instances and delegate stubs stay apart. A tail call is counted like a call (over-estimates by at most the caller's frame). ldr pc, [rT, rI, lsl #2] is a switch table, not a call.
  • Contexts. depth = context_bytes + dispatch chain + deepest entry. The dispatch chain is the fixed way from the task function to the runnables (task function, event loop, delegate stubs); each step's own frame stays on the stack below the next, and each step's direct subtree is a candidate for the deepest point on the way. The entries are what the context calls through function pointers (runnables, lifecycle transitions, console commands).
  • Indirect calls. A reached indirect call without a resolution in the profile makes the context incomplete; its number is then a lower bound, and the report lists the call sites. Virtual calls are recognised (ldr rV, [rObj] … ldr rF, [rV, #off] … blx rF) and labelled with their vtable offset to help the reviewer, but not resolved automatically: resolving a slot over all vtables of the image merges unrelated classes (tried on the demo: one cycle of 444 functions and a meaningless 14.9 KB). The profile names the targets per caller, globally or per context, each with its source.
  • Recursion. Strongly connected components of the graph. A cycle is an open item unless every member is listed in bounded_recursion with the number of times it can be on the stack (default 1); the tool then counts each member that many times.

  • Interrupt stack. Handlers of one NVIC level cannot preempt each other; the nested bound is, per level, the deepest handler plus one exception frame (exception_frame_bytes), summed over all levels. That is an upper bound: it assumes every level is active at its deepest point at the same moment.

  • Interrupt stack budget. A task-kind context with on_isr_stack: true runs on the interrupt stack itself (reset handler, constructors, main() up to the scheduler); every interrupt level can nest on top, so the interrupt stack must hold its depth plus the nested bound (checked against isr_stack_bytes).

  • Vector table coverage. With vectors: the tool reads the vector table and requires every handler to be an entry of an interrupt context (or of the start-up context), a named default handler, a weak stub that only branches to one, a generated wrapper that calls only the wrapper_hooks and a default handler (an unused vector), or a named non-interrupt. A handler linked later (pin events, sample group, fast control loop) is UNCOVERED until the profile gives it a context; --strict then fails.
  • Guard below the interrupt stack. With isr_stack_guard_bytes the guard must hold the largest frame on the interrupt stack plus the larger of that frame and the exception frame (a function may reserve its frame and write its locals later); while a context on the interrupt stack is incomplete, the largest frame of the whole image counts.
  • Interrupt stack and guard as linked. Sizes are a project value (memory.application.isr_stack_size / isr_stack_guard_size) or the family default; the tool reads them from the image (__StackTop - __StackLimit, __StackGuardEnd - __StackGuardStart via arm-none-eabi-nm, or --image-symbols <nm output>) and checks budget and guard against them. A guard that does not end at __StackLimit is unusable input (exit 2); the profile values only apply to an image without these symbols.
  • Tables of function pointers. A target table:<section> names every function whose address a section holds (.init_array).
  • Accepted lower bound. lower_bound_accepted: <reason> lets a task-kind context stay a lower bound under --strict (never for a safety context or an interrupt level).
  • Floors of the BSW task stacks. A context with bsw_task: <task> takes its stack from the build (<build>/generated/rte/tasks/BswTasks.h, or --bsw-tasks-header; else the profile's stack_bytes) and its worst case is compared with the floor (min_stack_bytes of ecu/configuration/taskStacks.yaml, or --task-stacks); a worst case above the floor fails the run (exit code 1, also without --strict). A task merged into another one has no stack of its own and is refused. The report gets a table "Floors of the BSW task stacks" (safety review 2026-10-01, S1).
